exp.0:6:
The explanation says that the land of Judah is in ruins. Its cities have been burned, and foreigners eat the produce of its fields while the people watch, unable to stop it. The word for "desolate" in the verse above is the one used here: it means laid waste or stripped bare. The phrase for "burned with fire" means set on fire.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, sent by God to Judah. The verses before this one describe the people as a body wounded from head to foot because of their rebellion. Many think this refers to an enemy invasion, perhaps that of Assyria, though scholars do not fully agree on the exact time. What matters is that God shows the consequences of sin and calls the people to return to Him.

For today: do not ignore the signs that something is wrong in your life. Wounds that are not treated get worse. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge what is harming you, and let Him heal and restore what has been broken.
exp.0:7:
It says that Jerusalem, called "the daughter of Zion", was left very alone and fragile. It is like a hut that a watchman builds in a vineyard, or a shelter in a field of cucumbers: poor, temporary shelters that are abandoned after the harvest.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. He has just described the people as a body wounded from head to foot, and the land as devastated by invaders. Scholars debate which invasion is meant, but the point is clear: the people's rebellion brought painful consequences. Even so, the next verse speaks of a small remnant that God preserved.

For today: when you feel your life lies in ruins because of your own choices, do not hide the wound. Bring it honestly before God, because he preserves a remnant and can heal and restore.
exp.0:10:
God asks, sadly, what use he has for so many sacrifices. He says he is already full of the burnt offerings of rams and of the fat of well-fed animals. He takes no pleasure in the blood of bulls, lambs, or male goats. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah kept up its temple rituals, yet it lived with injustice, as the following verses show. God is not rejecting here the sacrifices that he himself commanded, but he rejects them when the heart is far from him and there is no obedience.

For today: attending church, singing, or giving offerings is not enough if I mistreat others. Today I can ask myself whether my daily life, my words, and my fair treatment of others match my worship of God.
exp.0:14:
God says that when his people lift up their hands to pray, he will hide his eyes from them, meaning he will not look on them with favor. Even if they offer many prayers, he will not hear them. The explanation for this comes at the end: their hands are full of blood, that is, of violence and injustice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah. The people kept up their rituals, sacrifices, and festivals, but they oppressed the weak. God does not reject prayer itself, but the religion practiced without justice or repentance. The verses that follow show this: he calls them to wash themselves clean and to do good.

Today, it is not enough to pray or go to church if we live harshly toward others. We can ask forgiveness, correct an injustice, and help someone in need. In this way our prayer comes from a sincere heart.
exp.0:17:
God invites the people to come and "reason together," that is, to talk the matter through and settle it, as in a fair trial. He says that even if their sins are like the deepest scarlet or crimson dyes, which are hard to wash out, He will make them as white as snow or as clean wool.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah, a people who kept up their religion but oppressed the fatherless and the widow. First He asks them to change their conduct and do justice; then He warns that obedience brings good and rebellion brings ruin. Forgiveness is offered together with a call to return. Some read this as a question or as irony, but the central idea is the same.

If you carry guilt, come to God honestly, ask for forgiveness, and take one concrete step of justice or kindness toward someone who needs it.
exp.0:21:
It says that what was once valuable in Jerusalem has been ruined. "Dross" refers to the worthless residue left behind when a metal is refined. Wine mixed with water becomes watered down, of lower quality and deceptive.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just lamented that the faithful city, Jerusalem, has become like a prostitute, unfaithful to God. The silver and the wine are images of her moral corruption: justice and loyalty have been degraded. The verses that follow make this concrete: the leaders accept bribes and neglect the orphan and the widow.

For today: examine which part of your faith has been diluted, like wine with water. Ask God to purify you, and look for one concrete act of justice or compassion toward someone who is vulnerable.
exp.0:25:
God promises that he will set good judges and counselors back in Jerusalem, like those who served in the best days of his people. When this happens, the city will be known as the city of righteousness and the faithful city.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he had told them that the city was corrupted, and that he would cleanse it the way metal is purified, removing the impurities. This restoration comes after a judgment that purifies. Some understand that it was partly fulfilled after the exile, and others also see a future fulfillment in Christ; interpreters explain it in several ways.

God does not settle for punishing; he wants to heal and restore. If today we see injustice or a lack of integrity, we can pray for our leaders and begin by being faithful and just in our home, our work, and our church.
exp.0:26:
Zion, that is, Jerusalem, will be saved and restored through judgment, meaning through God's just action. Its ones who turn back to God, those who repent, are the people who will be rescued by righteousness, because God acts with uprightness. The idea of those who turn back can also be understood as those who return.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. They had become corrupt, with unjust judges and an empty religion. God promises to cleanse them the way metal is refined, removing the dross. The text then warns that the rebels who abandon God will be destroyed.

For today: God corrects because He wants to restore, not merely to punish. If He shows you something you need to change, do not harden your heart; return to Him with humility and trust that His correction seeks to heal you.
exp.0:29:
It says the people will be like a large tree whose leaves fall off and dry up, and like a garden or orchard that lacks water. The word for the tree is not fully certain, so some translations name a different kind of tree instead. It is an image of weakness and of life that is coming to an end.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which had abandoned the LORD and practiced the worship of idols, probably under trees and in gardens, as the previous verse suggests. Those who trusted in those places will find that they cannot hold them up. So the judgment shows that what seemed strong had no life of its own.

For today: what gives us strength is not what we admire or what appears firm, but staying connected to God. We can ask ourselves what we depend on most, and turn back to Him again each day.
exp.0:30:
The explanation says that the strong man will be as fragile as tow, the flax or hemp fibers that burn very quickly. What that man made, his work, will be like a spark. Both will catch fire together, and no one will be able to put out the fire.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Judah. They practiced idolatry, worshiping under trees and in sacred gardens, and they lived with injustice. Many understand "the strong" as the leader or the rich man who trusted in his power; others see it as the people themselves or their idols. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not put your trust in your strength, your achievements, or anything made by human hands. All of that can burn up quickly. Seek God with humility and place your security in Him, for He alone endures.
exp.1:1:
It says that in a future time ("the last days"), the mountain where God's temple stands will be firmly established and recognized as the most important, above all other mountains and hills. People from all the nations will come flowing toward it.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks to a people living under threats and spiritual failures. Before the warnings of judgment, God shows them a hope: one day Jerusalem will be a center of peace and teaching for everyone. Some understand this as the kingdom of Christ and the church; others as something future and literal. Christians have read it in both ways.

For today: when the world seems confused or violent, remember that God has a plan of peace. Draw near to Him with a desire to learn His ways and to live in them.
exp.1:6:
It says that the land of Judah was full of silver and gold, with riches without limit. It also had a great many horses and war chariots, so many that they could not be counted. In other words, the country had plenty of money and military strength.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Before this verse, he calls them to walk in the light of the LORD, but he acknowledges that they had turned away from God, mixing themselves with foreign practices and fortune-tellers. Afterward, the text says that their land was also full of idols. Wealth and power were not evil in themselves, but they trusted in these things more than in God.

Today we can ask ourselves where our heart rests: in money, in security, or in God. Be thankful for what you have, but place your trust first in the Lord.
exp.1:12:
It says the day of the LORD will also come against the cedars of Lebanon, tall and majestic, and against the oaks of Bashan. In other versions, Bashan is associated with oaks or terebinths; the Hebrew word is translated in different ways. These trees are famous for their height and strength.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He warns them that God will judge all human pride. The cedars and the oaks work as images of people, powers, and things that seem imposing. Many understand that this is not an attack on trees, but poetic language about arrogance.

For today: examine what you trust in to feel secure or important, such as your money, your position, or your achievements. Hand that over to God and ask for a humble heart, because only He remains firm.
exp.1:15:
This verse continues a list of great things that people admired. It says that the day of the LORD will also come upon all the ships of Tarshish, meaning the large trading vessels, and upon all the pleasant pictures, meaning beautiful and valuable works of art. Tarshish was a distant place; scholars are not sure where it was.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He warns that God will judge everything they trusted in: mountains, towers, wealth, and luxury. The following verses explain the reason: human pride will be brought low, and only the LORD will be exalted.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, achievements, and beautiful things are not evil in themselves, but they become dangerous when they take the place of God. Today, give thanks for what you have and offer it to Him with humility.
exp.1:19:
In that day, people will throw their idols of silver and gold, the ones they had made to worship, to the moles and to the bats. In other words, they will cast them into dark and abandoned places, as something useless.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had filled their land with silver, gold, and idols. He announces a day when the LORD will appear in his majesty and judge human pride. On that day, what once seemed valuable will be shown to be worthless. Many understand "that day" as a judgment of God; some also connect it to the end of time.

For today: ask yourself where you are placing your trust, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Give that place to God, because he alone is worthy to be worshiped.
exp.2:0:
He says that God, the Lord of hosts, is going to take away from Jerusalem and from Judah everything that holds them up. Those who give support are taken away, and so are those who provide protection. He will also take away all the bread that sustains them and all the water they need, that is, the basic food and water needed to live.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. The next chapter lists leaders and capable people who will be gone: judges, prophets, elders, and counselors. The message is a judgment for the people's injustice and pride, since they trusted in their own resources and not in God. Scholars understand the exact timing in different ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not place your security only in your work, your money, or your leaders. Be thankful each day for what God gives you, and trust Him first.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues a list of leaders that God will remove from Jerusalem and Judah. It names the captain of fifty (the leader of a small group of soldiers), the honourable man (someone respected and in authority), the counsellor, the cunning artificer (a highly skilled craftsman), and the eloquent orator (someone who knows how to speak with wisdom and persuasion).

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the Lord will do because of the people's sin. Taking away these leaders and supports was a judgment: without wise and capable people, disorder would come, and the people would be left in the hands of immature rulers, as the verses that follow say.

For today: value and pray for those who guide you, whether in the church, the family, or the workplace. And remember that a society is not sustained by talent alone, but by humility before God. Ask Him for wisdom to serve where He has placed you.
exp.2:4:
It says that when a society falls apart, people mistreat one another. Each one oppresses his neighbor. The young man shows no respect for the elder, and the common man, that is, the person of low standing, rises up against the person of rank and honor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the kingdom of Judah. He announces that he will take away its capable leaders, such as judges, counselors and skilled craftsmen, because of the people's injustice. In their place will come immature rulers, and the disorder will be so great that no one will want to lead.

For today: when respect and justice are missing, everything begins to crumble. We can start at home, treating elders and younger ones with honor, and praying for our leaders.
exp.2:12:
God stands up, like a judge in a courtroom, to present his case and pass sentence. To plead a cause means to argue on behalf of a matter in court, and the people mentioned here refers to his own people and, more broadly, to the nations. God is not a passive observer: he acts against injustice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in Judah, at a time when its leaders were abusing the people. Just before this verse, the text speaks of guides who lead people astray, and afterward God accuses the elders and princes of devouring the vineyard and crushing the poor. God himself calls the judgment because his people are being mistreated.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it to serve and not to take advantage of others. And if you have suffered injustice, rest in the knowledge that God sees and will judge with truth.
exp.2:15:
Here Jehovah speaks about the women of Jerusalem. He says they are proud: they walk with their necks held high, look around with flirtatious or brazen eyes, and step along with exaggerated steps, making the ornaments on their ankles jingle.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he accused the leaders of oppressing the poor. Now he points to the pride and luxury of the women of the city, probably a reflection of a society that lived comfortably and vainly while others suffered. The verses that follow announce that God will strip away those ornaments and their false sense of security.

For today: let us examine where we draw our sense of worth. God does not condemn beauty, but pride and indifference toward those in need. Let us ask him for a humble and generous heart.
exp.2:17:
It says that, when the day of judgment comes, God will take away from the women of Jerusalem their adornments. The phrase about the ankle ornaments seems to refer to striking anklets or foot jewelry. The hair nets were ornaments or nets for the hair. The crescent ornaments were pieces shaped like half moons. The exact meaning of some of the Hebrew words is uncertain, and translations vary.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just accused the daughters of Zion of pride: they walked with airs of superiority and made noise to draw attention. This list of jewelry shows a wealth and vanity that hid injustice among the people. By taking them away, God shows them that what they boasted in could not save them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we find our worth. God does not condemn beauty, but he does condemn the pride that seeks admiration. Let us ask him for a humble heart.
exp.2:18:
It says that the Lord will take away from the women of Jerusalem their adornments: the necklaces, the pendant earrings (hanging jewels), and the bracelets (wristbands). It is part of a long list of jewelry and accessories that the prophet mentions. Some of the Hebrew terms in this list are difficult, and the translations vary a little.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem, the daughters of Zion. The problem was not the jewelry itself, but the people's pride, luxury, and injustice (see Isaiah 3:16 and 3:14-15, where the poor are oppressed). God warns them that what they took pride in would disappear.

For today: ask yourself where you are placing your worth, in what you have or in God. And check whether your comfort goes hand in hand with indifference toward those in need.
exp.2:19:
This verse continues a list of adornments worn by the women of Jerusalem. The bonnets were embroidered caps or head coverings. The ornaments of the legs were small chains or decorations for the ankles. The headbands probably were ribbons or jewels for the hairstyle, though translators do not fully agree. The tablets were small flasks of perfume, and the earrings were earrings or charms.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. He announces judgment on Jerusalem, whose women, proud and luxurious, stood for a society that had forgotten justice and trusted in its wealth. The Lord says he will remove all that splendor.

For today: examine what your security rests on. What can be lost, such as money or appearance, should never be your foundation. Trust God first.
exp.2:20:
The verse says that the Lord will take away the adornments of the women of Jerusalem: the rings, and the nose jewels, that is, the hoops or rings hung from the nose. It is part of a long list of fine jewelry and clothing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The daughters of Zion walked proudly and vainly (v. 16), while the people lived unjustly toward the poor. God warns them that he will remove what gave them pride and security. Some scholars see here a criticism of luxury; others, an announcement of the fall of the city.

Today we can ask ourselves what we depend on to feel valuable: clothing, money, or image. God does not condemn beauty in itself, but pride and indifference toward others. Let us ask him for a humble and generous heart.
exp.2:21:
It says God lists more of the luxury items of the women of Jerusalem. The fine clothes worn for special occasions are changeable suits of apparel, the short capes or cloaks are mantles, the things that covered or adorned are wimples, and the small items that were probably purses or pins are crisping pins; scholars translate that last word in different ways.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's message to Judah. The women of Zion were proud and vain (v. 16), and the list of adornments points to a society that trusted in its appearance and wealth. God warns that all that brilliance will be taken away: mourning, loss, and humiliation will come through judgment.

For today: it is not wrong to dress simply, but it is worth asking where we place our security. If our worth depends on what we have or how we appear, it is fragile. Let us instead seek a humble and thankful heart before God.
exp.2:22:
This verse continues a list of ornaments and fine clothing worn by the women of Jerusalem. The mirrors were made of polished metal. The fine linen garments were pieces of fine cloth or fine fabric. The gauzy garments were dresses of very thin, see-through cloth. The hoods were ornaments or head coverings worn on the head.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah and Jerusalem. He warns of a judgment coming because of their pride and their injustice. The list of luxuries shows a vanity that led them to forget the poor. The verses that follow announce that all that splendor will be replaced by loss and sorrow.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we care for more than people. Examine whether your security rests in your appearance or in what you own, and ask God for a humble and generous heart.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that the women of Jerusalem will lose their luxury and their beauty. Instead of fine perfume there will be a bad smell; instead of an elegant belt or sash, a broken rope or cord; instead of carefully arranged hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, rough sackcloth worn in mourning; and instead of beauty, marks of burning, perhaps from slavery or captivity.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. He warns that their pride, their luxury, and their injustice will bring judgment. The verses that follow show that war, death, and desolation will come, and the city will be left like a woman sitting on the ground, weeping.

For today: taking care of our appearance is not wrong, but let us not place our security or our worth in it. Let us ask God for a humble, generous, and just heart, one that values more what lasts forever.
exp.3:5:
It says there will be a shelter, that is, a kind of booth or tent that gives shade, to protect people from the heat of the day. It will also be a refuge and a hiding place from the storm with strong wind, and from the downpour of heavy rain.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks to Judah and Jerusalem, who had fallen into sin and faced judgment. The verses before this one speak of a cleansing that God would bring and of his presence as a cloud and fire over Zion, as in the desert with Israel. This verse closes the promise: God himself will be the protection. Some see here a hope for Israel's future; many Christians also connect it with Christ, although the text does not say so in those words.

When you go through heat, pressure, or storms, do not rush to hide only in your own strength. Draw near to God in prayer, ask him to cleanse you, and trust that his presence is a real refuge.
exp.4:0:
He says the prophet is going to sing a song for his beloved, and that the song is about his beloved's vineyard. This vineyard was on a fruitful hill, that is, a slope on a mountain, a place of good, productive soil.

The one speaking is Isaiah, who begins as if he were a singer dedicating a love song. The verses that follow show that it is a parable: the vineyard represents God's people, Israel and Judah, and the beloved is God himself. The prophet uses a song so that the people will listen and then realize that the judgment applies to them.

For today: God has given us care and good opportunities. Ask yourself honestly what fruit of love, justice, and faithfulness your life is bearing in response.
exp.4:1:
He says that the owner of the vineyard cared for it with great diligence: he cleared the stones from the ground, planted the best vines, built a tower to watch over it, and prepared a winepress, which is the place where grapes are trodden to get the wine. He expected good grapes, but the vineyard yielded wild grapes, that is, sour and worthless ones.

Isaiah sings a song in the name of his beloved, who represents God. Shortly after, the text explains that the vineyard is the people of Israel and Judah. God had given them care, law and protection, but he looked for justice and found injustice (Isaiah 5:7). The final question asks the listeners to recognize the problem.

For today: God has given us much, and he hopes that this will show in our lives through love, honesty and justice. Today we can ask ourselves what fruit we are bearing and ask him for help to change whatever needs changing.
exp.4:2:
In this passage God, speaking as the owner of a vineyard, calls on the people of Jerusalem and the men of Judah to act as judges. He asks them to decide fairly who is in the right: himself or his vineyard.

Isaiah is telling a song or parable. The one who is loved is God, and the vineyard, as verse 7 of the same chapter makes clear, stands for Israel and Judah. God did everything to care for it: he cleared away the stones, built a wall around it, and planted good vines. But it produced wild grapes, that is, bitter ones. God puts the people in the role of jury so that they can see their own failure.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly what fruit we are bearing after so much care from God. This week, think of one area of your life where you have received a great deal, such as teaching, family, or forgiveness, and ask God for help to bear good fruit there, with justice and love.
exp.4:3:
God asks what more could have been done for his vineyard. He had done everything that was needed: he tended it, protected it, and planted it well. Even so, he expected good grapes and received wild grapes, that is, sour fruit with no worth.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf, with a song or parable addressed to the people of Jerusalem and Judah. He asks them to be the judges of the case. Later, the prophet explains that the vineyard represents God's people, who, despite so much care, answered with injustice and wickedness instead of justice and righteousness.

For today: God has given us much, such as his Word, his care, and his grace. We can ask ourselves humbly what fruit of love, justice, and faithfulness we are bearing, and ask him to help us change wherever it is needed.
exp.4:6:
It says that the vineyard God had been speaking about is his people: Israel and Judah. God cared for them with affection, like a plant that gave him delight, meaning pleasing and precious to him. He looked for right judgment and justice, but found violence and wrongdoing. He looked for righteousness, but found a cry, the cry of those being oppressed.

Isaiah uses a song-parable about a vineyard. God, the owner, explains why he will take away his protection: his people produced bad fruit. What follows shows concrete examples, such as piling up houses and land without thinking of others.

For today: God is not looking only for religion, but for visible fruits of justice and fair treatment. Today you can ask yourself: how do I treat those who depend on me or have less than I do? Ask God to let your faith show in honest and compassionate decisions.
exp.4:10:
Isaiah says "Woe" to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink and keep drinking until night, until the wine sets them on fire, that is, inflames them and takes control of them. This is not a single slip, but a life given over to drinking from the start of the day.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, within the song of the vineyard (chapter 5). God denounces Judah for its injustice and greed. Feasts with music and wine filled their days, yet they ignored the work of God. For this reason he announces judgment to them: empty houses, poor harvests, and captivity.

For today: examine what occupies the first place in your day and the best of your time. It may be alcohol or some other pleasure. Ask God to be your first thought and your greatest joy.
exp.4:11:
It says that at this people's feasts the music and the wine never fail. The harps, the lyres (stringed instruments), the tambourines (hand drums) and the flutes fill the air. But they do not look at or consider what the Lord is doing; that is, they do not take time to recognize his hand or his work.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah. This verse is part of a series of woes, or laments, against the injustice and the careless living of the people. The people were given over to pleasure and forgot God. For this reason the text goes on to announce exile, because of their lack of knowledge of God.

For today: enjoyment is not bad in itself, but it can dull our attention to God. Look for a moment each day to stop, give thanks, and notice what God is doing in your life.
exp.4:13:
It says that the grave, like an enormous mouth, opens without limit to swallow the proud people of Jerusalem and Judah. There their honored people will go down, along with their crowds, their luxury and the noise of their festivities, and everyone who took pleasure in it. The place of the dead is what the Hebrew word Sheol refers to, and it is the place of the dead. Those who took pleasure in it were enjoying themselves.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he denounces a people who held banquets with music and wine but ignored what God was doing. For this reason he announces judgment, which would mean captivity, hunger and death. Scholars debate whether all of this refers to a single invasion or to several stages of judgment. What is clear is the message: God will be recognized as holy and just.

For today: examine whether your pleasures and your comfort make you forget God. Enjoying what is good is not a sin, but it is wise to set aside time each day to pray, read the Bible and give thanks to him.
exp.4:15:
He says that when God judges, everyone will see how great he is. The Lord of hosts is the Lord who commands all power. To be exalted means to be lifted up and recognized as supreme. To be sanctified means to be shown as holy, set apart, and perfect. His righteousness makes his holiness visible.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. In chapter 5, God compares them to a vineyard that produced bad fruit: injustice, pride, and abuse. Just before this verse, the proud are humbled. Here the result is shown: while human pride falls, God's righteousness is lifted high.

For today: when you see injustice and it seems that no one responds, rest in the fact that God is just and will see everything. And examine your own heart: ask him to take away your pride and teach you to live with honesty and fair treatment toward others.
exp.4:21:
It says that God cries out a warning of "woe" against those who pride themselves on being champions at drinking wine and experts at preparing strong drinks. What should bring them shame, they take as a source of pride.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. He is denouncing leaders and powerful people who have turned good into evil and evil into good. The verse that follows shows that this life of excess went hand in hand with injustice: they acquitted the guilty for bribes and took away the rights of the innocent.

For today: examine what you feel proud of. If something controls you, such as alcohol or any other pleasure, ask God for help and seek support from people you trust. A clouded or enslaved mind rarely acts with justice and clarity.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that God's judgment will fall on his people like fire that burns up dry stubble. The dry heads of grain and the dry stalks are consumed in an instant. The rotting of the root and the turning of the blossom into dust describe a people left without life or a future. The reason is plain: they rejected the law of God and despised his word.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the Lord to the kingdom of Judah, in the song of the vineyard and the woes of Isaiah 5. Before this verse, he denounces drunkenness and injustice: judges who acquit the guilty for a bribe and take away the rights of the innocent. The root problem was turning their backs on God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are treating God's word lightly, or bending it to our own convenience. A practical way is to read it each day with humility and to obey what we already understand, including in how we treat others with justice.
exp.4:24:
God was deeply angry with his people because of their wickedness, and he struck them with his hand. The anger is described as intense wrath; the hills shook with a terrible tremor, and the bodies lying dead in the streets show how severe the judgment was. Even so, his anger has not faded: his hand is still stretched out, ready to correct.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the kingdom of Judah. This comes from the song of the vineyard (chapter 5), where the people produced injustice instead of good fruit. The verses before it condemn those who accepted bribes and despised God's law. Scholars debate which past blow the shaking refers to: some think of an earthquake, others see it as a general picture of judgment.

For today: God takes justice seriously. Today you can examine whether you are honest in your work and your dealings, and return to his word with humility before the correction becomes harsher.
exp.4:25:
It says that God will raise up a signal, like a banner (a standard), to call nations who live very far away. He will also call them with a whistle, as one summons someone from the farthest corner of the earth. And those nations will come quickly, without delay.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, whom he earlier called his vineyard. The people rejected the Lord's law, and so God announces judgment. The verses that follow describe a strong and tireless army. From the context, many understand this to refer to Assyria, though some also see a broader warning. God is shown directing even the nations.

For today: let us not take God's word lightly. His correction seeks to wake us up, so when He speaks to us through His Word, let us respond promptly with humility and return to Him.
exp.4:26:
The army that God is going to bring will be strong and tireless. None of its soldiers will grow weary or stumble. They will not doze off or fall into drowsiness. Their belts will be fastened tight at the waist, and the straps of their sandals will not break.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, carrying God's message. He has just described Israel as a vineyard that yielded bitter grapes, despite God's care, because of its injustice and violence. God announces that he will use a distant nation as an instrument of judgment. The text does not say here which nation it is; many think of Assyria, and that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God takes justice seriously, but his correction seeks to bring us back to himself. Today you can ask him to show you something you need to set right, and to obey him without delay.
exp.4:27:
This verse describes a very well-prepared army. The arrows are sharp, and their bows are drawn tight and ready to shoot. The horses' hooves are as hard as flint, and the chariot wheels spin with the force of a whirlwind.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who had fallen into injustice and disobedience. In chapter 5, the prophet announces that God will bring a distant nation as judgment. Many believe it refers to Assyria, although the text does not give the name here. God is the one who calls that army.

For today: God does not overlook injustice, but his warnings aim to bring us back to him. Today you can ask God in prayer what area of your life needs correction, and respond with humility before the consequences grow.
exp.4:28:
This verse describes an enemy army as a lion. Its roar, or loud growl, is like that of young lions. It growls, seizes its prey, and carries it off with no one able to rescue it. It is a picture of strength, speed, and a people that cannot be stopped.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. After the song of the vineyard and several woes against injustice, God announces that he will bring a distant nation as judgment. Many believe this refers to Assyria, although the text does not give the name, and some think of Babylon as well.

For today: God takes justice and faithfulness seriously. If we have neglected something, we can return to him now with humility, knowing that his discipline seeks to restore us and that his mercy remains open.
exp.4:29:
He says that, on the day of judgment, the invading people will roar against Israel with a noise like the sea stirred up by a storm. If someone looks toward the land, they will see only darkness and distress. Even the light in the sky will be darkened.

"Roar" means to make a loud, deep, rumbling noise.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. He has just described the song of the vineyard, which represents Israel, and the injustices of the people. Then he announces that God will bring a distant nation as an instrument of discipline. The verses before this one paint their army as swift and frightening. Exactly who that army is, the text does not say here; many think of Assyria, but others see it in a broader way.

For today: God takes justice and faithfulness seriously. Instead of ignoring the warnings, we can ask him to show us where we need to change, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.5:2:
Here the seraphim, beings who stand around the throne of God, call out to one another and proclaim that God is holy three times. "Lord of hosts" means the Lord of the heavenly armies, the one who commands all power. They say that the whole earth is full of his glory, that is, of his greatness and his presence.

Isaiah describes a vision he had in the year King Uzziah died. The seraphim speak in praise, and their voice shakes the temple. Repeating "holy" three times is a way of giving the strongest possible emphasis, though some also see a hint of the Trinity; this is interpreted in several ways. Before this holiness, Isaiah feels unworthy and confesses his sin.

Today we can begin our prayer with awe, not only with requests. Before speaking of what we need, let us take a moment to acknowledge who God is. And as we look at creation, let us remember that it speaks of his glory.
exp.5:3:
This verse describes what happened when the seraphim proclaimed the holiness of God. The posts of the door, the frames on which the doors turn, shook at the force of that voice. The phrase about the house being filled with smoke means that the temple was filled with smoke.

Isaiah recounts a vision he had in the temple, when he saw the Lord seated on his throne. The seraphim, who are heavenly beings, sang that God is holy. Smoke often calls to mind the presence of God, although the passage does not explain this in detail. This scene leads Isaiah to feel himself a sinner and to be purified, and then to be sent out.

When one takes the holiness of God seriously, prayer stops being routine. Today we can draw near with reverence and humility, acknowledging our faults, and trust that God forgives and equips us to serve him.
exp.5:9:
He says God tells Isaiah to make the heart of this people fat, to make their ears heavy, and to shut their eyes, so that they do not see, do not hear, do not understand, do not turn back to God, and are not healed.

Isaiah has just seen God in the temple and offers himself as a messenger. God warns him that the people will not listen. Many understand that the passage describes how the people had already hardened themselves, and that God confirms that direction as judgment. Others stress that the language expresses the result of the mission. The text does not fully settle the question. Jesus quoted this passage when speaking of those who rejected his message.

For today: let us not assume that hearing the Word is enough. Let us ask God for a soft heart, and let us respond quickly when he speaks, before habit makes us indifferent.
exp.5:12:
It says that although God's judgment will be very harsh and almost everything will be destroyed, a tenth of the people will remain. Even that remnant will pass through the fire again. But just as a cut elm or oak leaves a stump that is still alive, a stump will remain: the holy seed, that is, a remnant set apart for God, from which the people can grow again.

Isaiah recounts his calling as a prophet. God tells him that the hardened people will suffer judgment and exile. Isaiah asks how long this will last, and God answers that it will continue until the land is left desolate. Even so, this last verse adds hope. Some scholars disagree about how parts of the sentence should be translated, but the central idea of the faithful remnant is clear.

For today: when everything seems lost, remember that God still cares for what belongs to him. Trust that he can bring forth new life where you see only a cut stump.
exp.6:0:
It says that in the days of King Ahaz of Judah, two enemy kings, Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel (the northern kingdom), went up to Jerusalem to attack it. But they could not conquer it. The older forms of the names in the source are rendered here as Ahaz, Uzziah, and Jerusalem, and the word for attacking it means to make war against it.

The book of Isaiah presents this event as a summary of the conflict. The verses that follow tell how the king and the people trembled with fear, and how God sent Isaiah to speak with Ahaz. Some scholars see here a summary of the whole conflict, with the details explained afterward. God wanted Ahaz to trust in Him and not in human alliances.

For today: when a threat seems bigger than you, remember that God can sustain you even when you feel your heart tremble. Before looking for hasty ways out, pray and ask Him to teach you to trust in Him.
exp.6:1:
A report reached the royal palace of Judah: Syria had made an alliance with Ephraim, that is, with the northern kingdom of Israel. When they heard it, the king and all the people were filled with fear. Here "shaken" means trembling, and the image is that of the trees of the forest swaying in the wind.

Here the narrator of the book of Isaiah is speaking. "The house of David" refers to King Ahaz and his court. Syria and Israel meant to attack Jerusalem, and Ahaz felt he had no defense. That is why, in what follows, God sends Isaiah with a message: do not be afraid, because those enemies were only smoldering stumps of firebrands, that is, logs nearly burned out.

For today: when bad news makes you tremble, do not rely only on what you can see. Stop, pray, and remember that God is greater than whatever threatens you.
exp.6:7:
It says that Syria has Damascus as its capital, and that its leader is King Rezin. In other words, Syria is nothing more than that: a human kingdom with limits. Then it announces that within sixty-five years Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) will be broken, meaning destroyed, until it no longer exists as a people.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid because Syria and Israel were planning to attack him. God tells him that those plans will not succeed. The sixty-five years are explained in different ways, and scholars do not agree on how to count them. What is clear is that the northern kingdom would fall.

For today: when problems seem enormous, remember that God rules above every human power. Trust in Him instead of letting fear control you.
exp.6:12:
Isaiah speaks to the royal family of Judah. He tells them that they already wear out the people, and now they also wear out God.

King Ahaz was afraid of his enemies. God offered him a sign to strengthen his faith, but Ahaz answered with words that sounded pious, saying he would not put the Lord to the test. In reality, he had already decided to trust in political alliances and not in God. That is why Isaiah rebukes him. Then comes the sign of Immanuel, which means God with us. Scholars understand it in several ways, and Christians see it fulfilled in Christ.

Today: be careful with excuses that sound spiritual but hide distrust. When God invites us to trust Him, let us respond with sincere faith and obedience.
exp.6:16:
God says he will bring a time of suffering upon King Ahaz, his people, and his family, a kind of hardship not seen since the northern kingdom (Ephraim) broke away from Judah. That punishment would come through the king of Assyria.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Ahaz, king of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and did not trust God; he preferred to seek help from Assyria. God had offered him a sign, but Ahaz refused it. So what Ahaz was relying on would turn against him. Scholars agree that this refers to the later Assyrian pressure, although they debate some details.

For today: when you are afraid, do not run first to human solutions that ignore God. Pray, ask for his guidance, and trust in him, because what looks like a safe way out can bring more trouble than the one you were trying to avoid.
exp.6:17:
It says that in that day God will call, as with a whistle, the fly from the far reaches of the rivers of Egypt and the bee from the land of Assyria. Here "whistle" means giving a signal to make them come. These are images of armies that will arrive in swarms.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who feared his enemies and did not trust God. Isaiah warns him that although those kings would fall, God would bring something worse: the invasion of Assyria. Egypt and Assyria were neighboring powers, and many understand the text to refer to their armies.

For today: God rules even what seems out of control. So instead of seeking security in alliances or human resources, we can trust Him and obey Him with humility.
exp.6:18:
They say the enemy armies, compared to flies and bees, will come in force and occupy the whole land: even the empty valleys, the holes in the rocks, the thornbushes and the shrubs. No corner will be left free of them.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and did not trust God. He looked for help to Assyria. The prophet warns him that this same empire, which he wanted to use as a protector, would bring very hard days upon Judah. Egypt also appears in the picture, and many scholars see there the clash of great powers in the region.

For today: when you are afraid, do not place your security in human solutions that seem easy but leave God out. Before deciding, pray and seek his guidance. Trusting in him is safer than leaning on what may later turn against you.
exp.6:19:
God says he will use the king of Assyria like a hired razor. The wording about being shaved is a plain image: with it he will take off the hair of the head, the hair of the feet, and even the beard. In those days, this was a sign of complete humiliation. The phrase about the far side of the river refers to the Euphrates River.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah. Ahaz was afraid of his enemies and looked for help from Assyria instead of trusting God. The prophet warns that this power, the one Ahaz asked for help, would end up as an instrument of judgment and harm for Judah. Some scholars see here a reference to later Assyrian invasions.

For today: when we are afraid, let us not look for security in human solutions that draw us away from God. What seems like help can cost us dearly. Let us pray first and trust in Him.
exp.6:21:
It says that when that time comes, whoever raises one cow and two sheep will have so much milk that they will eat curds, a kind of thick cream or soft cheese rather than butter as we know it, along with honey. The same food will be eaten by those who are left in the land, that is, the survivors who remain in the country.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz of Judah, who feared his enemies and sought help from Assyria. Assyria would be like a razor that God uses to bring judgment. The land would be left empty and poor, and the few who remain would live on simple things. Some understand that food as a sign of scarcity; others see it as a sign of provision for the survivors.

For today: trust that God cares for you even when everything is reduced to little. Instead of seeking security in human powers, rest in Him.
exp.6:22:
It says that in that time, a piece of land that had a thousand vines, each worth a thousand pieces of silver, would be abandoned and covered with thorns and thistles. A very valuable vineyard would turn into brush.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid of his enemies and sought help from Assyria instead of trusting God. Isaiah announces that judgment will come because of that lack of faith: the land would be left empty of people. Scholars agree that he speaks of an invasion, though they debate the exact details.

For today: what seems very valuable can be lost if we stop trusting God. We can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, in plans, or in the Lord. He cares for those who lean on Him.
exp.6:23:
It says that people will have to enter that land armed with arrows and a bow, because the whole field will be covered with thorns and thistles. There will no longer be crops, only weeds, and the land will be dangerous or used for hunting.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz of Judah, who was afraid of his enemies, Syria and Israel. God promises that this threat will pass, but He also warns of judgment: the land will be left abandoned and uncultivated. Interpreters often see here the invasion of Assyria, although the details are explained in several ways.

For today: when we trust in our own securities instead of in God, what seemed fruitful can become weeds. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our trust, and return to God with humility, knowing that He cares for those who seek Him.
exp.6:24:
It says that the hills which used to be worked with a hoe, that is, a tool for digging and cultivating, will no longer be planted. People will not go there because of the thorns and thistles that will cover them. Those lands will serve as pasture for oxen, and the lesser cattle will tread upon them, trampling them down.

Isaiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, in the days of King Ahaz, when the armies of Syria and Israel were threatening. God announces that the land will be left abandoned because of the judgment that is coming, and many understand this to refer to the invasion of Assyria. It is a warning because of the lack of trust in God.

For today: when everything seems lost, do not place your security only in your own resources. Trust in God and seek his direction before you decide.
exp.7:2:
Isaiah says that he came together with his wife, "the prophetess," and she became pregnant and had a son. Then God commanded him to give the boy a very long name: Maher-shalal-hash-baz. The name is usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the plunder."

Isaiah speaks in the first person. Judah was afraid of Damascus and Samaria, which were threatening it. God used the child's name as a sign: before he learned to speak, Assyria would defeat those kingdoms. The witnesses mentioned in the previous chapter testified that the announcement was made before it came to pass.

For today: when fear seems bigger than God, remember that He knows the future and keeps His word. Trust His promises instead of seeking security only in human strength.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the people turned down the waters of Shiloah, which flow gently and quietly, and chose instead to rejoice in Rezin and in the son of Remaliah. "Rejoice" here means that they took delight in them and placed their trust in them. Rezin was king of Syria, and the son of Remaliah was Pekah, king of Israel.

God speaks through Isaiah in a time of threat for Judah. Shiloah was a spring of water in Jerusalem, and here it probably stands for God's quiet protection, though some also interpret it as the house of David. The people trusted in human alliances more than in God. Therefore, the following text says, the mighty king of Assyria would come upon them like a flooding river.

Today, we sometimes trust in visible resources that seem strong more than in the quiet help of God. Before seeking security in other things, we can stop to pray and trust in Him.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that God will allow a great flood of strong and numerous rivers to fall upon the people. That flood represents the king of Assyria with all his powerful army. It will advance over all the channels of the river and overflow all its banks.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a time of military threat. The people had rejected the quiet waters of Siloam, which many understand as a symbol of God's gentle and dependable protection, and preferred to lean on alliances with human kings such as Rezin and the son of Remaliah. For this reason God warns that a much greater force would come.

Today, when we trust in our own securities more than in God, we may end up facing bigger problems. Let us take a moment today to place in God's hands the things we rely on most.
exp.7:10:
It says that God spoke to Isaiah with a strong hand, meaning with a powerful and clear pressure upon him. He taught him not to follow the way of most of the people. The phrase "with a strong hand" is rendered here by the verse's own wording, and the sense of being firmly instructed is what the verse conveys.

Isaiah speaks in the first person. Judah was threatened by enemy kings, and many people looked for security in alliances and schemes of conspiracy. God warns the prophet not to be swept along by that shared fear. The verses that follow call for trust in the Lord and reverence for him, not for human threats.

For today: when everyone around you is moving out of fear, rumor, or pressure, stop and pray before you decide. Ask yourself whether you are following the crowd or the voice of God in his Word.
exp.7:13:
He says that God himself will be a refuge, a holy place, for those who trust in him. But for those who reject him, he will be like a stone in the road that makes people fall, and like a trap or a net. A stumbling block is an obstacle; a snare is a trap; an inhabitant is a dweller. The two houses of Israel refers to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

Isaiah speaks in a time of political threat, when Judah feared the neighboring kingdoms and sought alliances out of fear. God asks his people not to fear what others fear, but to honor him as holy. Whoever does not do this stumbles over him.

Today we can ask ourselves what we fear most. When we give God first place in our hearts, he becomes our refuge and our peace, even in times of uncertainty.
exp.7:14:
It says that many among the people will stumble, fall, and be broken. They will also be snared, like an animal in a trap, and be taken captive.

Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God showed him. Judah and Israel were threatened by foreign powers and looked for safety in human alliances instead of in God. The verse before says that God would be a sanctuary for those who trust in him, but a stone of stumbling for those who ignore him. Scholars agree that this is a warning of judgment; the exact historical details are explained in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust most when we are afraid: in money, in people, or in God? Take a moment to bring your worry to God and to give him first place in your heart.
exp.7:15:
It says that God's message should be kept carefully. "Bind up" and "seal" are like closing an important document to protect it. The "testimony" and the "law" are the word that God spoke through Isaiah. The "disciples" are those who listen to him and learn from him.

Here Isaiah speaks, or according to some, the Lord speaks through him. Judah was rejecting God and sought security in political alliances instead of in Him. Many would stumble because they did not believe. That is why the message is entrusted to a faithful group, so that it would remain as proof when it came to pass. Scholars disagree about whether "seal" means keeping it hidden or simply making sure it is authentic.

For today: when many ignore God, do not be discouraged. Keep His Word in your heart, study it with other believers, and trust that God does what He says.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that the darkness to come will not be like the distress before. At first, God dealt lightly, or with little weight, with the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, in the north of Israel. Later, the burden grew heavier in the area along the way of the sea, on the other side of the Jordan, in Galilee of the nations, that is, of the foreign peoples. This phrase is difficult, and translators understand it in different ways: some see a contrast between the past affliction and a future relief.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, threatened by the invasion of Assyria. The lands of the north were the first to suffer the blow, and the prophet announces that this darkness will not have the last word, as the following verse shows.

Today, when we go through dark times, we can remember that God knows where we suffer and that our pain is not the end of the story. Let us wait on Him with confidence.
exp.8:2:
The verse says that God made the people grow, but before, that growth did not bring true joy. Now, before God, the people will rejoice like those who gather the harvest after much labor, or like soldiers who divide the plunder after winning a battle. The goods taken from a defeated enemy are the spoils of war.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat of Assyria. The northern regions, Zebulun and Naphtali, were the first to suffer invasion. The prophet announces that God will bring light and freedom where there was darkness and oppression. Some translations read the text a little differently, since the Hebrew original presents a difficulty, but the central idea is the same: joy that comes from God.

Today you can remember that having more, whether people, achievements, or things, does not fill the heart. True joy is born when God sets free and restores. Ask him to give you that deep joy.
exp.8:6:
The explanation says that the government of the promised child will grow and that his peace will never end. He will reign on the throne of David, and he will make it firm with judgment, that is, with righteous decisions, and with justice. This holds from now on and forever. The passage ends by affirming that God himself will accomplish it through his zeal, his burning and determined love for his people.

Isaiah speaks to a people threatened by war and darkness, in the time of the divided kingdom. Earlier he had announced the birth of a child with divine titles. Then the text returns to the judgment on Israel for its pride. Christians see Jesus here, the son of David, although Israel first heard it as a promise of a just king.

For today: when the world seems unstable, trust that God will do what he has promised. Ask him for his peace and seek to live with justice in your home and your work.
exp.8:9:
It says that the people of Israel, after suffering a blow, respond with pride. The bricks were simple materials, and the hewn stone is carved stone, stronger and more costly. The sycomores were wild fig trees, of little value; the cedars were noble and expensive wood. They say: "The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones; the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars."

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom (Ephraim, Samaria). They had already suffered calamities, but instead of repenting, they spoke with arrogance. God warns that more enemies will come, because their hearts had not changed.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when a difficulty strikes us, we only want to rebuild with our own strength and plans. God may be calling us to stop, to acknowledge our mistakes, and to return to Him in humility before we raise anything up again.
exp.8:15:
It says that the leaders of the people were leading them down the wrong path, and that the people, by following them, had gone astray. The words that describe the leaders as those who guide or direct, and the phrase saying that they made the people wander by means of falsehood, belong to the same idea of misleading. Those who let themselves be guided are the ones who were led, and the people who were lost were left confused and without direction.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the northern kingdom, Israel, in the eighth century B.C. God had already disciplined them, but they still did not turn back to Him. The previous verse accuses elders and prophets who taught lies. Here the explanation of the result is given: false leaders and a people who followed them.

For today: do not follow anyone blindly. Compare what you hear with the Bible, pray asking for wisdom, and if you are a leader, guide with truth and humility.
exp.8:16:
God says that he will take no pleasure in the young men of the people, nor will he have compassion on their fatherless and widows, because all of them have fallen into wickedness. The young men are those who are in their youth; the impious are those who do not honor God; and those who do evil are the wicked. Even so, God's anger has not subsided: his hand remains stretched out, ready for judgment.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, Israel, also called Ephraim. The leaders and the false prophets had deceived the people, and the corruption reached everyone, even the weakest. Some understand the outstretched hand as judgment, and others also see a door left open to repentance.

For today: let us guard our words and whom we follow. Let us ask God that our mouths speak truth and that our hearts turn to him with humility.
exp.8:18:
It says that because of God's anger the land has been left in darkness, and that the people will be like wood for the fire. In addition, people will lose all tenderness: no one will have compassion for their own brother.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, Israel (also called Ephraim and Manasseh). The people lived in lies, wickedness, and injustice, and they did not repent. That wickedness is described as a fire that gets out of control and ends up consuming them, through divisions and internal struggles. Many understand this as God's judgment through war and chaos.

Today we can remember that sin, if it is not confessed, destroys relationships as well. Let us ask God for a humble and compassionate heart, and let us seek to be reconciled with someone close to us before hardness grows.
exp.9:8:
The king of Assyria proudly asks whether some cities did not suffer the same fate. Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, and Damascus are cities he had already conquered. He means that none of them could resist him, and that Jerusalem will not be able to resist him either.

The Assyrian king speaks here, boasting of his victories. He does not know that God is using him to correct His people. Even so, his heart is arrogant and he wants to destroy without limit. Later, God will hold him accountable for that pride. Scholars debate the exact location of Calno.

For today: when we have success or power, let us remember that everything is under the hand of God. Boasting about our achievements draws us away from Him. With humility, let us give Him thanks and use what we have to serve.
exp.9:10:
What it says: Here the king of Assyria speaks with pride. He says that just as he destroyed Samaria and its idols, he will do the same to Jerusalem and its own. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and the idols are false gods made by human hands.

Context: God had used Assyria as a rod to correct his unfaithful people. But the Assyrian king believed himself master of everything and boasted of his victories, without acknowledging God. He also placed Jerusalem on the same level as the idolatrous nations. That is why, in the verses that follow, God promises to call him to account for his arrogance, after finishing his work on Zion.

For today: Everything we accomplish, whether work, studies or success, is a gift that God allows. When we believe we are the authors of everything, pride blinds us. Today, before celebrating an achievement, give thanks to God for it.
exp.9:12:
Here the king of Assyria speaks with pride. He says he accomplished everything by his own strength and wisdom. He boasts of having removed the bounds of the nations, of having robbed their treasures, and of having put down their inhabitants like a mighty man.

The bounds are the borders or limits between the nations. The phrase about those who sat on their thrones probably refers to kings or rulers seated on their thrones.

God had used Assyria to discipline his people, who had filled themselves with idolatry. But the Assyrian king did not acknowledge God; he credited himself with all the glory. That is why, in the previous verse, God says he will punish him for his arrogance. Here the king speaks, but the prophet Isaiah shows that God sees his heart.

For today: when something goes well for us, let us give thanks to God instead of boasting. Everything we have, strength, talent, and opportunities, is a gift from him.
exp.9:14:
It would be absurd for an axe to think itself more important than the person who uses it to cut, or for a saw to show off in front of the one who moves it. It is as if a staff could lift up the person who holds it, or as if a rod could claim to be in charge. In the end, they are all just wooden tools.

God speaks through Isaiah. Assyria, the empire God used to discipline Israel, boasted that it had achieved everything by its own strength and wisdom. God reminds it that it was only an instrument in his hands. That is why judgment comes upon its pride.

For today: everything we do well, our talents, achievements, and opportunities, comes from God. We can work with effort and joy, but without thinking we own the success. If we remember that we are instruments, we live with humility and gratitude.
exp.9:16:
God, whom Isaiah calls the light of Israel and the one who is holy to his people, will be like a fire and a flame. That fire will burn up in one day the thorns and briers, which are images of undergrowth: the people and the power that do harm. Burning means that it sets on fire, and destroying completely means that it wipes out everything.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria was like an axe or a rod that God used to discipline his people. But Assyria became filled with pride, as if the power were its own. God answers that he rules and that he will judge that arrogance. Scholars understand the undergrowth and the forest as the Assyrian army.

For today: do not boast of your achievements or your strength, because everything you have comes from God. And if you feel small before powerful people, remember that God is still just and has the final word.
exp.9:17:
It says that God's judgment will completely destroy the greatness of Assyria, pictured as a forest and a fruitful field. The phrase "soul and body" means, in plain terms, the whole person, every part of them, entirely. The image of a standardbearer who falls and collapses is one way to read the last comparison; others understand it as a sick person who wastes away. Both images speak of an end with no remedy.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks at a time when Assyria was a powerful empire. God used it to discipline his people, but Assyria filled itself with pride. Therefore the Lord announces that he will bring it down, and that a small remnant of Israel will once again trust in him.

For today: no power, success, or wealth lasts if it makes us forget God. Examine what you rest your security on, and rest in the Lord, who remains faithful.
exp.9:18:
It says that, after God's judgment, the trees left in Assyria's forest will be so few that even a child will be able to count them. Here "forest" is an image of a great army and a proud nation, not of real trees.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria had been used to discipline Judah, but it became arrogant. For this reason God announces that He will bring it down. Many understand that the forest refers to Assyria, although some also see a broader application. What follows shows the contrast: a small remnant of Israel will stop trusting the one who struck them and will trust in God.

For today: do not place your security in what seems large and strong, but in God. What impresses today can disappear soon; the Lord remains faithful to those who turn to Him.
exp.9:19:
It says that in the coming time, the few who survive from Israel will no longer lean on the one who struck them down. To lean on something means to rely on it or trust in it, like a person leaning on a walking stick. Instead, they will rely on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth, meaning with sincerity and faithfulness.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the kingdom of Judah, which was surrounded by threats. The one who struck them down is usually understood to be Assyria, though Judah also looked for security in alliances with other nations. God announces judgment, but he also promises a remnant: a small group who return to him after suffering.

For today: think about what holds you up when everything around you is shaking, such as money, other people, or your own strength. Even if these fail you or hurt you, you can return to God sincerely and rest your life on him.
exp.9:21:
It says that even if the people of Israel became as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant would return to God. The word for what is left over, the remnant, is the part that remains. The idea of turning back means they will come back. A decreed destruction is a punishment decided by God, and the judgment will be completely just.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who trusted in alliances with foreign powers, while Assyria was threatening them. The prophet announces that judgment will come, but also that a faithful remnant will stop leaning on the one who struck them and will trust in the Holy One of Israel. Some see here also a promise that Paul quotes in Romans 9:27.

For today: when the consequences of drifting away from God arrive, let us not trust in our own strength or in human support. Let us return to Him sincerely, because God is just and always leaves the door open for a return.
exp.9:25:
He says that God himself, the Lord of hosts, will punish Assyria with a scourge. It will be like when he defeated Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will also lift up his rod over the sea, as he did on the way out of Egypt. A scourge is a whip used for punishment, and a rod is a staff of authority. The sea is the sea.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had been used to discipline Judah, but it became proud and cruel. God comforts his people by reminding them of two past deliverances: the one over Midian, in the days of Gideon, and the one at the sea during the exodus. It is not known with certainty which sea is meant here, but the comparison points to the exodus.

For today: when you feel that evil oppresses you and seems to have no end, remember how God has delivered before. Trust that he has the final word and that he does not forget his own.
exp.9:27:
He comes to Aiath, he passes through Migron; at Michmash he leaves his baggage. The explanation says that an enemy army advances step by step toward Jerusalem. First it arrives at Aiath (also called Ai), then it passes through Migron, and at Michmash it leaves its baggage and counts its troops. The phrase about counting the army means that it reviews and organizes them. These are names of towns north of Jerusalem.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He describes the arrival of the Assyrian army, which draws near quickly. Scholars debate whether this is a real military march or a poetic picture of what could happen. What is clear is the message: the threat seems enormous, but God still governs and promises to bring an end to the power that oppresses.

For today: when a problem seems to advance without a brake, do not look at it alone. Remember that God sees every step and has the final word. Pray with confidence and take the next step in faith.
exp.9:28:
The explanation says that the enemy army crossed the passage (the ford of the river or ravine) and camped at Geba, a small town. Seeing it approach, the people of Ramah trembled with fear, and the inhabitants of Gibeah, the city where King Saul was born, fled in flight. The word that means they spent the night there is simply the verb used in the verse for taking up lodging.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He describes, with vivid images, the advance of the Assyrian army toward Jerusalem, naming towns north of the city. Many understand it as an announced march, not necessarily one that had already happened, and scholars discuss the exact route. What matters is that the previous verse promises that God will remove the yoke from his people, and the following text shows that the danger will not have the last word.

For today: when fear advances like an army, remember that God sees the danger and also the deliverance. Tell him honestly what you fear, and trust that he cares for you.
exp.9:32:
This verse says that God, the Lord of hosts, will lop the bough with terror, that is, break the branches of a tree with force. The high ones of stature will be cut down, and the haughty will be humbled.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The Assyrian army advances toward Jerusalem, and the text describes it as a great forest. When it seems that nothing will stop it, God himself intervenes and brings it down. Many understand the high ones as the proud leaders of Assyria, though others also see a general warning against all pride.

For today: when powerful people or great problems make you feel small, remember that God rules over all. Trust him, and examine your heart so that you may live with humility.
exp.9:33:
He says that God will cut down the densest part of the forest with iron, that is, with an axe, and that Lebanon, famous for its great cedars, will fall by a mighty power. The thickest part of the forest is the densest, most tangled growth of trees.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. Assyria, the empire advancing against Jerusalem, is described as an army that reaches Nob, near the city. The images of the forest and the tall trees stand for the pride of the powerful. Some think Lebanon speaks of Assyria itself; others, that it refers to the fall of its leaders. The text does not make this entirely clear.

God is not impressed by those who seem untouchable. If today you feel small in the face of something that seems enormous, remember that God cares for his people and humbles pride. And if you have power or success, learn to live with humility.
exp.10:0:
It says that from what seemed like a cut-down tree, the trunk of Jesse (the father of King David), a new shoot would come forth. The words for the young shoots that spring up from the roots are not used here; the verse itself speaks of a rod and a Branch growing from the roots. The idea of a branch that grows again after the tree has been cut is what this picture conveys.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Before this, chapter 10 announces that God would bring down the pride of Assyria, the way a forest is cut down. Now he offers hope: the family of David would look finished, but God would raise up a righteous king, filled with the Spirit. Christians see Jesus here, as the New Testament does; the original passage was addressed to Judah in a time of crisis.

For today: when something in your life seems cut off or without a future, remember that God can bring new life to grow where you no longer expect it. Trust him and keep taking small steps of faith.
exp.10:1:
He says that the Spirit of the Lord will remain permanently upon a future descendant of Jesse. That Spirit is described with six qualities, in three pairs: wisdom and understanding (seeing clearly and grasping things), counsel and might (planning well and having the power to carry it out), knowledge and fear of the Lord (knowing God and respecting Him with reverence). "Rest" means that the Spirit stays, not that it merely passes by.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and of weak kings. Jesse was the father of King David, so the stump and the shoot suggest that the dynasty seemed cut off, but God would cause something new to sprout. Christians see Jesus, the Messiah, here; Jews have read it as a promise of an ideal king.

For today: before deciding something important, ask God for wisdom and reverence toward Him, and do not rely only on your own cleverness or on what you see at first glance.
exp.10:5:
It says that animals that are normally enemies or prey will live in peace: the wolf with the lamb, the leopard with the young goat, the calf with the lion. And a little child will lead them.

The phrase "fatling" in the verse refers to an animal fattened and raised in the pen.

Isaiah speaks of a future king, whom Christians understand to be Jesus, of the line of David. His justice is described first: he defends the poor and the meek. This peace is the result of his just reign. Some read the images literally, others as a symbol of peace between peoples, and others combine both ideas.

For today: if God promises such deep peace, we can practice it now. Seek to be reconciled with someone with whom you have had conflict, and treat them with justice and gentleness.
exp.10:7:
This verse says that a nursing infant will play beside the hole of a venomous snake, and a child just weaned will put his hand into the den of a dangerous serpent, without suffering harm.

Isaiah, God's prophet, describes the reign of the Messiah, the descendant of Jesse, father of David. He speaks to a people struck by injustice and fear. Many understand these images as a picture of complete peace, and others see them as poetic language. The verses that follow say that this peace comes because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the LORD.

For today: God promises a peace that heals what we fear most. While it arrives in full, we can seek to know him better and be people who bring peace to our home and work.
exp.10:9:
It says that, when the time of the kingdom God promises arrives, the descendant of Jesse (the father of King David) will be like a banner raised for all the peoples. A banner is a flag or standard that gathers people together. The nations will seek it. Rest is a place of quiet and ease, and the verse promises that this rest will be glorious.

Isaiah, a prophet of God, speaks to a people who lived in fear of the neighboring empires. Before this verse he describes a righteous king who would come from David's family and bring peace even to all creation. Christians see in that king Jesus; Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:12. Afterward, God promises to gather the scattered of Israel.

For today: if Jesus is the banner that gathers all the peoples, let us seek rest in him and welcome people from every background.
exp.10:10:
He says that God, in a future time, will once again stretch out his hand to rescue the remnant of his people who have been scattered. The word "remnant" means the survivors, those who were left behind. The phrase "a second time" is often connected with the return from exile, although some see it fulfilled in Christ or still to come in the future. Christians interpret it in different ways.

The places named (Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the islands of the sea) show that they were spread across the whole known world at that time.
