The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat of powerful empires. After describing the righteous king who would come from the root of Jesse, the father of David, he announces that God will gather his people together.

For today: God does not lose sight of those who are far away or scattered. If you feel distant from Him, trust that He knows how to bring you back.
exp.10:11:
He says that God will raise up a sign or banner for the nations to see. With that sign he will gather the exiled Israelites and the scattered Jews, who are spread out to every corner of the earth. "Corners" means the edges or far ends, and "exiles" are those who were forcibly taken from their land.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks of a future king who comes from the root of Jesse, that is, from David's family. Many Christians see Jesus here; others connect it to the return of Israel, or to both. The peoples of the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah) were divided, and God promises to unite and restore them.

For today: God knows how to gather what is broken and scattered. If there is division in your family or church, seek peace by drawing near to Christ, who is the banner that unites us.
exp.10:13:
The explanation says that God's people, united and restored, will advance swiftly and forcefully against their former enemy neighbors. "They shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines" suggests a swift attack toward the west. "They shall spoil them of the east together" means they will plunder them. Edom, Moab, and Ammon, nations to the east, will be brought under their control.

Isaiah speaks to the kingdom of Judah, around the eighth century B.C., announcing what God will do through the future King from David's line (Isaiah 11:1-10). The verses before this one speak of gathering the scattered people and ending the rivalry between Ephraim and Judah. Many see here a promise of restoration; others understand it symbolically, as God's final victory. Interpretations vary.

For today: God can heal divisions among his people and turn rivalry into unity. Ask him to remove envy from you and to help you work in peace with other believers.
exp.10:15:
This verse promises that there will be a clear road for the rest of God's people who were left in Assyria, that is, those who survived and were scattered there. The word "remnant" refers to those who survived and remained. Their return will be compared to the departure of Israel from Egypt, when God brought them out of slavery.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking. In this chapter he announces the reign of the Messiah, a time of justice and peace. Then he says that God will gather his scattered people a second time. The dried-up rivers and seas recall the Red Sea. Some see here the return from exile, and others also see it fulfilled in future times; there are several interpretations.

For today: if you feel far away, exhausted, or without a way out, remember that God knows how to open paths where you cannot see them. Trust that he can guide you back and give you hope, even when your situation seems impossible.
exp.11:2:
God's people will draw water with joy from the springs of salvation. "Salvation" here means rescue and deliverance. The springs are the sources from which fresh water flows. The picture is of people who are thirsty and find plenty of water, without having to search for it in anguish.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had suffered God's anger because of their sin. This chapter is a song for the day when God will restore and comfort them. The verses before it say that God is their salvation, strength, and song. Some see here also a promise of the Messiah; interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: do not live your faith as a dry burden. Each day, come near to God in prayer and in his Word as one who goes to a spring, trusting that he gives you what you need, and let that provision fill you with gratitude and joy.
exp.11:3:
This verse calls for praising God out loud. The commands to sing and to shout for joy are calls to celebrate with gladness. To make his deeds known among the peoples means to make known among the nations what God has done. His name is exalted means that his name is lifted up, or made very high. The word for salvation in the previous verse means deliverance.

Isaiah 12 is a short song of thanksgiving. It announces what God's people will say in that day, that is, when God restores them after his judgment and comfort, as Isaiah describes in chapter 11. Scholars connect it with the restoration of Israel and, for many Christians, also with the work of Christ. Here the people, now saved, encourage others to praise.

For today: when God helps you with something, do not keep it to yourself. Tell a friend or family member, or share it in your church, so that others also come to know his goodness.
exp.12:2:
God himself has given the command to a group of people whom he has set apart for this task. "Sanctified" here means set apart or appointed by God for a purpose, not necessarily people who are perfect. He also called his warriors, his fighters, to carry out his anger. They rejoice in the greatness of God, or they take pride in serving him in this.

God speaks, through Isaiah, in a message against Babylon. The armies that would come are instruments that God uses to judge the pride and violence of that city. Scholars explain in different ways who these "sanctified ones" are: it is generally thought to be the Medes or another army, used by God, although they did not know it.

For today: God rules over the nations and over justice, even when we do not see it. We can rest in the knowledge that no evil goes unanswered, and we should live with humility, without trusting in our own power.
exp.12:7:
This verse describes the fear of the people when the day of judgment comes. They will be filled with terror, and pain will seize them like a woman about to give birth. They will be stunned, speechless with amazement, looking at one another. Their faces will be flushed and burning with distress.

Isaiah prophesies about God's judgment against Babylon (Isaiah 13:1). He speaks on God's behalf and warns that the day of the Lord is drawing near. Some scholars also see in these words an announcement of the final judgment of the whole earth, because the language is very broad. Both readings are possible.

For today: let us not live as if God did not see injustice and pride. Today we can come to Him in humility, ask for forgiveness, and trust in Christ, so that we can await His justice with peace and not with dread.
exp.12:8:
It says that the day of the Lord is coming near and will be harsh, full of anger and burning fury. Its purpose is to leave the land desolate and to remove the sinners from it. The harsh, cruel quality of that day is what the passage stresses, and the anger it describes is intense.

Isaiah prophesies about Babylon, the great power that would later be judged. God speaks through the prophet to warn that he will punish wickedness and pride. Many understand that the passage was fulfilled in part with the fall of Babylon, and that it also points to a final judgment of God on the world. Christians have read it in both ways.

For today: God is just and does not overlook evil or arrogance. This invites us to live with humility, to repent sincerely, and to trust that he will do justice, without taking revenge ourselves.
exp.12:9:
This verse says that the sky will grow dark: the stars and their constellations will not give their light, the sun will be darkened as soon as it rises, and the moon will not shine. The bright stars are called the stars that shine brightly, and light is what fills the sky with brightness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This chapter announces the day of the Lord against Babylon, a day of judgment against pride and wickedness. The darkness in the sky is poetic language that often describes a very great judgment. Some see it fulfilled in the fall of Babylon, and others also see a reference to the end of the age.

Today this text reminds us that God rules over the nations and that no human power is eternal. We can examine our hearts, lay down pride, and trust God with humility, knowing that his justice is true and that he offers forgiveness to those who come to him.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that on that day the people will flee in fear, like a startled and hunted deer, or like sheep without a shepherd. Each one will turn toward his own people and escape to his own land.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in his message against Babylon. He announces the day of the LORD, a time of judgment on that empire's pride and violence. The foreigners who lived there, without protection or leader, would try to return to their own countries.

For today: human powers may seem firm, but they are not our security. Trust in God, and in Christ, the Good Shepherd, who cares for his sheep and does not leave them lost.
exp.12:15:
It says that when Babylon falls, its children will be violently thrown down and dashed to pieces before their parents' eyes. The houses will be plundered, and the women will be violated. It is a very harsh description of what happens in a conquest.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, announcing God's judgment on a proud and violent nation. God says he will raise up the Medes as his instrument. The text does not celebrate cruelty, but warns how terrible war is and how terrible the sin of empires is. Interpreters see here both a historical warning and a sign of God's final judgment.

For today: let us not trust in power or wealth, because every human empire falls. And if we suffer violence or injustice, we can trust that God sees and will judge with justice.
exp.12:19:
It says Babylon will be so desolate that no one will live there for generations. Not even the Arab nomad will pitch his tent there, nor will shepherds bring their flocks to rest in a fold. It will be an abandoned place, like a warning.

Isaiah announces this message on behalf of God against Babylon, the proud great power that oppressed the nations. God compares it with Sodom and Gomorrah, cities that were judged. Some believe the prophecy was fulfilled gradually, through the slow decline of the city after the Persian conquest. Others see poetic and symbolic language pointing to the end of all human pride. It is interpreted in several ways.

Today it reminds us that no human power, success, or fame lasts forever. Let us ask God for humility and place our trust in what is eternal, not in what we boast of.
exp.13:0:
The explanation says that God will have compassion on Jacob, that is, on the people of Israel, and that He will choose them again. He will give them rest in their own land. Moreover, people from other nations will join them and be added to the family of Jacob. To join with them means to come near and become united.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. This message comes just before a song against the king of Babylon. It announces that Israel, who would suffer exile and oppression, would be restored. The verses that follow speak of a change of fortune among the nations. Some interpret this as referring to the return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment in the future.

For today: even if we have passed through hard times or have failed, God is faithful and compassionate. We can trust that He restores and gives rest, and welcome with open arms those who come near to Him.
exp.13:1:
Other peoples, the explanation says, will help Israel return to its own land, and the Israelites will have those same people as male and female servants. Those who once held Israel captive and oppressed them will now fall under Israel's rule. The old wording in the source means to rule over or dominate, and the word for "possess" is used in an older sense: to hold as property.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a promise from God to the people who would suffer captivity, especially under Babylon. The verse before speaks of the LORD's compassion, and the verse after prepares a mocking song against the king of Babylon. Interpreters differ: some see this promise fulfilled in the return from exile, while others also read it as a promise with a still wider scope.

For today: when you feel crushed by injustice, remember that God sees the pain and can change the course of history. Trust in Him, and let His justice, not your resentment, have the last word.
exp.13:2:
It says that a day will come when God will give his people rest. They will be relieved from heavy labor, from constant fear, and from the hard bondage they suffered. The word "rest" in this verse means relief and peace, and the bondage it describes is living under the control of others as a servant.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing the word of God. Israel lived under the threat of foreign powers, and Babylon would become its oppressor. For this reason, God promises restoration and justice. The verses that follow show that this relief would come with the fall of the king of Babylon. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see a wider hope.

For today: if you are exhausted or afraid because of a situation that weighs you down, remember that God sees your burden and promises rest. Pray with confidence, keep doing good, and wait on Him, without letting fear have the last word.
exp.13:4:
It says that God broke the power of the wicked. The "staff" and the "scepter" are symbols of authority: the staff can also be a rod for striking, and the scepter is the sign of a ruler. The "wicked" are those who live without respect for God, and the "rulers" are those who dominate others.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. He announces that, when God frees his people from harsh servitude, they will be able to sing a mocking song against the king of Babylon. He refers to an oppressor who treated the peoples cruelly. Scholars debate whether he speaks of one particular king or of Babylon's arrogance in general.

For today: no unjust power lasts forever. If you suffer abuse or pressure, trust that God sees and knows how to bring oppression to an end. In the meantime, be someone who uses their authority to serve and care, not to hurt.
exp.13:8:
It says that the place of the dead trembled at the arrival of this fallen king. Down there the spirits of the departed were stirred, and the ancient kings and rulers rose from their thrones to receive him.

The word translated here as the place of the dead is the Hebrew Sheol, which means the dwelling place of the dead, not necessarily the place of final punishment.

It is part of a poetic mockery that Isaiah directs against the king of Babylon, an oppressive nation. He imagines the scene of his arrival in the world of the dead. Many see in the passage a reference to a historical king; others also see a broader background about pride and the fall of Satan. Scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: power and fame do not save us from death or from the judgment of God. It is better to live with humility, using what we have to serve and not to dominate.
exp.13:15:
They that see you will look closely at you and consider you with wonder, and they will ask: "Is this the man who made the earth tremble and shook kingdoms?" The phrase about bowing down means they will stare at him up close. The word about shaking means he stirred up and destroyed the order of the nations.

Isaiah announces a prophetic mockery against the king of Babylon (v. 4). His pride went so far as to say he would be like the Most High, but he ends up in the grave. Some see in these verses also a wider look at pride and its fall; others limit them to the historical king. The texts do not fully settle this.

For today: power and fame do not last, and God opposes the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and use whatever influence we have to serve and care for others, not to dominate them.
exp.13:23:
Here God makes a solemn oath. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" means the Lord who commands over all powers. It says that what he has thought and determined will come to pass just as he planned it, and nothing will change it.

God speaks through Isaiah. He had just announced the fall of Babylon, and right away he announces that he will break the Assyrian in the land of Judah. With an oath, God gives assurance to his people, who lived threatened by powerful empires. The verses that follow show that his plan reaches all the nations.

For today: when the world seems dominated by unjust powers or by fear, you can rest in the fact that God keeps what he promises. Trust in him, pray calmly, and keep doing good.
exp.13:24:
He says that God himself will destroy the Assyrian army when it is inside the land of Israel, on the mountains of Judah. "Break" means to crush or shatter, and "trample" means to tread underfoot, as one tramples something that cannot resist. The "yoke" and the "burden" are images of the domination and weight that Assyria placed on the peoples. God promises to remove them.

The words are spoken by the LORD of hosts, through Isaiah. It comes right after the prophecy against Babylon, and here the focus shifts to Assyria, the power that threatened Judah. God affirms that his plan is sworn and no one will stop it. Scholars often connect it with the Assyrian defeat in the time of Hezekiah, though some also see it as an example of God's judgment on all nations.

For today: when you feel a burden that seems greater than you are, remember that God still governs. Hand it over to him in prayer and trust that he knows when and how to take it away.
exp.13:26:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, has already decided what he is going to do, and no one can cancel it. His hand is stretched out in action, and no one can make him withdraw it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God said about Assyria, a powerful empire that oppressed many peoples. God promises to break the Assyrian in his land and remove his yoke, that is, his heavy domination. The verse closes that promise by affirming that God's plan cannot be stopped. Scholars debate exactly how everything was fulfilled, but the central message is clear.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that no human power, however great it may seem, is stronger than God's purposes. When you face something that overwhelms you, pray and trust that he continues to govern.
exp.13:27:
This verse only marks the moment when Isaiah received a message. The king of Judah named Ahaz is the one who died, and the word translated "burden" means a solemn word from God, almost always an announcement of judgment. It says this happened in the year that King Ahaz died.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and behind him God himself. The message is directed to Philistia, a region neighboring Judah. Many think the year was around 715 B.C., although the exact dates are debated among scholars. The Philistines were rejoicing because a power that had struck them had weakened, but God warns them that their relief will not last.

For today: let us not celebrate too soon when a problem seems to be ending. God governs history, so let us trust him and not changing circumstances.
exp.13:28:
God tells Philistia not to celebrate too soon. The rod that struck them has broken, but from that same family of enemies something worse will come. The serpent is a snake, the viper is a poisonous snake, and the flying fiery serpent is a burning snake that strikes quickly.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, in the year King Ahaz died. It is not known for certain which rod was broken: some think of the death of King Ahaz, others of the death of an Assyrian king. What is clear is that a greater judgment would come, and no one could stop what God had decided.

For today: do not trust that a problem is over just because a visible threat has fallen. Before you celebrate, ask God whether there is something more in your life that needs correcting, and entrust your future to Him, not to circumstances.
exp.14:3:
It says that Moab's crying will be so loud that it will be heard from one town to another. Heshbon and Elealeh were Moabite towns to the north, and Jahaz was farther away, though its exact location is not certain. The armed soldiers are the warriors, who are normally brave, but now they howl, that is, they cry out in pain. Their life will be grievous to them means that each person will suffer deeply inside.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. He describes the fall of its cities with images of mourning: shaven heads, sackcloth, and streets full of weeping. Scholars debate when this happened, but the text shows that God rules over all nations.

For today: let us not trust in our strength, money, or security, because everything can fall. Let us place our trust in God and show compassion to those who suffer, as the prophet does in the following verse.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that the women of Moab will go about frightened and without direction, like a bird that flees its nest when it is startled. They will be at the shallow crossing places of the river Arnon, on the border of Moab.

God speaks through Isaiah about a judgment that falls on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab is in crisis and its people are fleeing. The verses before and after show them asking Judah for help. Scholars do not agree on every historical detail of this passage, so it is wise to read it with humility.

When life shakes us and we feel like that bird without a nest, we need not run aimlessly. We can seek refuge in God and offer shelter to anyone who is wounded or left without help.
exp.15:2:
It says that Moab, a people in trouble, must make a wise and just decision. Take counsel and act justly means to deliberate and then act with justice. Make your shadow in the midst of the noonday as the night is an image: give the pursued a shade so deep that they can hide even in broad daylight. The ones who were driven from their land are those who were expelled from their home, and the wanderers are the fugitives. They should not be handed over to their pursuers.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, and the Moabites ask help from Judah, which stands on Mount Zion. Moab flees before a destroyer, probably an invasion, though the text does not give the name with certainty. The suggested answer is that Judah should protect the refugees. Then a just and merciful kingdom is promised in the line of David.

For today: when someone flees violence or injustice, God calls us to be a refuge, not to hand them over. We can help with lodging, practical aid, or by defending the one who suffers.
exp.15:3:
It says that the outcasts of Israel (or of Judah) can take refuge in Moab, and that Moab should protect them from the spoiler. A hiding place is a place to hide; the one who tramples and oppresses is the oppressor; and the word for ending means that it will come to an end. The promise is that oppression will not last forever.

Isaiah announces judgment on Moab, and here he gives it a piece of advice: that it help the fugitives. Scholars disagree about who the spoiler is and who the outcasts are; they could be Jews fleeing an invader, or Moabites themselves. What can be seen is that it is followed by a promise of a throne of mercy in the house of David, and Moab's pride remains as an obstacle.

For today: God calls us to be a shelter for the one who flees or suffers. We can open the door, our time, or our help to someone vulnerable, trusting that God puts an end to all oppression.
exp.15:9:
This verse says that joy and singing have ended in the fields and vineyards of Moab. No one will shout with gladness or tread grapes in the winepresses (the vats where grapes were trampled to get the wine). The treader was the one who crushed the grapes with his feet. God says, "I have made their vintage shouting to cease," meaning the celebration of the harvest.

Isaiah announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring country of Israel, famous for its vineyards. God is the one speaking, but the prophet also shows sorrow: he weeps for Jazer, Heshbon, and Sibmah. The texts do not explain all the historical details of that destruction. We see that God judges pride, but He takes no pleasure in human suffering.

For today: let us not rejoice in the fall of others, nor trust in our harvests or achievements. May our hearts feel compassion, and may we seek God before the crisis arrives.
exp.15:10:
The explanation says that the grief over Moab goes very deep. The words that describe the inner self, the seat of the emotions, point to the heart and the core of the person, and the phrase about sounding like a harp speaks of a trembling or vibration, like strings that sound with sorrow. The name of the place mentioned at the end was an important city of Moab.

Isaiah prophesies God's judgment on Moab, a proud people who would be destroyed and would lose their vineyards and their joy. The one speaking expresses sorrow over that ruin. Some think it is the prophet, others that it reflects the feeling of God. The text does not make this fully clear, and both ideas can stand side by side.

For today: even when someone faces the consequences of their pride or their mistakes, we should not rejoice in their fall. We can ask for justice and also feel compassion, praying for that person.
exp.15:12:
This verse says that what Isaiah has just announced about Moab was not something new. God had already spoken it long before, from that time, that is, from some time ago. The word "spoke" means that God declared it openly.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, conveying the message of the Lord. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, proud and trusting in their gods of the high places. Earlier, the prophet showed grief over their fall. Then, in the following verse, God sets a near deadline: three years. Scholars debate which exact historical events this fulfillment refers to.

For today: God does not speak at random or change his mind without reason. His warnings are an opportunity to turn back to him in time, instead of trusting in our own strength or in things that cannot save us.
exp.15:13:
God announces that within three years Moab will lose its glory. In that sense, the deadline will be precise. Moab's large population will be reduced to a small, weak remnant.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Moab was a neighboring people of Israel, and the preceding chapters mourn its downfall. Moab trusted in its high places and its gods, but they would not save it. Now God sets a date. We do not know for certain which historical event fulfilled this; scholars interpret it in various ways.

For today: do not place your security in what seems great, such as money, prestige, or empty religion. All of that can fall quickly. Seek God sincerely now, not only when you are tired and in trouble.
exp.16:0:
It says that God announces judgment on Damascus, the capital of Syria. "Burden" means a heavy message, a prophetic pronouncement. The city will cease to be a city and will be left as a heap of ruins. It is a strong image of total destruction.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, delivering the word of the LORD. Damascus had allied itself with Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, and the next verse says that Ephraim's help would also come to an end. Many understand this as referring to the fall of Damascus before Assyria, around 732 B.C. Some also see a broader fulfillment, but that is debated.

For today: no human power is as firm as it appears. Trusting in alliances, riches, or our own strength is fragile. We can rest in God, who governs the nations and fulfills what he says.
exp.16:1:
It says the cities of Aroer will be abandoned and will become grazing land for flocks. The sheep will lie down there, and no one will frighten them.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in an oracle, a message of judgment, against Damascus, the capital of Syria. Damascus had allied itself with Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel) against Judah. Aroer was probably in territory east of the Jordan, though it is not certain which Aroer is meant. The message announces that this alliance will collapse and that places once inhabited will be left empty.

Today we can remember that no human power or political alliance is safe forever. Trusting in God, and not in what appears strong, gives a peace that does not fall apart.
exp.16:4:
It says that what is coming upon Israel will be like a harvest: the reaper gathers the stalks of wheat, takes them in one hand, and with his arm cuts off the heads of grain. It is also compared to someone who gathers loose heads of grain in the valley of Rephaim. The mature crop is the grain standing in the field, and the heads are the tips of the stalk where the kernels are. The image speaks of almost everything being taken away, with very little left behind.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces judgment on Damascus and on Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, which had allied itself with Syria. It is thought that the valley of Rephaim lies near Jerusalem and was known for its harvests, though its exact location is debated.

For today: do not place your security in alliances, money, or power, because all of these can vanish. Trust in God, who even in judgment leaves a remnant and invites us to turn our eyes back to Him.
exp.16:6:
This verse says that after a time of judgment and loss, the people will once again look to God. The word "Maker" means Creator, the One who made us. "The Holy One of Israel" is a title for God that stresses that He is pure and set apart from everything else. "Look" here means to fix one's attention and trust on Him.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks on God's behalf. He announces judgment on Damascus and on the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim) for their idolatry and their alliances. Very little will remain, like a few olives left on the branch after the harvest. But in the midst of that loss, some will leave their altars and idols and turn back to God.

For today: sometimes God allows us to lose things we were trusting in, so that we lift our eyes toward Him. Today you might ask yourself: where am I placing my security? Give it to God in prayer, and look to Him again.
exp.16:10:
He says that someone plants with great care and sees that their plants grow quickly, even sprouting in the morning. But when the day of the harvest comes, everything is lost. Instead of joy, there remains a sorrow with no remedy, a grief that cannot be healed. The seed is what is planted, and gathering in the crop is the harvest.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom, Israel, together with its ally Damascus. He rebukes them for having forgotten God, their salvation and their rock. They looked for security in alliances and in strange and beautiful plants, and this probably refers to practices or supports foreign to God. Some interpreters see idolatry in this; others see political strategies.

We can work hard and see quick results, but if we leave God out, nothing endures. Today you might ask yourself: on what do I base my security? Before making plans, pray and place your projects in his hands.
exp.16:12:
They say that many nations will make a great noise, like the roar of mighty waters. But God will rebuke them with his word, and they will flee far away. They will be swept off like the chaff, the light husk that is left over when the grain is threshed, which the wind carries away from the mountains, or like the dust that a whirlwind lifts up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C., when Judah faced threats from neighboring powers. This passage follows a message against Damascus and Ephraim. Many understand it to refer to armies, probably Assyria, that attack God's people. The next verse shows that their noise comes to an end in a single night. Scholars do not agree on identifying every historical detail.

Today, when problems seem loud and enormous, remember that God is greater. Bring your fear to him in prayer and trust that he has the final word.
exp.17:2:
It says that all the inhabitants of the earth will see a sign lifted up on the mountains and hear the sound of a trumpet. A "banner" is a standard raised to draw attention, and the trumpet serves to give a warning. Both things announce that God is about to act, and no one will be able to ignore it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. A powerful nation, which many understand to be Ethiopia (Cush), sends messengers seeking alliances, probably in the face of the threat from Assyria. Scholars disagree about who raises the banner, but the context shows that God is the one who directs events, watching calmly and intervening in his own time.

For today: when the world seems agitated and we look for security in alliances or human plans, let us remember that God is still in control. We can trust and wait with peace, knowing that he acts in his own time.
exp.17:4:
It says that, just before the harvest, when the grape or fruit is nearly ready and the flower has passed, God cuts off the tender shoots with pruning tools and removes the branches. It is a farming image: the farmer steps in at the right moment, before the fruit is gathered.

Isaiah speaks in God's name to a distant nation, Ethiopia (Cush), in chapter 18. God says he watches in silence, with calm, while the moment comes. Scholars disagree about whom the pruning refers to: it may be the judgment on the nations that threatened Judah, or on the people themselves. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: even when God seems silent, he is not absent. He acts in his own time, and his pruning, though painful, is not carelessness. We can wait with confidence and ask him for patience.
exp.18:0:
The explanation says that God speaks of a judgment against Egypt. The word "burden" means a heavy message, a serious warning. The Lord appears riding on a swift cloud, that is, he arrives quickly and no one can stop him. The Egyptian idols shall be moved, that is, they tremble before him. The phrase about the heart melting means that the courage of the Egyptians melts away like wax.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, announcing what Jehovah will do. Egypt was a power with many gods and great confidence in its strength. Some in Judah looked to Egypt for protection against other empires. Scholars disagree about the exact historical moment this prophecy refers to.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, power or security, begins to totter when he acts. We can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and return to resting in him.
exp.18:5:
The explanation says that the rivers of Egypt will be turned far away, meaning their flow will drop until they are dry. The canals or channels that carried water will be emptied, and the plants along the banks, such as the reeds and flags (a plant similar to the rush), will be cut down or will wither.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God, the Lord of hosts, against Egypt. In that country everything depended on the Nile: food, work and trade. When the river dried up, God's judgment would strike the foundation of its security. Scholars debate exactly which historical events it refers to, and some also see a broader meaning.

For today: ask yourself what things you place your security in, such as money, employment or health. All of these can fail, but God remains. Trust Him first.
exp.18:10:
They say that the leaders of Egypt, those of the city of Zoan, are fools. The counselors who thought themselves very wise no longer know what to do; their counsel has vanished, meaning it has disappeared and is of no use. God asks with irony how they dare tell Pharaoh that they are descendants of the wise and of ancient kings. Zoan was an important city in Egypt.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message of judgment against Egypt. Earlier, the crisis in its economy is described: linen, nets, and fish. Now its leaders are pointed out, people who boasted of inherited wisdom but cannot understand what God is doing.

For today: human wisdom, prestige, or experience is not enough without God. Before trusting in our own plans, it is good to ask him for direction with humility and to listen to his Word.
exp.18:11:
God asks Egypt where its wise men and counselors are, the ones who prided themselves on their discernment. He challenges them to tell the king what the Lord of hosts has decided concerning their country. If they were truly wise, they would know God's plan.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message against Egypt. Pharaoh's counselors, in Zoan and Noph (Memphis), took pride in their wisdom and their lineage. But their advice failed, and the text says that God himself confused them, showing that no human wisdom stands above him.

For today: It is good to seek advice and to keep learning, but we should not trust our own intelligence or that of others as if it were the final word. Before deciding something important, seek God's direction in prayer and in his Word.
exp.18:16:
The explanation says that Judah, the land of God's people, will cause fear in Egypt. Every Egyptian who remembers it will be left frightened, that is, they will be astonished. The reason is the counsel of God, which here means his plan or decision, and which he himself determined against Egypt.

Isaiah prophesies about Egypt, which was a great power. Earlier, the text says that no leader or ordinary person will be able to save it, because God will act with his mighty hand. Some understand that Judah becomes a cause for dread because Egypt recognizes that the God of Judah is the one who rules. Interpreters do not agree on how or when this was fulfilled. What follows shows that God's judgment also opens the door for Egypt to come to know him.

For today: let us not trust in power, money, or human leaders. God's plans come to pass, and his judgment often seeks to restore. Trust in him.
exp.18:18:
It says that a day will come when Egypt, an old enemy of Israel, will have an altar dedicated to the Lord in the middle of its land. The word "pillar" here means a column or monument set up as a sign, and "border" means the edge of the country. In other words, there will be a visible reminder of God right at the country's boundary.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, announces what God will do. Before this, he speaks of judgment on Egypt, but now he shows hope: Egypt will come to know the Lord. Scholars disagree about when this will be fulfilled. Some think of Jews and believers in Egypt centuries later, others of the time of the Messiah, and others of a time still in the future.

God does not give up on anyone, not even on peoples who seem most distant. Today we can pray for people or nations we see as enemies, trusting that God can transform them.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that the altar and the monument to the Lord in Egypt will be a sign and a witness that God is present there. When the Egyptians suffer under their oppressors, they will cry out to the Lord, and he will send them a saviour, a great one, who will defend them and set them free.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in God's name about the future of Egypt, a nation that had once been an enemy of Israel. It is a surprising promise: Egypt too would come to know the Lord. Interpreters differ about who this saviour is. Some think of a historical deliverer, and many Christians see a promise that points to Christ. It cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: God hears the cry of anyone who is oppressed, whatever their background. When you suffer, cry out to him with confidence, and let his great mercy teach you to pray also for those who seem far from God.
exp.18:21:
God says he will strike Egypt, but not to destroy it; he will strike it in order to heal it. The blow is a correction. Afterward, the Egyptians will turn back to the Lord, and he will receive them with kindness.

Isaiah the prophet speaks, announcing a message from God about Egypt, a nation seen in Israel's thinking as an enemy and oppressor. The immediate context shows that Egypt would cry out to God in its suffering, and God would send them a deliverer. Interpreters differ about when and how this is fulfilled, but all of them see an announcement of hope for the nations.

For today: when God corrects you, do not see it as rejection. His aim is to heal you and draw you closer to himself. Also remember that his mercy reaches even those who seem most distant.
exp.18:22:
It says that a time will come when there will be an open road between Egypt and Assyria, two nations that were once rivals. People will go back and forth from one country to the other without fear. And together, Egyptians and Assyrians will worship the LORD.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking, on God's behalf, within a message about Egypt. First he announces judgment, but he ends with hope: God wounds in order to heal. Assyria was a feared power. Interpreters differ on when this is fulfilled: some see a partial historical fulfillment, others see it in Christ or in the future.

For today: God can bring together those who seem to be enemies. Ask Him to help you let go of a grudge and take a step toward reconciliation with someone.
exp.19:0:
This verse marks the time when what follows takes place. It says that Sargon, king of Assyria, sent a high military commander (called Tartan in some other versions) to Ashdod, a Philistine city. There he fought against the city and captured it.

The passage is a historical fact that serves as an introduction. Assyria was the dominant power, and Ashdod had looked toward Egypt for help. That is why God speaks right away through Isaiah: Egypt and Ethiopia would not be a safe refuge either. Historians usually place this event around 711 B.C., although the exact dates are debated.

Today we can learn not to place our security in human strengths that seem firm, such as money, connections, or power. When crises come, only God is a refuge that does not fall. Trust in Him first.
exp.19:1:
Here God gives the prophet Isaiah a strange command: to take off the sackcloth from his waist and the sandals from his feet. Sackcloth was a rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance. Isaiah obeyed and went about naked and barefoot. It is likely that "naked" means without his outer cloak, wearing only his undergarment, though some think he went further than that.

The Lord speaks at the time when Assyria conquered the Philistine city of Ashdod. Judah was tempted to trust in Egypt and Ethiopia for protection. God used Isaiah as a living sign: in this way the Egyptians and Ethiopians would be led captive, and they would not be able to save anyone. According to the text that follows, Isaiah did this for three years.

Today, the lesson is to trust in God and not in human powers that seem secure. It also invites us to obey God even when it costs us shame or the opinion of others.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that some people will be frightened and put to shame, because they had placed their hope in Ethiopia and took pride in Egypt. They will be filled with fear and confusion. Here, the things they boasted in or leaned on with pride were their own sources of security.

God speaks through Isaiah. Isaiah walked without his outer clothing and barefoot as a sign for the people. The inhabitants of the region, probably Judah, were seeking alliances with Egypt and Ethiopia to defend themselves against Assyria. God warns that Assyria would defeat them, and that confidence would end in shame.

Today we can ask ourselves what we rely on for our security: money, influence, a job, or powerful people. All of these can fail. It is good to use the resources we have, but our deepest trust should rest in God, who does not fail.
exp.20:12:
Here God announces a "burden", that is, a message of judgment, concerning Arabia. He says that the travelling companies of Dedanim, who were merchants with caravans, will have to spend the night hidden in the thickets or among the bushes, far from the known roads, because they are fleeing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The verses that follow show that these travelers are escaping from war: swords, bows, and battle. The people of Tema are asked to bring them water and bread. Scholars do not know with certainty which invasion is in view; it is often linked to some military advance of the period, but this is debated.

For today: when someone arrives weary and fleeing from a difficulty, God calls us to offer concrete help, such as a plate of food or a cup of water. Small acts of kindness reflect his care for those who suffer.
exp.20:14:
It says the people flee from four things: the swords, the drawn sword (the sword that is out of its sheath), the bent bow (the bow that is strung and ready to shoot), and the weight, or harshness, of the battle. These are people who escape from a war and seek to save themselves.

Isaiah announces a burden, that is, a message of judgment, concerning Arabia. He speaks in the name of God. The fugitives arrive in lands such as Dedanim and Tema, and those peoples are asked to give them water and bread. Afterward God announces that within a year the glory of Kedar, another Arab tribe, will be broken. Scholars are not sure which specific invasion is meant.

For today: God sees the exhausted person who flees and calls us to help them. This week, share bread, time, or a kind word with someone who is going through a hard struggle.
exp.20:15:
God tells Isaiah that within a year, counted precisely, the way a hired worker counts his years of service, all the glory of Kedar will come to nothing. A hired worker is one who receives a fixed wage for a set period of time, so the term will not be extended by even one day.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert, known for its archers and its wealth. The passage announces that war will strike them, while the people of Tema are to help the fugitives with water and bread. Scholars do not agree on the exact historical event the passage refers to.

For today: human strength and reputation are passing, but God governs history. Trust in Him more than in your achievements, and when you see someone fleeing or exhausted, offer them concrete help, such as water and bread.
exp.21:5:
Elam and Kir are said to be preparing an army to attack Jerusalem. Elam carried the quiver, the case for arrows, and came with chariots of men and horsemen. Kir uncovered the shield, that is, he took off its cover to make it ready for battle. It is a picture of an armed and determined army.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, and he is deeply sad over the suffering of his people. The valley of vision is usually understood to refer to Jerusalem. God allows this attack, and the text shows that the city trusted more in its weapons than in Him. Scholars are not completely sure which specific enemy is described, or when it happened.

For today: let us not rely only on our defenses, plans, or resources. Preparing ourselves is good, but God should be our first security. When difficulty comes, let us return to Him with humility.
exp.21:6:
It says that the most beautiful valleys of Jerusalem, which had once been quiet and fertile, were filled with war chariots. The horsemen took up positions in front of the city gate, ready to attack. The horsemen are not named in the verse above, so I should not refer to them that way. Instead, the explanation describes them simply as the horsemen who took their stand at the gate.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Jerusalem, which is called the valley of vision. The city faced an invasion, and its people trusted in their weapons and walls, but they did not seek God. Scholars debate which exact attack is described: it may be the Assyrian threat or a later event. The text does not make this fully clear.

For today: it is not enough to prepare defenses and plans if we forget God. Before crises arrive, we can draw near to Him and entrust our security to Him.
exp.21:8:
It says that the people of Jerusalem saw that the walls of the city of David had many cracks or breaches, and that there were more and more of them. So they gathered the water of the lower pool (the pool, or reservoir, is the one named in the verse) to have water during an attack.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, sent by God. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy, and the people made practical preparations: repairing walls, storing water, and checking their weapons. The problem, according to the next verse, is that they did not look to God, who had made and formed that city. Scholars debate the exact moment this refers to, but the central message is clear.

It is good to plan and work wisely, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before solving a problem, let us seek God in prayer and place our trust in Him.
exp.21:9:
The explanation says that the people of Jerusalem counted the houses of the city and tore down some of them to get stones and space, in order to strengthen the wall. The word "Jerusalem" refers to Jerusalem itself, and to fortify means to make something stronger so that it can be defended.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy army. The people made practical plans: they inspected the defenses, gathered water, and repaired the wall. The problem, according to the following text, is that they did not look to God, who had made and directed the city. They did what was human, but they ignored what was spiritual.

For today: it is good to plan and work hard in the face of difficulties, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before we set our plans in motion, we can pray and seek God's guidance, and then work wisely, trusting in Him.
exp.21:10:
The explanation says that the people of Jerusalem built a channel between the two walls, using the water of an old pool (the word translated here as "pool" refers to a pool or reservoir of water). They did all this to defend themselves, but they did not take God into account, the one who had made and shaped everything long ago.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by an enemy, and the people rushed to strengthen walls, houses and their water supply. They were preparing well, but they did not even think of seeking God. Afterward, instead of repenting, some of them said, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Scholars debate exactly which pool is meant.

For today: It is good to plan and prepare, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before facing a problem, let us bring it to prayer and ask God for direction.
exp.21:11:
He says that the Lord God of hosts called the people on that day to weep, to lament, to tear out their hair, and to put on sackcloth, which was a rough cloth worn as a sign of grief and repentance.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was under threat, and its people trusted only in walls, torn-down houses, and stores of water, but they did not look to God, who had made all of it. God asked for humility, but they answered with feasting and with the attitude of "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

For today: when a crisis comes, make your plans wisely, but do not leave God out of them. Stop, pray, and humbly acknowledge your faults, instead of distracting yourself so you do not have to think about what matters.
exp.21:12:
This verse describes a feast. Instead of weeping and repenting, the people slaughter cattle and sheep, eat meat, drink wine, and say, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die." Slaying here means killing the animal by cutting its throat.

The Lord had called Jerusalem to weep and to dress in mourning, because the city was under threat. But the people chose to ignore the danger and did not turn their eyes to God, who governs all things. That is why God later says this sin would not be forgiven until they died. It is a very serious judgment, and scholars understand it as a hardness of heart without repentance.

For today: when a difficulty comes, let us not cover it with entertainment or distractions. Better to stop, pray, and return to God with humility, for He does listen to us and restore us.
exp.21:15:
God asks Shebna a sharp question: "What are you doing here? Who are you, to have carved yourself a tomb here?" He speaks of a tomb cut out in a high place, hewn into the rock.

Isaiah brings this message from God to Shebna, a high official, the palace steward. It seems he used his position to seek his own honor, with a luxurious tomb, as if he were of royal blood. We know no more details of his life; the text shows only a man more concerned with his fame than with serving. God announces that he will be removed from his post and will die far away.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I work to serve, or to be admired? God gives us responsibilities to bless others, not to raise a monument to our own name.
exp.22:4:
When the news of Tyre's fall reaches Egypt, the Egyptians will be filled with anguish. "Report" here means news or rumor, and the word translated "report" means news. Some translators understand that Egypt will suffer because of what happened to Tyre; others understand that it will be distressed as it was when it heard the news of another disaster. The Hebrew text allows several readings.

Isaiah announces God's judgment on Tyre, the great trading city of the sea. Egypt was one of its partners, since it supplied Tyre with grain from the Nile. If Tyre fell, Egypt would lose a good customer and would see that not even the most secure powers hold firm. God is the one who speaks through the prophet.

For today: let us not place our security only in money, work, or business. All of that can change suddenly. Let us first trust in God, who endures.
exp.22:7:
This verse asks a question: who decided the fall of Tyre? Tyre was a city famous for its trade, and it was described as a city whose power and fame made it admired. Its merchants were so wealthy that they had the standing of princes and nobles.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks a message of judgment against Tyre. The question is rhetorical: the answer comes in the next verse, where God himself has decreed it. Tyre trusted in its riches and its reputation, and God shows that no human glory is beyond his authority.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or reputation. All of that can change suddenly. Be thankful for what God gives you, use it with humility, and trust in him more than in what you have.
exp.22:10:
He stretched out his hand over the sea and shook the kingdoms. He also says that the Lord has given a command against Canaan, which here refers to Phoenicia, the region of trading cities such as Tyre and Sidon, that its strongholds be destroyed. The sea is the Mediterranean, from which its wealth came.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter is a message against Tyre, a powerful city made rich by sea trade. The verse before explains the reason: God wants to humble the pride of all human glory. Neither the sea nor riches protect someone who thinks they are untouchable.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, success or reputation. All of that can totter, but God does not. Trust Him first and use what you have with humility.
exp.22:12:
Look at the land of the Chaldeans, that is, Babylon. That people had no importance before. Assyria founded it or strengthened it for people who lived in the wilderness. They raised up towers and palaces, but in the end that land was left in ruins. The text is difficult, and it is not known for certain who "he" was that brought it to ruin: it may be Assyria, or God working through it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in a message against Tyre, the great trading city. He uses the example of Babylon to show that even what seems firm can fall. Tyre should not have trusted in its wealth or its reputation.

Today, let us not place our security in money, success or power, because all of that can change. Let us trust in God, who remains forever.
exp.23:1:
What it says: The verse lists pairs of people: the people and the priest, the servant and the master, the one who buys and the one who sells, the one who lends and the one who borrows. It says that judgment will come to all alike.

Context: Isaiah is the prophet who speaks in God's name. In chapters 24 to 27 he announces a judgment on the whole earth because of human wickedness. Here it is shown that no one is left out: not those who hold authority, not those who have money, and not those who serve. Some understand this passage as judgment on Judah and the nations of his time, and others also see it as an announcement of the final judgment.

For today: God shows no favoritism. Our position, money, or prestige does not protect us from having to give an account to him. Today we can examine our hearts with humility and live honestly, whatever our place in society.
exp.23:2:
This verse says that the land will be completely emptied and stripped bare, like a house that thieves have entered and cleared of everything. The words "utterly" and "utterly" stress that nothing will be left. The reason given is simple: God himself has spoken it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Chapters 24 to 27 describe a judgment that reaches the whole earth, without distinction of rank: priest and people, master and servant. The verses that follow give the reason: the people broke God's laws and violated his covenant. Some see here a judgment on the world of that time, others a foretaste of the end of days; the text allows both readings.

For today: let us not trust in what can be lost, such as money, position, or success. God calls everyone alike to live justly and to return to him with humility, because only his word endures.
exp.23:4:
The earth was defiled because of the people who live on it. Its being defiled means that it was made dirty and corrupted. The inhabitants disobeyed God's laws, twisted justice, and broke the everlasting covenant.

Isaiah the prophet announces what the LORD says will come upon the whole earth. This judgment is not a whim: it comes as a consequence of sin and injustice. Some think the everlasting covenant refers to the covenant with Noah; others, to God's law in general. It is not certain which it is.

Today we can take seriously that what we do has consequences. Let us ask God for help to be honest and just in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in our dealings with others.
exp.23:6:
It says that the new wine has spoiled, that the vine has dried up, and that those who once lived with joy now grieve. Where the wording reads as it does here, the verse itself speaks of the wine mourning and the vine languishing, and the sense is the same: a plant that weakens and no longer bears fruit. The wine and the vine were common symbols of joy and celebration.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the earth. In the verses before, he explains the cause: the people broke the laws, twisted justice, and broke the everlasting covenant. Some understand this covenant as the one made with Noah, others as the law given to Israel. Scholars interpret it in different ways. Here the sorrow is the result of sin.

For today: let us not look for joy only in things that can come to an end, such as festivities, money, or success. Living justly and faithfully before God gives a joy that is more firm.
exp.23:7:
It says that the music and the feasting are over. The tambourines (percussion instruments) no longer sound, the noise of those who were celebrating has ended, and the harp has fallen silent. It is a picture of sorrow: where there was once celebration, there is now stillness and grief.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks in a section that describes a judgment upon the whole earth. According to the text, the cause is that its inhabitants broke God's laws and the everlasting covenant (v. 5). Scholars debate whether it refers to a specific historical event or to a final judgment; the passage may carry both meanings.

For today: the joys of this world can end suddenly, so let us not place our security in them. Let us enjoy with gratitude what God gives, but trust in Him, who remains forever.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that God has been a firm refuge for the poor and the needy when they suffer. He is like a coat in the storm and a shade in the strong heat. The needy are those who lack what they need, and the violent blow of the wicked is like a heavy rain beating against a wall, the very face of a wall or building.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks in the form of praise to God. It is in a section where God announces that he will bring down proud and oppressive cities. It is not stated with certainty which city is meant; scholars understand it in several ways, perhaps as a symbol of human pride in general. Afterward, God prepares a banquet for all peoples.

For today: when you feel weak or pressured, turn to God in prayer before looking for other ways out. He cares for the fragile and can be your refuge.
exp.24:8:
This verse describes a shout of joy from the people on the day when God acts. They will say, "This is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us." They repeat that they waited for the Lord, and now they rejoice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and the verse is the people's response to what God promised before: to remove the veil covering the nations, to destroy death, and to wipe away every tear. After that, the text speaks of judgment on Moab, a symbol of pride against God. Interpreters debate whether this is fulfilled at a moment in history, at the end of time, or in both.

For today: waiting on God is not wasted time. While you wait for an answer, remember what He has promised, pray with patience, and keep alive the hope that His salvation will come.
exp.24:9:
He says that the hand of God, that is, his power and his care, will rest securely upon this mountain, which is Zion, where God reveals himself. But Moab will be trodden down like straw that is crushed in the dunghill, the place where manure is piled up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He comes from a great promise: God will defeat death, wipe away every tear, and save his people. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears as an example of pride against God (the following verse). Some believe it represents all who oppose God; others think it speaks of the historical Moab.

For today: trust that God has the last word. If you feel small before injustice, rest in his hand and give up pride, which God resists.
exp.25:0:
This verse announces a song that will be sung in Judah when God restores his people. It says they have a strong city, but their security does not come from stones; it comes from God himself. In this context, "salvation" means rescue or deliverance. The walls and bulwarks are the protection that God himself provides in full.

It is the prophet Isaiah who speaks, describing a future song of praise. It comes after the judgments against the nations (chapters 13 to 25). "In that day" refers to a time of future deliverance. Some see it fulfilled in part after the return from exile, and others see it also pointing to the final restoration. The verses that follow speak of the righteous entering and of peace.

For today: when you feel fear or insecurity, do not first look for refuge in your own resources. Remember in prayer how God has saved and cared for you, and sing to him, even if only quietly, with gratitude.
exp.25:8:
Here the prophet says that he desires God with his whole being. At night he longs for him with his soul, and while he has life and breath ("spirit") he will rise early to seek him. He also says that when God's judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn what is right.

Isaiah speaks in a song of trust on behalf of the people of Judah. They wait on God, who is upright, while they see evil all around them. The verses that follow show that not everyone learns: the wicked, even when shown kindness, keeps doing evil. For this reason some understand "judgments" as God's corrections, and others as his acts of justice.

For today: set aside a moment at the beginning or end of the day to seek God sincerely. Before the news or your phone, speak to him, listen to his Word, and ask him to teach you to live righteously.
exp.25:10:
The verse says that, although God's hand is raised to act, the wicked do not see it. They are blind to what He is doing. But in the end they will see, and those who envied God's people will be put to shame. And the fire, that is, divine judgment, will consume His enemies.

Isaiah speaks in a song of confidence that the people of Judah will sing. Shortly before, the prophet says that the wicked receive kindness and still do not learn righteousness. That is why the verse acknowledges that some do not understand even when God acts. Then the song affirms that God will give peace to His own.

Today, if you see that those who mock God seem to get their way, do not become bitter or envy them. God sees everything and works in His own time. In the meantime, seek God steadily, as the passage says, and trust that He puts everything in its place.
exp.25:12:
The explanation says that the people acknowledge the Lord as their God. Other lords ruled over them, that is, governed them, but those masters stood apart from you, that is, without reckoning with God. Even so, the people declare that only through God will they remember and honor his name. Having been ruled by others means they exercised power and control.

The speaker is the people of Judah in a song of trust found within Isaiah 24 to 27. They have lived under foreign powers and oppressors. The verses before it speak of peace that comes from God, and the verses after it say that those rulers died and were wiped out. Interpreters debate exactly whom it refers to, but the general sense is clear: God is stronger than any human power.

Today we can ask what things hold authority over our hearts: money, fear, the opinion of others. Today you can choose deliberately to put God first, giving thanks for his name and seeking him in prayer.
exp.26:0:
In that day, it says, God himself will intervene with his sword, which is hard, great and strong, against Leviathan. This is a sea monster described as a swift, gliding serpent and as a twisting, coiled serpent full of bends. He will also slay the dragon of the sea.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do at the end of a long section about his judgment on the nations. Leviathan and the dragon are poetic images of evil and chaos that threaten his people. Some believe they represent enemy powers; others, a spiritual force. The text does not make this clear, and it is interpreted in several ways. Next comes the song of the vineyard protected by God.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that evil, however great or twisted it may seem, does not have the last word. God will defeat it, and in the meantime he cares for his own.
exp.26:3:
He says that God is not angry with his vineyard, which is his people. If someone were to set thorns and briers, that is, enemies or wickedness, as if they were going to fight against him, God would advance against them, trample them underfoot, and burn them all together.

The Lord speaks, and in the passage he tends his vineyard with tenderness, watering it and guarding it day and night. Here God's anger is not against his people, but against whatever threatens them. Scholars debate some details of the image, but the general meaning is God's protection and his invitation to make peace with him.

Today you can trust that God cares for you, even when you feel surrounded by problems. If you have felt that he is angry with you, remember that he invites you to make peace with him. Come near to him sincerely and rest in his care.
exp.26:5:
It says that a time will come when the people of God, called Jacob and Israel, will be like a tree that puts down roots, blossoms, and sends out new shoots. They will bear so much fruit that the face of the world (the surface of the earth, the whole world) will be filled. The word "fill" here means to be full.

He speaks within a song about his vineyard (Isaiah 27:2-5). He says that he has no anger against it and invites his enemies, like thorns and thistles, to make peace with him. After the discipline, he promises restoration. Some see here a future fulfillment for Israel, others a blessing that reaches the nations through the people of God.

For today: even when you go through trials or correction, God does not leave you there. His goal is for you to take root again in him and bear fruit. Trust in his process and seek peace with him.
exp.26:8:
This verse says that God will purge the wickedness of the people of Israel (Jacob). The intended result is that sin is taken away, and it is seen when the altars of the idols are broken down until they are like chalkstones that are beaten to pieces. The groves and images are not to stand up again.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, passing on what God said. It comes after speaking of the measured punishment God gave his people. His purpose was not only to punish but to cleanse Israel of idolatry. Some scholars see this fulfilled after the exile, and others think it will also be fulfilled later on.

For today: God corrects in order to heal. Ask him to show you which "altars" have taken his place in your heart, and let them fall with confidence.
exp.26:9:
It says that a city which seemed very strong will be destroyed and abandoned. Where there were once people, there will be a desolate place. The animals will graze there and feed on the branches that grow up.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Israel. The verses before this one speak of purging Jacob of idolatry. Commentators do not agree on which city is meant: it may be Jerusalem, Samaria, or an enemy city. What is clear is that judgment comes because of the people's lack of understanding and faith.

For today: there is no lasting security in what we build without God, whether money, reputation, or power. We can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and return to God with humility. He corrects, but He also desires to restore.
exp.26:11:
The passage says that on that day God will act from the river Euphrates, from the riverbed itself, all the way to the stream of Egypt, a brook on the southern edge of the promised land. Here the word for God's action is understood as shaking or striking, the way an olive tree is shaken to gather its fruit. And the children of Israel will be gathered one by one, that is, personally, leaving no one behind.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Earlier he announced judgment on a city that lacked understanding. Now the tone changes: after the punishment comes the hope of restoration. Interpreters disagree about whether this refers to a historical return or to something still in the future.

For today: God does not treat his people as an anonymous mass; he seeks you one by one. If you feel far away or scattered, you can trust that he knows your name and invites you to come back.
exp.26:12:
In that day God has appointed, a great trumpet will sound, a sign of calling. The Israelites who were scattered in Assyria and those driven out or exiled in Egypt will return. They will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to a people who would be punished for their lack of understanding and their idolatry. After the judgment, God promises to gather his people one by one. Assyria and Egypt represent places of exile and oppression. Some see here the return after the exile; others also see a future or spiritual fulfillment. Believers have understood this in several ways.

For today: even if you feel far away, lost, or scattered because of your mistakes or your circumstances, God keeps calling. His discipline is not his final word; his aim is to restore you so that you worship him again. Respond to his call today.
exp.27:3:
He says that the beauty of Ephraim, the thing it was so proud of, will fade like a flower that dries up. Its city sat on a fertile valley, but it will be like the early fig of summer: as soon as someone sees it, they pick it up and eat it right away. The word "fading" describes a flower that withers; the phrase about it being swallowed up speaks of a quick destruction; and "in his hand" means within easy reach.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf against the northern kingdom, called Ephraim, and its capital, Samaria. Its leaders lived in luxury and drunkenness, trusting in their wealth. Isaiah announces that a strong invader will come like a storm. Many understand that he is referring to Assyria, although the text says it through images.

Today, beauty, success, or security can end quickly. Put your trust in God, not in what you boast about. He is the lasting crown.
exp.27:4:
On that day, the explanation says, God himself will be like a crown of glory and a beautiful headpiece for the rest of his people. "The remnant" means those who are left, the faithful few. A "diadem" is a crown or ornament worn on the head.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he had announced the fall of Ephraim (the northern kingdom), whose leaders took pride in their adornments and drank themselves into a stupor. In contrast to that passing crown, which will be trampled underfoot, God promises to be the true crown for those who remain faithful to him. Some believe that "that day" points to the judgment of Assyria, while others see a broader hope.

For today: do not look for your worth in success, fame, or pleasure, which wither quickly. Fix your eyes on God, who gives lasting beauty and dignity to those who trust in him.
exp.27:5:
This verse continues the promise from the verse before: God himself will be a crown for his faithful people, and he will also give a spirit of judgment to the one who sits in judgment, that is, wisdom and justice. He will also give strength to those who turn the battle to the gate, meaning those who push back the enemy and hold it at the entrance of the city.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. He has just announced punishment for proud Samaria, compared to a flower that withers. Then he shows that God will care for those who remain faithful to him. Right after, he criticizes the leaders of Judah, priests and prophets, who were drunk and judged badly. That is why the contrast is so strong.

For today: if you have responsibility over others, in the home, the church, or the workplace, ask God for wisdom and firmness, and take care of your own clarity of mind and character.
exp.27:6:
They also stagger from wine and reel from strong drink: the priest and the prophet reel from strong drink, they are swallowed up by wine, they stagger because of strong drink. They go astray in vision, they stumble when they judge.

The explanation says that the spiritual leaders of Judah, the priest and the prophet, drank so much wine and cider (a fermented drink, usually made from apples or other fruit) that they were unsteady on their feet and confused. Their confusion is described as losing sound judgment. That is why they failed in their vision, that is, in receiving and passing on the word of God, and why they stumbled in judgment, that is, when deciding just cases.

Speaking on God's behalf, Isaiah had announced that God would be a crown for the faithful. Now, in a sharp contrast, he denounces the leaders of Jerusalem, who were meant to guide the people with clarity. Their disorderly way of life left them unable to teach or to judge. The verses that follow show how repugnant their condition was.

For today: be careful about what clouds your mind, because whoever guides, advises, or decides for others needs to be sober and attentive to God.
exp.27:9:
It says that the teaching comes repeated and in small portions: one command after another, one line after another, a little here and a little there.

Isaiah speaks to priests and prophets who were drunk and who mocked his message. Many think this verse mimics their mockery, as if they treated Isaiah like a teacher speaking to infants. Others read it as a description of God's own teaching. It is not certain which reading is correct. In any case, since they would not listen, God would speak to them in a foreign tongue, probably through invaders.

Today: do not despise what is simple or repeated. Read a short passage each day, practice it, and return to it. In this way faith grows, little by little.
exp.27:12:
It says that the word of God, for this people, becomes teaching that is repeated: precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little. But they, instead of learning, stumble, fall backward, are broken and snared and taken.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Judah who mocked his message. God had offered them rest, but they would not listen. They trusted in covenants with death and in lies. Many think the repetitive tone imitates how they mocked the teachings, as if they were for children. Some also see it as a judgment: if they do not listen, that word will make them stumble.

For today: do not despise the simple or repeated teaching of the Bible. Listen to it with humility every day, because God often shapes us little by little.
exp.27:14:
They said the rulers of Jerusalem felt secure. They claimed to have made a covenant with death and an agreement with the grave, meaning they believed the punishment would not reach them. The overflowing scourge is a destructive storm or flood. Their refuge, they said, was a lie and falsehood.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God, addressing the mocking leaders of Jerusalem. With irony, he quotes what they themselves were saying. Many believe this refers to political alliances, perhaps with Egypt, to protect themselves from Assyria, although the text does not name it here. God then responds with a firm stone in Zion and with just judgment.

For today: examine what refuge you trust. Money, appearances, or a comfortable lie do not withstand the storm. Seek your security in God and in his truth, which does remain firm.
exp.27:16:
God says he will measure judgment and righteousness with a cord and a level, as a builder does to see whether a wall is straight. Then the hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters will flood the hiding place. "Refuge" is the meaning of the word rendered as "refuge of lies," and a "hiding place" is a place to hide.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. The leaders of Judah felt secure and said they had made a covenant with death, meaning that nothing would happen to them. They trusted in deceptions and false alliances. God answers them that he has placed in Zion a firm stone, and that his own rod of justice will reveal what is crooked.

For today: examine what you are leaning on. If your security rests on excuses, appearances, or lies, it will not withstand the storm. Seek the truth and trust in God, who is a firm foundation.
exp.27:17:
The explanation says that the agreement the leaders of Jerusalem believed they had with death and the grave will be annulled. They thought they were safe, but that will not be so. "Covenant" and "agreement" both mean pact. A "scourge" is a punishment that comes like an overflowing flood.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to rulers who mocked his warnings. In verse 15 they said they had made a pact with death and were taking refuge in a lie. Many think this refers to political alliances, perhaps with Egypt, but the text does not say so precisely. God offers them, as the alternative, the firm stone that He places in Zion.
