Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, in influence, or in excuses. Every false refuge collapses. Trusting in God is the only foundation that does not move.
exp.27:20:
He says that God will rise up to act, as he did at mount Perazim and in the valley of Gibeon. In both places God fought on behalf of his people against their enemies (2 Samuel 5:20; Joshua 10:10-12). Here, however, his judgment will come against his own people. That is why he calls his work "strange": it is not what he most delights in, but it is necessary.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the proud leaders of Judah, who mocked his warnings and trusted in political alliances to protect themselves. God warns them that the judgment is real and that their false refuges will not cover them, like a bed that is too short.

Today, mockery in the face of God's correction hardens the heart. If God points something out to you, listen to it soon and return to him with humility, because his correction seeks to restore you.
exp.27:21:
Now therefore, do not keep mocking, or your chains will grow tighter. He says that they should stop mocking God and his warning, so that their bonds will not be made stronger. The bonds are the chains of punishment that were already threatening them. Complete and determined destruction is what the phrase about consummation and end means. The prophet states that he heard this directly from the Lord, the LORD of hosts, that is, the God of the armies of heaven.

Isaiah speaks to the rulers of Jerusalem, who were mocking his warnings and trusting in political alliances to protect themselves. The preceding text recalls God's past victories at Perazim and Gibeon, but now his strange work would be to act against his own people. Scholars debate historical details, but the message is clear: mockery would not save them.

For today: when the Bible or our conscience corrects us, let us not take it as a joke. Let us listen with humility and change in time, because God corrects in order to rescue.
exp.27:24:
He says that the farmer, once he has leveled the ground, plants each seed with care. The fitches are a plant with aromatic seeds, similar to cumin. Each crop goes in its place: the wheat in rows, the barley in its marked spot, and the rye (or spelt, it is not known for certain) at its edge.

Isaiah speaks to the proud leaders of Israel and Judah who did not want to hear his warning. He uses the example of the field to show that the farmer does not act without order or without limit. The verses that follow say that God taught him. Thus, God also works with wisdom and measure when he corrects his people.

For today: trust that God knows what he is doing with you. If you go through a difficult time, it is not by chance or without limit. Ask him for wisdom and obey him with patience.
exp.27:25:
The explanation says that the farmer knows what to do at each step because God himself instructs him. The verse points to doing things with good judgment, sound sense, and in the right order. God teaches the farmer how to do his work properly.

Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Judah who mocked his warnings and trusted in their own alliances. He uses the example of the farmer to show that God does not act without measure: just as the plowman does not plow or thresh forever, God corrects with purpose and with limits. Some believe this speaks of God's discipline over his people.

For today: when you go through a trial, trust that God works with wisdom and not without meaning. Ask him for the wisdom you need for each task and each season.
exp.27:26:
Says that not all seeds are beaten the same way. The fitches (a small plant with delicate seeds) and the cummin (another aromatic seed) are not threshed with the heavy threshing instrument nor with the cart wheel. The fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod, that is, a gentler blow.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had become hardened and mocked God's correction. He uses the example of the farmer, who knows what to do at each sowing and harvest, because God teaches him. In the same way, God also knows how to treat his people with wisdom. Scholars understand that he is speaking of divine discipline, measured and purposeful.

For today: when God corrects you or you go through trials, trust that it is not harshness without meaning. He knows your strength and treats you with wisdom. And with others, correct with measure and not with more severity than necessary.
exp.27:27:
The explanation says that the farmer threshes the bread grain (wheat), but does not do it without stopping. He does not keep crushing it over and over with the wheel of his cart, nor break it apart with the teeth of the threshing sledge, which was an instrument with sharp edges or stones used to separate the grain from the straw.

Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Judah, who felt secure and mocked his warning. He uses the example of the farmer, whom God himself instructs, to show that God corrects with measure and purpose. Many understand that this refers to God's judgment on his people: it is serious, but it does not seek to destroy. The text gives no further detail.

For today: when you go through a trial or correction, remember that God knows how much pressure is necessary. Trust his wisdom and allow yourself to be shaped, without despairing.
exp.27:28:
This verse says that the farmer's wisdom is not his own but comes from God. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" is a title for God that stresses his power and authority. "Counsel" means plan or way of acting, and "wonderful" means admirable. The small-seeded plant and the heavy threshing tool are farming items used to separate the grain.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who felt secure and did not want to hear God's warning. Earlier, the prophet describes how a farmer treats each seed according to its need: with gentleness or with more force. In this way he teaches that God also works with wisdom, and that his correction has a purpose and a limit.

For today: when you go through a trial, remember that God does not act at random. Trust that his dealings with you are wise, and ask him to teach you what he wants to form in you.
exp.28:2:
Here God says he will surround Jerusalem with an enemy army. The phrase for pitching camp is what it means to set up camp around a city; the siege engines are war machines used to attack it; and the siege ramps are towers or earthen mounds raised to assault the walls.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The city is named here as Ariel, a name for Jerusalem, and the text links it to David and to the sacrifices of the temple. Its exact meaning is debated. The people kept up their ceremonies, but without a sincere heart, and God warns that he will bring them low. Many believe this refers to the Assyrian siege, though it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: it is not enough to perform rituals or religious customs if the heart is far from God. We can honestly ask ourselves whether our faith is real or only routine. God corrects us to wake us up, and we can always return to him with humility.
exp.28:6:
The explanation says that all the nations that gather to attack Ariel (another name for Jerusalem) will vanish like a dream of the night, which fades away when one wakes up. The siege engines and weapons of attack, and the encirclement that leaves her distressed and with no way out, are what the verse refers to when it speaks of her munition and her distress.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Jerusalem, a city that felt secure but lived with a shallow faith. God announces that he will first correct her, and then rescue her from her enemies suddenly. Scholars debate the exact moment he has in mind, perhaps the time of King Hezekiah and the threat from Assyria, though some also see a broader scope.

For today: when a problem seems enormous and threatening, remember that God is greater. Give him your fear in prayer and trust that he can undo what weighs on you today.
exp.28:12:
It says the people come close to God with words and praise, but their heart is far from Him. Their respect toward God no longer comes from loving Him, but is a rule learned from people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at a time when Jerusalem lived with a religion that was only for show, while it trusted in its own plans and alliances. The verses before show that the people did not understand what God was saying, like someone holding a sealed book. Then God announces that He will act and will put human wisdom to shame.

For today: before you sing, pray, or go to church, ask God to examine your heart. Let your worship be sincere, and let your obedience come from loving Him, not just from habit.
exp.28:13:
God says that he will once again astonish his people with a great and amazing work. The result is that the wisdom of the wise men will perish and the understanding of the prudent men will vanish, that is, it will disappear or become worthless.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah, in Jerusalem. They practiced a religion of the lips, with fine words but with their hearts far away, following human rules. In addition, they trusted in their own plans and tried to hide them from God. For this reason he shows them that human intelligence cannot hide anything from him or take his place. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 1:19.

Today, examine whether your faith is only a habit or whether it comes from the heart. Before making a decision, pray and ask for God's guidance, instead of relying only on your own judgment.
exp.28:16:
What it says: Isaiah asks whether it is not yet a very little while before Lebanon, a place of thick forests, is turned into a fertile field (Carmel), and before Carmel, already fertile, is regarded as a forest. Being turned means being changed, and being regarded means being considered. It is a picture of great change: what once looked one way will be seen another way.

Context: The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Earlier he rebuked those who pretended to obey God and made their plans in secret, as if God did not see them. Afterward he promises that the deaf will hear and the humble will rejoice. Interpreters differ: some see here a future restoration, others a reversal of values, where the proud fall and the humble are lifted up.

For today: God can transform situations that seem unchangeable. We can stop hiding things from Him, trust Him with humility, and wait for His work, even when today we see little change.
exp.28:18:
God says that, when he acts, humble and needy people will be filled with a joy that keeps growing. The phrase about joy increasing means their gladness will become greater and greater. The most needy among people are the ones meant here, and the Holy One of Israel is a title for God, the only one who is perfect and set apart from evil.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people with proud leaders and a religion that is only on the lips. First, the prophet announces a surprising change: the deaf will hear and the blind will see. Then he promises that the violent and the mockers will fall. Scholars debate whether all of this was fulfilled in Isaiah's own time, in Christ, or also in the future.

For today: if you feel small or lacking, you do not have to wait until everything is settled before you can rejoice. Today you can draw near to God with simplicity and look to Him for your joy.
exp.28:20:
This verse describes those who will be removed when God brings justice: people who used their words to make others guilty, who set traps for the one who corrected them in court, and who twisted what was right with empty arguments. The gate was the public place where the elders judged. The phrase about turning aside the just with worthless reasons means that they denied justice to the innocent with arguments that had no value.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. He announces that God will put an end to the oppression of the corrupt leaders in Judah, and that the humble and the poor will rejoice. Then God promises that his people will not be put to shame.

For today: let us guard our words and not attack the one who corrects us with sincerity. If something troubles us, let us seek truth and justice, and honestly defend those who have no voice.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that God, who saved Abraham, makes a promise to the family of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel: they will no longer suffer shame, nor will their faces turn pale with fear. The word "redeemed" means that God rescued them and set them apart for himself.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he announces the end of the violent, the mockers, and those who twisted justice at the city gates, where judgment was made. Then he promises that the children of Israel will recognize God as holy, and that those who have gone astray will learn. It is a promise of restoration. Scholars debate exactly when it is fulfilled: whether in the return from exile, in future times, or in both.

For today: if you place your trust in God, who has been faithful generation after generation, you can face your fears with hope. Ask him today to give you calm and to help you live with honesty.
exp.28:22:
Isaiah says that Jacob will see his children, whom God calls "the work of my hands," living among his people. They will honor God's name, that is, they will treat him as holy and set apart. Here "sanctify" means recognizing God as sacred. The reverence the verse describes is not fear in the sense of being frightened, but deep respect shown toward him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he spoke of unjust people who accused others with lies and persecuted those who corrected them at the gate, which was the place where judgments were made. Now God promises to restore his people so that they will no longer be ashamed. Scholars debate when this is fulfilled; many see it in the return from exile and also in a future time.

For today: God continues to work in his people with patience. We can trust that he corrects and renews, and respond by honoring him with sincere respect in what we say and do.
exp.28:23:
They who went astray in their thinking and in their way of living will come to understanding with wisdom. Those who complained and criticized will also learn to receive correct teaching. Those whose hearts or minds have wandered away from the truth are the ones who went astray in spirit. People who grumble under their breath, especially against God or against their leaders, are the ones who murmur.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In this chapter he rebukes a people whose hearts are far from him, but now he promises restoration. God will give Israel children who honor his name and fear him. Some understand this promise as hope for Israel in its own time, while others also see a greater fulfillment in the future. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: if you have been complaining or confused, do not stay there. God keeps teaching those who allow themselves to be corrected. Ask him for humility to listen to his Word and to change your attitude.
exp.29:2:
The explanation says that the protection Judah was looking for in Pharaoh would not help them. On the contrary, what they saw as a secure strength would end up bringing them shame. The word "refuge" here means protection or shelter, and the shame of being let down is what the passage is describing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The leaders of Judah, threatened by a neighboring power, sent envoys to Egypt to ask for military help, without consulting God. Many understand that the threat came from Assyria. God rebukes them because they chose to trust in a human power and not in Him.

It is easy to look first for a human solution and leave God for last. Using the resources we have is not wrong, but it is wrong to place in them the trust that belongs only to God. Before deciding something important, pray, seek His guidance in the Bible, and ask for wise counsel.
exp.29:3:
This verse describes the leaders of Judah and their messengers, who have already arrived in Egypt. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities, and there the princes (leaders) and ambassadors (envoys) were seeking an alliance with Pharaoh. Some scholars doubt exactly where Hanes was located, but all agree that it was a place in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was threatened by Assyria, and instead of seeking God, its leaders looked for military protection in Egypt. God warns them that this help will bring them shame and will not do them any good.

Today, when we are afraid, it is easy to rush first to our own solutions. Before deciding, let us ask God for direction in prayer and seek his Word. We may use the resources we have, but without placing our final trust in them.
exp.29:5:
It says that Judah sends a caravan loaded with riches toward Egypt, the south. To get there, it crosses a dangerous desert full of lions, vipers, and swift poisonous snakes. They carry the treasure on donkeys and camels, but the people they are taking it to will be of no use to them.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The leaders of Judah, threatened by Assyria, were seeking a secret alliance with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities. God warns them that they will pay a high price for help that will do them no good.

For today: when we are afraid, let us not spend the best of ourselves on solutions that promise much but cannot sustain us. First let us turn to God in prayer, and then use wisely the means He gives us.
exp.29:13:
It says God will break this sin and those who lean on it, the way a clay pot is broken: without pity, and into pieces so small that none of them is any use. Small fragments are tiny bits of broken pottery. A shard is a piece of baked clay. Not even one fragment is good for carrying coals from the fire or for drawing water from a well.

The Holy One of Israel speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah had rejected his word and trusted in violence, injustice and political alliances, probably seeking help from Egypt, as the chapter suggests. God warns that this false security will suddenly collapse. He then reminds them that their strength lay in quietness and in trusting Him, but they refused.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are resting our security on: money, influence or our own plans. In humility, let us ask God to teach us to rest in Him and to obey His word before what we hold on to breaks.
exp.29:18:
The explanation says that God's people will once again live in peace in Zion, in Jerusalem. There will be no more weeping, because God, who is compassionate, will show pity to them. When they cry out to Him, He will answer them right away. The word "dwell" in the verse above is the key idea here: it means to live and remain in a place.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to a people who, instead of trusting Him, were looking for protection in Egypt against their enemies. He warns them that consequences will come, but he also promises that God waits patiently to show them mercy. Some think the promise points to relief in the near future, and others think it also points to a fuller restoration to come.

For today: when you feel afflicted or have strayed from the right path, you do not have to hide or solve everything on your own. Cry out to God sincerely. He listens, He has compassion, and He still guides those who return to Him.
exp.29:22:
It says that when the people turn back to God, he will send rain on the land that has been sown. There will be bread from the produce of the earth, and it will be rich and full of substance. The animals will graze in peace in wide pastures, that is, broad meadows. The sown land is the field that has been planted.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, the prophet announces that God will guide them with his voice and that they will abandon their idols of silver and gold. The promise is one of forgiveness and restoration after repentance. Scholars understand these blessings as a picture of real provision, and some also see a broader future hope.

For today: when you have gone astray, returning to God is not a loss but a receiving of care. Place today in his hands a worry about money or provision, and leave behind any false security that steals your peace.
exp.29:23:
The oxen and the young donkeys that work the ground will eat fodder of very good quality. It is clean grain, winnowed with the shovel and the fan, that is, separated from the chaff with tools that clean it. It is choice food, not leftovers.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who had sought help in Egypt and in idols instead of trusting in Him. This passage describes what will come if they turn back to God: they will abandon their idols, and there will be rain, abundance, and healing. Scholars read it as a promise of near restoration and also as a foreshadowing of future blessings.

For today: God cares even for the small details of our lives. If we set aside what has taken His place and trust in Him, we can wait in peace for Him to provide.
exp.29:24:
It says that upon the lofty mountains and the high hills there will be rivers and streams of water. This will happen in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. A raised hill is a high ridge, and the towers may stand for strongholds or for human pride.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting God. He announces that God will judge the proud, but also that He will restore His people with abundant blessing. Scholars disagree about whether the day of the great slaughter refers to the fall of Assyria, to a future judgment, or to both. The text joins judgment and blessing in one moment.

For today: God can bring life where we least expect it, even in hard times. Trust in Him and not in your own towers, such as money, status, or human plans. He knows how to care for His people.
exp.29:26:
It says that God draws near from far away, like a judge coming to act. The reference to his anger against evil comes through in the phrase about his face burning with it. His weight is hard to bear, and his lips and tongue, like a consuming fire, speak words of judgment that cannot be stopped.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was looking for help in Egypt instead of trusting God. The passage announces judgment on the nations, probably Assyria according to many interpreters, and at the same time comfort for God's people. The same God who punishes pride also heals his people's brokenness.

For today: do not take God's holiness lightly, but do not forget his care. When you face an unjust situation or feel wounded, trust that God sees, judges with justice, and knows how to heal. Go to him instead of looking for easy ways out.
exp.29:27:
This verse describes God's judgment with powerful images. His breath is like an overflowing river that rises up to the neck. Sifting with a sieve means shaking and separating, the way grain is sifted. The bridle in the jaws is like the one put on a horse to lead it where it does not want to go; here it causes the peoples to turn aside.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Assyria was the threat. The text promises that God will heal his people and judge the nations that oppress them. Scholars debate how this is fulfilled in detail, but the central message is clear: God rules over all peoples.

Today we can rest in the fact that God is just and in control. When we feel fear or injustice, instead of depending only on human resources, we can pray and trust in Him.
exp.29:30:
This verse says that Assyria, which struck others with a rod, that is, with force and violence, will be destroyed by the voice of God. The name for Assyria here is the old form of the word, which is rendered in English as Assyrian, the great enemy empire of that time. The word for being broken means broken into pieces, defeated completely.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was afraid of Assyria and looked for help from Egypt instead of trusting in God. For this reason he reminds them that God is the one who has real power. Earlier, Isaiah speaks of songs of joy for God's people; afterward, he speaks of judgment on Assyria. Scholars debate which exact historical event is in view, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel that someone or something stronger than you is oppressing you, do not place your hope only in human solutions. Pray and trust that God has the last word over all injustice.
exp.30:0:
God laments the attitude of those who go down to Egypt seeking help. They place their trust in horses, chariots, and horsemen, because there are many of them and they are strong. But they did not look to the Holy One of Israel, nor did they seek the Lord. The word for horsemen here means riders, soldiers on horseback.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks in a time of threat from Assyria. Judah's leaders were seeking a military alliance with Egypt instead of trusting in God. Historians agree that it was a time of great political pressure. Isaiah reminds them that Egypt is only human, not God, and that God is wise and keeps his word.

Today we can trust more in our resources, contacts, or plans than in God. Planning is not wrong, but the question is: to whom do I turn first? Before seeking human solutions, let us pause to pray and seek God sincerely.
exp.30:3:
Isaiah says that the Lord spoke to him in an image: a lion roaring over its prey, which is not frightened even when a group of shepherds comes shouting against it. A group of men is the company of shepherds, and the uproar of many voices is the noise they make. In the same way, God will come down to fight for Mount Zion, which is Jerusalem, and for its hill, that is, the height on which the city stands.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. They were looking for help in Egypt, with its horses and chariots, instead of trusting in God. The prophet reminds them that the Egyptians are only men. There are different views on whether the lion here shows God protecting Jerusalem or also his firmness toward it; the context that follows favors the idea of protection.

For today: when you feel pressure and want to lean only on human resources, remember that God is not intimidated. Do what you can with wisdom, but place your trust in Him.
exp.30:8:
It says that Assyria, the mighty empire, will lose its strength through fear. Its stronghold (its rock or place of refuge) will pass away in terror, and its leaders will be struck with dread at the banner (the sign of war). The Lord declares all this, the one whose fire and furnace are in Zion and Jerusalem, that is, his presence that judges and purifies.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking military help in Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. The prophet promises them that God himself will defend Jerusalem and defeat Assyria, without any need for human armies. Some understand the fire and the furnace as protection, and others as judgment; perhaps it includes both.

Today we can remember that no power or problem is greater than God. When you feel fear, or the temptation to rely only on human resources, pray and trust first in the One who cares for his people.
exp.31:1:
This verse says that the righteous king will be like a shelter for his people. He is like a place where a person hides from the strong wind, a refuge from the storm, fresh water in the desert, and the shadow of a great rock when the sun beats down. A hiding place from the wind is a shelter, and a covert from the tempest is a refuge from the storm.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived in fear and injustice because of wicked leaders and threats from other nations. He announces a king who will rule with justice. Many Christians see here a sign of Jesus, the Messiah; others think it first refers to a king like Hezekiah. It can be read in both ways.

For today: when you are tired or afraid, turn to Christ in prayer, and at the same time try to be a refuge for others: listen, help, and treat with justice and tenderness anyone who needs it.
exp.31:4:
This verse says that a time is coming when things will be seen as they really are. The stingy person, the one with a small heart, will no longer be given the reputation of being openhearted, a word that here means generous and noble. And the one who clings tightly to what he has will not be called bountiful either.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a promise about a righteous king (Isaiah 32:1). Under that reign, people regain their sight, their hearing, and their understanding. The verses that follow explain that the selfish person shows himself by his actions: he leaves the needy hungry and harms the poor.

For today: do not be impressed by appearances or by reputation. Look at how someone treats the weak. And examine your own heart: ask God to make you truly generous, not just generous in words.
exp.31:5:
The explanation says that the vile person, that is, the one who acts with wickedness and selfishness, speaks and thinks according to what is in his heart. He plans evil, lives without respect for God, and speaks with mockery against the Lord. Furthermore, he leaves the hungry person empty and denies water to the thirsty.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He announces a time when justice will reign, and so people will no longer be confused: the selfish person will not be called generous. This verse shows what the heart of the vile person is really like, and the next one contrasts it with the generous person.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our words and actions reflect a generous heart. One practical way is to help someone with a concrete need this week, such as food or companionship, without expecting anything in return.
exp.31:6:
This verse says that the greedy man (the stingy or wicked person who thinks only of himself) misuses his power. He plans how to deceive the simple, that is, plain and naive people, with clever words. He also uses the courts, or tribunals, to attack the poor and take away what they have.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, in Judah. He is describing the righteous kingdom that will come, and by contrast he shows how fools and wicked people behave. Just before this, he says that the stingy man will no longer be called generous: his actions reveal his heart. Afterward, the text presents the noble person, who plans to do good.

For today: review how you use your words and your influence. May they never be used to take advantage of someone who has less than you. Use what you know and what you have to help with honesty.
exp.31:11:
This verse describes a time of mourning. The people will beat their chests, showing grief, over the fields that once brought them joy and over the vine that bore good fruit. The phrase about the pleasant fields refers to fields that were lovely and agreeable.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the comfortable and self-assured women of Jerusalem. They were living at ease, without thinking about the consequences of their spiritual neglect. The prophet announces that the harvest will fail and a great loss is coming. Some understand the beating of the chest as a gesture of mourning; others render the phrase differently, but the general sense is the same: deep sorrow.

For today: comfort can give us a false sense of security. It is wise to examine whether we trust in what we have more than in God, and to return to him with humility before loss forces us to do so.
exp.31:12:
It says that the land of God's people, which once gave harvests, will be filled with thorns and thistles, that is, weeds that grow where no one tends the field. Even the houses of pleasure and the joyful city will be left deserted. The houses of pleasure were the homes where people enjoyed life in comfort.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the women who are at ease and feel secure, that is, those who live quietly and confident in themselves. He warns them that their false sense of security will come to an end through a coming judgment. Scholars disagree about the exact historical moment, but the message is clear. Still, the passage ends with hope: the Spirit will come from on high, and everything will be restored.

For today: let us not place our security in comfort or in what we have. Let us ask God that his Spirit renew our hearts.
exp.31:15:
It says that when God renews all things, judgment (uprightness, acting with fairness) and righteousness will live in every place: both in the wilderness, a dry and abandoned land, and in the fruitful field, land that is cultivated and fertile. In other words, nothing will be left outside its reach.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. Before this, he announces ruin: empty palaces and cities laid waste because of their sin. But he adds a hope: "until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high." Many Christians see here a promise of God's Spirit; others connect it with the future restoration of the people. Then the text says that righteousness will bring peace and security.

For today: even where you see areas of dryness in your life, family, or work, ask God's Spirit to renew them, and practice righteousness with honesty in small things.
exp.31:17:
This verse promises that God's people will live in a peaceful place, with safe homes and places of rest. A peaceable habitation is a home without fear. Sure dwellings and quiet resting places mean places of calm rest, free from hurry and threat.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name. Just before this, he describes a time when a just king will reign and the Spirit will be poured out from on high (v. 15). There, justice produces peace. Some believe the promise points to the reign of Hezekiah, others to the Messiah and the future. Then comes a warning of judgment against the proud city.

For today: true peace grows where people live with justice and trust in God. Today you can care for honesty at home and at work, and rest by handing your worries over to God.
exp.31:18:
This verse says that when the hail comes, it will fall on the forest, and the city will be completely destroyed or brought low.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. Earlier, he promises a just kingdom, with peace and security for his people. This verse is difficult: some think it announces judgment on the proud (the forest and the city as symbols of power), while others believe it contrasts the judgment outside with the peace of God's people. There is no single certain interpretation. Then the text speaks of blessing for those who sow beside the waters.

For today: do not place your security in what seems strong, such as money or reputation. All of that can fall. Trust in God, whose justice gives a peace that truly lasts.
exp.31:19:
They are blessed who sow beside all waters and let the ox and the donkey roam freely there. "Blessed" means happy or fortunate. The phrase about letting the animals walk through the ground refers to allowing livestock to tread on wet land, something done on moist soil, perhaps to sow or to trample the earth. Scholars do not have one single exact explanation for that image.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. The chapter announces a time of justice, of the Spirit poured out, and of peace for God's people, after judgment. This verse closes the promise with a scene of calm and fruitful work, where the land yields its harvest without threat.

For today: work with hope and generosity, even when you do not see the fruit right away. Sow kindness, prayer, and honest labor, trusting that God cares for what you do in his name.
exp.32:3:
It says that the plunder the enemy left behind will be gathered up, like when caterpillars strip a field. The people will rush over it, back and forth, like locusts. The words about the spoil and what was taken are explained by the verse itself: the spoil is what is taken in war, and the gathering is simply the collecting or seizing of it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of threat, probably when Assyria was pressing against Judah. First he prays to God asking for help, and then he announces that the nations flee before Him. Here he describes how God's people will gather, with great speed and abundance, what the enemy abandoned. Some think the picture is of looting; others, that it describes how the people strip the defeated enemy. The text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel that a problem is bigger than you, go to God with confidence, as Isaiah did. He can turn around what seemed like a total loss, and your part is to wait on Him and give thanks.
exp.32:7:
The highways lie empty, and no traveler walks them anymore. Someone has broken the agreement, looked down on the cities, and shown no respect for anyone. The word for the great roads is one the verse itself doesn't use, so the explanation's note on it can be dropped, and the phrase about the agreement being annulled simply means that an agreement was broken.

The prophet Isaiah describes a time when Assyria threatened Judah, when King Sennacherib invaded the land. The messengers of peace weep because their efforts to make a treaty were ignored. Many understand that the one who broke the covenant was the invader; others see it in a more general way. After this picture of ruin, God himself says that he will rise up.

When everything seems abandoned and broken, do not place your hope in human promises, which can fail. Trust in God, who remains faithful and acts in his own time. Today you can pray about the situation that worries you and rest in him.
exp.32:8:
The earth mourns and grows weak. Lebanon, famous for its cedars, is put to shame and cut down. Sharon, a fertile plain, looks like a wilderness. Bashan and Carmel, known for their pastures and trees, are shaken, that is, left without leaves.

Isaiah speaks in a time of threat from Assyria. The treaties were broken, the roads stood empty, and even the messengers of peace were weeping. Many understand that the land reflects the consequences of violence and of trusting in human alliances. Interpreters explain it in several ways, but the picture is clear: without God, everything withers.

For today: when everything around you seems to be drying up, do not place your security in human promises. Bring your anxiety to God, who remains the Lord, and listen to his voice.
exp.32:14:
This verse describes the person who can live near God. He walks in righteousness and speaks with truth. He turns away from money gained through violence. He shakes his hands so as not to accept bribes, which are payments meant to corrupt judgment. He stops his ears from hearing plans of violence or bloodshed, and he closes his eyes so as not to look on evil with pleasure.

Isaiah writes in a time of threat for Judah. God has shown his power, and the hypocrites in Zion tremble. Then the question arises: who can stand before a holy God, compared to a consuming fire? This verse and the next answer: the one who lives with integrity will receive protection, food, and will see the King.

For today: practice integrity in small things. Refuse an unfair advantage, do not repeat harmful gossip, and turn your gaze away from what pushes you toward wrong. In this way your life shows that you want to be close to God.
exp.32:16:
This verse promises that those who have remained faithful will see the King in all his beauty, and they will also look out over a wide and distant land. "Beauty" speaks of his glory and splendor. The phrase about a distant land can be understood as an expansive territory free from threats, or as a faraway place that has been promised. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah at a time of threat from Assyria. Before this, he describes the righteous person who will live securely. Afterward, the people will remember with relief the fear they once knew, when foreign invaders were besieging them. Many see God or a just king in view here, and Christians also see Christ.

Today, when fear or injustice weighs heavily on us, we can live with integrity and keep our eyes fixed on God, trusting that He has the final word.
exp.32:19:
Isaiah tells the people to look upon Zion, the city where the feasts of the LORD were celebrated. There they will see Jerusalem as a place of rest and peace, compared to a sturdy tent: its tent pegs will never be pulled up, and its cords will never be broken.

Isaiah speaks to Judah at a time when Assyria was threatening and fear was great. Before this, the people remember with dread the foreign officials who counted and collected tribute. Afterward, the prophet explains the reason for this security: the LORD is judge, lawgiver, King, and Savior. The promise rests on God, not on the walls.

For today: when you lack stability, do not place your peace in things that can be broken, such as work, money, or plans. Take a moment today to pray and remember that God is your King and your firm refuge.
exp.32:20:
In Zion, the Lord himself will be our strength and our protection, as if the city were surrounded by wide rivers and streams. But those rivers cannot be crossed by a rowed vessel, nor by a great ship. That is to say, the enemies will not be able to come near.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of foreign threat. Jerusalem had no great river to protect it, so the image is symbolic: God is a better defense than any wall or river. The verses that follow confirm this: the Lord is judge, lawgiver, and King, and he will save.

For today: when you feel fear or lack resources, remember that your security does not depend on your own defenses, but on God. Pray, trust in him, and walk with peace.
exp.32:21:
This verse says that God fills three roles for his people: he is our judge, the one who decides with justice; our lawgiver, the one who gives the laws for living well; and our king, the one who rules with authority. For that reason it concludes that he himself will save us. The word "lawgiver" refers to the one who establishes the laws.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived threatened by foreign powers. Before this verse, he describes Jerusalem as a secure city, like a firm tent whose stakes are never pulled up. Afterward, he compares the enemies to a poorly built ship that sinks. God is the one who gives the victory and forgives sin.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember that God is not merely a distant helper. He guides, corrects, and rules with justice. You can entrust your decisions to him and trust that he sustains you.
exp.33:0:
God says he calls all the nations to come near and listen. The word for "come near" means the same as the verse's "come near," and "listen" means to pay close attention. The phrase about what fills the earth refers to everything that is in it, that is, the living beings on the earth. The phrase about what the world produces refers to everything the world brings forth. It is a summons to all of creation, as in a court of law.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The verses that follow explain the reason: the Lord is going to judge the nations for their wickedness. This chapter uses very strong and poetic language. Many understand that the mention of Edom, later on, is an example of that universal judgment.

Today we can take seriously what God says, without thinking it does not concern us. Before speaking or defending ourselves, we can pause and listen to his voice in the Bible with humility, and let it correct us and draw us closer to him.
exp.33:2:
They say that the bodies of the dead will be thrown out, unburied, and that the stench of the corpses will rise up. The text also says that the mountains will be melted, that is, they will dissolve and their soil will be washed away, because of so much blood spilled.

The one speaking is God through the prophet Isaiah. He calls all the nations to listen, because God is angry with them and hands them over to judgment. It is poetic and very intense language. At the end of the chapter the judgment focuses on Edom, though some scholars see here also an image of the final judgment. Interpreters debate how much of this is historical and how much is symbolic.

For today: this text reminds us that God takes injustice seriously and that no one escapes giving an account to him. That should move us to live with humility, to seek his forgiveness, and to trust that he will do justice in the end.
exp.33:5:
This verse uses the image of a sacrifice to speak of God's judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood and with fat, like the animals offered on the altar: lambs, goats and rams. The word "fat" here simply means the fat of the animals. The city of Bozrah was an important city of Edom, and "slaughter" refers to a great destruction.

Isaiah announces God's judgment against the nations, and here he focuses on Edom, a neighbor of Israel and a frequent enemy of his people. The animals are a poetic picture of Edom's fall. The passage speaks of vengeance and of the cause of Zion, that is, God defends his people and sets right the injustice done to them.

For today: God does not ignore the evil and suffering of his people. We can rest in the fact that he will do justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. And his holiness invites us to live with humility and to repent in time.
exp.33:9:
It says that the fire and smoke of judgment against that land will not stop. The image is of a place destroyed forever, where no one will ever pass through again or live.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter announces judgment on the nations, and especially on Edom, which here stands as an example of those who oppose God and his people. The case of Zion shows that God defends his own and does justice. The images of pitch and sulfur recall Sodom. Many understand them as poetic and prophetic language, not as a literal description.

For today: God takes justice seriously, and evil will not have the last word. This invites us not to take revenge ourselves, but to trust him, and to live with humility and reverence, seeking his mercy while there is still time.
exp.33:16:
God himself divided the land among the birds and wild animals, like one who casts lots and measures out ground with a measuring line. That land will belong to them forever, and they will live there from generation to generation.

Isaiah speaks of God's judgment against Edom, which had been left desolate. Where people once lived, desert creatures would now dwell. The prophet invites readers to examine the book of the LORD to confirm that everything happens just as God said. Some interpreters see in Edom a symbol of all the nations that oppose God.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. We can trust that everything he says comes to pass, and for that reason it is worthwhile to read his Word with seriousness and faith.
exp.34:1:
It will blossom abundantly and be filled with joy and singing. It will receive the glory of Lebanon, known for its cedars, and the splendor of Carmel and Sharon, green and fertile lands. The people will see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who have endured judgment and fear. He announces a promise of restoration: the dry land becomes life, and this shows that God himself is coming to save. The verses that follow call for encouraging the weak. Many understand this as hope for the return from exile; others also see it pointing to the work of Christ.

For today: if you feel dry or weary inside, God can make bloom what seems dead. Trust his promise, and encourage someone today who is discouraged.
exp.34:2:
It says that we should give strength and encouragement to those who are exhausted and weak. The phrase that means to strengthen or encourage is not needed here, and neither is the word that means to make firm or give vigor. Hands that are tired and knees that tremble describe people without strength, who are afraid or discouraged.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to God's people with a message of hope. Before this, he describes a desert that blossoms, an image of the restoration that God promises. Then he says that God himself will come to save. For this reason, this call is directed to those who already believe and who should encourage one another while they wait. Scholars debate the exact moment the prophecy refers to, but the central encouragement is clear.

Today we can look out for someone in our family, church, or work who is tired or worried. A phone call, a prayer together, or a concrete offer of help will remind them that God has not forgotten them.
exp.34:4:
This verse promises that God will heal. The blind will see and the deaf will hear. The word "Then" points to a future time, when God will act to save his people.

Isaiah speaks to a people who are tired and afraid. He asks them to strengthen those who are weak and to tell them not to fear, because God is coming to save them. The chapter uses images of a desert that blooms and of people being healed to describe that restoration. Christians see a partial fulfillment in the miracles of Jesus (Matthew 11:5), though many understand that the complete promise still awaits its fullness.

For today: if you are tired or afraid, remember that God does not forget you. Encourage someone who is weak with a word of hope or with concrete help, and trust that God is still at work and that one day he will restore everything.
exp.34:6:
This verse says that the dry ground, scorched by the sun, will become a pool, and the thirsty land will become springs of water. "Parched ground" is very dry earth, and "springs" are the places where water rises up. Even the place where the jackals used to lie down, wild animals of the desert, will be filled with grass, reeds, and rushes, plants that grow where there is water.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of God, who lived among threats and discouragement. This chapter is a promise of restoration: God will bring healing, joy, and a safe road for the redeemed. Many believe it speaks of the return from exile and also of a greater hope, still in the future. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: if there is an area of your life that feels dry, do not lose hope. God knows how to bring life where it seemed impossible. Pray with confidence and take one small step of faith today.
exp.35:1:
The explanation says that the king of Assyria sent his spokesman, named Rabshakeh, with a great army from the city of Lachish to Jerusalem, where Hezekiah was king. Rabshakeh is not a personal name but probably the title of a high official. He camped beside the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field, that is, where clothes were washed and worked.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sennacherib had already conquered many fortified cities of Judah and was now pressing Jerusalem to surrender. The place mentioned also appears in Isaiah 7:3, when Ahaz received another message from God there. That can remind us that God had already spoken in that place.

For today: when problems seem like giants and surround your life, do not just stand there staring at the threat. Put your trust in God, who remains faithful.
exp.35:3:
Here Rabshakeh, an official of the king of Assyria, speaks to Hezekiah's envoys. He asks them to carry a message: the great king of Assyria wants to know what Judah is relying on to feel secure. Rabshakeh seems to be a title rather than a personal name, and it is usually understood as the chief cupbearer or a high-ranking officer. "Confidence" means security or hope placed in something.

Assyria had invaded Judah and was now threatening Jerusalem. Rabshakeh speaks with pride and wants to discourage the people. His question aims to show that Judah has nothing to trust in, neither its army nor Egypt.

For today: the question serves to examine us. When pressures come, where does my heart rest? Rabshakeh used it to intimidate, but we can answer it honestly before God, who is worthy of trust.
exp.35:6:
Here the verse says that if the people answer that they trust in the Lord their God, that God would be the same one whose high places and altars Hezekiah had removed. Furthermore, Hezekiah ordered that Judah and Jerusalem worship before only one altar. "High places" are places of worship on the hills.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and make them surrender. He twists what Hezekiah did: that reform aimed to purify worship, but he presents it as if it had offended God. His argument is that of an enemy, not a voice from God.

For today: when someone uses half-truths to sow doubt about your faith, do not let yourself be intimidated. Compare what you hear with the Word of God and keep obeying him, even when others misread your decisions.
exp.35:7:
The Rabshakeh, a messenger sent by the king of Assyria, mocks Jerusalem with sarcasm. Offering to hand over pledges here means making a bet or a deal, and his polite-sounding request is really a taunt. He offers two thousand horses, but he doubts that Judah has enough riders to mount them. The riders are the horsemen.

The Rabshakeh speaks for King Sennacherib around the year 701 BC. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem and wants to discourage Hezekiah and the people so that they will surrender. He stresses that Judah is militarily weak. Although he claims to speak on behalf of the LORD, his words are propaganda, and the biblical account portrays him as a proud man who mocks God.

Today, voices that belittle us often point out our weaknesses so that we will stop trusting God. We can listen calmly, acknowledge our limitations, and still place our trust in God, not in the taunts or in our own strength.
exp.35:10:
Here the three officials of King Hezekiah ask Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, to speak in Syriac (Aramaic), a language they understood, and not in Hebrew. They did not want the people listening from the wall to understand what was being said. The request is that he speak to them in the language they understood and not in the language of the people, in hearing of those on the wall.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Assyrian army. Rabshakeh was trying to spread fear and break the people's trust in God and in Hezekiah. The officials wanted to negotiate in private, but Rabshakeh refused and shouted in Hebrew so that everyone could hear him. His plan was to sow panic.

For today: when words arrive that only aim to frighten and discourage you, do not let yourself be carried away by them. You can ask for wisdom to respond with calm, to guard what you listen to, and to remember that your trust is in God, not in the noise of those who threaten you.
exp.35:12:
Rabshakeh stands up and shouts loudly in Hebrew, the language of Judah, so that everyone can hear him. He calls on them to listen to the words of the great king, the king of Assyria.

Rabshakeh was a senior officer of King Sennacherib, who had Jerusalem under siege. The officials of Hezekiah had asked him to speak in Aramaic so that the people would not understand. He did the opposite: he spoke in Hebrew to frighten the ordinary people on the wall and to take away their trust in their king and in God.

Today too there are loud voices that try to sow fear and doubt about God. Before you let yourself be carried along by them, stop, pray, and remember what God has promised. His voice is more trustworthy than the voice of fear.
exp.35:18:
Here the spokesman of the king of Assyria mocks and asks where the gods of Hamath, Arphad and Sepharvaim are, and whether the gods of Samaria were able to save it.

Speaking is Rabshakeh, envoy of King Sennacherib, before the walls of Jerusalem, in the days of King Hezekiah. He wants the people to lose hope and surrender. He places the LORD on the same list as the idols of other nations, as if He were no different. The Assyrians had indeed conquered those cities, but Rabshakeh overlooks that idols are human handiwork, while the LORD is the living God.

For today: when voices of fear or mockery compare God to anything else, do not become anxious or argue endlessly. Keep silent as the people did, and seek God in prayer, trusting that He is different and faithful.
exp.35:21:
Three officials of King Hezekiah returned to him with their clothes torn. Eliakim was the one in charge of the palace, Shebna the scribe or secretary, and Joah the recorder, that is, the one who kept the records of the kingdom. They told him what Rabshakeh had said, a senior spokesman of the king of Assyria. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief, distress, or horror.

The Assyrians had surrounded Judah, and Rabshakeh was mocking the LORD, saying that no god had saved his people. The officials obeyed the king's order not to answer him. Now they return to report, troubled by the threats and by the insult against God.

For today: when news or pressure overwhelms you, there is no need to pretend to be strong. You can bring your pain honestly before God, as Hezekiah did, who quickly sought the LORD in prayer.
exp.36:6:
God tells King Hezekiah, through Isaiah, that He will put a spirit in the king of Assyria. This means that God will influence his mind or his decisions. That king will hear a rumor, that is, a piece of news, and return to his own land. There he will fall by the sword, that is, by the sword.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by Assyria, and its messengers had mocked God. Hezekiah was distressed, and God calmed him. Afterward, the Assyrian king hears that Tirhakah of Ethiopia is coming to fight against him, as the following account shows.

For today: when you feel fear over a threat that seems bigger than you, hand it over to God in prayer. He can act in ways we do not expect, and He still rules over every situation.
exp.36:7:
This verse tells how Rabshakeh, the officer sent by the king of Assyria, returned from Jerusalem and found his king fighting against the city of Libnah. The king had already left Lachish, another city he had been attacking.

It is part of the account of King Hezekiah and the threat from Assyria. Rabshakeh had insulted God in front of Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah had already said that God would act and that the Assyrian king would hear a report and return to his own land. Here events begin to move, but the outcome is not yet in view. The Assyrians are still sending threats.

For today: when God promises to help you, you will not always see the result right away. Between the promise and its fulfillment there may be new pressures. Trust what God has said and keep praying, as Hezekiah did.
exp.36:9:
Here the king of Assyria sends a message to Hezekiah, king of Judah. He tells him not to let his God deceive him, since that God promised that Jerusalem would not fall into the hands of Assyria. To be deceived means to be made to believe something false, and to be given into the hand of the enemy means that the city would be surrendered to them.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, speaks through messengers. He was at war and had learned that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, was coming to attack him. He wanted to frighten Hezekiah so that he would surrender. With his words he treats God as if he were just one more of the gods of the defeated nations. Later, God would show that this idea was a mistake.

Today there are also voices that tell us that trusting in God is an illusion, especially when problems seem enormous. Like Hezekiah, we can bring those threats to God in prayer and not decide by fear alone.
exp.36:10:
Here the king of Assyria says to Hezekiah: "You know what the Assyrian kings have done to all the countries: they destroyed them completely. Do you think you will be spared?" It is a question meant to frighten and to strip away all hope.

The one speaking is Sennacherib, king of Assyria, through messengers. Jerusalem was under threat. He learns that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, is coming to fight against him, and even so he sends this message to pressure Hezekiah into surrendering. He mocks Judah's trust in God, and he compares the Lord to the gods of other nations.

For today: when threats seem bigger than your faith, do not measure your situation only by what has happened to others. Bring your fear to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and trust that He is greater than any voice that intimidates you.
exp.36:13:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah received a letter from the messengers sent by Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He read it, went up to the temple of the Lord, and spread it out before the Lord, that is, he opened it and laid it in front of God, as if showing it to Him.

The writer describes a moment of crisis. Assyria had conquered many cities and now threatened Jerusalem. The letter mocked God and said that He could not deliver His people, just as the gods of other nations had not saved theirs. Hezekiah did not respond with fear or with a hasty alliance, but by bringing the problem before God.

For today: when news comes that troubles you, a message, a diagnosis, or a debt, before reacting, bring it to God with sincerity. You can lay it out before Him in prayer, tell Him what you feel, and entrust the outcome to Him.
exp.36:14:
This verse says that King Hezekiah, after receiving a threatening letter, began to pray to God. Hezekiah is the name used here, and God is the one he calls on. It is a simple sentence that introduces the prayer that follows.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who is talking about Hezekiah, king of Judah. The Assyrian king Sennacherib had sent messengers with letters that mocked God and demanded surrender. Hezekiah took the letters to the temple, spread them out before the Lord, and prayed. He did not look first for a human solution but for the presence of God.

When you receive news that frightens or overwhelms you, do what Hezekiah did: bring it to God as it really is, with honesty. Before rushing to find solutions or giving in to fear, take a moment to lay everything before Him in prayer.
exp.36:16:
What it says: King Hezekiah asks God to listen and to look carefully. He uses human images: bending down to hear and opening the eyes, like someone who draws near to pay full attention. He asks God to hear the words of Sennacherib, who sent messengers to insult the living God. To blaspheme means to speak with contempt against God.

Context: Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks while the Assyrian army surrounds Jerusalem. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had sent a letter mocking Judah's trust in God. Hezekiah took the letter to the temple, laid it before God, and prayed. He did not ask for help out of pride, but because the honor of God's name was at stake.

For today: When a threat or a mockery overwhelms you, do not carry it alone. Present it to God honestly, as Hezekiah did with his letter. Tell him in detail what you are facing, and trust that he sees and hears.
exp.36:17:
It says that the kings of Assyria did indeed lay waste many nations and their lands. "Countries" refers to the territories around a city or nation. Hezekiah does not deny Assyria's power; he acknowledges it honestly before God.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks here, in prayer within the temple. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was threatening him with a letter, mocking God. Hezekiah presents the actual facts and then recalls that the gods of those nations were made of wood and stone, while the LORD is the living God.

For today: when you face a great problem, there is no need to pretend it does not exist. You can tell God sincerely how serious it is and, at the same time, remind both him and yourself who he is.
exp.36:18:
This verse says that the kings of Assyria threw the gods of the nations they conquered into the fire. Hezekiah explains that those gods were not real gods, but things made by human hands, out of wood and stone. That is why they could be destroyed.

The one speaking is King Hezekiah, in prayer, in the temple. Assyria was threatening Jerusalem, and Sennacherib mocked the God of Israel as if he were just one more of the idols of the nations. Hezekiah acknowledges what the Assyrians did, but he marks the difference: the LORD is the living God, not a human work. That is why he asks him to hear and to act.

For today: when something big threatens you, do not just stare at the size of the problem. Pray as Hezekiah did, remembering who God is. And check where you have placed your trust, because what we build or make with our own hands cannot save us.
exp.36:19:
Here King Hezekiah asks God to rescue him from the power of the king of Assyria. He is asking to be saved from the king's power. He makes this request so that all the nations will know that the Lord, Jehovah, is the only true God.

Hezekiah prays in the temple. Assyria had conquered many countries and burned their idols, and now it threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah recognizes that those gods were only wood and stone, but that Jehovah is different. His request seeks the glory of God, not only his own safety. God answers quickly through the prophet Isaiah.

When you face a big problem, you can pray sincerely and ask God for help. And you can add a deeper desire: that, whatever the outcome, your life will show who God is and honor him.
exp.36:22:
God asks Sennacherib, king of Assyria, pointed questions: whom have you mocked and spoken against, and against whom did you raise your voice with such pride? The words that were used for insulting and speaking with contempt, and the phrase describing a haughty attitude, all point to arrogance. The answer is clear: he did it against the Holy One of Israel, that is, against God himself.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Hezekiah, who had prayed asking for help. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel, believing his army was unbeatable. God answers that these mockeries will not go unnoticed.

For today: when you feel small before a threat or a taunt, pray as Hezekiah did and trust that God sees everything. And remember that human pride, however powerful it may seem, is not above God.
exp.36:26:
They say the people of the conquered cities had lost their strength, were defeated and put to shame. They were as fragile as the grass of the field, as tender green plants, or as the grass that sprouts on rooftops, which dries up quickly because it has no deep root. The phrase about being "before it is grown" means before it has grown up and ripened.

Here God speaks through Isaiah to King Sennacherib of Assyria, who boasted of his conquests and mocked the God of Israel. God answers him that those victories were not his own merit, since God had allowed them from long before. Assyria was only an instrument, and its pride would be judged.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated by powers that seem invincible. God governs history and is greater than any threat. Trust in Him and avoid pride, because everything we have comes from His hand.
exp.36:28:
God tells the king of Assyria that his pride and his rage against Him have risen up to heaven. Therefore He promises to put a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth, the way one controls an animal, and to make him return by the same road he came.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for God here. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah and mocked the God of Israel while threatening Jerusalem. God answers King Hezekiah, who had prayed in distress, and assures him that the invader will not have the final word.

For today: when someone powerful seems to be in control of everything, remember that God is still greater. You can bring your fear to Him in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and trust that He governs even what you cannot control.
exp.36:29:
God gives Judah a sign: this year and the next they will eat what grows on its own, what springs up without being sown. In the third year they will be able to sow, reap the harvest, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Hezekiah. The army of Assyria, under King Sennacherib, threatened Jerusalem and had ruined the fields. God promises to deliver his people and give them back a normal life. Scholars debate the details of those years, but the message is clear: restoration will come.

For today: when you go through a time of scarcity or little progress, trust that God can sustain you step by step. He cares for you today and prepares better times.
exp.36:32:
God promises that the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, will not enter Jerusalem. He will not shoot even one arrow there, he will not approach with shields, and he will not build a siege ramp against the walls.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. Assyria had invaded Judah and threatened to take Jerusalem. Hezekiah had prayed with humility, and God answered with this promise. The verses that follow say that God would defend the city for his own sake and for the sake of David, to whom he had made promises. The text then tells how the Assyrian army withdrew.

For today: when a threat seems bigger than you are, bring the problem to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. He is faithful to his promises, and we can rest in his care, even when we do not always know how or when he will act.
exp.36:34:
It says that God himself will defend Jerusalem and deliver it. The word translated "defend" means to protect, shelter, and care for. God gives two reasons: he does it for his own sake, that is, for his name and his faithfulness, and for the sake of his servant David, because of the promise he made to that king.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. King Hezekiah was terrified because the Assyrian army, led by Sennacherib, surrounded Judah and mocked his God. Hezekiah prayed, and God answered with this promise. Afterward, an angel struck down the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, pray as Hezekiah did and rest in the fact that God is faithful to his promises. Your security does not depend on your own strength but on the character of God.
exp.36:35:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord went out during the night and struck down 185,000 soldiers in the Assyrian camp. When the others got up, they saw only dead bodies.

King Sennacherib of Assyria had surrounded Judah with threats and mocked God. King Hezekiah prayed, and God answered through the prophet Isaiah, promising to defend Jerusalem for his own honor and because of his promise to David. This account also appears in 2 Kings 19. The Bible does not explain how it happened; it only says it was the work of God's angel.

When you find yourself surrounded by a problem that is bigger than you are, do as Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer with sincerity. He can act in ways you cannot imagine, and his faithfulness does not depend on your strength.
exp.37:3:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Isaiah. The word "came" is the old form of the word that the verse uses, so the sentence can be read as plain speech about a message arriving. The phrase "the word of the Lord" means that God himself gave him a message. It is a short phrase, but it marks an important moment: God answers.

Here the narrator speaks, telling what happened. King Hezekiah was seriously ill and had received the news that he would die. He turned his face to the wall, prayed, and wept. God did not delay in answering. Right away he sent Isaiah with a reply: God had heard his prayer and seen his tears.

For today: when you pray sincerely, even weeping and without many words, remember that God hears you. He does not always answer in the same way, but he is always attentive to you and to your need.
exp.37:5:
It says that God promises to save King Hezekiah and Jerusalem from the power of the king of Assyria. "Deliver" means to rescue or bring out of danger, and "defend" means to protect and watch over.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah was very sick, had prayed in tears, and God granted him fifteen more years of life. In addition to that, God renews the promise to defend the city, which was threatened by Assyria. God answers his prayer with personal help and also for his people.

For today: when you face an illness or a threat that overwhelms you, pray sincerely, even with tears. God hears and cares for you. You can trust in his protection, even though he does not always respond in the same way.
exp.37:6:
It says that God will give Hezekiah a sign, that is, a visible proof, that he will fulfill what he promised. "The LORD" is the name of God. The phrase ends with a colon because the sign is explained in the following verse: the shadow on the dial will go back.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, carrying a message from God to King Hezekiah. The king was seriously ill, had prayed weeping, and God promised him fifteen more years of life and protection against Assyria. The sign confirmed that promise. Some think it was a miracle in the sun or in the shadow; the text only says that the shadow went back, and does not explain how it happened.

For today: God hears our prayers and does not despise our tears. When you doubt his promises, remember how he has kept his word before, and trust him simply.
exp.37:8:
This verse is a short introduction. It says that what follows is a writing by King Hezekiah of Judah, made after he had been sick and was recovered. The word "writing" here means a written text, something like a poem or a written prayer.

The context is that Hezekiah was very ill, and God promised him more years of life. As a sign, he made the shadow on the dial of Ahaz go back. The speaker in the verse is the narrator of the book, and then Hezekiah himself speaks. His writing recalls his distress before possible death and his gratitude for having been healed.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not let it pass by. Write down what you lived through, your fears and your gratitude. Writing it will help you remember God's faithfulness and encourage others.
exp.37:14:
He says that Hezekiah cannot find words to describe what he is going through. He acknowledges that God himself was the one who spoke and the one who acted. Then he resolves to go softly, moving slowly and thinking with seriousness, remembering the bitterness of his soul all the years of his life. Some understand that he says this with humility, and others with a sense of solemn reverence.

The speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, after a serious illness. Isaiah had announced that he would die, but he prayed and God added years to his life. This song is his response of gratitude. His suffering has passed, but he does not want to forget what he learned.

For today: when God brings you out of a difficult trial, do not let it lie buried. Write down what you felt and what God did for you. Review that memory from time to time, so that your gratitude and your humility stay alive.
exp.37:20:
Here the text says that Isaiah had already given an instruction to heal King Hezekiah. They were to prepare a lump of figs, that is, figs pressed until they formed a paste, and place it on the boil, which is a sore or inflammation. The promise is that in this way he would recover.

The book presents Hezekiah as very sick, and God adds years to his life after his prayer. This verse seems like a separate detail, placed almost at the end, that explains how the illness was treated. The text does not say exactly what the boil was, so it cannot be specified. Some see here a common remedy of the time used under the word of the prophet.

For today: God can heal, and He can also use simple means, such as medicine or the care of others. Praying and receiving practical help are not opposed; we can trust God and thank Him for both.
exp.37:21:
It says that King Hezekiah had asked what sign he would have that he would go up again to the temple. "Go up to the house of the Lord" means going to worship God in the temple in Jerusalem, which stood on a hill. A "sign" is a visible proof or confirmation. It is a question asking for assurance.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and God promised to heal him and add fifteen years to his life. After his song of thanksgiving, this verse adds a detail: Isaiah had ordered a poultice of figs placed on the sore, and Hezekiah asked for a sign. In 2 Kings 20 it is told that God gave him as a sign that the shadow would go back. Some think the verse is out of its proper place, but that does not change its message.

Asking God for assurance is not always a lack of faith. If you have doubts, bring them to him honestly, and remember that healing and giving thanks lead you into the community of worship.
exp.38:1:
Hezekiah was pleased with the envoys from Babylon and showed them everything he had: the house of his treasures, the silver and the gold, the spices and the precious ointment, and the house of his armour. Nothing was held back.

The text presents this as a fact. Babylon had sent letters and gifts when they learned that Hezekiah had recovered from his illness. Soon after, Isaiah will confront him. Interpreters do not fully agree: some see pride, others a lack of political wisdom or trust placed in resources rather than in God. Later, it would be Babylon that carried those treasures away.

For today: when God blesses us or heals us, it is easy to boast about what we have. It is wise to give glory to God and to be careful about whom we show everything to, and why.
exp.38:2:
Isaiah the prophet comes to King Hezekiah and asks him two questions: what those men said, and where they came from. Hezekiah answers that they came from a far country, from Babylon. Notice that he answers only the second question; he does not say what they had told him or what he showed them.

The messengers of the king of Babylon had come to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery. He was glad and showed them all his treasures and weapons. Isaiah asks as a messenger of God, since he is about to announce a judgment. Some think Hezekiah became proud or sought human support; the text does not explain all his motives.

Today, God invites us to be sincere and to guard our hearts when we receive praise or success. Everything we have is a gift from God; let us give the glory to Him.
exp.38:3:
Here the prophet Isaiah asks King Hezekiah a second question: what things the messengers saw in his palace. Hezekiah answers frankly that he showed them absolutely everything, keeping nothing back. "Treasures" are his riches and stored goods.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The envoys from Babylon had come from far away, and Hezekiah, pleased with their visit, showed them all his wealth and his weapons. The Bible does not detail everything he was thinking, but God's response in the following verse shows that this was a serious mistake: Babylon would later carry off all of that.

For today: it is worth asking ourselves where we place our trust and what we boast about. Everything we have is a gift from God and can pass away. Before others, it is better to give glory to God than to proudly display what we possess.
exp.38:4:
Isaiah tells King Hezekiah to listen carefully to a message that does not come from him, but from God. The title "Lord of hosts" speaks of the Lord as the one who rules over all power, even over kings and nations.

The prophet Isaiah speaks after Hezekiah showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon. Hezekiah saw no problem in doing so.
