Many understand that there was pride or overconfidence in his riches, although the text does not say it in so many words. That is why the prophet confronts him and announces what God will say next.

Today we can learn to listen to the word of God even when it is not pleasant. Everything we have is a gift from Him, and trusting in our possessions instead of trusting in Him puts us at risk. Let us ask Him for humility to receive His correction.
exp.38:5:
Here God announces that a time will come when everything in the palace of Hezekiah, including the riches that his ancestors stored up, will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, delivering a message from the LORD. Hezekiah, king of Judah, had shown all his treasures to Babylonian envoys who visited him. His pride or excessive confidence in human alliances receives a warning here. Babylon was not yet the great power, and the prophecy was fulfilled later, though the historical details are understood in different ways.

For today: what we accumulate is not secure forever. It is wise to receive God's correction with humility, to use what we have with gratitude, and to trust Him more than our possessions or the support of others.
exp.38:6:
God announces through Isaiah that some of King Hezekiah's descendants will be taken away to Babylon. The word "eunuchs" probably refers to servants of the royal court, though some understand that it could also mean they would be made eunuchs.

Isaiah speaks to King Hezekiah after he proudly showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon. The prophet warns him that this nation, which now seems friendly, will one day carry off the riches and also part of his family. Later, the Bible shows that Babylon conquered Judah.

For today: what we boast about or hold onto with pride is not secure forever. It is wise to live with humility, to be thankful for what God gives, and to also think about the good of those who will come after us.
exp.39:1:
God commands that Jerusalem be spoken to tenderly. He announces three things to her: her time of hard struggle or forced service is over, her sin has been pardoned, and she has received double for her sins.

God speaks to his messengers, probably the prophets, to comfort his people. Isaiah looks ahead to the exile in Babylon, when Jerusalem would lie in ruins. The word "double" is understood in several ways: a punishment that is fully sufficient, or a measure equal to her guilt. The verses that follow announce that God himself is coming to his people.

If you carry guilt that has already been forgiven, remember that God does not speak to you with contempt, but with tenderness. Today you can comfort someone with words of hope, and receive God's forgiveness yourself with confidence.
exp.39:3:
This verse describes a road being prepared for the Lord. The valleys are raised up, the mountains and hills are brought low, the crooked is made straight, and the rough places become level. It is the language of preparing a real road for a king to pass.

God comforts Jerusalem: her punishment has been completed and her sin has been forgiven. A voice in the wilderness calls for a way to be opened for Jehovah. Many understand this as speaking of the return from exile in Babylon. The Gospels apply this voice to John the Baptist, who was preparing people for Jesus.

For today: preparing the way for God means removing what gets in the way in the heart, such as pride, bitterness, or hidden sins. Today you can speak to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and set straight one specific thing, such as making peace with someone.
exp.39:4:
It says that God will reveal his glory, that is, his power, his goodness and his presence, in such a clear way that all flesh, that is, all people, will see it together. The word "revealed" means that it will be shown plainly. What it states is certain, because the very mouth of God has spoken it.

Isaiah announces comfort to the people of Israel, who are discouraged and in exile. A voice commands that the way of the Lord be prepared, as when a road is leveled for a king. Christians see in this an announcement of John the Baptist and of the coming of Jesus, as the Gospels do. Afterward the text contrasts human frailty with the firmness of God.

For today: when you feel small or doubt God's promises, remember that his word does not fail. Prepare the way for him with humility, letting him straighten what is crooked in your heart.
exp.39:11:
This verse asks questions to show the greatness of God. It asks who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, who set the heavens in order with the span of a hand, who gathered the dust of the earth in a measure, and who weighed the mountains in scales. The hills are the hills. The answer is: only God.

The prophet Isaiah comforts the people of Israel, who were discouraged and felt that God had forgotten them. Just before this, God appears as a tender shepherd who carries the lambs. Here the same God is presented as the enormous and powerful Creator, so that they may trust in Him.

For today: when your problems seem enormous, remember that the God who holds up the universe also cares for you with tenderness. Give that worry to Him today in prayer.
exp.39:14:
It says that, compared with God, all the nations weigh very little. They are like a drop that falls from a bucket, or like the fine dust that clings to the scale of a balance and that no one takes into account. The islands, distant and great as they seem, are to Him like light dust.

In this chapter, the prophet Isaiah brings comfort to God's people. The verses before ask who could ever have advised or taught the Lord, and the answer is that no one could. God depends on no one. This encourages a people who felt small in the face of powerful empires.

Today, when governments, the news, or the pressure of the world make you feel afraid, remember that God is still greater than all of that. Rest in Him and pray with confidence, without ceasing to act responsibly.
exp.39:15:
It says that not even all the wood of Lebanon would be enough to light the fire for a sacrifice worthy of God, nor would all its animals be enough to offer. Lebanon was famous for its cedar forests and its abundance. Even so, all of that falls short before the greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, discouraged and far from their land. He wants to comfort them by showing them who their God is. Before and after this verse, the nations appear as a drop or as dust, and he asks how anyone could make an image of God. Some understand that it is also stressed that God does not need our offerings.

Today we can remember that we do not draw near to God because of how much we give or do. We can worship him with humility and trust, and rest in the fact that he is greater than our fears.
exp.39:19:
The explanation says that a person of little means, who cannot afford gold or silver for an idol, looks for a wood that will not rot. Then he hires a skilled craftsman to make a carved image that will stay firm and not fall over. Presenting it as an offering to his god is what the source's first quoted phrase refers to, and the second quoted phrase means that it is fixed securely in place.

God speaks through Isaiah to comfort his people, who were or would be in exile, surrounded by idols. With a certain irony, he shows how absurd it is to compare the Creator with something a man makes and must secure so that it does not fall. Right after this, he reminds them who God truly is: the one who stretches out the heavens.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can trust in things that we must hold up ourselves, such as money, success, or our image. Rest better in the God who holds you up.
exp.39:22:
He says that God brings the mighty to nothing, that is, the princes and people of great authority. He also makes the judges or rulers of the earth like something empty, meaning without lasting worth.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who felt small and discouraged before the empires of their time. To comfort them, he reminds them who God is: the Creator who is above the whole earth, before whom the inhabitants are like grasshoppers. Before Him, no king has the final word.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated or dazzled by human power, whether political, economic, or social. Governments and great figures pass away, but God endures. Trust in Him, pray for those who govern, and have peace, because your life is in the hands of the Lord.
exp.39:25:
Isaiah 40:26 tells us to lift up our eyes to the heavens and consider who created the stars. God brings out their whole host and calls each one by name; not one is missing.

The verse's wording for the star-host refers to the stars as a whole, and the phrase about God's great might and strength is rendered as "by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power."

Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who are discouraged and feel that God has forgotten their situation. Earlier in the chapter, the text showed that powerful rulers wither like plants before God. Then the people complain that their way is hidden from the Lord. This verse answers them: the God who knows every star also knows his people.

For today: when you feel forgotten or small, go outside at night, look at the sky, and remember that God sustains everything with care. If not one star is lost, neither is your life lost to him. Bring your worry to him today with confidence.
exp.39:27:
Doesn't this verse ask whether we have not known or heard that the Lord is the everlasting God? He is the one who created the ends of the earth. He never grows tired or weary, and no one can fully grasp his wisdom.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, also called Jacob, who felt forgotten and thought God did not see their suffering. So the prophet reminds them who God is: the Creator who calls the stars by name. Then he promises that he gives strength to the weary.

For today: when you feel exhausted or believe God does not see your situation, remember that he does not grow tired or forget you. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that his wisdom is greater than what you are able to understand.
exp.39:28:
This verse says that God gives strength to the one who is worn out, and that to the one who has no strength left at all, he increases what little remains. "Strength" here means power or courage, and "increases" means he makes it grow greatly. It speaks not only of bodily tiredness, but of the person who feels they can go on no longer.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, comforting the people of Israel, who were discouraged and believed that God no longer saw their situation. That is why, just before, he reminds them that the LORD is eternal, the creator of all things, who never grows weary and whose wisdom is immense. Many scholars think he is addressing the Israelites in exile, although the exact time is debated.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not pretend that you are fine. Tell God honestly that you are tired, and wait on Him with confidence, asking him for help to take the next step.
exp.40:4:
It says that the islands, that is, the distant peoples by the sea, saw what God was doing and were filled with fear. Even the most remote corners of the earth were frightened. Then they gathered together and drew near. The words "ends of the earth" mean the far edges or limits of the world.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that he raises up a conqueror, and many believe this is Cyrus, although the text does not give the name here. God affirms that he directs history. The nations react with fear, and what follows shows that they organize themselves and encourage one another to make idols, instead of seeking the living God.

Today, when the world is stirred up and people look for security in what they make or in mutual support, we can remember that God still governs. Instead of relying only on what is human, we can pray and trust him.
exp.40:14:
God tells his people that he will make them into a new threshing sledge, a heavy tool with sharp edges or teeth that was used to separate the grain from the straw. With it they will crush mountains and hills until they are reduced to chaff, the fine straw that the wind carries away. These are figurative images, not literal ones.

God himself speaks to Israel and calls them a worm because of their weakness and smallness. He tells them not to be afraid because he is their Redeemer. The mountains represent the enemies and obstacles that seem enormous. The strength will not come from Israel, but from God, who holds them by the hand.

For today: when a problem looks like a mountain to you, do not trust your own strength. Bring it to God, who takes you by the hand, and move forward in faith, knowing that he gives you what you need for each step.
exp.40:16:
The explanation says that there are people who are afflicted and poor who desperately seek water and do not find it; their tongues are dry from thirst. The word for "poor and needy" refers to those in need, and "forsake" means to abandon. Facing that distress, God promises to hear them and not leave them alone.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, a small and weak people surrounded by powerful nations. Shortly before, he had called them not to fear and promised them strength to overcome their enemies. Then he announces that he will turn the desert into rivers, springs and trees. The thirst can be understood as a real need and also as an image of their difficult situation.

For today: when you feel dry, tired or without a way out, bring your need to God with sincerity. He hears and promises not to abandon you, even though his answer does not always come as or when we expect it.
exp.40:17:
God says he will make water break out where it seems impossible: rivers on the bare heights, springs in the middle of the valleys, pools where there had been desert, and flowing springs in dry ground.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to his people Israel, who felt weak, poor, and without resources. Just before this, the verse describes the poor and needy who search for water and find none, and God promises to hear them and not forsake them. Water is an image of provision and care. Scholars understand it both as a concrete promise of help and as a picture of renewal.

For today: when you feel dry or without a way out, bring your need to God honestly. He does not ignore the one who is thirsty, and he can supply what you need in ways you did not expect.
exp.40:19:
This verse says that God will do all these wonders so that the people may see, know, pay attention, and understand that it was the hand of the Lord who did it. The word translated "consider" here means to take notice or pay attention. The phrase "created it" means that God made it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were tired and afraid, as if in a desert. God promises to turn dry places into rivers, springs, and forests. Then, in the verses that follow, He challenges the idols to show whether they can do anything similar. Many understand this as a promise of comfort and restoration.

For today: when God helps you in a dry or difficult time, do not credit it only to luck or to your own effort. Stop, recognize His hand, and give thanks to Him out loud. In this way your gratitude will also become a witness to others.
exp.40:21:
Here God challenges the idols and those who worship them. He tells them to bring forward their evidence: to announce what is going to happen and to explain what took place from the beginning.

The Lord, the King of Jacob, speaks as in a courtroom. The nations and their gods of wood or metal are called to defend their case. The challenge is that a true god must know and direct history. Later, God himself will show that he does announce what is coming, and the idols fall silent.

For today: our trust can be placed in many things that promise security, such as money, success, or fashionable opinions. Ask yourself which of them can truly guide you through what is uncertain. Rest in the God who knows the beginning and the end.
exp.40:27:
He says that God looks among the idols and the nations, searching for someone who can explain what is happening or give good counsel, and He finds no one. He asks them, and no one answers even a word. A counsellor is someone who guides with wisdom. None means that there is no one able to answer.

The Lord speaks here in the middle of an imagined trial against the idols and the nations that follow them (Isaiah 41). He challenges them to show that their gods know the past and the future. Since they cannot announce anything, it becomes clear that they are not gods. By contrast, God announced long ago His plans for Zion and Jerusalem, and He promises to send good news.

Today we can ask ourselves what we place our trust in: money, success, opinions, or our own plans. If these cannot give us firm answers or peace, let us return to God, who speaks the truth and does what He promises.
exp.41:0:
God presents his servant and says that he will uphold him. He calls him "my chosen one," in whom he delights, that is, in whom he finds great pleasure. He says that he has put his Spirit upon him, and that he will bring forth judgment to the nations, or in other words, bring justice to the nations.

God himself is speaking here, within the Servant Songs in Isaiah. In the original setting, the people were discouraged and needed hope. Jews have seen Israel in this passage, and others have seen a special individual. Christians, following Matthew 12:18-21, see Jesus here, whose justice is gentle: he does not break the bruised reed or snuff out the smoldering wick.

For today: if God works with tenderness and firmness, we can draw near to him even when we are weak or weary. And in how we treat others, let us seek justice without crushing those who are already broken.
exp.41:1:
This verse says that God's servant will not cry out, nor raise his voice, nor make himself heard with commotion in the squares, which were the public places where people gathered. "Cry out" here means to shout loudly; "make his voice heard" refers to making noise to attract attention.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He presents his chosen servant, whom he upholds and fills with his Spirit, to bring justice to the nations. Many Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the Gospel of Matthew (12:18-21) quotes it this way. The point is that his manner of acting will be humble and gentle, not noisy or proud.

For today: we can serve and bear witness with gentleness, without fighting or seeking applause. Truth does not need shouting; it needs love, patience, and steadfastness.
exp.41:5:
God speaks to his Servant and tells him that he has called him in righteousness, that is, with a right and faithful purpose. He promises to take him by the hand, to care for him and to protect him. He appoints him as a covenant for the people, meaning as someone through whom God joins himself to his people, and as a light for the nations, who are the non-Jewish peoples.

The Lord speaks, the Creator who gives life and breath to all. This passage is one of the Servant songs in Isaiah. Some see it as referring to Israel, and Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus, whom the New Testament calls a light to the nations. God assures him of his support in opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners.

For today: if God calls you to serve, he also promises to sustain you. Walk with confidence, not in your own strength, and let your life bring his light to others.
exp.41:7:
He declares that God presents himself with his proper name: Jehovah, the God of the covenant, who is always faithful. He affirms that he will not share his glory, that is, the honor that belongs to him alone, with anyone else. Nor will he give his praise to carved images, that is, idols made by human hands.

God himself is speaking, addressing Israel, which lived surrounded by idolatrous nations. Just before this, he presents his Servant, who would be a light to the nations and would free the prisoners and those who live in darkness. Many Christians see Jesus in that Servant. God makes clear that only he can accomplish this and that no idol will do it.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts: money, success, or the opinion of others. Let us give God the gratitude and the first place that belong to him.
exp.41:9:
This verse calls everyone to sing a new song to God and to praise him from the farthest places on earth. It asks those who travel the sea, everything that is in it, and also the islands with their people, to sing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he alone is the Lord, that he will not share his glory with idols, and that he announces new things before they happen. That is why the song is "new": it responds to the new thing God is about to do. Many understand it to refer to the Servant of the Lord in the previous passage, although how that is fulfilled is debated.

For today: when God shows you his faithfulness, do not keep your thanks silent. Write or choose a new song, and sing it today, at home or with others, to give him thanks.
exp.41:11:
This verse is an invitation to give God the honor he deserves. To "give glory" to the Lord means to acknowledge who he is and to praise him. To "declare his praise" means to announce and proclaim what he is like and what he has done. The "islands" were understood as distant lands, beyond the sea.

Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking. He has just presented the Servant of the Lord, who will bring justice and hope. For this reason he calls for a new song from the desert to the sea and the mountains. The praise is not only for Israel but for distant peoples. Afterward, God appears as a warrior who acts after a long silence.

Today we can praise God without keeping it to ourselves. This week, tell someone close to you or far away something specific that God has done in your life, and thank him out loud.
exp.41:12:
What it says: This verse describes God as a powerful warrior who goes out to fight.

Context: The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Before this, the peoples of the desert, such as Kedar, sing praise to God. Afterward, the Lord himself says that he has kept silent for a long time, but now he will act. It is a poetic image. Many see it as a promise that God will deliver his people and overcome injustice, in connection with the Servant in chapter 42.

For today: When it seems that God is silent in the face of evil or your pain, remember that his silence is not weakness or forgetfulness. Trust that he will act in his time, and in the meantime, praise him with hope.
exp.41:14:
Here God says that he will turn mountains and hills into desolate places, that he will dry up all the grass, that the rivers will become islands (that is, banks of dry land), and that he will dry up the pools.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he will come out like a warrior, after a long silence. The images of drought show his power over nature and his judgment against those who trust in idols. Interpreters debate whether this is figurative language or whether it also refers to concrete events. What follows shows that his aim is to guide his people, like the blind, toward the light.

For today: God is not indifferent or powerless, even when he seems silent. You can trust that he guides your steps, even along paths you do not know, and stop leaning on things that cannot save you.
exp.41:22:
God asks his people a question: who among you will listen to this? Who will pay attention and hear, thinking about what is coming? To "listen" here means to give close attention. Being alert to what is ahead means thinking about the future and learning for what comes next.

Here God speaks through Isaiah. Israel has been plundered and humbled, and the people do not understand why. God reminds them that he himself allowed that defeat because of their disobedience. The question is a call, and also a rebuke, because they were not listening or learning.

For today: when we go through hard times, let us not only ask that they end. Let us stop and listen to God, think about what he wants to teach us, and obey him again. Listening today changes what comes tomorrow.
exp.41:24:
He says that God poured out on Israel the heat of his anger and the violence of war. It was like a fire that surrounded them on every side, yet the people did not understand what was happening. It burned them, and still they did not take it to heart.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of the defeat and exile that Israel would suffer for having turned away from God. In the verses before, it is acknowledged that it was the Lord who allowed the plundering, because the people refused to walk in his ways or obey his law. Many understand this to refer to foreign invasions, such as that of Babylon, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when difficulties come, it is not enough simply to endure them; it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God what he wants to teach us. He corrects in order to restore, not to destroy.
exp.42:5:
God says he will tell the north to give up its captives, and the south not to hold them back. In this way he will bring back his sons and daughters, even if they are in the farthest parts of the earth.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people scattered and discouraged. Earlier he had told them that he loved them and that they should not fear, because he was with them. This promise to gather them from every direction points first of all to the return from exile. Some also see it fulfilled in a broader way in the gathering of people from all nations into God's people.

If you feel far away, forgotten, or lost today, remember that God knows where you are and has not let you go. Pray with confidence, leave your fear in his hands, and return to him, because his love is seeking you and calling you by name.
exp.42:8:
All the nations and peoples are said to be gathered together as if for a trial.

The reader is challenged to bring forth someone who announced ahead of time what was going to happen, or who can explain the former things, that is, earlier events that have already been fulfilled. Let them bring their witnesses to prove they are right, and let those who hear them agree that it is true.

God speaks to Israel, his people, who are weary and surrounded by nations with idols. Earlier, the people are described as blind and deaf, even though they have eyes and ears. God calls them to be his witnesses. The challenge shows that only the LORD announces the future and then fulfills it; the idols are silent. Scholars debate which exact events are meant, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when many voices compete for your trust, remember how God has been faithful in your life and in his Word. Write down those signs of his faithfulness and tell someone about them this week.
exp.42:9:
God says to Israel: "You are my witnesses and my chosen servant." He chose them so that they would know him, believe in him, and understand that he alone is God. The phrase about being "formed" refers to the fact that no other god was made before him, and none will be made after him. God has no beginning and no rival. The name of God is the one the verse calls "the Lord," and the older spelling of certain words has been updated to modern usage.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is like a courtroom: he calls the nations to bring forward witnesses who can show that their gods have announced or done anything. Israel, though spiritually blind and deaf, did see God announce things and save them. In this way, their history proves that the Lord is the only true God.

For today: God also invites us to be witnesses through our lives. Think of a time when God helped you or held you up, and tell someone about it today with simplicity and gratitude.
exp.42:13:
God presents himself as the Redeemer of his people and the Holy One of Israel. He says that, for their sake, he acted against Babylon: he brought all of them down like fugitives, and the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) cried out in anguish in their ships. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translators understand it differently.

God speaks to Israel, who would be carried off captive to Babylon. He promises them that this mighty empire will not have the last word. He announces its fall to set his people free, and he does this so that they will recognize that he alone is God.

Today: when you feel that something greater than you has you trapped, remember that God is your Redeemer and that no power stands above him. Trust in his care and pray with hope.
exp.42:14:
It says that the Lord presents himself with three titles: he is the "Holy One" of his people, the "Creator" of Israel, and their "King." "Holy One" means unique, set apart, perfect. "Creator" is an older way of saying "Creator" (the word "creator" as it appears in the verse). It is God affirming who he is and what place he holds with his people.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were about to be taken to Babylon, and God promises to act on their behalf and defeat their enemies. Before and after this verse he reminds them that no one can stop his hand, and that he has already made paths through the sea, as in the Exodus. With these titles he strengthens Israel's confidence.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember who your God is. Before asking him for something, take a moment to declare who he is: holy, Creator, and King. That affirms your trust.
exp.42:16:
It says that God is the one who brings out a powerful army, with chariots, horses and soldiers. But that same army falls down together and does not rise again. It is put out like a wick, the thread of a candle or lamp, and goes out completely.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah to his people Israel. He reminds them how he made a way through the sea, most likely alluding to the exodus from Egypt, when Pharaoh's army was defeated. He encourages them in the midst of their distress, because he is still their King and Savior, and right after this he promises to do a new thing.

For today: no human power is so great that it can stop God. If you face a problem today that seems impossible, trust that God has rescued before and can open a new way. Rest in him and not only in your own strength.
exp.42:18:
God says he is doing something new, and that it will soon sprout up, like a plant coming out of the ground. He asks whether the people will not notice it. He promises to open a way where there is only desert and to make rivers run in the wilderness.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israel, who was in exile or was about to be. Earlier, he reminded them how he defeated the Egyptian army at the sea. Now he asks them not to stay bound to those memories, because he is going to act again to rescue his people, who were created to praise him.

For today: if you feel that your life is a desert, do not conclude that God has finished working. Remember with gratitude what he has done, but keep your eyes alert and your heart open to see the new thing he is beginning.
exp.42:22:
God tells Israel that they did not bring him the sheep and goats for their burnt offerings, and did not honor him with their sacrifices. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar. A grain or food offering was given to God, and incense was the sweet smoke that rose from the altar. God makes it clear that he did not burden them with those offerings or wear them out by demanding incense.

God speaks through Isaiah and addresses Jacob and Israel. He reminds them that he made them to praise him, but they did not seek him. It is understood that their offerings were empty or did not come from a grateful heart, though scholars debate the details. What is striking comes next: God forgives by his own grace, not because of their merits.

For today: do not use your religious activities to try to satisfy God. Seek him with a sincere heart, and remember that your forgiveness rests on his love, not on your efforts.
exp.42:23:
God says that Israel did not buy him sweet cane, the fragrant oil or fine incense used in worship, nor did they please him with the fat, the best part of the sacrifices. Instead, they made him serve under their sins; that is, they burdened him with their wickedness and wearied him with their faults.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who offered little from the heart and lived in rebellion. He does not say that sacrifices were wrong in themselves, but that there was no sincere love behind them. Right after, in verse 25, he promises to forgive for the sake of his own name.

For today: performing rituals or religious gestures is not enough if the heart remains far from God. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge your failures, and trust in his forgiveness, which is not earned with gifts but comes from his grace.
exp.42:24:
God says that He Himself, and no one else, is the one who wipes out the rebellions of His people. He does this for His own sake, that is, for the sake of His own name and His merciful character, not because the people deserve it. And He promises that He will not remember their sins, meaning that He will not hold them against them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel. The people had neglected their sincere offerings and, worse still, had burdened God with their wrongdoing. Even so, He offers forgiveness. Then He invites them to a court-like exchange, a dialogue in which they can present their defense, and He reminds them that sin goes back a long way.

Today, if you repent, you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry old guilt. Come to God with sincerity, receive His forgiveness as a gift, and live with gratitude.
exp.43:0:
It says that God speaks to his people and asks them to listen carefully. The opening words mark a shift: after rebukes, a word of comfort comes. God calls Jacob and Israel his servant and reminds them that he chose them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were living under judgment and discouragement, and perhaps felt forgotten. So God reminds them of their identity: they are not an abandoned people, but a chosen one. The verses that follow confirm this with promises of help, of not fearing, and of pouring out his Spirit and his blessing.

For today: when you feel far from God or afraid, stop and listen to what he says about you. Your worth does not depend on your failures, but on his love and his calling. Read his Word and rest in his faithfulness.
exp.43:7:
God tells his people not to be frightened or shaken. He reminds them that he had already announced long ago what he would do. That is why they are his witnesses, that is, people who can vouch that he is faithful. He declares that there is no other God besides him. The word "Rock" here means a secure refuge, and he says he knows of no other.

The Lord himself is speaking, presenting himself as the King and Redeemer of Israel. His people were surrounded by nations that worshiped idols, and God reminds them that only he announces what is coming and then fulfills it. He then contrasts this with idols, which neither see nor understand.

Today, when the future unsettles you, remember the times God sustained you. Tell those stories to others; your testimony strengthens your own trust and that of those who listen to you.
exp.43:8:
This verse says that those who make idols of wood or metal live in vanity, that is, in something empty. Even what they value most in those figures is of no use. The idols themselves bear witness against their makers, because they neither see nor understand, and so they expose how absurd it is to worship them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he alone is God, that he announced what would happen, and that his people are witnesses to it. Now he contrasts the living God, who speaks and guides, with idols made by human hands, which can do nothing.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval. If they depend on us and cannot sustain us, it is worth returning to trust in God.
exp.43:11:
He describes a smith who takes his tools, works the metal in the coals, shapes it with hammer blows, and forms it with the strength of his arm. But he grows tired: he becomes hungry, loses his strength, and if he does not drink water, he faints. The tongs are what the smith uses to hold the hot metal, and the coals are the glowing embers.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He mocks idolatry with irony. He shows that the one who makes an idol is a limited human being, who wears himself out and needs to eat and drink. How could such a weak being create something that could be a god?

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by our own hands, such as work, money, or success, we are treating as if they could save us. Only God, who never grows weary, deserves our complete trust.
exp.43:12:
The carpenter measures the wood with a ruler or a cord, marks the outline with red ochre (a reddish dye), carves it with planes, and shapes it with the compass. In this way he makes a figure with the look of a beautiful man, so that it may stand in a house, as an ornament or a shrine.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people tempted by idolatry. With irony, he describes step by step how craftsmen make idols. The point is to show that a god made by human hands cannot be God. The verses that follow show that the same wood serves for warming oneself, cooking, and also for worship.

For today: let us ask ourselves which things made by us, such as money, fame, or success, we treat as if they could save us. Only the Creator deserves our complete trust.
exp.43:17:
They do not know nor understand those who make and worship idols. The explanation of the word meaning covered over, like a crust that covers the eyes, is left out here. Because of this, they cannot see the truth, and their hearts cannot grasp it. It is a spiritual blindness that they themselves do not notice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel. He mocks idolatry with sadness: a man uses half of a log to warm himself and cook, and with the rest he makes a god and asks it for help. The verse explains why he does something so absurd: his heart is closed and deceived.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we put in place of God: money, success, approval. Ask God to open your eyes, and look honestly at whether you trust in something that cannot save you.
exp.43:21:
God says that He has already blotted out the rebellions and sins of His people, the way the sun makes a cloud or a mist disappear. Then He invites them to return to Him, and the reason is that He has already redeemed them, that is, bought them back and set them free.

The Lord speaks to Israel, also called Jacob. Shortly before, He mocked idolatry, which is like feeding on ashes and trusting in a lie. Now He reminds His people that He formed them and that they are His servant. First God acts by forgiving and redeeming, and then He invites them to return. That is why a song of praise follows.

If you feel trapped by your failures, do not wait until you have fixed yourself before drawing near to God. He invites you to return because He already offers forgiveness. Confess today what weighs on you and rest in His mercy.
exp.43:22:
This verse calls all of creation to celebrate. The heavens, the lower parts of the earth, the mountains, the forest and every tree in it are told to sing and shout for joy. The reason is that the Lord has done it: He has rescued His people. To redeem means to pay the price to set someone free. To break forth means to burst out into singing. To be glorified means that God will show His greatness in Israel.

The prophet Isaiah passes on what God says to a people who have failed and feel forgotten. Just before, God reminds them that He has wiped away their sins like a cloud that fades away, and He invites them to return to Him. Then He presents Himself as Redeemer and Creator of all things.

For today: when you doubt that God will forgive you, remember that He has already wiped away your sins. Respond with gratitude: take a moment today to thank Him out loud for His forgiveness.
exp.43:23:
God presents himself with three titles: the Lord, your Redeemer, and the one who formed his people from the womb. That is, he knows them and cares for them from their very beginning. Then he says that he makes all things, and that he alone stretched out the heavens and the earth. In today's language, stretching out the heavens is like unfolding them, and "by myself" means that no one helped him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people who would be taken into exile. He has just told them that he blotted out their sins and redeemed them. Now he affirms his power as Creator, so that they will trust in him and not in diviners or human wise men, as the following verses show.

For today: the God who created everything and knows you before you were born can also forgive you and sustain you. When you feel fear or uncertainty, pray and rest in his care, instead of seeking security in other sources.
exp.43:25:
This verse says that God makes true what his prophets announce. The phrase about his servant's word means that he confirms it and fulfills it. His messengers are the prophets who spoke on his behalf. God promises that Jerusalem will again have inhabitants and that the cities of Judah will be rebuilt. The idea of raising up the decayed places means that he himself will restore what has been destroyed.

The Lord speaks, presented as Redeemer and Creator. Isaiah writes to a people who would be taken into exile, or who were already living it, depending on how one understands the book. God shows himself superior to diviners and to the wise men of the world. In the following verse he names Cyrus, who would have a role in the rebuilding.

For today: when you feel that something in your life has been left in ruins, remember that God keeps what he promises. Trust his word and wait for his work, while faithfully doing what is yours to do.
exp.44:3:
God says that he called someone by name and gave him a title of honor, even though that person did not know him. The reason is his affection for Jacob and Israel, his chosen people. A servant is someone who serves God. A title of honor is a name given in recognition of someone's standing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the previous verse (45:1) he names Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he calls his anointed. God would use him to open the way for the release of Israel from exile in Babylon. Cyrus was a pagan king, but God would use him to care for his people and to show that he alone is God.

Today we can trust that God works even where he is not recognized. If you are going through a difficult situation, remember that he can move people and circumstances in favor of his children. Rest in his care and give him thanks.
exp.44:4:
He says that the Lord is the only God; there is no other beside him. He also promises to gird someone, that is, to clothe him with strength, equip him, and prepare him for a task, even though that person did not know him.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. In this passage he addresses Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he names long before his reign. God would use him so that the people of Israel, in exile in Babylon, could return to their land. The verses before say that all this is for the sake of Israel, his chosen people. In this way everyone would know that only the Lord governs history.

For today: God can work in your life and in your world, even when you do not see him or recognize him. Trust that he is still in control, and seek to know him better.
exp.44:6:
It says that God is the creator of all things: he forms the light and creates the darkness, he makes peace and creates calamity. The Hebrew word translated here as "calamity" can mean disaster, misfortune or judgment, not necessarily sin. The word "create" in the verse is the same one that means to bring something into being, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

God himself speaks, addressing Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he would use to free Israel from exile in Babylon, although Cyrus did not know him. In that time many peoples believed in several gods, one of light and another of darkness. God declares that there is no other power beside him; everything, including calamities, is under his control and purpose.

For today: when you live through dark or confusing times, remember that nothing escapes the hand of God. You can pray with confidence, even if you do not understand everything, because he still governs and is just.
exp.44:11:
God says that he made the earth and created human beings on it. With his own hands he stretched out the heavens, and he gave commands to all their host, that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars.

The Lord, the Holy One of Israel, speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were in trouble and doubted how God was acting. So God reminds them that he is the Creator and that he is in control. Right away he announces that he will raise up Cyrus to free the captives. Many understand that this is the meaning of the passage that follows.

When something in your life does not make sense, remember who God is. The one who holds up the universe also cares for you. You can pray with confidence, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.44:16:
Israel receives salvation from the Lord, and that salvation lasts forever. Here "salvation" does not mean being healthy, but being saved and rescued. The promise is that God's people will not live in shame for all time.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and the context sets this against those who make idols, who will indeed be confused and put to shame. Idols cannot save, but the God of Israel, though at times he may seem hidden, does save. Scholars differ on how this promise applies to Israel today; some see it fulfilled in Christ and his people, while others also see a future fulfillment for the nation.

For today: if you trust in God and not in what you build yourself, you can rest. He does not fail, and whoever takes refuge in him will not be ashamed.
exp.44:22:
God says he made an oath by himself, because there is no one greater by whom to swear. What has gone out of his mouth is righteous and will not be canceled: every knee will bow before him and every tongue will swear, that is, will declare its loyalty to him.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people in exile who feel forgotten. God presents himself as the only God, Savior, and righteous one, and calls all the nations to look to him and be saved. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, applying it to Christ. Some debate how that final acknowledgment will take place, but the text emphasizes that God has the last word.

Today we can rest: even though the world may seem chaotic, God fulfills what he promises. Decide today to honor him with your life, and trust him when you feel insecure.
exp.45:2:
God calls his people: "Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel." He reminds them that he has carried and sustained them since before they were born, from the womb of their mother. The word "womb" here refers to the place where a baby is formed, and the idea of being carried means being held up and supported.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, Babylon had gods such as Bel and Nebo, idols that had to be carried on animals when defeat came. In contrast, the Lord is not carried by his people; he is the one who carries his people. He speaks to those who remained of Israel, probably in times of crisis and captivity.

For today: when you feel tired or insecure, remember that God is not one more burden. He has sustained you your whole life. Rest in his care and speak to him with confidence today.
exp.45:3:
He says that God himself will care for his people all their lives, even into old age and gray hairs. The word "carry" here means to bear up and hold, not merely to put up with something. God repeats "I" several times: he made them, he will carry them, he will uphold them and keep them safe.

The passage speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It compares the idols of Babylon, which had to be carried on animals when they fell, with the God of Israel, who has carried his people since before they were born. The idols are a burden; the Lord is the one who carries the burden. He addresses a people who were facing captivity.

When you feel tired, old, or without strength, remember that God does not ask you to hold yourself up alone. You can give him your burdens in prayer, trusting that he walks with you through every stage of your life.
exp.45:4:
God asks a question to make us think: to whom can God be compared? The words "liken" and "equal" mean placing someone on the same level. "Compare" means measuring one thing against another. The implied answer is that no person and no thing is like him.

The Lord speaks to his people Israel, who were surrounded by nations with idols. Earlier he reminded them that he carried them from birth and will carry them into old age. Then he describes how people make idols out of gold and silver, and then the idols must be carried because they cannot move or respond. The contrast is clear: the living God carries his people; idols have to be carried.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we carry as if they could save us: money, success, or approval. When you feel weary, rest in the God who sustains you and listens to you.
exp.45:5:
Some people, the explanation says, take gold out of their bag or purse and weigh silver on scales. With that money they pay a goldsmith, a craftsman who works metals, to make them a god. Then they bow down before what they had made themselves and worship it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he presents himself as the God who made, carries, and sustains his people into old age. He then compares that faithfulness with the idols of Babylon, which have to be carried on people's shoulders, do not move, and do not answer. God wants his people to come to their senses.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we are putting in God's place, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Everything we make ourselves and then expect to save us falls short. Today we can once again trust the God who sustains us.
exp.45:6:
Here the passage speaks of people who make an idol. They lift it onto their shoulders, carry it, and set it in its place. There it stays, unmoving. If someone cries out to it, it does not answer, and it cannot save anyone from their distress.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he asked to whom they could compare him. Then he describes how people pay a goldsmith to make a god of gold and silver, and then they worship it. God contrasts that motionless image with himself, who does act and does save. After this, he calls his people to remember and return to him.

For today: ask yourself what you are holding onto to feel secure, such as money, status, or success. If it depends on you to keep it up, it cannot keep you up. Bring your distress to God today, for he does hear.
exp.45:12:
God promises that his righteousness will draw near and will not stay far away. He also says that his salvation will not be delayed. He will place salvation in Zion, which is Jerusalem, his people, and he will show his glory in Israel.

God himself is speaking through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he will call a man from far away to carry out his plan; many understand this to refer to Cyrus, king of Persia, although the text does not give the name here. God speaks to those who are stubborn of heart, people who doubted his help and lived far from what is right. In contrast with the idols of Babylon, which must be carried, God himself carries and rescues his people.

For today: when you feel that God's help is taking too long, remember that he does what he says. Trust his timing, and instead of hardening your heart, come to him with humility and wait for his salvation.
exp.46:1:
It says that Babylon, once proud and pampered, will be brought low like a slave. She will have to grind grain at the mill, hard work fit for servant women. The words that refer to the hair are the lock of hair; removing the veil and baring the legs to cross the rivers speaks of being left exposed, like a captive led away into exile.

God speaks through Isaiah. Babylon had dominated other peoples, even the people of God, and had believed herself eternal and without rival. God announces that her fall will come, and that He Himself will do justice. Scholars agree that it is an image of humiliation, though not all of them agree on every detail.

For today: pride and power seem firm, but they do not last. God sees injustice and is the Redeemer of his own people. Today you can live with humility and trust that He cares for you and brings about justice in his time.
exp.46:12:
This verse mocks Babylon's trust in its advisers. It says she has grown weary of so many counsels, and it challenges them: let the ones who watch the sky, the ones who study the stars to predict the future, and those who announce the months now stand up and save you from what is coming.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Babylon, pictured as a proud queen. She trusted in astrology and enchantments, but God announces a sudden judgment that no divination will be able to stop. The verses that follow show that these advisers will not be able to save even themselves.

For today: when we are afraid of the future, let us not place our security in horoscopes, superstitions, or people who promise to control what is to come. We can bring our worries to God in prayer and trust Him, who truly holds our days.
exp.46:13:
They say that the astrologers and fortune-tellers of Babylon will be like stubble, that is, light chaff that the wind carries away. The fire will consume them, and they will not even be able to save themselves. No good ember will remain to warm yourself by, nor a fire to sit beside; the fire will be destructive, not a comfort.

God speaks through Isaiah against Babylon, portrayed as a proud queen who trusted in magic, omens, and the study of the stars. He mocks those securities: if they are of any use, let them defend her now. The text stresses that her counselors will not be able to deliver her from judgment.

For today: examine what you trust in to feel secure. It may be horoscopes, superstitions, money, or your own plans. All of these can fail. Hand your fears over to God, who can truly save.
exp.46:14:
They say that all those who have stood with Babylon for years, her partners and merchants from her youth, will abandon her. Each one will go off on his own way, every one to his own direction, continuing on his course without looking back. No one will come to rescue her when judgment arrives.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Babylon, a symbol of pride and of trust in human power. She depended on astrologers, counselors and trade alliances, and believed herself safe. God shows her that none of that will be able to save her. Many understand that he also speaks of a pride that goes beyond a single city.

For today: examine where you have placed your security, whether money, connections, reputation or plans. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who never abandons anyone who draws near to him with humility.
exp.47:2:
He says that God had announced long before what was going to happen. He spoke it with his own mouth, made it known, and then carried it out suddenly, and everything happened just as he had said.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, the people of Jacob. They boasted of being God's people and swore by his name, but without truth or righteousness, that is, with their lips and not with their hearts. God reminds them that he gave warning beforehand, so that they would not credit what happened to their idols, as the following verses say.

For today: God is faithful to his word. We can trust what the Bible says and give him the credit, not luck or other things. And our faith must be sincere, not just words.
exp.47:4:
God says that long ago he told his people what was going to happen, before it took place.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a stubborn people, whom he describes as having a neck of iron and a forehead of bronze. Many understand this to refer to the years of exile in Babylon, when people were tempted to credit their fate to idols. God shows that he alone knows the future and directs history.

For today: when something good comes into your life, do not credit it to luck, money, or your own effort. Stop and give thanks to God, who cares for you and works even before you notice.
exp.47:12:
God says that his hand laid the foundations of the earth and that with his right hand he measured the heavens, marking them out with a span, that is, with the width of an open hand. When he called to them, they came together at once, presenting themselves all at the same time, ready to obey.

God himself speaks to Israel, his people, who were in exile and were always tempted to trust in idols. He reminds them that he is the first and the last, the Creator. That is why he can announce in advance what he will do in Babylon and then carry it out.

For today: if the God who formed the earth and the heavens calls you and cares for you, you can entrust him with your worries. What seems enormous to you is not great to him. Rest in his power and in his faithfulness.
exp.47:16:
The explanation says that the Lord, who redeems his people and is completely holy, presents himself as their God. He is the one who teaches what truly benefits, what is good and useful for them. He also guides and directs them along the way they should walk.

Here God himself speaks to Israel, who was in exile in Babylon. Earlier he reminded them that he does not speak in secret and that he directs history. Then he laments that his people did not pay attention to his commandments, for otherwise they would have had peace like a river and numerous descendants. It is an invitation given with tenderness and also with sorrow.

For today: if God leads us for our good, it is worth listening to him before we decide. You can set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and pray, asking him for direction, and be willing to obey what you see, even when it costs you.
exp.47:21:
It says that those who live in wickedness do not have true peace. "Wicked" refers to the ungodly, that is, to those who turn away from God and live against His will. "Peace" is more than calm: it is complete well-being and tranquility of the soul.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. God has just invited His people to leave Babylon, where they were held captive, and He reminds them how He cared for them in the desert. This sentence closes that section as a warning: deliverance is for those who trust in Him. Those who reject Him will remain without inner rest. Some scholars see here a call not to stay bound to Babylon.

Today we can examine what takes away our peace. If there is something we know does not please God, we can confess it and turn back to Him sincerely. His forgiveness and His guidance restore a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.48:6:
God, who is the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, speaks to someone who is despised and rejected by the nations and who serves under harsh rulers. He promises that kings and princes will see him, will rise to their feet as a sign of respect, and will bow down in worship. The reason is that God is faithful, and it was he who chose him.

This is the second Song of the Servant. The one speaking is God, and he addresses the Servant, whom he sends to restore Israel and to be a light to the nations. Christians often see Jesus here, who was rejected and then exalted. Others also see a reference to Israel as a people. Both readings are possible.

For today: if you feel despised or ignored, remember that your worth does not depend on what people think of you, but on the faithfulness of God. Trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.48:9:
They shall not hunger or thirst, and neither the heat nor the sun will harm them. God, who has compassion on them, will lead them like a shepherd to places where fresh water flows.

The Lord speaks in the second song of the Servant. He addresses his Servant, whom many Christians see fulfilled in Jesus, and also the people returning from captivity. God promises to free the prisoners and bring them back along safe paths. Some scholars see this as a promise for Israel of that time, while others add a broader spiritual fulfillment.

For today: when you feel weary or in need, remember that God cares for you like a shepherd. Trust his guidance, ask him for direction each day, and rest in his compassion.
exp.48:12:
The explanation says that the whole universe should sing for joy: the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. The reason is that God has comforted his people and has compassion on the afflicted. The word "break forth" means to burst out with force in praise. "Afflicted" here refers to the humble and those who suffer.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Israel, who lived in exile, far from their land. God promises to bring them back from distant places. This song announces that hope. But in the following verse Zion feels forgotten, and God answers that he will never forget her, as a mother does not forget the baby at her breast. So the praise rests on God's promise, even though the people did not yet feel it.

Today, when you feel lonely or abandoned, you can praise God for what he has said about his faithfulness, even though you do not yet see the change. His comfort is real, and it can grow in you as you praise him.
exp.48:18:
God tells Zion (Jerusalem) that the ruined, destroyed and empty places of her land will now be too small for her, because many people will come to live there. The destruction of those places will be complete, and the land that was made narrow will have no room left to hold the crowd. Moreover, those who destroyed her will be sent far away.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people who felt abandoned and exiled. Zion is pictured as a woman alone and without children. God promises that her children will return in great numbers, so many that she herself will be amazed. Many see this as a promise of return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment.

For today: even if your life seems to be in ruins, God can restore it beyond what you imagine. Keep waiting on Him and pray with confidence, without counting out what He is able to raise up.
exp.48:20:
It says that Zion, the city of God, will be amazed to see so many children around her. She felt bereaved of her children, alone, with no settled home, and cast out of her land. So she asks who raised all these, since she had been left abandoned.

God is speaking to Jerusalem, which represents his people in exile in Babylon. They felt forgotten, but God promises to restore her and fill her with people. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a broader fulfillment in God's family, which includes the nations.

For today: when you feel alone, fruitless, or forgotten, remember that God can work in silence and surprise you. Keep trusting in him, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.48:22:
He says that God promises to restore Zion, his people. Kings will be their protectors who care for and raise children, and queens will be wet nurses. Bowing with the face to the ground and licking the dust are Eastern images of great honor and submission. The result is that Zion will know that God is the Lord, and that those who wait for him will not be put to shame.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israel, which felt abandoned, alone, and exiled in captivity. God answers that he himself will lift up his hand and bring his children back. Interpreters debate whether the language of kings bowing down is literal or a picture of the honor God would give his people. Many Christians also see here a look toward the Messiah.

For today: when you feel forgotten or are waiting for an answer, remember that God does not forget his own. Keep trusting him with patience, because his faithfulness does not leave those who wait for him ashamed.
exp.48:24:
God answers a hard question: who can take the prey away from a strong warrior? He says that he will. The captives of the mighty will be set free. "Contend" means to argue a case or take up a dispute in court, so God promises to defend the cause of his people. "I will contend" means that he himself will take up their case. He also promises to save their children.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Zion, that is, to Israel in exile, who felt abandoned. Their oppressors seemed impossible to overcome. God declares that his power is greater, and so everyone will know that he is Savior and Redeemer.

When you feel that a problem is too big for you, do not face it alone. Bring it to God in prayer, trust that he defends his own, and keep waiting on him, even when the solution takes time.
exp.48:25:
God promises that those who oppressed his people will suffer the consequences of their own violence. The images are very strong: they will eat their own flesh and be drunk with their own blood as though it were sweet wine. Many understand this as figurative language of judgment, in which the oppressors destroy one another. The goal is that all flesh, that is, all of humanity, will know that the Lord is the Savior, the Redeemer, and the mighty One of Jacob.

The Lord speaks to Israel in exile, a people who felt abandoned and trapped by a greater power. God answers that he himself will defend their cause and rescue his children, even though the captor may seem invincible.

For today: when you feel crushed by an injustice or by a situation stronger than you, do not take revenge. Entrust your cause to God, who sees, defends, and redeems. Rest in the fact that he is faithful to his own.
exp.49:2:
God says that he clothes the skies in darkness, that is, he covers them with gloom, as if he were putting them in mourning. And that their covering, or their cloak, he makes like sackcloth, a rough, dark cloth that was used for grief and sorrow. It is an image of God's power over all creation.

The LORD speaks to the people of Israel, who felt abandoned, like a wife who had been sent away. God answers that the people were punished for their own sins, and that his hand has not grown too short: he is still able to save. If he can dry up the sea and darken the heavens, he can also deliver his own people. Some think the darkness recalls the judgment on Egypt, although the text does not say so.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, do not doubt his power. Acknowledge your mistakes, return to him, and trust that he can help you.
exp.49:5:
Here the servant says that he gave his body to those who struck him. He offered his cheeks to those who pulled out his beard (the phrase is rendered here as tearing out the hair, meaning pulling hard on the hair or the beard). He did not hide his face from insults or from spit. The ones who strike are the smiters.

This is the third Servant Song in Isaiah. It speaks of a servant of the Lord who listens to God every morning, obeys, and does not turn back. Christians read it as a foreshadowing of Jesus, since the Gospels recount that he was struck and spat upon. Others also understand it as the experience of the prophet or of the faithful people. His confidence rests in God helping him and vindicating him.

For today: if you suffer for doing what is right, you do not have to repay evil with evil. Listen to God each day, and rest in the knowledge that He sustains you and knows your cause.
exp.49:9:
What it says: Isaiah asks who among the people fears the Lord and obeys the voice of his servant. Then he encourages anyone who walks in darkness (dark moments with no way out) and has no light (hope or guidance) to trust in the name of the Lord and lean on Him, that is, rest on Him like a firm walking staff. "Fear" here means to respect God with reverence.

Context: This is the third Servant Song. Before it, the servant speaks, trusting that God helps him. Here the prophet seems to address the people. Scholars debate who the servant is: some think of Isaiah, others of Israel, and Christians see in him Jesus. Afterward, God warns those who trust in their own light, a light made of human fire.

For today: When you don't understand what is happening in your life, do not invent your own light with hasty solutions. Pray, listen to the Word, and keep trusting God, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.49:10:
They say there are people who light their own way with their own fire, that is, with their own plans and resources, and not with the light of God. They are surrounded by sparks. God tells them to keep walking by that light if they want, but the result will come from his hand: they will end up in sorrow.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and at the end God himself speaks. The verse before shows two groups: the one who walks in darkness but trusts in the Lord, and the one who prefers his own light. Many understand the servant to be the Messiah, though it has also been interpreted in other ways. The passage invites trust in God and warns against self-sufficiency.

For today: when you are in the dark, do not invent your own way out. Pray, trust in God, and lean on his Word, even when you cannot yet see the path.
exp.50:0:
God calls on those who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord to listen. He asks them to look back to the rock from which they were cut, like a quarry, and to the pit from which they were dug, that is, to their humble origin.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a weary people, probably in a time of exile or discouragement. The verses that follow make clear that this rock is Abraham and Sarah: God called one man, blessed him, and multiplied him. If God made a people out of so little, he can keep his promise to comfort Zion.

For today: when you feel small or without strength, remember where God took you from and how faithful he has been before. That remembrance strengthens your confidence that he can do something new with you.
exp.50:2:
God promises that he will comfort Zion, that is, Jerusalem and his people. Her ruins and abandoned places will be made like the garden of Eden. Where there was desert, there will be a garden like the garden of the Lord. In place of sorrow there will be joy, gladness, thanksgiving and the voice of singing.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to those who seek righteousness and trust in him. He asks them to remember Abraham and Sarah: God called one man alone, blessed him and multiplied him. If he did that with a childless couple, he can raise up his people from their ruins again.

When your life feels like a desert, remember how God has acted before. His comfort is not just an emotion; it is a promise of restoration. Wait on him and give him thanks now.
exp.50:4:
God says that his righteousness is near and that his salvation has already gone out, meaning it is already on its way. With his arm, which represents his power, he will judge the peoples. The distant lands, which in the Bible often point to faraway regions, will wait on him and place their hope in his power.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to a weary and discouraged people. He has just promised comfort for Zion and that his law and his judgment will be a light to the nations. Then he asks them to look at the heavens and the earth, which will pass away, and to trust in his salvation, which lasts forever. Scholars debate exactly which moment he has in mind, but the message of hope is clear.

For today: when you feel tired or without a way out, remember that your hope rests not on passing things but on the faithful power of God. Today, bring to him in prayer whatever you cannot resolve.
exp.50:5:
God invites his people to look at the sky and the earth, which seem solid and firm. But he says the heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth will wear out like an old garment. Its inhabitants will also pass away. His salvation, however, will last forever, and his righteousness will never come to an end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a discouraged people, probably in a time of exile or pressure. He wants them to trust in him and not in human powers. The verses that follow encourage them not to fear the mockery of people. Some understand the statement that they will vanish literally and others as poetic language; the central message is the same.

For today: when fear, criticism, or insecurity weighs on you, remember that the most solid things in this world are temporary. Place your hope in God's salvation, which endures. Today, bring him one specific worry in prayer.
exp.50:7:
The explanation says that God's enemies and the enemies of his people will disappear like a garment that the moth and the worm gradually eat until it is gone. What God does, on the other hand, endures forever. "Righteousness" here includes his faithfulness and his action to rescue, and "salvation" means deliverance or rescue. "Forever" means without end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who are weary and exposed to mockery and pressure. He tells them not to fear the contempt of men, because their power is passing. Then the people respond by calling on God to awaken his arm, as in the past.

Today we can remember that the criticisms, threats, and fears of this world wear away with time. When someone despises you for following God, rest in the knowledge that his salvation does not come to an end. Place your trust in what lasts.
exp.50:11:
It is God himself who comforts his people. "I, even I" repeats the phrase to give force and assurance. Then he asks, almost tenderly: who are you to be afraid of a mere human being? The verse speaks of a man who will die, and of a son of man who will fade like grass, which soon withers and disappears.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were under pressure and fear before powerful oppressors. God reminds them how he opened the sea to rescue his own, and he promises that the redeemed will return to Zion with singing. His purpose is that they look to their Maker and not to their enemies.

When fear of people overwhelms you, remember who holds you up. Pray honestly, and place your fear before the power and faithfulness of God, which is greater.
exp.50:13:
The prisoner is said to be in a hurry to be set free, so that he will not die in the dungeon, which is a dark, underground prison, nor be left without food. Other translations read the Hebrew differently: the bowed-down captive will soon be set free, will not die in the pit, and will not lack his bread. It is a somewhat difficult text.

God speaks here, presenting himself as the comforter of his people. Many understand that he is addressing Israel in captivity, or on the verge of it, in Babylon. He reminds them that the oppressor is mortal and that the Creator, who gave freedom to his people before, can give it again.

Today, if something or someone has you bound by fear, debt, or anguish, remember that God sees your need. Speak to him honestly and trust that he cares for you, even in the everyday things, like bread.
exp.50:14:
This verse says that it is the Lord who divides the sea, that is, who stirs up or splits the sea, and its waves roar. The phrase "The Lord of hosts" is a title that speaks of his power over all that he has made. God reminds his people who he is: the mighty God who rules even the fiercest waters.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to a people in exile who were afraid of their oppressors and had forgotten their Creator. Earlier he rebuked them for fearing a mere man who passes away. Now he comforts them with his greatness. Some see here a memory of the Red Sea, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: when your fears seem like giant waves, remember that God rules the sea. Before you think about your problem, take a moment to pray and to recall who he is.
exp.50:17:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to a mother, was left alone and without support. Among all the sons she bore and raised, none guides her or takes her by the hand to help her.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem after God's harsh punishment. She has drunk the cup of God's wrath, an image of divine judgment. Her leaders and her people lay fallen and without strength. The abandonment shows how deep the pain was. But this passage prepares the comfort that God offers right after.

For today: when you feel without support, with no one to take you by the hand, do not stay silent or alone. God sees your pain and remains your comfort. And if you know someone who is alone or weary, be the one who reaches out a hand to them.
exp.51:2:
The explanation says that God speaks to his people. "For nothing" means freely, without receiving anything in return. Israel was sold without anyone paying a fair price for them. That is why they will also be redeemed "without money": their freedom will not be bought with silver.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem, which lives in captivity and humiliation. God calls her to awake and rise up. Her oppressors did not pay a real price for them, so God owes no ransom to them. He will act on his own account and out of love for his name, which is blasphemed.

For today: if you feel bound by guilt or failure, remember that the freedom God gives is not earned through effort, nor is it paid for. Christians of many traditions see in this a foreshadowing of redemption in Christ. Today you can receive it with gratitude and rise up.
exp.51:6:
This verse speaks of a messenger who comes running over the mountains with good news. His feet are beautiful because they bring joy: peace, good, and salvation. "Salvation" here means deliverance or rescue. The central message is: "Your God reigns!" "Zion" is Jerusalem, the people of God.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who are oppressed and exiled, whose name was mocked. God promises that He will make Himself present. The watchmen of the city see the messenger coming and sing for joy, because God will comfort and redeem Jerusalem. The New Testament quotes this text in Romans 10:15 to speak of those who proclaim the gospel.

Today we can bring words of hope to someone who suffers. You do not need to be an expert: it is enough to tell them, with love, that God has not abandoned them and that He reigns.
exp.51:7:
The explanation says that the watchmen, that is, the lookouts who guard the city from the walls, lift up their voices and sing together for joy. They see clearly, face to face and up close, that the Lord is bringing back Zion, that is, Jerusalem, his city.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who were living in exile or in the aftermath of it. The watchmen were waiting for news of liberation, and the messenger had already announced that your God reigns. Many understand this as referring to the return from Babylon, and others also see a broader fulfillment in God's work in Christ. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: God does not leave his people forgotten. Even in difficult times, we can live alert and full of hope, and praise him together, remembering that he is faithful to restore.
exp.51:8:
