This verse calls the desolate places of Jerusalem, meaning the ruins and abandoned areas of the city, to break into singing and joy. The word "together" in the verse means all of them joining in as one. The reason for such joy is that the Lord has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem, that is, rescued and freed it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who had lived through exile and the destruction of their city. Just before this, watchmen announce that God is returning to Zion and reigning. What follows shows that God acts before all the nations. The message speaks as if the deliverance were already a certain fact. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of salvation in Christ.

For today: if there are areas of your life that you feel are in ruins, you can begin to praise God before you see everything restored. He is faithful to comfort and rescue.
exp.51:10:
This verse is an urgent call to leave a place and separate oneself from what is unclean. "Depart" means to go away. "Unclean" means impure or contaminated. Those who carry "the vessels of the Lord" are the ones who bear the sacred objects of the temple, and they are asked to make themselves clean.

God speaks through Isaiah to his people, who are in exile in Babylon. He has just announced comfort and redemption for Jerusalem. Now he invites them to return home. He promises that they will not leave in a hurry, because he will go before them. Many see here a reference to the temple objects that were to be returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:7-11).

For today: if God has redeemed us, he also calls us to live differently. Think of a habit or environment that pulls you away from him, and take one concrete step to leave it, trusting that he goes ahead of you.
exp.51:11:
It says that God's people will not leave in a hurry or escape like fugitives. God himself will go ahead of them as their guide, and he will also watch over their rear.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what God will do. The people were captive in Babylon, and they are called to leave and to live in holiness. The departure from Egypt was in haste (Exodus 12:11); this one will be different, under God's care. Right after this comes the suffering Servant, and many Christians see Jesus there.

For today: when God calls you to leave something harmful or to start over, do not act in panic. Pray, walk one step at a time, and trust that he goes before you and stays with you.
exp.52:3:
This verse says that the servant of the Lord took upon himself our sicknesses and our pains, that is, our suffering and our burdens. Yet the people thought God was punishing him: they saw him as struck down, smitten of God, and humbled.

Here a group speaks, looking back with surprise and regret. They had despised him before, but now they understand that his suffering was not punishment for his own fault. The verses that follow make this clear: he was wounded for our rebellions. Christians see Jesus in this passage, though some scholars debate how the passage was originally understood.

For today: when you see someone suffering, do not rush to judge them. And when you suffer, remember that Christ knows pain and walks with you in compassion.
exp.52:6:
It says that the Servant of the Lord suffered greatly, yet he did not defend himself or protest. He is compared to a lamb led to be slaughtered and to a sheep that stays silent while it is being sheared. The shearers are those who cut the wool. The word for the place where animals are killed is slaughter, the place where they are put to death.

This is the fourth song of the Servant in Isaiah. The prophet speaks of this Servant's suffering on behalf of others, who had gone astray like sheep. Jews have read this in different ways (as Israel, or as a righteous man), but Christians see Jesus here, as Acts 8:32-35 does.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, you do not always have to respond with anger or revenge. Jesus shows you another way: to trust God, even in pain. And remember that this silence was for love of you.
exp.52:10:
He says that the Servant of the LORD, after suffering greatly, will see the fruit of his pain and be content. Through his knowledge, he, being righteous, will make many righteous, because he will carry their guilt. "Iniquities" are sins and wrongdoings; to "justify" means to declare righteous or free from blame; to be "satisfied" means to be content.

It is part of the fourth Servant song in Isaiah. God speaks and announces that the suffering of this Servant has a purpose and ends in victory. Jews have interpreted it in various ways, for example as referring to Israel; Christians, from the New Testament onward, see it fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:24).

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through your own effort. You can rest in what Christ has done for you and respond with gratitude, forgiving others as God forgave you.
exp.52:11:
This verse says that God will reward his Servant with a portion among the great and the strong, like a victor who divides what he has won. The reason is that he poured out his life even to death, was treated as a wrongdoer, bore the sin of many, and interceded for those who did him wrong. "Transgressors" are those who disobey God's law. "Was numbered" means that he was treated as one of them.

Here God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the fourth Servant Song. Christians see this passage fulfilled in Jesus, and the New Testament quotes it in this way (Luke 22:37). Jewish interpreters have understood it in other ways, for example as referring to Israel.

For today: if Christ prayed for those who mistreated him, we can ask him for help to pray for someone who offends us, and trust that God sees and rewards what is done in love.
exp.53:0:
God invites the barren woman, the one who never had children, to sing and shout for joy. The reason is that the children of the forsaken woman will be more than those of the married wife.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, right after the chapter about the suffering Servant (chapter 53). The woman represents Jerusalem or the people of God, who felt abandoned and without a future during the exile. God promises them restoration and growth. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4:27 and applies it to the children of promise.

When you feel empty or unproductive, do not decide by what you see today. Praise God with confidence, because He can bring life where it seems impossible.
exp.53:3:
God tells a woman not to be afraid or to feel humiliated, because she will not be put to shame. He promises that she will forget the shame of her youth and will no longer remember the disgrace of her widowhood.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for God. The woman represents Jerusalem, or the people of Israel, who felt abandoned after the exile. Earlier, God asks her to enlarge her tent, because a great growth is coming. Then God presents himself as her husband and redeemer, that is, the one who rescues her and cares for her.

If you carry a shame from the past or a feeling of abandonment, you can hand it over to God. He does not define you by your failures or your losses. Trust that he can give you a new future, and prepare your heart to receive it.
exp.53:7:
This verse says that God turned away from his people only for a moment and with a small anger, but now he embraces them with a love that never ends. "I hid my face" means that he withdrew his favor and his closeness. The one who rescues and pays the price to set someone free is the one who redeems them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, which had suffered the punishment of exile because of its unfaithfulness. The people felt like an abandoned wife. God promises restoration and compares his faithfulness with the promise he made after Noah's flood: his mercy will not move, even if the mountains move.

For today: if you feel that God is far away because of your mistakes, remember that his correction is brief, but his mercy is eternal. Return to him with confidence.
exp.53:13:
God promises to clothe his people in righteousness, like an adornment that makes them beautiful. He also promises to keep them far from oppression, that is, from the mistreatment of the powerful. Because of this, they will no longer be afraid, since terror will not come near them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Jerusalem, described as a woman who was abandoned and afflicted, but who will now be restored. Many understand that the promise looks toward the return from exile, and others also see a broader fulfillment in the people of God. Righteousness and peace come from Him, not from human effort.

For today: when fear or injustice surrounds you, remember that your security rests in the character of God and not in your circumstances. Pray asking Him for peace, and seek to live justly in your daily dealings with others.
exp.54:5:
It says we should seek God now, while he lets himself be found, and call on him while he is near. "Seek" means to approach him with a sincere desire. "Call on" means to invoke him, to speak to him in prayer. The words "found" and "near" show that God wants to be found.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a passage where he invites everyone, even nations that did not know him, to come to him. The verses that follow explain the call: that the wicked person should leave his evil way and return to God, who pardons generously. Some think that "while he may be found" is a call not to let the opportunity pass; the text does not give an exact date.

For today: do not put off your prayer or your drawing near to God. Today itself, set aside a few minutes to speak to him sincerely and ask him for forgiveness and guidance.
exp.54:8:
It says that the heavens are much higher than the earth, and that in the same way God's ways and thoughts are above ours. "Ways" refers to the way he acts, and "thoughts" refers to his plans and the way he sees things.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who are generally understood to have been in exile or close to it, and he invites them to return to him. Just before this, the wicked person is called to leave his evil way, because God is abundant in pardoning. This verse explains why he can forgive so much: his heart and his plans are not like those of humans.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows, or find it hard to believe that he truly forgives, trust that his wisdom and mercy are greater than your view. Come to him with humility.
exp.54:11:
It says that God's people will go out with joy and be led back in peace. The joy is so great that creation itself joins the celebration: the mountains and the hills will break forth into singing, and the trees of the field will clap their hands, that is, they will applaud. The hills are low rises or small mountains. The people will be brought back again, that is, they will be led home.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were, or would be, in exile, far from their land, and God promises them deliverance. The verses before this one say that his word, like the rain, accomplishes its purpose. Many understand this going out as a reference to the return from Babylon, although some also see a broader promise of salvation.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, trust that God keeps what he promises. Write down one of his promises and repeat it in prayer, waiting with peace and gratitude.
exp.55:3:
Here God speaks to the eunuchs, men who in that time were often shut out from the congregation of Israel. He tells them that if they keep his Sabbaths (the days of rest), choose what pleases him, and hold fast to his covenant (his agreement with him), they will have a place among his people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The eunuchs and the foreigners felt rejected, afraid of being left out, like a dry tree with no future and no descendants. God answers that their acceptance does not depend on their background or their condition, but on their faithfulness to him.

Today, if someone feels excluded or without worth, they can remember that God looks at a willing heart. We can draw near to him with confidence and also welcome others who feel left out.
exp.55:4:
God promises faithful eunuchs a place in his house and within his walls, that is, a sense of belonging among his people. He gives them a name better than that of sons and daughters, an everlasting name that will never be erased.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Eunuchs and foreigners felt excluded, and the law placed restrictions on them (for example, Deuteronomy 23:1). Moreover, a eunuch had no children to carry on his name. God answers that whoever keeps his Sabbaths, chooses what pleases him, and holds fast to his covenant is welcome and remembered forever.

If you ever feel set aside, or believe you lack something needed to be valued before God, remember that he looks at the faith and obedience of the heart. Draw near without fear, and welcome with the same warmth those who feel left outside.
exp.55:5:
The explanation says that foreigners who draw near to God to serve him, who love his name and want to be his servants, are also welcome. They are asked to keep the Sabbath without defiling it, that is, without treating it as an ordinary day, and to hold firmly to God's covenant.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. At that time, Israel's law limited the participation of eunuchs and foreigners in certain aspects of worship. Here God declares that his house will be open to them, and that what matters most is loving and obeying him, not the person's origin or condition.

For today: if God receives with joy those who come to him with sincere love, we too should welcome into the church those who arrive from other countries, cultures or backgrounds. You might greet someone new today and offer them a place beside you.
exp.55:6:
God himself says he will bring a group of people to his holy mountain, that is, to Jerusalem, where the temple stands. There he will fill them with joy. Their whole burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be welcomed, that is, well received. And his house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The words before this one are addressed to foreigners who join themselves to the Lord, love him, and keep his covenant. In that time many thought they were left outside. God promises them a place, a name, and a full welcome in his house.

For today: if God opens the door to all who come to him with sincerity, we too should do the same. This week, invite or warmly welcome someone who feels like an outsider in your church or community, and pray with that person.
exp.55:9:
It says that the watchmen of the people, that is, their leaders, are blind and know nothing. They are like guard dogs that do not bark: they give no warning of danger. "Watchmen" are sentinels who keep watch from a tower. Those who are drowsy and lying down describe people who spend their time stretched out, and loving to slumber shows that they prefer comfort to their duty.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah after the return from exile. He has just promised to gather the scattered, and he also invites the nations. But now he denounces the leaders of Israel who neglect the people and seek their own gain, as the following verses show. Interpreters differ on exactly who these leaders are and when this took place.

Today: if you have any responsibility, whether in your family, your church, or your work, do not grow drowsy. Ask the Lord for open eyes, and speak with love and truth when you see a danger.
exp.55:10:
They say the people's leaders are like greedy dogs whose appetite is never satisfied. They are also shepherds who do not understand what they are doing. Each one goes off on his own path, looking out for his personal gain, every one for his own side, without caring about the others.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that foreigners and outcasts would be welcomed into his house. Then he accuses the watchmen, or lookouts, of Israel of being blind and asleep, failing to warn of danger. That is why the people are left exposed, like sheep before wild beasts. The next verse shows that they think only of feasting and drink.

Today the message invites us to examine our hearts if we lead others, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace. Ask yourself: do I care for people, or do I seek my own comfort? Ask God for a shepherd's heart that watches and serves.
exp.55:11:
Here the wicked leaders of Israel invite one another to a party. They say they will bring wine and get drunk on strong drink, which in this version is a potent beverage, not the apple juice of today. They expect tomorrow to be just like today, or even better.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just described the watchmen and shepherds of the people as blind, silent, and selfish. Instead of caring for and warning the people, they only seek their own pleasure. This verse shows their attitude: pleasure today and great confidence that tomorrow will stay the same.

For today: let us not live with the idea that there will always be time later. Whoever leads others, in the church or in the family, must care with responsibility and not merely seek their own comfort. Let us ask God to keep us alert.
exp.56:1:
This verse says that the righteous person enters into peace. When they die, they rest in their beds, a poetic way of speaking about the rest of death. Walking uprightly means living with sincerity, aware that God sees us. Beds are places of rest.

God speaks through Isaiah. Many righteous people died and no one noticed or asked why. The previous verse says the righteous are taken away before calamity, and many understand this as God's protection from the evil that was coming. Afterward, God addresses with harshness those who mocked and lived in rebellion.

For today: if you live faithfully before God and feel that no one values it, remember that He does see it. Your faithfulness is not lost, and your final rest is in His hands.
exp.56:2:
God firmly calls out a group: "Come closer, you children of the sorceress." A fortune-teller is someone who predicts the future through signs or magic. The words for adulterer and adulteress speak of unfaithfulness, and here they refer mainly to spiritual unfaithfulness: abandoning God for other gods. It is a way of saying that this people followed the bad example of their parents.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he comforted the righteous person who dies without anyone noticing, and now he addresses those who mock and practice idolatry. The contrast is strong: the righteous enter peace, while the rebels are called to account.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we place our trust in instead of God, such as superstitions, horoscopes, or modern idols. God invites us to return to him sincerely, without mocking those who follow him.
exp.56:6:
He says that the people set their bed on a high and lofty mountain, and that there they also went up to offer sacrifices. The bed is an image of the place where they gave themselves to other gods. "Lofty" means very steep and high.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Israel of being unfaithful, like a wife who leaves her husband. High mountains were places where idolatry was practiced. Many understand the bed as a symbol of spiritual adultery, not only of a literal act. Some details of the passage are debated, but the central message of unfaithfulness is clear.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we give the time, effort and heart that belong to God. God does not want divided loyalty. We can return to Him sincerely, knowing that He receives us with mercy.
exp.56:11:
God says he will reveal the "righteousness" of his people and their works, that is, everything they believe makes them good. But he says it with irony: those works will do them no good at all.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. He is addressing a people who had turned away from him, looking for support in idols and human alliances. They were worn out from all their effort, yet they did not want to return to God. The text then shows that those supports will be carried off by the wind, while whoever trusts in God will inherit the land.

For today: we can ask ourselves what we are trusting in to feel secure or accepted. Our works, though good, do not save us. We can rest in God and come to him with humility.
exp.56:12:
It says that when the people cry out for help, the idols and alliances they trusted will not be able to save them. Their "companies" are the groups gathered around them, that is, what was put together for protection. "But" is the word that turns the verse toward its contrast. The wind and the breath show that all of that is fragile. By contrast, whoever trusts in God will receive the land and will live on his holy mountain.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He rebukes a people who had forgotten Him, sought other gods, and feared people more than Him. Many understand that the land and the holy mountain speak of Jerusalem and the restoration; others also see a broader spiritual promise. Then God promises nearness to the humble.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, success. Those things help, but they do not sustain the soul. Today, hand over to God one specific worry and trust Him with it.
exp.56:16:
He says that God was angry with his people because of their greed, that is, their desire to gain more and more by unjust means. For this reason he punished them and turned his face away from them, meaning he withdrew his nearness and his favor. The phrase about being angry with force means that he was angered intensely. Even so, the people remained rebellious, walking wherever their heart wanted to go.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Isaiah. Shortly before, he is presented as the High and Exalted One, but also as one who dwells near the humble and the broken. Here he reminds them that his anger was a just correction, not an eternal rejection. In the next verse he announces that, although he saw their wicked ways, he will still heal them and comfort them.

For today: when you feel that God is correcting you, do not take it as abandonment. Examine honestly whether there is some craving or desire that is pulling you away from him, and return to him with humility. His discipline seeks to heal you, not to destroy you.
exp.56:17:
God says that he has seen how his people have lived, with their mistakes and their stubbornness, and yet he promises to heal them, to lead them as a shepherd does, and to give them comfort. For the phrase about leading them, the verse speaks of guiding and caring for them, and the wording about giving comfort is clear on its own. The ones who mourn are those who weep and grieve.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he said that he had been angered by the greed of the people, and that they kept on rebelling. But God does not want to stay angry forever, since the human spirit would break under it. His discipline has a limit, and his aim is to restore. Some scholars think this refers to the people in exile, though the message reaches anyone who turns back in repentance.

For today: if you feel wounded by your own mistakes or by a loss, do not hide from God. He already knows your path and offers you healing. Bring him your pain and your guilt today in prayer, and let him lead you.
exp.57:6:
The explanation says that the fasting which pleases God is shown in acts of kindness: sharing your food with someone who is hungry, welcoming into your home the poor who have no place to live, clothing the one who has no clothes, and not turning your back on your own flesh, that is, your relatives or anyone in need, who is of your very same human nature. Those who are wandering without direction or shelter are the ones described here.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people fasted with great outward religiosity, yet they continued to oppress others. God makes clear to them that he does not want only external rituals, but justice and compassion. Afterward he promises light, healing, and his closeness to those who live this way.

Today we can ask ourselves: who near me needs concrete help? It may be sharing a meal, giving away clothing in good condition, or supporting a family member. Praying and fasting are good, but God also calls us to love through deeds.
exp.57:13:
He says that if someone honors the Sabbath and stops pursuing their own profit on that day, God promises them three things: that they will delight themselves in the Lord, that he will make them ride upon the high places of the earth, and that he will feed them with the inheritance of Jacob. The promise that he will feed them with the inheritance of Jacob refers to the land and the blessings promised to Jacob's descendants.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and practiced their religion, but neglected justice and mercy. Before this verse, God asks them to honor the Sabbath as a day of delight and not of their own interests. The final phrase emphasizes that the promise is certain.

For today: set aside time each week to rest and be with God, leaving work and distractions behind, and ask him to teach you to delight in him.
exp.58:4:
They hatch vipers' eggs and weave spiders' webs. The wicked are like someone hatching eggs of venomous snakes and spinning webs. Those who are venomous serpents are deadly, and the one who eats of their eggs dies, and if they are crushed, a viper comes out. In other words, what they produce brings only harm and death.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He explains that God is neither deaf nor powerless; what separates them from Him is their sins: violence, lying, and injustice. Their webs are no use for clothing; in other words, their works cannot cover their guilt.

For today: examine what you produce with your words and decisions. What seems small, like a lie or an injustice, can bring harm. Ask God to cleanse you and guide you to act with truth and justice.
exp.58:5:
What it says: The verse compares the actions of wicked people to spider webs. A spider's web is fragile and cannot be made into clothing; it does not warm or cover anyone. In the same way, what these people do gives them no benefit and does not protect them. Their hands are full of injustice.

Context: Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel and explains why they feel that God is far away. The problem is not that God cannot save, but that the people have filled themselves with lies, violence and injustice (vv. 1-2). The prophet describes real sins and shows them with strong images, such as viper's eggs and spider webs.

For today: What is built on deceit or on abuse does not give true security. Today we can ask ourselves whether our work, our words and our businesses are honest. Doing what is right may cost more, but it is the only thing God blesses and the only thing that truly covers us.
exp.58:14:
Here the verse says that truth was lost in society: it was no longer allowed to act. Whoever turned away from evil was left as prey, that is, they were attacked or stripped of what they had. God saw this, and it grieved him that there was no justice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and describes their sin: lies, slander, and corruption in the public square, where justice was supposed to be done. This explains why God seems far away. The verses that follow show that God does not simply watch: he himself acts to save and to correct.

Today, if you are called to be honest and that costs you, do not be discouraged. God sees when truth is trampled and is not indifferent. Even so, keep speaking the truth with respect, and seek to be just in your work, your family, and your community.
exp.58:15:
What it says: God looks at his people and sees that no one stands up to set right so much injustice. He is astonished that there is no intercessor, that is, someone who steps in between and defends what is right. So he himself acts: his arm, which represents his power, brings salvation, and his own righteousness sustains him.

Context: The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people full of lies, violence and oppression, where even the one who avoided evil was persecuted. God does not ignore this: he sees it, and it grieves him. The verses that follow describe him as a warrior who puts on righteousness as his armor. Many Christians see here a sign of Christ, although the original text speaks first of the liberation of Israel.

For today: God is the one who saves, but he also seeks people willing to intercede and to defend the weak. Today you can pray for someone who suffers injustice and, if it is within your reach, help them with courage and humility.
exp.58:16:
He puts on a suit of armor, like a soldier about to go into battle. The breastplate is the piece of armor that protects the chest, and here it stands for righteousness. The helmet is the head covering, and it stands for salvation or deliverance. The "vengeance" is like the clothing that covers him: it refers to God doing justice and correcting evil. The "zeal" is his intense and steadfast love for his people and for what is right.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of a people full of injustice, lies, and violence. No one was defending what was right, and God was astonished that no one stepped in. So He himself acts. This passage presents God as a warrior who rescues and judges. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of the work of Christ, although Isaiah says it in the context of Israel.

Today we can trust that God is not indifferent to injustice. While He is at work, let us ask Him for the courage to defend the truth and help those who suffer, without taking personal revenge.
exp.58:18:
People from every part of the world, from where the sun sets to where it rises, will come to revere the name of the Lord and to acknowledge his glory. Here "fear" means to honor with awe. The verse also says that the enemy will come like a flood, that is, with overwhelming force, but the Spirit of the Lord will raise a standard against him. Some translators render this as the Spirit will put him to flight; the Hebrew text allows both ideas.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name. The people were living in injustice and sin, and no one was interceding. So God himself acts as a warrior who puts on righteousness as a breastplate. Then he promises a Redeemer for those who turn away from evil.

For today: when you feel that your problems are sweeping you along like a river, remember that God does not leave you alone. Come to him sincerely and trust that his Spirit sustains you.
exp.58:19:
God says he will send a Redeemer, that is, someone who rescues and sets free, to Zion, meaning Jerusalem and its people. This salvation is for those who turn from wickedness in Jacob, which is another name for Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the people are accused of injustice and sin, and God sees that no one can save them. So he himself acts. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:26-27, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. How it applies to Israel in the future is understood in different ways.

For today: salvation is a gift from God, but it is received by turning back to him. If there is something you need to leave behind, today you can confess it honestly and trust in the forgiveness that the Redeemer offers.
exp.59:0:
It says that God calls his people to arise and shine. The phrase translated here as "light" means light, and the word about the light having come refers to God's light rising like the sun at dawn. The glory of the Lord, that is, his presence and his beautiful character, is revealed upon them. They do not shine by themselves; the light comes from God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, which is discouraged and in darkness after hard times. Many believe he is addressing a people who are returning from exile or who are waiting for it. God promises to restore them and says that other nations will see that light and draw near. Some Christians also see here an announcement of Christ and his church, although this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if you are tired or discouraged, do not wait to feel strong before getting up. Fix your gaze on God, receive his light, and let it show in your kind treatment, your honesty, and your hope toward those around you.
exp.59:8:
This verse says that the isles, that is, distant lands along the sea, will place their hope in God. The ships of Tarshish, large trading vessels, will bring back the sons of Zion from far away, together with their silver and their gold. All of this will be to honor the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and the Holy One of Israel, who glorified his people. To "wait" here means to trust and to look forward in expectation.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, which had gone through judgment and punishment. Here he promises restoration: the scattered will return and other nations will join in worship. It is not known with certainty where Tarshish was; some think it lay in the western Mediterranean.

Today we can remember that everything we have, our work, resources, and talents, can be offered to God with gratitude. He also restores those who return to him.
exp.59:10:
It says that the gates of Jerusalem will always stand open, by day and by night, and will never be shut. In this way the wealth of the nations will be able to come in freely, and their kings as well, who will be brought to the city, that is, led or guided there.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who had suffered punishment and destruction. He promises them restoration and mercy. The gates were normally shut at night out of fear of enemies; here it is announced that the peace will be so secure that there will be no need to shut them. Some see here a fulfillment in history, and others a future or spiritual fulfillment.

For today: our lives and our church can live with confidence in the peace that God gives, keeping our doors open to receive and welcome everyone with generosity, without living dominated by fear.
exp.59:12:
It says that the finest trees of Lebanon, famous for its fine timber, will be brought to Zion to beautify the temple. The trees named in the verse are the fir, the pine, and the box, all trees with fine wood. The phrase "the place of my feet" refers to the sanctuary, where God makes his presence felt among his people. God promises to honor that place.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, encouraging Jerusalem after its humiliation. He promises restoration and says that the nations will bring their riches. Some see its fulfillment in the return from exile, others in Christ and the Church, and others in a future time. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: God delights in beautifying and honoring the place where he dwells. Offer him the best of your life, your time, and your talents, trusting that he restores what seemed abandoned.
exp.59:14:
Jerusalem (Zion) went through a period of abandonment and contempt. She was rejected and hated, so lonely that no one even passed through her. But God promises to change that situation: he will make her an everlasting excellence, that is, an honor that does not fade, and a joy that will pass from parents to children.

The passage is God speaking through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Zion. The people had suffered punishment and humiliation, and the text announces their restoration. The nearby verses speak of enemies bowing down and of God as Savior and Redeemer. Many see here a partial fulfillment after the exile and another still to come; interpreters understand it in different ways.

If today you feel forgotten or looked down upon, remember that God can turn abandonment into hope. Trust in his faithfulness, even though the process may take time.
exp.59:16:
It says that God will change what is poor and worn out into something better: instead of copper, gold; instead of iron, silver; instead of wood, brass; and instead of stones, iron. Furthermore, he will make peace the ruler of his people and righteousness the one who collects what is owed. A tribute is what is paid to an authority, and those who collect it do so with harsh demands.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who felt abandoned and despised. He promises restoration and glory. Many understand this as hope for the return from exile, and others also see a future fulfillment in the kingdom of God. Interpreters explain it in various ways.

For today: when you feel that your life is worn down, surrender that area to God and ask him to place his peace and his righteousness in it, trusting that he knows how to restore.
exp.59:17:
It says that in the land of Israel there will no longer be violence, ruin, or destruction within its borders. The source's explanation of a word for serious damage and the word for territory's limits must be rewritten: "Ruin" in the verse's sense means serious harm, and "borders" are the limits of the land. The walls will be called Salvation (safety, protection) and the gates Praise. That is, security will come from God, and the people will respond with gratitude.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who had suffered wars and exile. He promises them restoration: peace instead of oppression, and Himself as light and Savior. Some understand this as the restoration after the exile; others see it as a hope looking toward God's final kingdom.

For today: when you live with fear or wounds, remember that true security comes from God. You can "name" your walls: instead of repeating your fears, give thanks today for a concrete protection you have received.
exp.59:18:
This verse says that the sun will no longer be needed to light the day, and the moon will no longer be needed to light the night. God himself will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a city that had gone through suffering and exile. Before this verse he promises peace, justice, and an end to violence. After it he says that the days of mourning will come to an end. Some understand this as a restoration after the exile, and others as a promise that will be fully fulfilled in the future. Revelation 21:23 uses a similar image, and this helps us read it with Christian hope.

Today, when you sit in darkness because of sadness or uncertainty, pray and remember that the LORD is your steady light. Seek him every day, because his presence does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.59:19:
It says that the sun of Jerusalem will never set and its moon will not wane, because God himself will be its light forever. The verse's word "wane" means to lessen or fade out. The days of mourning, the sorrow over a loss, will come to an end.

It is a promise from God through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who had suffered violence and destruction. It speaks of a restored Zion, where there will be salvation and praise. Some believers see it partly fulfilled in the return from exile, others in the work of Christ, and others in the final restoration, as in Revelation 21:23.

For today: when you go through dark moments, remember that God is not merely a temporary help but a light that endures. Place your hope in him, and let his presence sustain you while you wait for the end of your tears.
exp.60:1:
It says that God's servant comes to announce a year of the Lord's good pleasure, that is, a time of favor and grace. It also speaks of a day of vengeance, which points to God's justice against evil. And his mission is to comfort all who mourn, that is, those who weep and suffer.

The one speaking is a servant anointed by the Spirit, and the passage goes on to speak of good news for the brokenhearted. It was probably addressed to a battered people living among ruins. Jesus read this text in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18-19), but he stopped before the day of vengeance, and that suggests this aspect is reserved for his return. Some interpret it this way; others see it differently.

For today: if you are grieving or weary, God sees you and wants to comfort you. Tell him your pain in prayer, and also look for someone you can comfort this week.
exp.60:2:
This verse promises that God will change the grief of his people into blessing. Ashes and mourning were signs of deep sorrow; in exchange, God gives beauty, the oil of joy (the oil used at festivals), and a garment of praise in place of a heavy spirit. Those who mourn are the ones who weep. In the end, the people are called trees of righteousness, planted by God to display his glory.

The speaker is a servant anointed by God's Spirit, sent to comfort. Isaiah addresses a people struck by exile and ruin. Jesus read the preceding verses in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied them to himself (Luke 4:16-21).

For today: if you are going through grief, bring your sorrow to God with sincerity. He can comfort you and, in time, cause something new to grow in you. Let others walk with you through that process.
exp.60:6:
This verse promises a complete reversal. Where there was shame and dishonor, there will be praise. The word "portion" in the verse refers to the share of land that falls to each person. The idea of "double" means twice as much. So God says the people will receive twice what they lost, and they will have joy that does not end.

The message comes from the prophet Isaiah, speaking on God's behalf to a humbled people, probably returning from exile. God promises to restore them and to make them his priests before the nations. Christians see here an announcement of the work of Jesus, who quoted the beginning of this chapter in Luke 4.

For today: if you carry shame over past mistakes or losses, do not stay there. Bring them to God in prayer and trust that he restores. His joy can replace what hurt you.
exp.60:7:
God says that he loves justice, that is, what is right, and that he hates robbery mixed in with offerings, as if an offering could cover over what was stolen. For this reason he promises to support the work of his people with truth and to make with them an everlasting covenant, a bond that never ends.

Here God himself speaks, in a message of comfort for a humbled people. Before this, he promises to change their shame into honor and their sorrow into joy. Many understand that his justice is the basis of that restoration. Christians also see in this passage, which Jesus read in Luke 4, a promise that points to Christ, although there is discussion about how all of it is fulfilled.

For today: God does not want offerings or service while we practice injustice. Review your work, your dealings, and your money, and seek to be honest and fair. In this way your worship will be sincere, and you can trust that God keeps his promises.
exp.60:10:
It says that just as the earth brings forth its bud, and as the garden makes the things sown in it spring up, God will make righteousness and praise spring forth before all the nations. A new shoot is a bud, and the seed is what is sown. The nations are the peoples of the earth.

The one speaking seems to be God's anointed messenger, who comes announcing good news to the afflicted (Isaiah 61:1-3). Christians often see Jesus here, who read this passage in Nazareth (Luke 4). God will restore his people, clothe them with salvation and righteousness, and the nations will see that God has blessed them.

For today: you cannot force a seed to grow, but you can plant it and trust. Plant patiently works of kindness, truth, and prayer, and let God bring forth the fruit in his time.
exp.61:2:
Verse 3 says that Zion, that is, God's people in Jerusalem, will be like a beautiful crown and a royal ornament. What matters is where it is: not on its own head, but in the hand of the LORD. A royal diadem is a crown or royal band. Glory speaks of beauty and honor.

The speaker seems to be the prophet Isaiah, although some think it is the Messiah. He says he will not keep silent for Jerusalem. The people were discouraged, with the city in ruins. God promises to restore it, give it a new name, and show his righteousness to the nations.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements or on what others think of you. God holds you in his hand and rejoices over you. Today, when you feel discouraged, remember that you belong to him and that he cares for you.
exp.61:6:
It says that those who pray for Jerusalem should not give God any rest. Rest here means a break or pause. They are to keep pressing until he makes it secure and firm, and makes it a source of praise throughout the earth. To make it firm means to establish it, leaving it safe and steady.

Isaiah speaks to a people who were waiting for Jerusalem to be restored. God has set watchmen on its walls, and they keep reminding the Lord of his promises. This is not because God forgets them; rather, persistent prayer joins us to his purpose. Some understand the watchmen to be prophets, while others understand them to be the whole faithful people.

For today: persevere in prayer for what God has promised, whether for your family, your church, or your community. Pray with constancy and hope, trusting that God finishes what he begins.
exp.61:7:
God has made a solemn oath. The phrases about his strength and power speak of his might. He promises that he will never again hand over his people's grain for their enemies to eat, nor let foreigners drink the wine that his people worked to produce. Outsiders, meaning oppressors, are the people in view here.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem. Before this, enemies would carry off the people's harvests. Many readers understand this message as encouragement for those who had been exiled or had only recently returned, who were suffering poverty. God assures them of restoration: the fruit of their labor will be for them, and for praising him.

Today, we can trust that God cares for those who work and wait on him. When you feel that your effort is being lost, pray with perseverance, like the watchmen of the previous verse, and rest in God's faithfulness, while continuing to work honestly.
exp.61:10:
God has made an announcement that reaches to the farthest corners of the world. The message is for the daughter of Zion, that is, the people of Jerusalem: their Savior is coming. The reward and the work are understood as what God brings with him: the prize, the restoration, and the fruit of his labor on behalf of his people. Here, hearing means making known.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to a people who are returning from exile or waiting to be restored. The verses before this one call for preparing the way and raising a signal for the nations. What follows promises that they will be called a holy people and the redeemed of the Lord. Christians also see here a sign pointing to Jesus, the Savior.

Today we can live with active hope: God is coming to rescue and to restore. Prepare your heart by removing a specific stone, such as a grudge or an excuse, and share a word of encouragement with someone.
exp.62:0:
This verse presents a question and an answer. Someone asks who this figure is who comes from Edom, from the city of Bozrah, with garments stained a deep red. He looks glorious and walks with great strength. He himself answers: he speaks in righteousness and is mighty to save.

Edom was a neighboring people and a frequent enemy of Israel, and Bozrah was one of its important cities. In the verses that follow, the figure appears as a warrior who judges the nations. Many Christians see here the Lord himself, and some connect him with Christ, although there are different interpretations of the details. Edom may represent God's enemies in general.

For today: we can trust that God is just and also mighty to save. When we see so much injustice, we do not have to take revenge; we can hand everything over to him and keep doing good.
exp.62:1:
Here the prophet asks the warrior who is approaching why his clothing is stained red, like the clothing of someone who has trodden grapes in the winepress, the vat where the juice of the grapes was squeezed out. The reddish color is so intense that it is compared to deep red.

The prophet Isaiah sees God coming from Edom, a people hostile to Israel, as both judge and savior. He himself answers afterward that he has trampled the nations in his anger, and that his clothing was stained. Some understand this as historical judgment on God's enemies; others see it as a announcement of the final judgment. Christians also connect it with Revelation 19, although how it connects is debated.

For today: God is not indifferent to injustice. We can hand over our pain to him, trust that he will do justice, and reject personal revenge. He also saves and redeems his people.
exp.62:2:
He says God trod the winepress alone, the place where grapes were pressed to get the wine. No one was with him. He trod the peoples in his anger and crushed them in his fury, and their blood stained his garments. It is a strong image: the red juice of the grapes is compared with judgment on the nations.

The Lord speaks, arriving from Edom and Bozrah, a land hostile to Israel. He answers the question of why his clothing is red. It is poetic language that shows God as a warrior who executes justice and rescues his people. Some see here a foretelling of the final judgment; others, a specific historical judgment.

For today: we do not have to carry revenge or all the injustice of the world. We can trust that God sees evil and will act with justice, and so let go of resentment and seek peace.
exp.62:10:
The verse says that, after God had become an enemy to his people because of their rebellion, someone remembers the days of old, when Moses led Israel. It asks: where is the God who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of his flock, and who put his Holy Spirit within them?

This passage is a lament prayer. Some interpreters think the people themselves are speaking, and others think God is speaking as he remembers; the Hebrew text allows both readings. What is clear is that the people, in the middle of the punishment, look back and remember how God rescued them at the Red Sea.

When you feel God is far away, do what Israel did: remember how he has helped you before. That memory can sustain your faith and lead you to cry out with hope.
exp.62:12:
He says God led his people through the deep waters of the Red Sea with as much sureness as a horse walking across open, level ground without stumbling. The wilderness here is understood as open country or grassland, not as difficult sand. The picture is one of firm, calm steps with no stumbling.

The speaker is the prophet, speaking on behalf of the people, in a prayer of lament. He recalls the exodus with Moses in order to appeal to God: if God cared for them so well before, where is that same help now? The people feel far from God and ask that he show his compassion again.

For today: when you go through a situation that feels like a deep abyss, remember how God has helped you before. That memory can sustain your prayer and your trust, even when today you do not see the way clearly.
exp.63:2:
This verse recalls a moment when God came down and acted with power. The phrase about the mountains means that the mountains melted or trembled before his presence, as if they were nothing.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, praying on behalf of the people of Israel. He seems to ask God to intervene once more, as he did before, probably recalling the exodus from Egypt and Sinai, although some see it as a more general reference. The people feel far from God and need his help.

For today: when you feel tired or without hope, remember what God has already done in your life and in his history with his people. Pray with confidence, asking him to act, and wait on him with humility.
exp.63:4:
He meets those who gladly do what is right, that is, those who remember you and walk in your ways. Then the people admit that God was angry because they had sinned. The phrase "in those is continuance, and we shall be saved" is hard to understand. It could mean that there is ongoing life and hope of salvation in God's ways, or it could mean that their sin lasted a long time and they still hope to be saved.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of repentance. They remember God's mighty works in the past and ask him to act again. They acknowledge that their spiritual condition is bad, as the following verses show.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God. Admit your sin honestly, remember how faithful he has been to you, and return to his ways, trusting that he gladly receives anyone who seeks him.
exp.63:9:
What it says: The people describe with sorrow how the land has been left. The holy cities are empty, Zion (the mountain where the temple stood) looks like a wilderness, and Jerusalem is a lonely place, without people. "Desolation" here means a place that has been abandoned and laid waste.

Context: The prophet speaks on behalf of the whole people of Israel, in a prayer of repentance. They have just acknowledged that God is their Father and their potter, and they ask him not to remember their sin forever. Many believe it reflects the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile, though some also see it as a prophetic look toward that grief.

For today: When your life feels empty or in ruins, do not hide your pain. Bring it honestly before God, acknowledge what has gone wrong, and trust that he, as the potter, can still rebuild what has been broken.
exp.64:1:
God says that he spread out his hands all day long, meaning that again and again he reached out with open arms to a stubborn people. That people does not walk in the good way; they follow their own thoughts, that is, their own ideas.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The verses before this one show that he let himself be found even by those who were not looking for him. Then he describes Israel, who offended him with idolatrous practices. Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10:20-21 and applies it both to the Gentiles and to Israel.

For today: if God still holds out his arms, do not wait until everything is settled in your life. Ask yourself in what area you are following only your own ideas, and return to him with humility and simplicity.
exp.64:2:
This verse speaks of a people who offend God openly, "to my face," and who keep doing it without stopping. Their sin was false worship: they offered sacrifices in gardens, that is, in orchards used for pagan worship, and they burned incense on altars made of brick, probably altars they had built for themselves. Some scholars think it refers to idolatrous rituals, although the exact detail is understood in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he stretched out his hands all day to a rebellious people who sought him little, and now he shows the pain and seriousness of that rebellion. God was patient, but they kept following their own path.

For today: examine whether your way of worshiping God is sincere and according to his Word, or whether you are following your own ideas. Come to him with humility and obedience, not out of habit or appearance.
exp.64:5:
It says that God keeps a record of what this people has done, and that he will not stay silent. The phrase about his coming to act means that he will come to take action. The phrase about repaying into their bosom means that he will give them back what they deserve, so that they receive it in full. The bosom is the chest or lap, where what was given was received.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He addresses a rebellious people who practiced idolatrous customs, such as eating what was forbidden and considering themselves holier than others. Their religion was false and proud. Even so, the passage goes on to show that God preserves his faithful servants, for he will not destroy them all.

For today: God sees everything, including what we do in secret and the pride with which we look down on others. Instead of boasting of being holy, we can humbly ask him to cleanse us and teach us to treat others with mercy.
exp.64:7:
God uses the image of a cluster of grapes where new wine is still found. Someone sees it and says, "Do not throw it away, for a blessing is in it." In the same way God promises that, for the sake of his servants, he will not destroy the whole people. Here "destroy" means to ruin or throw away.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just announced judgment on a people who burned incense on the mountains and offended him with their idolatry. But even in the midst of punishment, God makes clear that he will preserve a faithful group. He then promises to bring descendants from Jacob and Judah, and that his chosen ones will live again in the land.

For today: God sees value in those who are faithful to him, even if they are few, and he does not lose them in the midst of crises. If you feel small or alone in your faith, remember that he cares for you. He also invites us to live with sincerity, so that we do not keep following what offends him.
exp.64:9:
He says that God will turn two places into lands of rest and abundance for his people. Sharon was a fertile plain beside the Mediterranean Sea, good for grazing. The valley of Achor lay on the other side of the territory, near Jericho, and its name is associated with distress. A fold is a pen or place where livestock rest. A safe pasture is what is meant by the phrase. The promise is for those who sought God.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces that, although the people have been rebellious and will be judged, he will not destroy everything. He will preserve a faithful remnant. The contrast is clear: those who seek him receive restoration, and those who worship Fortune and Fate face judgment.

For today: God can transform our valleys of distress into places of rest. If we seek him sincerely, we can trust that he cares for and restores his own, even after difficult times.
exp.64:11:
God says he will hand over to judgment those who rejected him. The verse's wording points to a sword and a slaughter. Being put to the sword and bowing down to the slaughter show that they will not be able to escape. The reason: God called them and they did not answer, he spoke and they did not listen, and they chose what was evil in his sight and what he did not delight in.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a group of the people who had left him and worshiped false gods of luck and fate. Scholars debate the exact details of who they were, but the point is clear. God contrasts this group with his faithful servants, who will be blessed.

For today: God still calls. Today we can put our trust in luck, money, or success instead of him. Let us listen to his voice soon and answer with humility, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.64:13:
It says there will be two very different outcomes. God's servants will sing for joy, with hearts full of gladness. Those who rebelled will cry out in pain, with wounded hearts, and they will howl, that is, lament with loud groaning, because their spirit will be broken.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people where many, although God called them again and again, did not respond and chose what is wrong. God contrasts those who are faithful to him with those who reject him. The verses that follow promise that the past troubles will be forgotten for the faithful.

Today we can examine whether we are responding when God speaks to us. Listening to his voice and obeying it today leads us to a deep joy, while ignoring it brings an emptiness that later hurts.
exp.64:15:
This verse says that in the future God promises, people will seek blessing and make oaths only in the name of the God of truth, that is, the faithful God who keeps his word. To swear is to affirm something by calling God as witness. It also says that the troubles of the past will be forgotten and hidden from his eyes.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is separating those who despise him, who will suffer, from his servants, who will have joy. Right after this he announces new heavens and a new earth. Some see here a restoration after the exile, others the final renewal of all things; some see both.

For today: if your past or your pain weighs on you, trust that God is faithful and able to heal. And strive to make your words and promises true, as he is.
exp.64:17:
The explanation says that God's people should be glad and rejoice forever in what God is creating.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who have suffered greatly and need hope. He promises new heavens and a new earth, where the pain of the past will be forgotten. Some scholars see here a near restoration, and others see the final promise of a new world. It can also be read as both.

When you are going through a trial, remember that God has not given up on his creation. Take a moment today to thank him for something good you already see, and to trust that he can turn your sorrow into joy.
exp.64:19:
In the renewed Jerusalem, it says, there will no longer be babies who die after only a few days, nor old people who die without having lived a full life. Dying at a hundred years old will be seen as dying young. And the sinner who reaches a hundred years will suffer the curse, that is, the consequences of his sin.

God speaks through Isaiah. He promises his people new heavens and a new earth, where weeping and crying will come to an end. Christians understand this in different ways: some see it as a picture of eternity, and others as a stage before it. All agree that God will restore life and justice.

For today: when death or pain weighs on you, trust that God promises to restore everything. In the meantime, care for the lives of others and live with integrity.
exp.64:22:
God promises that his people will no longer live with efforts that come to nothing. What they work for, they will enjoy. Nor will they have children for sorrow or disaster, since the phrase about bearing children for a curse speaks of raising children who suffer calamity. They and their descendants will be blessed by the Lord.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises new heavens and a new earth to a people who had suffered losses, injustice and exile. Before, others ate what they had planted; now God gives them back peace, security and joy. Some see here a complete future fulfillment, others also see a foretaste in the restoration of Israel.

For today: when work or family wear you down or worry you, entrust them to God in prayer. He promises a future where nothing is lost. In the meantime, work with faith, knowing that God sees and cares for your effort.
exp.64:23:
This verse says that God will answer his people even before they ask him for help. And while they are still speaking, he has already heard them.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is describing a future restoration, a new heavens and a new earth (v. 17), in which his people will live in peace, without working in vain or suffering injustice. Scholars debate whether this is fulfilled in the return from exile, in the age of the church, or at the end of time. Many see a mixture of these ideas.

For today: you can pray with confidence, knowing that God is neither distant nor slow to hear you. He knows your need. Keep praying, but do it with rest, without thinking that you must convince him to attend to you.
exp.65:0:
God says the heavens are his throne, and the earth is the footstool where he rests his feet. Then he asks: what house could be built for him, and what place could be his resting place? God cannot be contained in any building.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This is the end of the book, and he addresses a people who valued the temple and the sacrifices very highly. The verses that follow show that God is not concerned with rituals offered without a sincere heart. He looks to the humble person, the one who respects his word. Scholars debate which temple is in view, but the central message is clear.

For today: it is not enough to attend a place or keep religious customs. Today you can draw near to God with humility, listening to his word with respect and obeying it from the heart.
exp.65:2:
God says that the offerings of certain people are as repugnant to him as murder or a pagan sacrifice. The grain offering, the incense, and the pig, an animal unclean for Israel, are also mentioned in this passage. Those people chose their own way and loved their abominations.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that heaven is his throne and that he does not need a temple made by human hands. He looks to the humble person who trembles at his word. Some believe the people mixed the worship of God with idolatrous practices; the text does not spell this out.

Today: it is not enough to keep rituals, go to church, or give offerings. God seeks a humble heart that obeys his word. Ask him to examine your heart.
exp.65:3:
God says that He too will choose the punishment that fits them: He will bring upon them the very thing they feared. The reason is that He called them and no one answered; He spoke and they would not listen. They did evil in His sight and chose what does not please Him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people practiced a religion that was only for show: they offered sacrifices, but with their hearts far from God, and for this reason He compares those offerings to detestable things. God contrasts this group with those who are humble and tremble at His word, that is, who take it seriously with reverence.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly answer when God speaks to us through His Word. Before carrying out religious acts, it is good to listen with humility and obey. God looks for an attentive heart, not just ceremonies.
exp.65:6:
It says that Zion gave birth suddenly, without going through the usual process. Normally childbirth brings long pain and a period of waiting; here everything happens in reverse.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just comforted the faithful who are rejected by their own brothers, and he promises that those who rejected them will be put to shame. Then he announces a restoration so swift that it seems unbelievable: a nation born in a day. Scholars debate whether this refers to the return from exile, to the church, or to a future fulfillment, and it may include several of these meanings.

For today: when your situation seems to move very slowly or has no way out, remember that God does not depend on our timing or on what seems possible. Remain faithful and wait on him with confidence, because he finishes what he begins.
exp.65:7:
God asks questions to show something astonishing. No one has seen or heard of such a thing: that an entire land would be born in a single day, or that a nation would appear all at once. "Zion" is Jerusalem, the people of God. The phrase "was in labor" means she suffered pains to give birth. Yet as soon as the labor began, she already had her children.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is comforting his people after times of judgment and sorrow, and he promises to restore Jerusalem. Interpreters differ: some see a return from exile, others the arrival of God's renewed people, and others a fulfillment that is still future.

For today: when your situation seems slow or impossible, remember that God can work in ways you do not expect. Trust that he finishes what he promises, and in the meantime, pray and wait with hope.
exp.65:9:
The explanation says that all who love Jerusalem and have mourned for her are invited to rejoice and celebrate with her. "Rejoice" means to take delight with joy, and "mourn" means to be in grief, sad and hurting.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do. The verses before it say that God brings a nation to birth suddenly, and that Zion will have children. Then comes the promise of comfort and peace like a river. Many understand this to refer to the restoration of God's people; others also see a future fulfillment. Interpreters differ on this point.

For today: if you are sad over situations that hurt, such as a family, a church, or a community, God promises comfort. Trust that your sadness is not the end, and let Him lead you little by little into joy.
exp.65:10:
It says that those who love Jerusalem will be like a nursing baby who feeds and is satisfied at its mother's breast. That breast gives comfort, that is, consolation. The idea of drawing out milk with delight refers to the abundance of the restored city, and its glory and beauty are the fullness of the restored city. It is an image of nourishment, rest, and complete joy.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah at the end of the book. After the exile, the people were grieving and the city lay in ruins. God promises to restore Jerusalem like a mother who nurtures her children, and the verses that follow confirm this: he himself will comfort them as a mother does. Many also see here a broader hope for the future.

For today: when you are tired or sad, do not look for comfort only in distractions. Turn to God in prayer and to the community of believers, where he often gives nourishment and rest to the soul.
exp.65:11:
God himself promises to bring peace to Jerusalem, and that peace will be abundant, like a river that never runs dry. It also speaks of the riches of the nations that will come like a stream that has overflowed its banks. The people are described as a child: they will nurse, be carried in arms, and be bounced on the knees, being shown tender affection.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. His people had gone through pain, punishment and disappointment. God promises them restoration and joy. The verses that follow compare his comfort to that of a mother. Some understand this as a promise to the restored Israel, and others also see an announcement of God's future kingdom.

For today: if you are weary or wounded, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Come to God honestly and let him comfort you, as a child rests in its mother's arms.
exp.65:19:
It says that people from all the nations will bring your "brothers" back, that is, the scattered people of God, to Jerusalem. They will bring them as an offering to the Lord, on horses, in chariots, in litters (stretchers or seats carried by people or animals), on mules, and on camels. It compares this to the Israelites who brought their offering in clean vessels to the temple.

God himself speaks at the end of the book of Isaiah. He announces that he will gather all the nations so that they see his glory. He will send messengers to distant lands that have never heard of him. Scholars understand who these "brothers" are in different ways: scattered Jews, or believers from all peoples. The text that follows speaks of priests taken from among them, which is a very open idea.

For today: God wants his glory to reach all peoples, and every person brought to him to be a clean offering. We can pray for someone far from God and help draw them near with love and patience.
exp.65:20:
God promises that he will take "of them" to be priests and Levites. Priests and Levites were those who served God in the worship of the temple. The word "them" seems to refer to people brought from the nations, although some scholars think it refers to scattered Israelites who return. Both readings exist.

The Lord speaks near the end of Isaiah. He has just announced that his survivors will carry his glory to distant nations that never heard of him. Then he promises new heavens and a new earth, where all flesh will worship him. What is surprising is that priestly service, once limited to one family, is now opened up in a broader way.

For today: God does not look at our origin, but calls us to serve him. Ask him how you can serve others with what you have, without thinking that you are not fit for it.
exp.65:21:
He says that God is making new heavens and a new earth, and that this new creation will last forever before him. In the same way, he promises that the descendants of his people and their name, or their identity, will also endure. "Descendants" here means offspring. "Endure" means to stand firm and not disappear.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. After speaking of judgment, he announces hope: people from all the nations will be brought to worship him in Jerusalem, and some will even become priests. Interpreters debate whether this refers to Israel, to the church, or to both, and whether it is fulfilled in the present time or in the future.

For today: if your life feels fragile or uncertain, remember that God upholds what he promises. You can entrust your future and that of your family to the one who will make a creation that never ends.
exp.12:1:
It says to raise a banner on a barren hilltop, a signal that everyone can see. A loud call is made and a hand is waved to gather an army. "Call aloud to them" means shouting to the soldiers. That army is to enter "the gates of the nobles," that is, through the entrances of the lords and rulers of Babylon.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, and God himself gives the command. He wants to show that he directs the nations and that Babylon's power is not final. Interpreters explain in different ways which historical events the passage refers to, but the central message is that God judges the pride of empires.

For today: trust that God governs history, even when the powers of the world seem untouchable. This invites us to live with humility and not to place our security in money, politics, or prestige.
exp.49:3:
The explanation says that God has given the Servant "the tongue of discipleship," meaning a tongue shaped by teaching, so that he can sustain the weary with a word. Every morning God awakens his ear so that he listens as a disciple does, with attention and a readiness to be taught.

The Servant of the Lord speaks in the third of Isaiah's "Servant songs." Before this, God rebuked Israel because no one answered his call. Now the Servant does answer and listen. Many Christians see Jesus here, who suffered without rebelling, as the following verses show. Others first emphasize the meaning for the prophet or for Israel.

For today: before speaking with someone who is exhausted, begin by listening to God yourself, in the morning, in prayer and in his Word. In this way your words will be timely and will bring encouragement, not just opinions.
exp.51:9:
The explanation says that God "has bared his holy arm," meaning he has rolled up his sleeve to act with power, like someone getting ready for hard work or battle. It is a "holy" arm, pure and faithful to his character. He has done this in the sight of all the nations. The phrase "all the ends of the earth" refers to the far limits of the world, and "salvation" means the rescue or deliverance that comes from God.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were in exile. The watchmen, or sentinels, announce that God is returning to Zion and comforting Jerusalem. A deliverance so clear is promised that even the nations will see it. Many Christians also see in this a announcement of salvation in Christ, and the New Testament connects it with the gospel.

For today: when you feel weak, remember that God acts with power and faithfulness. Trust in his work and share it with others, because his salvation is for everyone.
exp.61:5:
God says he has posted watchmen (guards, sentinels) on the walls of Jerusalem. They will never be silent, whether by day or by night. Then he speaks to "you who call on the LORD," that is, those who keep reminding him of his promises, and tells them to take no rest.

Here God speaks through Isaiah, or the prophet himself speaks, to a people who felt abandoned. God has just promised that Jerusalem will no longer be forsaken, but loved, like a bride. These watchmen keep up prayer and waiting until the promise is fulfilled. Some think they are prophets; others, that they are those who pray. The text does not fully clarify this.

Today we can pray steadily for what God has already promised, even when it takes a long time. Choose a promise from the Bible and bring it before God each day, with confidence and without growing weary.
exp.3:1:
After judgment, God promises to bring something beautiful for his people. "The Branch of the LORD" is a new shoot, and "the fruit of the land" is the harvest that comes from the ground. Both will be a source of beauty and glory, and a matter of pride, for the people of Israel who survive.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. The chapter before announces a harsh judgment on Jerusalem, so severe that seven women would seek a single man just to be called by his name and take away their shame. This verse shifts the tone and offers hope. Many understand "the Branch" as a picture of the Messiah, that is, Jesus; others see it as the restoration of the land, and some see both.

For today: even when we go through loss or painful consequences, God can make something new grow. Trust that his final word is restoration, not ruin.
exp.43:16:
This verse describes a man who takes part of a log to cook his food and warm himself, and from the rest he makes an idol. Then he bows down before it, worships it, and prays to it, saying, "Save me, for you are my god." The rest of the wood is what remains after he has burned part of it, and the carved figure is the image he shapes from that leftover piece. To bow down is to lower oneself in worship before the figure.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who lived surrounded by nations that worshipped idols. With irony, he shows how absurd idolatry is: the same wood serves for the daily fire and for a "god." The verses that follow say that this person does not reflect, because his mind is closed.

For today: let us review what we are placing in God's place, even good things, such as money, work, or success. They cannot save us. Let us ask God to help us trust in him alone.
exp.7:3:
God says that, before the boy knows how to cry "Father" or "Mother," the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria. "Will be carried off" means they will lose their power. "Plunder" is the goods taken in war.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. King Ahaz of Judah was afraid of Syria (Damascus) and of Israel (Samaria), who were threatening him. God gives him a sign through the son of the prophet, named Maher-shalal-hash-baz, a name usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the prey." The witnesses recorded the prophecy before it was fulfilled.

For today: when enemies or problems seem enormous, remember that God governs history. Trust in Him instead of seeking security in human alliances or in your own cleverness.
exp.23:12:
It says that when God judges the earth, very few people will be left among the nations. It is like an olive tree after it has been harvested, or like the leftover grapes someone gathers after the grape harvest is finished. The explanation calls these few leftover grapes "gleanings," and the grape harvest is the "vintage." Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking. Chapters 24 to 27 describe a judgment on the whole earth for its sin, and joy disappears. But this verse looks ahead to a small remnant that survives. According to the context that follows, that remnant lifts up its voice and praises the LORD.
