Some scholars see here a historical judgment, and others see an announcement of the end of time; the text allows both readings.

For today: even in dark times, God cares for those who are faithful to him. You can choose to praise him today, even when everything around you seems lost.
exp.40:13:
Do not fear, says God to his people. He calls them "you worm, O Jacob," an image of weakness, and speaks to "you few men of Israel," meaning a small group. Then he promises: "I will help you." He identifies himself as "your Redeemer," the one who rescues and frees, and as "the Holy One of Israel."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a frightened people, surrounded by powerful nations. He reminds them that he holds them by the hand and that their enemies will be reduced to nothing. He does not praise their strength; he shows them that their security lies in the one who rescues them. Then he promises that they will be like a new threshing sledge, a tool from the field, and that they will end up rejoicing in God.

When you feel small or without strength, do not trust in what you have. Remember who holds you up. Pray today like this: "Lord, you are my help; take my hand."
exp.41:19:
This verse describes someone who sees many things but does not keep watch over them, and who has open ears but does not hear. The explanation of the Hebrew word translated "keep watch" is "pay attention" or "notice." It is like seeing and hearing without really understanding or obeying.

God speaks through Isaiah to his people Israel, whom he calls his servant. He had given them his instruction and his works, but they did not respond. The verses that follow speak of their ruin as a consequence. Some understand that the one described is Israel in its calling, while others connect it with the ideal Servant. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

We can hear sermons and read the Bible, and yet change nothing. Today, before reading or listening to the Word, ask God for an attentive heart, and choose one specific thing you will obey this week.
exp.21:7:
He says that God has uncovered the defenses of Judah, that is, he has exposed its weakness. The "defenses" are what shelter and protect the city. Then the people looked toward the weapons in the House of the Forest, a storehouse of arms that Solomon had built (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17). In other words, they sought safety in military means.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the message about the "valley of vision," which is Jerusalem. The city is surrounded by enemies, and its inhabitants rush to build walls, secure water, and prepare weapons. But the prophet rebukes them for not looking to God, who allowed that crisis (v. 11). Scholars debate which exact moment he has in mind, perhaps the Assyrian threat in the time of Hezekiah.

For today: preparing and planning is wise, but we should not trust only in our own resources. Before rushing to find solutions, stop and ask God what he wants to tell you in the difficulty.
exp.2:24:
This verse announces that the men of Jerusalem will die by the sword, and that its warriors, that is, its military strength, will fall in battle. "Your men" are the men, and "by the sword" means by the sword. "Your warriors" refers to the fighters who defended the city.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. Before this, he described the pride of the women, who trusted in their jewels and their beauty, and announced that all of that would be lost. Now judgment reaches the men. Many understand this as a warning of invasion, although the text does not give exact details of when it happened.

For today: do not put your security in what is passing away, such as appearance, money, or strength. Trust in God, and let Him correct your pride before life does it with blows.
exp.0:24:
God says that he will turn his hand against Jerusalem to purify it, as one does with metal. The impurities that rise to the surface when silver is melted down are the dross, and the lesser metal mixed in with it is what the verse calls impurities. God says he will thoroughly purge away the dross and remove all of it. He promises to take away what contaminates.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he denounced the leaders of Judah for accepting bribes and not defending the fatherless or the widow. His hand here is correction, not only punishment, since the following verse promises to restore righteous judges and a faithful city.

For today: God corrects because he wants to heal, not to destroy. We can ask him to show us what dross is in our hearts, such as selfishness or injustice, and accept his correction with trust, seeking to help those who most need it.
exp.40:15:
God says he will make the enemies like chaff that is blown away. To "winnow" grain is to toss threshed grain into the air so the wind carries off the chaff. The verse says a wind will carry them away and a gale will scatter them, meaning the enemies will be swept off and dispersed. Then the verse turns. "But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel." Where the enemies are scattered, God's people will rejoice and take pride in knowing the Holy One of Israel.

God speaks to Israel, calling them worms and few, that is, weak and small. He encourages them not to fear, because he is their Redeemer. He compares them to a new threshing sledge, a tool that crushes grain, to say that God will use them with power against what looks like a mountain. Interpreters debate exactly who these enemies are; the text does not name them here.

For today: when you feel small before an enormous problem, do not put your trust in your own strength. Bring your fear to God and seek your joy in him, rather than in everything turning out well.
exp.35:8:
This verse shows the Assyrian commander mocking Judah. He asks how they could expect to repel even a single officer from the least important of the servants of the king of Assyria, since they are depending on Egypt for chariots and horsemen. An "officer" here means a commander or military leader. To "repel" means to push back or defeat. "Horsemen" are soldiers who ride on horses.

Rabshakeh, a senior spokesman for King Sennacherib of Assyria, speaks before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and Hezekiah, so he tells them that Egypt will not save them. His words are war propaganda; he mixes truths, taunts, and half-truths, even when he speaks about God.

For today: when someone tells you that your situation has no way out, do not measure everything only by visible strength. Evaluate honestly, but place your trust in God, not in human resources or in voices that try to frighten you.
exp.39:17:
To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him? The question is rhetorical. It means "with whom will you set Him as an equal?" To "make an image" means to shape or assemble a figure. The expected answer is: with nothing and with no one.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, probably during the exile in Babylon, where idols were everywhere. Earlier he had said that the nations are like nothing before God. Then he mocks the idols with irony: a craftsman makes them, a goldsmith covers them with gold, and they must be fastened so they will not fall over. In this way he contrasts the Creator with objects made by human hands.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God: money, success, or the opinion of others. None of them can sustain us. Trust God as he is, not as you imagine him.
exp.39:16:
It says that all the nations, compared with God, are like nothing. The phrases "as nothing" and "nothingness and emptiness" are a strong way of saying that, next to God, the peoples have no weight or worth that can be compared with his. The word "nations" in the verse means nations or peoples. A "bucket" is a small pail, and "dust on the scale" is usually understood as the fine powder left on a balance.

The prophet Isaiah comforts a tired people who are afraid before powerful empires. He reminds them that God is greater than any power, and that not even all of Lebanon, with its forests and animals, would be enough to offer him a worthy offering. Then he goes on to ask who can be compared with God, and he mocks the idols made by craftsmen.

For today: when the fear of governments, crises, or powerful people weighs on you, remember who God is. Pray with confidence, and do not put your hope in anything made by human hands.
exp.33:1:
Here Isaiah says that the LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. The original word for "destroy" means that God will bring them to ruin, and the image of a place where animals are put to death is a strong picture of judgment. The word "armies" can refer to their forces and to all their power.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and calls all peoples and the whole earth to listen. It is a solemn announcement of worldwide judgment, and the chapter then focuses on Edom. Scholars debate whether it refers only to events close at hand, to the end of time, or to both. What is clear is that God is sovereign over all the nations.

Today we can remember that no human power stands above God. That invites us to trust in Him, to live with humility, and to seek His forgiveness, which is offered in Christ, rather than depending on our own strength or on governments.
exp.5:4:
Isaiah says that he feels lost and ruined. "I am ruined" means that he believes he is under judgment, and "a man of unclean lips" means that the way he speaks is not pure. He also lives among a people whose speech is unclean. And yet his eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. He has just seen a vision of the temple, with seraphim proclaiming the holiness of God. Faced with such purity, Isaiah sees his own sin. He does not defend it or hide it; he admits it. Then, in the next verse, God cleanses him with a coal from the altar.

For today: when we draw near to God, we do not need to pretend that we are perfect. We can honestly admit our sins, including those of our words, and trust that God forgives and cleanses those who humble themselves before Him.
exp.8:5:
It says that a child is born, a son who is given to his people. The "government will be upon His shoulders" means that the rule will rest on him and be under his authority. The phrase "He will be called" simply means that these names will be used for him. His names describe who he is: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under the threat and oppression of foreign powers. First he announces that God will break the yoke that oppresses them, as in the days of Midian (Judges 7). Then he promises a kingdom without end on the throne of David. Christians see Jesus here; some scholars also see a first fulfillment in a king of that time.

For today: when you feel that everything weighs on you or you don't know what to do, bring your burdens and decisions to Jesus. He counsels with wisdom and gives a peace that the world cannot give.
exp.24:5:
God, the LORD of hosts, will prepare on his mountain a lavish banquet for all peoples. The food described is the finest available: choice meat, the richest and most nourishing food, and finely aged wine. It is a picture of abundance and joy.

Isaiah speaks in a song of praise to God, who protected the poor and humbled the proud. After that judgment, God invites all peoples, not only Israel. Many understand "this mountain" as Zion, Jerusalem. The passage that follows speaks of God taking away death and tears.

For today: when you feel weary or in need, remember that God is preparing for you a future of abundance and comfort. In the meantime, share your table with someone who needs it.
exp.13:10:
It says that the pride of the king of Babylon and the music of his harps went down to Sheol, the realm of the dead, along with him. Sheol is the place where the dead are gathered, and the harps are stringed instruments used at his feasts. Instead of a comfortable bed, he will have maggots beneath him and worms over him as his blanket.

Isaiah delivers this poetic mockery against the king of Babylon, who oppressed the nations. The dead, once powerful kings, receive him in astonishment: he is now no more than one of them. Some see in the passage that follows a reference to Satan, but others understand it only as the human king. Christians have interpreted this in different ways.

For today: power, money, and prestige do not accompany us to the grave. It is worth asking God for a humble heart and using what we have to serve, not to dominate others.
exp.23:20:
In that day, it says, the LORD will call to account and punish both the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below. Here "punish" is not a gentle word. It means God himself stepping in to judge.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in chapters 24 to 27, which describe a judgment over the whole earth because of its sin. Scholars understand "the host of heaven above" in several ways: as rebellious spiritual forces, as the heavenly bodies that were worshiped, or as exalted human powers. The text does not fully make this clear. The conclusion is clear: God will reign.

For today: do not place your ultimate trust in any human power, because only God reigns forever. Live with humility and hope.
exp.20:13:
Isaiah 21:14 is a call to help. The people of Tema are asked to bring water to the thirsty and to meet the refugees with food. The verse asks them to act with care toward those who arrive in need.

The verse belongs to a message of judgment about Arabia. Travelers from Dedan, people of the caravans, are described as hiding at night in the forest because they are fleeing from war, as the verses that follow make clear. Tema was an oasis, which is why it is asked to show hospitality. Scholars do not agree on who the invader is, but the text announces that the glory of Kedar will fall within a year.

Even in times of crisis, God calls us to be generous. Today we can help in concrete ways, such as with food or companionship, for someone who flees from violence or need.
exp.36:11:
Here the king of Assyria asks whether the gods of other nations were able to rescue the peoples that his forefathers destroyed. He names places such as Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who lived in Telassar. "Rescued" means "saved." "Nations" refers to the peoples of other lands. "Of Eden in Telassar" means "of Eden living in Telassar."

Sennacherib speaks through his messengers as he threatens Jerusalem. He wants King Hezekiah to surrender, and to that end he compares the God of Israel with the idols of other peoples. He overlooks the fact that the Lord is not just one god among many.

For today: when threats or voices of fear tell you that God cannot help you, do as Hezekiah did. Bring your worry to God in prayer, lay it before Him, and trust in His power rather than in what you can see.
exp.58:7:
They have not known the way of peace, the explanation says. There is no justice in how they act, and they have turned their paths into crooked ones, that is, twisted and dishonest. Paths are small roads. No one who walks those roads will find peace.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He shows them that their sins, such as violence and injustice, stand as a barrier between them and God (v. 2). Then, in the verses that follow, the prophet includes himself with the people, as one who confesses a shared sin.

For today: peace is not found through shortcuts or at the expense of others. Examine today one area where you act with deceit, harshness, or injustice. Confess it to God and ask Him to straighten that path. He forgives and guides anyone who returns to Him sincerely.
exp.48:2:
God speaks to his servant and calls him "Israel." He assures him that God will display his glory through him. The verse says, "You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory," so the phrase "in whom I will display My glory" means that God will make his glory seen in this person.

The one speaking is the servant, who tells how God called him from before he was born. Here there is a detail that is interpreted in several ways: some see in this servant the people of Israel; others, a faithful figure within Israel; and many Christians see Jesus, who fulfills what Israel did not accomplish. The next verse shows weariness, but also trust in God.

For today: even if you feel tired or think your effort is not worth it, your worth does not depend on results. God has called you, knows you, and can display his glory in your life. Rest in Him.
exp.1:16:
The verse says that human pride will be brought down and people's arrogance will be humbled. In the end, God alone will be lifted up and honored as the only one who is truly great. The pride in view is both the pride of each individual and the pride of people as a whole, and it means thinking of oneself as superior to others and even to God. To be "brought low" means to be lowered or put down. "That day" points to the day of the Lord, when God will act in judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who trusted in their wealth, their fortresses, their trading ships and their idols. The verses just before this one mention towers, walls and the ships of Tarshish, all symbols of power and prosperity. Isaiah warns that none of these will save them when they stand before God. Scholars debate exactly which moment "that day" refers to, whether a near judgment, the end of time, or both.

Today we can ask where we place our security: in money, achievements or prestige. It is better to humble ourselves now before God than to be humbled later.
exp.27:7:
The verse describes a disgusting feast. The tables are covered with vomit, and there is no clean spot anywhere. The word "vomit" refers to what is thrown up after drinking too much, and the filth around it is the mess that comes with it. It is a deliberately raw image.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the leaders of Judah, including priests and prophets. These men were supposed to guide the people with clarity, but they were drunk on wine and strong drink (fermented drink). Because of this they made mistakes when seeing visions and when pronouncing judgments. Then they mock God's teaching, as if it were meant for children.

Today we can ask ourselves what things cloud our minds and keep us from hearing God. It is not only alcohol; it can be any vice or excess. If we want to guide others with wisdom, we need a sober heart that is attentive to his Word.
exp.28:1:
He says that God himself will constrain Ariel, that is, bring it into anguish, trouble, and siege. The city will be left full of mourning and lamentation. And at the end he says she will be like an altar hearth before God. The name Ariel can sound like "lion of God," but it has also been understood as "altar hearth," and so there are several interpretations.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Ariel is a name for Jerusalem, the city of David. The people kept up their feasts and sacrifices, but their hearts were far from God. So the Lord announces a siege that would bring them low.

For today: routine religion does not replace a sincere heart. Ask yourself whether your prayers and your service come from love for God, and ask him to correct whatever is empty in you.
exp.63:8:
The explanation says the people ask God not to be angry beyond measure and not to remember their sin forever. The phrase "do not be angry beyond measure" is the wording of the verse itself. They ask that he look upon them, because they are his people.

The passage is a prayer spoken by the prophet Isaiah on behalf of the nation. He confesses that the people turned away from God and are suffering the consequences. The verses that follow describe deserted cities and the temple burned, which many understand as the destruction of Jerusalem. Scholars disagree about the exact moment in which the prayer is set.

We can come before God with sincerity, acknowledging our failings without making excuses. Even so, we rely on his relationship with us, not on our own merits. God is a Father who listens to anyone who returns to him with humility.
exp.58:10:
The explanation says that the people groan in deep distress, like bears that growl and doves that moan. They were hoping that God would set things right, but it did not come. "Justice" here means things being put right, and "salvation" means deliverance or rescue. The phrase "far from us" describes something that stayed at a distance.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, joining himself to them with the word "we." He acknowledges that the injustice and darkness they live in come from their own sins, as the following verses say: lies, rebellion, and turning away from God. God had not lost his power; sin had created a barrier.

For today: when you feel that justice or help is slow in coming, examine your heart honestly. Confess what God shows you, and return to Him with confidence, for He receives whoever draws near with humility.
exp.45:9:
He says that God announces the future from the beginning, that is, he speaks of things that have not yet happened. Where it says "my purpose will stand," it refers to his plan, which is not cancelled. "All my good pleasure I will accomplish" means he will carry out everything he intends, and nothing stops him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who were tempted to trust in idols. For that reason he asks them to remember the past and to recognize that he alone is God. The "man of my counsel" that appears later is usually understood to be Cyrus, king of Persia, although the text here does not name him.

For today: when your life feels uncertain, remember how God has sustained you before. Pray with confidence, knowing that his plan is firm even when you cannot see the whole way ahead.
exp.53:2:
It says that God's people, who seemed small and without a future, will spread out in every direction, "on the right and the left." Their descendants will take possession of other nations and will fill again the cities that lie in ruins, that is, cities that were destroyed and abandoned.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem or Israel, which is compared to a barren and abandoned woman. The people were living through the pain of exile and desolation. God promises them restoration and calls them to enlarge their tent in faith. Scholars debate whether the fulfillment refers only to the return from exile or also to the church, which includes people from all nations.

For today: when your situation looks barren or without a way out, do not shut yourself in with fear. Trust God's promises and take steps of faith, praying and serving, preparing room for what He can do.
exp.28:11:
This verse speaks of a scroll that is handed to a person who cannot read. When they are asked to read it, they answer that they cannot. The image is the second in the passage: before, the scroll was sealed; now, the one who receives it simply cannot read it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing the people of Jerusalem. He tells them that, because of their hardness, they could not understand his message, as if they were in a deep sleep. The verses that follow show the problem: they honored God with their lips, but their hearts were far away. Some interpret the image as a spiritual inability; others, as a judgment of God upon them.

For today: having a Bible or knowing religious words is not enough. Ask God for a humble and willing heart, and read his Word eager to obey it, not merely to keep a custom.
exp.43:18:
The explanation says that the man who makes an idol does not stop to think. He uses part of the wood to warm himself, bake bread and roast meat, and with what is left he makes a god. Words like "consider" mean to think something through; "abomination" means something detestable in God's sight; and "bow down" here means to bend low in order to worship.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, which was surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. With irony, he shows how absurd it is to worship a block of wood that was used for the daily fire. Then he calls Israel to remember that he formed them and does not forget them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by us, such as money, success or image, we are treating as if they could save us. Stop, think calmly, and return to the God who made you.
exp.29:7:
God tells the prophet Isaiah to write his message on a tablet in front of the people and to inscribe it on a scroll. The word "vision" refers to the message God gave him. The phrase "a witness forever and ever" means that the words are meant to stand as a lasting record for the days to come.

God speaks to Isaiah. Judah was looking for help from Egypt against its enemies, instead of trusting in the LORD. God warns that Egypt will be of no use to them. Because the people were rebellious and did not want to hear the truth, God orders the message to be left in writing, so that later it can be seen that he had spoken clearly.

Today we can learn not to run away from God's words when they make us uncomfortable. If you are about to make an important decision, ask yourself whether you are looking for a flattering answer or for the truth. Read the Bible with humility, and trust that God guides you better than any human support.
exp.7:20:
They will roam the land, dejected and hungry. Because of their hunger they will become enraged, and they will curse their king and their God. The phrase "they will curse" means speaking with anger and contempt. The phrase "looking upward" shows that they will look up toward the sky in anger and defiance. The word "land" probably refers to the land described earlier, though some understand it differently.

Isaiah speaks in a time of crisis in Judah, when many sought answers from diviners and spirits instead of from God. Isaiah tells them to return to the law and to the testimony, the word of God. Whoever rejects it is left without light and ends in distress and darkness, as the following verse says.

For today: when need comes, let us not blame God or seek answers in dark things. Let us first seek his Word, where there is light and hope.
exp.58:8:
The people believed God would bring them justice and a good way forward, but justice stayed far away and did not reach them. They hoped for light and found only darkness. Here "justice" means what is right, and "light" refers to moments of clarity and hope, which the verse expresses with the word "light."

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel and includes himself with the word "we." Before this verse, he describes the violence, the injustice, and the crooked paths of the people. His message is that sin and wickedness raise a barrier between the people and the blessing of God. The verses that follow show his confession and his despair.

For today: if we feel that we walk in darkness, it is good to examine ourselves humbly and see whether there is something we should correct. We can confess it to God and seek again the paths of justice and peace, trusting that he is merciful.
exp.23:17:
It says that no one will be able to escape God's judgment. Whoever runs away from the sound of panic will fall into a pit (the "pit" is a deep hole in the ground), and whoever climbs out of the pit will be caught in a trap. The "windows of heaven" that are opened call to mind the flood of Noah (Genesis 7:11), and the shaking "foundations of the earth" show that everything is shaken.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, in a section describing God's judgment on the whole earth. The cause is that the inhabitants have been unfaithful and have broken the covenant with God. Scholars debate which historical events it refers to, and many also see it as a picture of the final judgment.

For today: we cannot hide our sin or flee from God by our own means. The wisest course is to turn back to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy, for the righteous receive glory (v. 16).
exp.40:0:
God calls the islands, that is, the distant lands, and all the peoples to be silent and listen to him. He asks them to renew their strength, come forward, and present their case. The phrase "let us together draw near for judgment" means they will gather together for a debate or a court, where it will be seen who is right.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah. The verses that follow ask who raised up a righteous man from the east and gave him victory over kings. Many believe this refers to Cyrus of Persia, though some understand it differently. The central idea is that the Lord directs history, and not the idols of the nations.

For today: before you let fear or the voices of the world carry you away, be still and remember who governs history. Bring your concerns before God with confidence, because he can withstand any examination.
exp.28:15:
The explanation says that the people have turned things upside down, and this is shown by the phrase "You have turned things upside down" in the verse. Treating the clay as though it were wiser than the potter is absurd. Can what is formed say to the one who formed it, "He did not make me"? Can the pottery say of the potter, "He has no understanding"?

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Jerusalem. Its leaders were making plans in secret, without consulting God, and they thought no one was watching. They acted as if they were cleverer than He was. So God shows them how ridiculous that attitude is. Then He promises that the deaf will hear and the blind will see.

For today: before deciding something important, lay your plans before God with humility. He knows you and formed you, so trust that His wisdom surpasses yours, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.4:17:
It says that it will be terrible for those who drag their wickedness along as if they were pulling a load behind them with ropes. "Deceit" here means something false or misleading. The ropes are the cords used to pull a cart. The image is of people who carry their sin with effort, dragging it along and making it heavier each time.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God, within a song about the vineyard of Israel and a series of "woes." God accuses the people of injustice. In the verses that follow, it is seen that they mock God's judgment, as if it were a threat of no importance. Some understand that the ropes show how sin binds them more and more tightly.

For today: do not let yourself be deceived into thinking that a small sin does not weigh anything. If something is tying you down, bring it to God sincerely today, and ask a trusted person to help you loosen it.
exp.59:2:
The explanation says that peoples from other nations will walk guided by the light that shines over Jerusalem, and that even kings will come drawn by its brightness. The word "nations" means peoples who are not Jewish. "Dawn" here refers to the rising of the light, as when the sun comes up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, a people who had come through punishment and discouragement. God promises restoration. The light is not their own merit: it is the glory of the LORD rising over her. Many Christians see here an announcement of Christ, the light of the world, though others read it mainly as a promise for a restored Israel.

For today: if God has brought light into your life, do not hide it or boast about it. Live with honesty and kindness, and let his glory be seen in you. Many people in the middle of their darkness will draw near, not because of you, but because of the light that shines on you.
exp.48:1:
He says that God made the Servant's words powerful and piercing, like a sharp sword. He also hid him in the shadow of his hand, keeping him close and protected. He made him like a polished arrow, ready to be shot, and hid him in his quiver, the case where arrows are kept.

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, who calls out to the islands and distant peoples to listen to him. God called him from before he was born. In the text, this Servant is called "Israel," and many Christians see in him Jesus, who carries out the mission that Israel was not able to accomplish. Others understand him also as Israel or a faithful remnant. God prepares him and takes care of him before sending him out.

God cares for and prepares his servants, even in times that seem hidden or silent. If you feel kept in the quiver, not doing much, trust: God knows when and where to send you.
exp.31:0:
This verse announces that a time is coming when a king will reign in righteousness, and his officials will also rule with justice and fairness. "Princes will rule with justice" means that they will lead and decide matters fairly and rightly.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had suffered under unjust rulers and under the threat of Assyria. After harsh warnings, the prophet offers hope. Many Christians see here an anticipation of Jesus, the righteous King, though some think the first meaning points to King Hezekiah. Both readings have been held, and they need not be set entirely against each other.

For today: trust that God has not forgotten justice. While that King reigns in full, seek to be, in your home, work, or church, someone who protects, listens, and acts uprightly, without taking advantage of any authority you hold.
exp.49:1:
God asks why, when he came to his people, no one was there, and why no one answered when he called. Then he asks whether his hand is too short to redeem them, meaning too weak to rescue. He answers by showing his power: with a single rebuke he dries up the sea and turns the rivers into a desert.

The Lord is speaking to the people of Israel in exile. They felt that God had abandoned them, like a wife who had been sent away. God answers that the problem was not a lack of power or love on his part, but the people's wickedness and rebellion. He did come and call, but no one answered.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, honestly examine whether you have been attentive to his call. He still has the power to rescue, and he invites you to respond to him today with confidence.
exp.48:8:
God says that the Servant will be used to tell the prisoners, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves." And like a shepherd, God will lead them along the pathways, and they will find pasture even on the barren hills.

Here the LORD speaks to the Servant, who was seen as despised and worthless. God promises that He will be faithful to him and that He will use him to set others free. Some understand the Servant to be Israel; many Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus. Both readings have been held.

Today, if you feel trapped by guilt, fear, or sadness, God invites you to come out into His light. And if you know someone like this, you can encourage them, with love, to trust in the Shepherd who cares for and provides for them.
exp.4:12:
It says that God's people would go into exile because they lacked understanding: they did not know or consider God and his ways. For that reason their dignitaries would be starving, and the masses would be parched with thirst. The verb is in the future tense, describing something God presents as certain to happen.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah. It comes after a "woe" against those who lived among feasts and wine, without looking at what God was doing. Many understand that it announces the exile that would come later, though some see it as a general warning of judgment.

For today: do not let noise, entertainment, or routine dull your attention to God. Set aside time each day to read his Word and reflect on it.
exp.18:3:
God says that he himself will hand Egypt over to the power of a harsh master, and that a fierce king will rule over them. "Harsh master" means a ruler without mercy. The wording about this ruler's control means that he will govern them by force. All of this is declared by the Lord GOD of Hosts, that is, the God who has power over everything.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a message against Egypt. Before this, he announces divisions and confusion among the Egyptians, and that they will look for answers in idols and in fortune-tellers. It is not known with certainty which king he means; scholars have understood it in various ways, since the prophecy does not give a name.

For today: trusting in what is passing, such as power, money, or the occult, leaves us empty. Let us seek the guidance of God, who governs over all nations and is just.
exp.2:13:
God says he himself will bring the elders and leaders of his people to account, that is, their rulers. He charges them with having devoured the vineyard, an image of God's people, which Isaiah 5 also compares to a vineyard. He also says that the plunder of the poor is in their houses, meaning what they took from the needy. The word "charge" here means an accusation brought before a judge, where the case is presented and decided.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, on behalf of God, to Judah and Jerusalem. God appears as a judge who brings his case against the leaders. They were supposed to care for the people, but instead they deceived them and took advantage of the weakest.

For today: if you have any authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it to protect and serve, not to gain advantage for yourself. God sees how we treat the most vulnerable.
exp.43:9:
Here God asks a question that sounds like a serious mockery: who would be foolish enough to make a god or cast an idol that profits him nothing? The words "fashions" and "casts" speak of shaping and casting metal. "Profits him nothing" means that it neither helps nor benefits the one who made it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who were surrounded by nations with idols. God reminds them that he is the only God and that they are his witnesses. He shows them how absurd it is to worship something made by human hands, in order to give them confidence and so that they will not be afraid.

For today: anything we make and then ask to give us security, such as money, success, or the approval of others, can become an idol. Today you can ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and bring that fear to God in prayer.
exp.35:9:
Rabshakeh asks: "Was it apart from the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it?" In other words, he claims that the God of Judah sent him to attack Jerusalem. The phrase "apart from the LORD" means the same as "without his permission or approval."

Rabshakeh speaks as the spokesman of the king of Assyria, before the envoys of King Hezekiah. He wants Jerusalem to surrender without a fight, and so he weakens their trust in God. There is no evidence that he actually received such an order from the LORD; it seems to be war propaganda. Isaiah 10 shows that God can use a nation, but it also judges that nation's pride.

For today: do not accept every voice that claims to speak in God's name. Compare what you hear with Scripture, especially when it tries to frighten you or pulls you away from trust in Him.
exp.42:3:
God tells his people that he values them deeply. "Precious" means of great worth, and "honored" means respected. Because he loves them, he is willing to give other men and nations in exchange for them. "Life" here refers to the whole life of the person.

The LORD, the Holy One of Israel, speaks to Israel, a people facing exile and fear. The verses before it promise his presence in waters and fire, and the verses after it promise to gather his children from far away. The references to Egypt, Ethiopia and Seba belong to the language of rescue, and scholars interpret them in different ways, so it is best not to force an exact historical explanation.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements or on what others think of you. When you feel insignificant, remember that God loves you and is with you. Rest in that, and treat others as someone whom he also loves.
exp.24:0:
Isaiah says that the LORD is his God, and that he will lift Him up and praise His name. The reason is that God has worked wonders. To "exalt" someone means to lift them up very high. The "plans formed long ago" are the purposes God set in place well before they came to pass, and "perfect faithfulness" means a faithfulness that never fails.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, after the judgments announced in the earlier chapters. From the verses that follow, the fallen city is a symbol of a proud power that God brought down. It is not known with certainty which city is meant; scholars interpret it in several ways. Isaiah responds with a song of thanksgiving, because what God planned has been fulfilled.

For today: when you look back, make a list of the times God was faithful to you. Give him thanks for them in prayer. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens your trust when the future looks uncertain.
exp.58:0:
It says that God is indeed able to save and indeed able to hear. "The arm of the LORD is not too short" means that his power has not grown weak. "His ear too dull to hear" means that his hearing has not become impaired, like someone who can no longer hear well. Isaiah affirms that this is not the case.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who felt that God was far away and did not answer. The verses that follow explain that the problem was not God, but the sin of the people: violence, lying, and wickedness were separating Israel from their Lord.

For today: when you feel that God is not listening to you, do not begin by doubting his power. Examine your heart honestly, confess whatever needs to be confessed, and return to him, for he remains ready to forgive and to save.
exp.29:11:
God, here called "the Holy One of Israel," says that his people rejected his message. The word for "rejected" means that they set it aside. Instead of trusting in God, they put their security in oppression and deceit, and leaned on these as on a walking staff.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who did not want to hear warnings. They asked the prophets to say only pleasant things. Moreover, they sought protection in political alliances, especially with Egypt, rather than trusting in God. That is why God announces the consequences to them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we want to hear only what pleases us. God loves us, and for that reason he sometimes corrects us. Listening to his Word with humility, even when it is uncomfortable, is a firmer foundation than any false support.
exp.59:3:
It says that Zion, or Jerusalem, should lift up her eyes and look around her. A crowd has gathered and is coming toward her. Her sons return from far away, and her daughters are carried in the arms. The phrase about being carried on the arm means they are held close and carried carefully, like small children. The words "look around" simply mean to see everything that is happening around her.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a promise of God to his people. After a time of sorrow and scattering, God promises restoration. His light and glory will shine over Jerusalem, and even the nations will draw near. Scholars connect this with the return from exile, and many Christians also see a broader fulfillment in Christ and his Church.

For today: when you find yourself in darkness or alone, lift up your eyes. God can restore what seems lost, so pray with hope for those who are far from him or from your family.
exp.57:8:
Isaiah 58:9 promises that when the people live with justice, God will answer their prayers right away. The words "call" and "cry" mean asking God for help. "Here I am" means "I am here." But the verse sets a condition: remove the yoke from among you, which is the oppression of others, the pointing of the finger, which is accusing and looking down on people, and malicious talk, which is speaking words that are cruel, false, or harmful.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and seemed religious, yet oppressed their workers and were harsh toward those in need. God tells them that their faith is not genuine if it is not shown in justice and compassion. The verses before this one speak of sharing bread and clothing the naked.

For today: before asking something of God, examine how you treat others. Stop criticizing and accusing, and help someone who is in need.
exp.1:14:
It says that the day of the LORD will also come against every high tower and against every fortified wall. The towers and walls were defenses and symbols of human security. "Fortified" here means strongly built, hard to bring down.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He announces a day of the LORD in which God will bring down everything that people raise up in pride: mountains, cedars, towers, ships, and riches. The list in the nearby verses ends by saying that human haughtiness will be humbled and that only the LORD will be exalted. Interpreters debate when and how this is fulfilled: some see historical judgments, others also a final day.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, reputation, work, or your own strength. Having things is not sin, but trusting them more than God is. Today you can hand over to God your "walls" and rest in Him.
exp.12:20:
This verse describes Babylon as an abandoned place, where no people live anymore and only wild animals remain. "Desert creatures" are animals of the wilderness; "howling creatures" are probably animals that cry out, though the Hebrew term is uncertain; "ostriches" are the birds that will dwell there; and "wild goats" are animals that leap about.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, announcing judgment against Babylon, the proud power of its time. It is a warning that no empire, however great it may seem, stands above God. Interpreters debate when and how this was fulfilled: some see it in the city's gradual fall, others in a fulfillment that is still broader.

For today: do not place your security in what seems great and strong, such as money, power or prestige. Trust in God, who always endures.
exp.47:15:
Come near to me and listen. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time it happened, I was there. And now the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit. The phrase "come near" matches the call to come near to him, and "listen" matches the call to hear this.

The context is that God calls Israel, who is in exile and tempted to trust in idols, to remember that he announced ahead of time what he would do, even against Babylon. Who speaks at the end of the verse is a matter of debate: some see the prophet Isaiah, others the Servant of the Lord, and many Christians see here a shadow of the Messiah. The mention of the Lord GOD and his Spirit alongside the one who is sent is remarkable, although it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God does not act in secret or leave us in the dark. Come near to him, read his Word, and trust that his promises will be fulfilled in his time.
exp.28:5:
God himself, the LORD of Hosts, will come to visit the city with powerful displays: thunder, earthquake, a loud noise, windstorm, tempest, and a consuming flame of fire. "You will be visited" here does not mean a gentle visit, but God's arrival to act. A windstorm is a wind that spins with great force.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, which is called Ariel. First God humbles her for her pride and her religion of lip service. Then, however, he intervenes against the enemies who attack her. Interpreters debate whether this visiting refers to Jerusalem under judgment or to the defense of the city against its enemies. The following context favors the second.

For today: when you feel surrounded or without strength, remember that God rules over every threat. Trust in him, but also let him correct your pride.
exp.1:18:
He says that when God rises in power to judge the earth, people will flee to hide in caves in the rocks and holes in the ground. They will be afraid because of the terror of the Lord and the splendor of his majesty. Here "terror" means something that causes fear and awe. The phrase about shaking the earth speaks of a judgment that shakes all of humanity.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He warns them that human pride and idolatry will not withstand the day of the Lord, a time when God will show that he alone is great. Scholars debate whether the text refers to a near historical judgment, a final one, or both.

For today: examine what you depend on in place of God, such as money, reputation, or your own strength. Today you can surrender these to him with humility, without waiting for everything to be shaken.
exp.54:3:
God has placed someone as a witness to the nations, that is, someone who makes known who God is and what He does. He has also made him a leader and commander of the peoples, that is, a guide who leads and instructs.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just invited His people to come and listen, and to receive the enduring mercies shown to David. For this reason, many understand this "him" to be a descendant of David, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. Some also apply it to the people of Israel, and this is debated. In any case, God's blessing reaches the nations.

For today: before looking for other guides who do not satisfy, listen to Jesus, and let His teaching direct your decisions this week.
exp.50:6:
God calls out to those who know what is right, the people who have his law in their hearts. He tells them not to fear the scorn of other people, and not to be broken by their insults and mockery.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a faithful people who feel weak and surrounded by people who ridicule them. Before and after this, God reminds them that the world is passing away, like clothing eaten by moths, but that his righteousness and his salvation last forever. For this reason they should not fear what is temporary.

If you are criticized or mocked for living your faith with honesty, remember that those words pass away, but what God says remains. Keep his Word in your heart and let it weigh more than the opinion of others.
exp.3:4:
God says that he himself will cover and protect all of Zion, both the homes where his people live and the places where they gather to worship him. Here "will create" means "will make." By day there will be a cloud of smoke, and by night a glowing flame of fire. A canopy is like a roof stretched overhead, and over all the glory there will be a covering of protection.

Isaiah is speaking to Judah and Jerusalem. Earlier he spoke of judgment and cleansing for sin; now he promises that those who remain, called holy, will have God's protecting presence. The cloud and the fire bring to mind how God guided Israel in the wilderness, though the text does not say this directly. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others apply it to the church.

After being cleansed, God does not leave us alone. If today you feel exposed or afraid, remember that his presence covers you. Ask him to cleanse you, and rest in his care.
exp.28:3:
This verse describes Jerusalem brought low, fallen so far that her words seem to rise up from the ground. Her speech will be muffled and quiet, as if it came from the dust. The image is of a voice that sounds weak and hidden, like a faint whisper from underground.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The name for Jerusalem used here is one that some take to mean "lion of God" or "altar of God"; there is no single certain interpretation. God warns that he will allow a siege against a city that is proud and religious only in appearance. But the message continues: in the end, God himself will intervene against the enemies.

For today: when pride or false security fill us, God may humble us in order to correct us. If you feel brought low today, cry out to him with humility; he lifts up those who sincerely draw near.
exp.35:19:
Here the spokesman of the king of Assyria asks mockingly which god of the other nations ever saved his land from the power of Assyria. By this he means that the Lord will not be able to rescue Jerusalem either. The words "delivered" and "from my hand" mean rescued or saved from someone's power. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high-ranking officer sent by King Sennacherib. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem, in the days of King Hezekiah. He wants to frighten the people into surrendering and not trusting in God. He compares the Lord with the gods of conquered nations, as if he were just one more of them. Hezekiah's officials keep silent, as the king had ordered, and afterward they report everything to him with their clothes torn, a sign of distress.

Today too there are voices that tell us God will not be able to help us, comparing our situation with cases that seem hopeless. Instead of arguing with fear, we can do as Hezekiah did: bring the problem to God in prayer and trust that He is different from everything else.
exp.13:21:
God himself declares that he will rise up against Babylon and wipe it out completely. The phrase "cut off" means to pull up or erase entirely. "Remnant" refers to the survivors, what is left over. "Her offspring and her posterity" speaks of descendants: neither its name, nor its remnant, nor its heirs will remain.

God speaks here as "the LORD of Hosts," that is, the Lord of all power. The verse sits within a taunting song against the king of Babylon, a proud and cruel ruler who oppressed many nations. Isaiah announces that this power will not last. Scholars debate whether the king is one particular person or a symbol of imperial arrogance, and the text leaves that open.

For today: do not lose heart when injustice seems to be winning. God sees and has the last word. Trust that he will do justice in his own time, and examine your own heart so that you do not live with the pride that God so strongly opposes.
exp.55:7:
The Lord God, who gathers the dispersed of Israel, says he will not stop there. He promises to gather still others to join those already gathered. The word "dispersed" means people who have been scattered or driven apart.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he promises that foreigners who love him and serve him will be welcomed into his house of prayer, which will be for all peoples. For this reason, the verse shows that God's people will grow larger. The verses that follow change in tone and criticize the leaders who do not care for the people. Some understand this as a reference to the future inclusion of the nations.

God opens his arms to those who feel distant or left outside. We can imitate him by warmly welcoming the new or overlooked person in our church, and not treating the group as closed.
exp.36:0:
When King Hezekiah heard the news, he tore his clothes as a sign of grief, put on sackcloth (a rough cloth worn in times of mourning and humiliation), and entered the house of the Lord.

The passage is about Hezekiah, king of Judah. Assyria, under its king Sennacherib, had invaded the land, and its spokesman, Rabshakeh, mocked God and threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah felt the weight of the crisis and of the blasphemy. He immediately sent his officials to ask the prophet Isaiah to pray.

When a piece of news crushes us, the first response does not have to be panic or looking only for human solutions. We can come before God honestly, acknowledge our weakness, and also ask for the prayer of people of faith.
exp.8:20:
The explanation says that the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim were brothers who fought against each other, and then joined together to attack Judah. God's "anger" is his wrath. The phrase "his hand is upraised" means that his hand was still raised to punish. Although the people were already suffering, the judgment had not ended.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel, which is sometimes called Ephraim. He describes God's punishment for their pride and rebellion. The war, the hunger and the violence between brothers show a people destroying themselves. Scholars understand this as a description of the internal struggles of that time, although not all of them agree on the specific events.

Today this verse invites us to examine our quarrels with family, church or neighbors. When pride and resentment take control, everyone is hurt. Let us ask God for humility, and seek peace before division consumes us.
exp.32:13:
The sinners in Jerusalem (Zion) were filled with fear when they saw God's judgment. Those who trembled were the ungodly, people whose lives did not match their claims. The phrase "trembling grips" means they were left shaking. The "consuming fire" and "everlasting flames" describe the holiness of God, who does not tolerate evil. The question is: who can stand close to such a God?

The prophet Isaiah speaks here after announcing punishment against the nations that were enemies of Judah. God calls both those far away and those near to recognize his power. Some understand the fire as God's judgment; others understand it as his holy presence. The answer comes in the verses that follow: the one who lives with justice and righteousness.

For today: it is not enough to only appear good. Ask God for a sincere heart, and practice honesty in small things, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.23:0:
This verse says that God himself is about to lay waste the earth and leave it in ruins. "Laid waste" means that it is left without its riches and its beauty. The phrase about twisting its surface means that he changes the appearance of the earth, disfiguring it. And the phrase about scattering its inhabitants means that the people who live there will be dispersed, sent far away.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God. This chapter opens a section where the judgment reaches the whole earth, not just one nation. The verses that follow explain that no one escapes, neither priest nor servant, neither rich nor poor. Scholars debate whether it refers to a near historical event, to the final judgment, or to both.

For today: let us not place our security in things that can be lost, such as money, status, or plans. Let us place our trust in God, who remains when everything else is shaken.
exp.35:14:
Here Rabshakeh, a spokesman for the king of Assyria, tells the people of Jerusalem not to let Hezekiah persuade them to trust in the Lord. The message is: "Don't think that God is going to save you, because this city will indeed be handed over to the king of Assyria."

Jerusalem was under siege by the Assyrian army. Rabshakeh shouted in Hebrew so that the people on the walls would understand him and be filled with fear. He wanted to take away their confidence in God and in their king so that they would surrender without fighting.

Today too there are voices that present faith as an illusion when trials arrive. When someone tells you that trusting in God does no good, remember that He is faithful. Speak to Him in prayer and seek His word before giving in to fear.
exp.37:1:
He says that King Hezekiah, when he received the news that he would die, turned toward the wall and prayed to God. "Turned his face to the wall" means that he turned over in bed so that he was facing the wall. "LORD" is the name of God, and "Hezekiah" is Hezekiah.

The prophet Isaiah had just told him on God's behalf that his sickness was fatal and that he should put his house in order. Hezekiah was king of Judah. Many think he turned away to have privacy with God, although the text does not explain his reason. Afterward, he prays and weeps, and God answers.

When we receive news that breaks us, we can step away for a moment from the noise and the stares to speak with God in complete honesty. He listens to the one who speaks to him with an open heart.
exp.53:14:
If someone attacks God's people, the explanation says, that harm does not come from God and does not have his approval. The verse's wording about attacking means joining with others to plot something harmful. Its phrase "it is not from Me" means God is not behind such a plan. The text adds that whoever attacks this people will fall, that is, they will fail.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, pictured as a woman who was once barren and is now restored. After the exile, God promises her protection, peace, and justice. Some interpreters read this as a promise to Israel, and others also apply it to the church. But it does not promise that attacks will never come. It promises that they will not have the final word.

For today: when you feel attacked or unfairly criticized, do not respond with revenge. Pray, do what is right, and trust that God cares for you and is just.
exp.56:18:
He says that God himself brings about praise on people's lips, words of peace, praise, and comfort. He announces peace to those who are far away and to those who are near, meaning those who are at a distance and those who are close. And he promises: "I will heal them."

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He has just said that he was angry because of his people's greed and rebellion, but that even so he wants to heal them and guide them. The ones who are far away and near are understood in several ways: Jews far from or near Jerusalem, or those who were estranged from God and those who already followed him. Then the text warns that the wicked who reject God have no peace.

For today: if you are far from God, it is not too late to return; his peace and his healing are waiting for you. If you are near, use your words to bring peace and encouragement to others.
exp.48:4:
Here the servant of the LORD says that the LORD formed him from the womb to be His servant and to bring Jacob back to Him, that Israel might be gathered to Him. Even though Israel does not gather or respond, he knows that he is honored in the sight of the LORD, and that his God is his strength.

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, who in this passage is called "Israel." He feels tired from work that seems to be in vain. Many Christians see here a prophecy about Jesus, while others first emphasize Israel as a people or a faithful servant within it. God answers by expanding his mission: he will also be a light to the nations.

For today: if you serve God and see little fruit, do not measure your worth by people's response. Rest in the fact that God knows you, honors you, and gives you strength to remain faithful.
exp.61:4:
The verse uses the image of a wedding. Just as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will be joined to you, Jerusalem. And as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

Isaiah speaks to a people who lived through exile and a city in ruins. God promises to restore them: they will no longer be called "Forsaken" but will be called by a new name that means "my delight is in her." The prophet wants to comfort and give hope with the most tender image of human love.

For today: even when you feel abandoned or without worth, God does not approach you with anger but with joy. Pray today by receiving that love, instead of trying to earn it.
exp.58:1:
It says that sin builds barriers between people and God. The "iniquities" are the wrongdoings and crooked deeds. "Hidden His face" means that God does not look on them with favor or respond. "So that He does not hear" explains the result: their prayers are not heard.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel. They thought God was far away or weak, but the verse before says that the Lord's hand has not been shortened, nor is His ear too dull to hear. The problem was not God but the sin of the people: violence, lies, and injustice, as the following text describes.

For today: if you feel distant from God, do not first blame Him. Examine your life with honesty, acknowledge your sin, and return to Him. The Bible teaches that God forgives those who repent (1 John 1:9).
exp.27:15:
God says that he lays in Zion a firm and precious stone, set as a cornerstone and as a secure foundation. A cornerstone is the stone that holds up and aligns the whole building. The phrase "the one who believes will never be shaken" means that the person who trusts will not be thrown into panic or grab at false escapes.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. The rulers of Jerusalem mocked and believed they were safe from any punishment because of deceptive agreements, which they called a covenant with death. God contrasts their refuge of lies with a true foundation. The New Testament applies this stone to Christ (1 Peter 2:6).

When pressures come, do not run after quick or deceptive solutions. Build your life on trust in God and in Christ, and wait calmly, because He sustains what is well founded.
exp.35:5:
It says Egypt is like a walking staff made of a fragile reed. A staff is a stick a person leans on when walking. If someone leans on it, the reed splinters, goes into the hand, and wounds it. The verse says the broken reed will pierce the hand, which means the wound will be deep. That is how Pharaoh is to all who trust in him.

Rabshakeh, an officer of the king of Assyria, speaks in front of the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and Hezekiah so that they will surrender. He mocks their alliance with Egypt and presents it as an empty hope. At this point, his criticism of Egyptian help was realistic, since Egypt was not a firm support. But Rabshakeh is an enemy and seeks to intimidate, so his words mix truth and pressure.

We may lean on things that seem strong, such as money, connections, or plans, and that fail us just when we need them most. It is wise to use them with discernment, but to place our final trust in God, who does not break.
exp.28:7:
The verse says that the nations who attack Jerusalem (Mount Zion) will end up disappointed. They are like a hungry man who dreams he is eating but wakes up still hungry, or a thirsty man who dreams he is drinking and wakes up faint and parched. The comparison to two dreams shows the enemy's hopes ending in the same frustrating way.

Isaiah speaks for God to Jerusalem, called Ariel, in a time of threat. God promises that He Himself will act, and that the vast enemy army will vanish like a dream. The verses that follow show that the people were also spiritually asleep. Some read this as a historical promise of deliverance, and others also see a wider announcement about God's judgment.

For today: the things that do not come from God promise much but do not satisfy. Seek your rest and your security in Him, who truly feeds the soul.
exp.5:0:
Isaiah tells us that, in the year King Uzziah died, he saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted. The word "exalted" means grand and lofty. The train of God's robe is the long part of his robe that trails behind him, and the phrase saying it filled the temple means that it covered the whole temple.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, remembering the moment when God called him. Uzziah had reigned for many years in Judah, and his death may have brought uncertainty. It is not known for certain whether the vision took place in the temple in Jerusalem or in a heavenly scene; it is interpreted both ways. What is clear is that, although a human king had died, the true King still sits on his throne.

When everything changes or someone you trusted is no longer there, remember that God still reigns. Ask him to give you peace and confidence, and praise him for who he is.
exp.54:12:
It says that where there used to be thornbushes and briers, good trees will now grow. The tree named here, the cypress, is a tall evergreen, and the myrtle is a shrub with green leaves and fragrant flowers. To be "destroyed" means to be wiped out or taken away. So this change will be a lasting sign that shows the greatness of the LORD.

God speaks through Isaiah at the end of his message of comfort to the people of Israel. He promises their return and joy after the exile. His word will accomplish what He intends. The thornbushes represent a land damaged by sin and punishment; the good trees show the change that God brings about.

For today: if there are areas of your life that feel like thornbushes, such as habits, wounds, or fears, trust that God can change them. Ask Him for His help and let His word keep working in you with patience.
exp.6:3:
God tells Isaiah to say to King Ahaz that he should calm down and not be afraid. Be calm and keep still, and do not be afraid or disheartened. The "two smoldering stubs of firewood" are pieces of wood that are nearly burned out and no longer have much fire. Rezin is the king of Aram, and the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, is the one pictured here. His anger looks terrible, but God sees it as weak smoke.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Judah was threatened because Aram and Israel (Ephraim) had joined forces against King Ahaz. He and his people were trembling like trees in the wind. God wants to reassure them and to have them trust in Him.

For today: When a problem seems enormous, remember that God is greater. Pray, breathe deeply, and trust in Him before acting out of fear.
exp.52:9:
It says that, although the Servant of the LORD was innocent, the LORD willed for him to suffer and to be crushed. "Crushing him" means beating him down, and "causing him to suffer" means placing him under affliction. A "guilt offering" is a sacrifice that deals with guilt. After that offering is made, the Servant will see his offspring, will live many days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in his hand.

Isaiah 53 is the fourth Servant Song. Here the prophet speaks, and in other passages it seems God is speaking. The verses before it show a righteous man who dies because of the people's rebellion. Christians see in this Jesus, as the New Testament does. Some Jews interpret it differently, for example, as referring to Israel.

For today: when pain seems meaningless, remember that God can bring life and good out of what looks like loss. Look to Christ with gratitude and trust.
exp.58:11:
The passage says the people have sinned greatly against God. Their wrongdoings are piled up before him, and their sins stand against them like witnesses giving evidence. Their transgressions are with them, and they admit their wrongdoing: "we know our iniquities." The guilt stays with them wherever they go, so they cannot pretend it is not there.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel and includes himself with the word "we." It is a shared confession. Earlier, the prophet explained that their sins had separated them from God (v. 2). That is why they live as if in darkness, waiting for justice and salvation that do not arrive. After this verse, they name their sins: lying, slander, and injustice.

For today: honest confession is the first step back to God. Instead of making excuses or blaming others, we can tell him sincerely what we have done, trusting that he forgives those who come near with humility.
exp.64:21:
It says that God's people will no longer live under the unfairness of working so that others end up with everything. No one will build a house for a stranger to live in, or plant so that someone else eats the harvest. The wording "enjoy fully" means they will keep and delight in what their hands have made for a long time. Their lives will be long, like the lifetime of a tree.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises his faithful people "new heavens and a new earth" (65:17). Many see here a future fulfillment; others think it also describes a restoration after the exile. Christians often see it as a hope that Christ will bring to completion.

For today: God sees honest work and does not forget it. You can work faithfully even when you do not yet see fruit, and you can also help others receive a fair reward for their effort.
exp.5:7:
Here is what the passage says: Isaiah heard the voice of the Lord asking, "Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?" Isaiah answered right away, "Here am I. Send me!"

The reader's wording has "Here am I" and "Send me!" The question in the Berean Standard Bible uses the capital "Us" for God, which some readers see as a sign of more than one person in God, while others understand it as a way of speaking about God's majesty. The text itself does not settle the matter here.

Isaiah is speaking, a man who has just seen the holiness of the Lord in the temple and felt lost because of his sin. A seraph touched his lips with a coal from the altar and declared him forgiven. After that forgiveness, the Lord asks who will go, and Isaiah answers. His mission would be difficult, since the people were not going to respond well.

For today: when we experience God's forgiveness, we can respond with gratitude and availability. We can say, "Here I am," even though we do not know everything that will be asked of us.
exp.24:4:
God subdues the uproar of foreign enemies who oppose him, as a burning dry land is brought under control. But then he compares it to the heat being cooled by the shade of a cloud: in the same way, God silences the song of the ruthless. The "foreigners" here are people who are both foreign and hostile; the "ruthless" are the strong and the tyrants. Their power fades like a plant that withers.

Isaiah speaks in a song of praise to God. He celebrates that the Lord protects the poor and the needy, and that he holds back the oppressors. Scholars do not agree on which city or power the text refers to; it may be a specific enemy or a picture of human pride in general. Then comes the promise of a feast for all peoples.

For today: there is no need to fear those who abuse their power. We can trust that God cares for the weak, and ask him to free us from our own pride too.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that the workers who weave fine cloth will lose heart, and that all the people paid to labor will be sick at heart. Those who work with cloth and the hired workers are the ones named here, and they are left in despair. The verse speaks of workers in general, with no mention of fishing or ponds.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God, in a prophecy against Egypt. He announces that the Nile, from which the whole country lived, would dry up. Without the river there is no work in the fields, no trade, and no cloth to weave. This shows that God can take away what Egypt believed was secure. The wise men of Pharaoh would not be able to prevent it.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in work, money, or plans. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else breaks.
exp.44:2:
God promises Cyrus, king of Persia, "the treasures of darkness and the riches hidden in secret places," that is, wealth stored away in hidden places. The purpose is that Cyrus will know that the Lord is the LORD, the God of Israel, the one who calls him by name. Calling him by name means that God knows him and gives him a place and a task.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Cyrus is called "anointed," that is, set apart for a task, even though he did not know God. The verses that follow explain that all of this is "for the sake of my servant Jacob," the people of Israel, who were in exile. Many understand this to refer to the riches of Babylon, but the text gives no further detail.

For today: God governs history and can use anyone to carry out his plans. When everything seems closed off or out of control, we can trust that he is still at work and still caring for his people.
exp.43:1:
God presents himself as the one who made Israel and formed it from the womb, that is, from its very beginnings as a people. He promises to help it and says, "Do not be afraid." He calls Jacob "My servant" and also "Jeshurun," a poetic name for Israel. "Chosen" means that God picked him out.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were living with fear and discouragement, and God reminds them that he has not forgotten them. In the verses that follow, he promises to pour out water on the dry land and his Spirit on their children, as an image of new life and blessing.

For today: when fear or weariness weighs on you, remember that God has known you from the beginning and does not let you go. You can speak to him with confidence, ask him for help, and rest in the knowledge that his care does not depend on your strength, but on his faithfulness.
exp.15:4:
In loving devotion, a throne will be established, and on it a judge will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David. This judge seeks justice and is quick to bring about righteousness.

The verse describes the rule of a king who is secure, because his throne rests on loving devotion. He sits in the line of David, meaning his family and royal house. He is a judge who pursues justice and acts promptly to make things right. His rule is marked by faithfulness, meaning he keeps his word and stays true to what is right.

Isaiah speaks these words to Judah about Moab, a neighboring people who have been destroyed and whose refugees are in desperate need. The Moabites are told to seek refuge in Judah. Many readers understand this throne of David to point to the ideal king, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus. Others see it first as a hope for the Davidic line in Isaiah's own time.

Today we can ask God for a heart that joins justice with mercy. If you hold authority, even in your home or workplace, treat the weak with compassion and do not delay in doing what is right.
exp.27:23:
He says that a farmer does not keep plowing and harrowing the soil every day without ever planting. Preparing the ground is only the first step; the time comes to stop working the soil and sow the seed. The verse mentions "nigella," a plant with aromatic seeds, and "cumin," a spice.

Isaiah speaks to scornful leaders of Jerusalem, whom he warns of a judgment coming from God. He uses the picture of the field to show that God does not punish without end or without purpose. Like a wise farmer, God has a plan and a time for each task. Verse 26 says that his God teaches him. Some understand that the judgment aims to correct and bring to fruit; the text suggests this, though it does not fully explain it.

For today: if you are going through a hard season, trust that God does not prolong it without purpose. And examine whether you yourself keep "plowing" in worries or blame, without taking the step of sowing.
exp.50:12:
God asks his people whether they have forgotten the LORD, their Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth. They have lived all day long in terror because of the fury of the oppressor, who seemed bent on destruction. Then God asks, "But where is the fury of the oppressor?" To "oppress" means to crush or make suffer.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people were in trouble, probably under the rule of foreign powers, and they were afraid. God has just told them that he is their comforter and that a mere human does not deserve so much dread. He reminds them who he is in order to restore their confidence.

For today: when fear of a person or a situation takes hold of you, remember that the God who created all things still cares for you. Pray and tell him what you fear, and go over his promises. The problems are real, but his power is greater and the threat does not have the last word.
exp.36:23:
The explanation says that the king of Assyria mocked the Lord through his messengers. He boasted that with his many chariots he would climb the highest mountains, up to Lebanon, and cut down its tallest cedars and its finest trees. The word "taunted" in the verse means insulted.
