The "finest of its cypresses" refers to the best of the trees. "The densest of its forests" describes the thickest, most fertile woodland.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Sennacherib, who had threatened Jerusalem and sent messengers to insult the Lord. God shows him that, although he feels invincible, he has actually offended the Holy One of Israel and does not have as much power as he believes.

For today: it is easy to trust in our achievements, resources, or strength and forget that we depend on God. Today we can stop, thank Him for what we have, and hand over our plans with humility, remembering that He is the one who sustains everything.
exp.44:18:
God says that he has never spoken in secret or from some hidden place in a land of darkness. He did not tell the descendants of Jacob, that is, Israel, to seek him in a wasteland. When God says "I speak the truth; I say what is right," he means that what he says is true and upright.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, and also the nations, at a time when many worshiped idols of wood that could neither speak nor save. God presents himself as the Creator who has made himself known clearly, unlike false gods and their hidden mysteries.

For today: you can seek God with confidence, because he wants to be found. Read his Word and pray sincerely, knowing that you are not searching blindly or in vain.
exp.60:5:
You will be called priests of the LORD, and others will speak of you as ministers of our God. You will feed on the wealth of nations and boast in their riches.

The explanation says that God's people will be recognized as priests of the LORD and ministers of our God. "Ministers" means those who serve; "you will feed on the wealth of nations" means they will enjoy the goods of the nations; and "boast in their riches" points to taking pride in what has come to them.

The one speaking is the anointed servant of the LORD (Isaiah 61:1), who brings good news to the afflicted. God promises to restore Israel after ruin and shame. Some see this as a promise for Israel; the New Testament also calls the Church a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). How the wealth of the nations comes about is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if God has called you to serve him, your daily life is a sacred service. Pray for others, serve with humility, and trust that God restores what seemed lost.
exp.15:8:
Isaiah says that he will weep for Moab with a grief as deep as the weeping of the people of Jazer over the vines of Sibmah. He says he will drench the cities of Heshbon and Elealeh, two cities of Moab, with his tears. The loud cheers that once rang out over the summer fruit and the harvest have now gone silent, because the land has been ruined.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Moab, a neighboring country of Israel famous for its vineyards. Its harvests will be destroyed by invaders. It is surprising that Isaiah does not rejoice but mourns for them. Some understand that this reflects the pain of God himself.

For today: even when someone faces the consequences of their actions, we can respond with compassion and not with mockery. Let us ask God for a heart that suffers with those who suffer.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that the Lord will raise up the enemies of Rezin, the king of Syria, and gather them together against him. The phrase "raised up" means to stir up or empower. Rezin was an ally of Israel, so God allows his enemies to turn against that alliance.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Ephraim, whose capital was Samaria. They had suffered blows, yet they answered with pride, saying, "The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with dressed stone." God warns that his judgment is still in progress. Some understand that Syria and Ephraim would be weakened by Assyria; the text does not detail this here.

For today: when life shakes us, it is not enough to rebuild with pride and carry on as before. God invites us to stop, listen to his correction, and return to him with humility, before making new plans.
exp.7:9:
It says that the plans of God's enemies will fail. "Devise a plan" means making plans or meeting to decide a strategy; "state a proposal" means giving orders or declaring what they intend to do. But none of it will succeed, "for God is with us."

The prophet Isaiah speaks at a time of great threat to Judah from the powerful army of Assyria. The people were afraid and looked for human alliances and conspiracies. Isaiah reminds them that God is with his people, and that no enemy power has the final word. The following verse asks them not to fear what others fear.

For today: when problems seem bigger than you, do not let yourself be carried away by the panic of the crowd. Do your part with wisdom, but rest in the fact that God is with you and still governs.
exp.12:21:
The explanation says that the fortresses and luxurious palaces of Babylon will be left empty and in ruins, and that only wild animals will live there. The hyenas and jackals of the verse are the creatures meant by that picture. The phrase that Babylon's time is at hand means that her end is very close, and the phrase that her days will not be prolonged means that it will not be delayed.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Babylon, a proud and violent power. God promises to judge her arrogance and her injustice. Scholars debate how and when each detail was fulfilled, since Babylon fell into the hands of other empires and declined gradually.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever. If you feel admiration or fear before powerful people, place your trust in God, who is just, and live with humility.
exp.25:17:
The explanation says that the people suffered like a woman in labor, but in the end nothing was born. The verse says, "We were with child; we writhed in pain; but we gave birth to wind." Their struggle produced only emptiness. The verse says they "have given no salvation to the earth." The word translated "salvation" means rescue or deliverance. Nothing they did was able to save the earth. The final phrase, "nor brought any life into the world," can be understood in two ways: that no new people were born, or that the oppressors were not brought down.

The people of God in Judah speak here, in the middle of trouble and discipline. They honestly admit that their own efforts failed to free them. That confession prepares the hope of the next verse: God himself will give life to the dead.

For today: when your efforts leave you with empty hands, do not give up or pretend otherwise. Bring your weariness to God honestly. He is the one who gives true salvation, and he can give life where we see only emptiness.
exp.31:3:
It says that under the just reign that Isaiah announces, people who previously did not understand will begin to comprehend. The "rash" here are hasty people or those lacking discernment, not necessarily foolish. The "stammerers" are those who speak with difficulty, and their tongue will speak clearly and fluently, moving from hesitation to smooth, confident speech.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks of a righteous king (Isaiah 32:1), whom many Christians relate to Christ, though some think first of Hezekiah. Before that, the people were spiritually blind and deaf. With that king, the truth would be seen and heard, and then the text contrasts this with the wickedness of the miser.

For today: if you find it hard to understand God's Word or to express your faith, ask Him for light and courage. He can give you understanding and clear, fluent words to speak of Him.
exp.44:10:
Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, the one who also made them, that he invites them to question him about what is to come. The one who "makes" is the one who shapes, like a potter. The question put to them, "do you question Me about My sons, or instruct Me in the work of My hands?", sounds sharp; many read it as a call to bring God their requests and concerns about his people, not as a challenge that God must answer to anyone.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were complaining about how he was acting. He was about to use Cyrus, a foreign king, to free the captives, and this seemed strange to some of them. God reminds them that he is the Maker and that his plan makes sense, even when they do not understand it.

For today: instead of arguing with God or doubting him when something does not make sense, bring him your questions and concerns in prayer. You can trust that the One who made you cares for you and for those you love.
exp.10:4:
It says that righteousness will be like the belt around this king's hips, and faithfulness like the sash around his waist. Both pieces of clothing sit close to the body and keep everything else in place. In that time, fastening the belt was a way of getting ready to work or serve. The idea is that justice and faithfulness are an inseparable part of his character and his work.

It is the prophet Isaiah who speaks. He describes a future king from the line of David, the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa. 11:1). Christians recognize him in Jesus, the Messiah. This king judges with uprightness, protects the poor, and brings a peace that changes even nature, as the image of the wolf and the lamb shows.

For today: ask God to make righteousness and faithfulness your belt. Keep your word and deal fairly with the weak, without letting yourself be swayed by appearances.
exp.65:16:
Isaiah 66:17 describes people who go through rituals to make themselves holy and clean in sacred groves, following a leader in the middle of the group, while they eat the flesh of pigs, vermin, and rats. The verse says that they will perish together. The sacred groves and the practices there suggest pagan worship, and the foods named are ones that the law of Moses forbade. The message is that they will all share the same fate.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In its setting, He comes to judge those who mixed their worship with idolatrous practices. He says that He knows their works and their thoughts. But judgment is not the final word: afterward He will gather the nations together so that they may see His glory.

For today: it is not enough to appear religious on the outside if the heart is divided. Examine honestly what place God holds in your thoughts and decisions, and ask Him to cleanse you truly, not merely in appearance.
exp.5:11:
It says the judgment will last until the LORD has driven people far away (the exile), and that the land will be left utterly forsaken. The phrase about the forsaken land means the land left desolate, without inhabitants. Here "utterly" means that the places left empty will be numerous.

Isaiah has just received his call in the temple. God assigns him to speak to a people who will not listen. Isaiah asks, "How long, Lord?", and God answers with this announcement of destruction. Many connect it with the Babylonian invasion and the exile, though some also see a broader scope. But the next verse leaves a hope: a stump remains, a holy seed.

For today: when you see that your efforts to speak of God bear no fruit, remain faithful. God disciplines, but never stops preserving a remnant and preparing a new beginning.
exp.50:10:
This verse promises that the redeemed of the Lord will return and enter Zion with singing. They will be crowned with a joy that never ends. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee far away, like someone running from danger.

God's people are suffering, probably in exile, and they ask God to act as he did before. They remember the exodus from Egypt and the crossing of the sea. Rahab and the dragon are poetic images of the power of chaos and evil. Then God himself answers with comfort, so that they will not fear human beings.

Today, if you are going through a painful time, remember what God has already done for his people. His past faithfulness encourages you to wait with hope. Pray with confidence and do not let fear rule your heart.
exp.7:18:
This verse warns that when someone tells you to seek answers from spirits or fortune-tellers, we should remember that God's people ought to seek their God. The "mediums and spiritists" are people who claim to contact the dead, and the voices they "whisper and mutter" are the murmuring sounds they use. The closing question means: why would anyone consult the dead on behalf of the living?

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Judah lived in fear because of threats from other kingdoms, and many people sought answers through the occult. Isaiah had decided to wait on the LORD, even though God seemed silent. Then he directs the people to "the law and to the testimony," that is, to what God had already said.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, do not run after horoscopes, mediums, or mysterious voices. Pray, open the Bible, and wait on God, even when the answer takes a long time.
exp.57:10:
This verse promises that God himself will guide and care for his people, much like a shepherd leads and protects his flock. The word "guide" shows what this means: leading and protecting. Times of great need are described as a sun-scorched land. The promise that God "will satisfy you" means that he will give you contentment. The promise to "strengthen your frame" speaks of giving strength and health. The people will be like a well-watered garden and like a spring whose waters never fail.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people fasted and appeared religious, but they oppressed others and did not practice justice. God tells them that what he truly desires is that they remove the yoke, give bread to the hungry, and help those who are suffering. Then the blessing will come.

When we generously help someone who is suffering, God takes care of our lives. This week, look for a concrete way to serve someone in need, and trust that God will sustain you.
exp.33:13:
It says the place will be left desolate and filled with wild animals. The "desert creatures" are animals of the wilderness, and in your verse they meet with hyenas, which are scavengers of the open land. The "wild goat" is a goat that roams untamed, and it calls out to its fellow. Some understand this wild goat as a goat-like creature of the desert, and some take it as a spirit of the wilderness. The "night creature" is a difficult term: some think of an animal that is active at night, others of a creature from legend. Whatever it is, it settles there and finds a place of rest.

The prophet Isaiah announces God's judgment against the nations, represented here by Edom. Its palaces, once full of power, will be abandoned. The message is that no human kingdom can defy God and remain standing.

For today: do not place your security in what the world calls great, such as money, power, or prestige. All of that can disappear. Trust in God, whose word endures, and seek first what lasts forever.
exp.64:24:
This verse describes a time of complete peace. The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, meaning animals that were once enemies or predators will live side by side without violence. The serpent's food will be dust, a sign that evil is brought low. On God's holy mountain, no one will harm or destroy.

Here God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises his people "new heavens and a new earth" (v. 17). Many see this as a hope for Israel and also as a foretelling of God's final kingdom; Christians read it in the light of Christ. Scholars debate whether the language is literal or symbolic.

For today: God promises a future without violence, and that invites us to be peacemakers now. Today you can choose to respond with gentleness at home, at work, or in church, trusting that God will complete the work of peace.
exp.24:2:
Isaiah 25:3 says that a strong people will honor God, and that the cities of ruthless nations will revere him. Here "revere" means holding God in deep respect and awe, not being terrified of him. "Strong" means powerful and mighty.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, praising God after announcing his judgment. God brought down a strong and proud city, and the text does not give its name, so scholars interpret it in several ways. Seeing how God cares for the poor and humbles the proud, even the powerful end up acknowledging him. It is a song of gratitude for God's faithfulness.

For today: even if you have power, success, or security, your true strength is in God. Today you can thank him for his works and treat with compassion those who are weak, as he does.
exp.15:11:
It says that Moab will wear himself out at his high places, where he worshiped his gods, until he is exhausted. Then he will enter his sanctuary to pray, but it will do him no good. The phrase "appears on the high place" means "is seen at the high place," and "the high places" were places of worship on the hills.

Isaiah announces a judgment on Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. The verses before this one describe the ruin of its vineyards and the end of its joy. God himself says he feels grief for Moab, and the prophet compares this to a harp that sounds sad. Even so, Moab trusted in its gods, and that trust was empty. Afterward it is announced that the judgment would come within three years.

For today: intense religiousness does not replace a real relationship with God. Praying only when everything is falling apart, and without trusting the living God, does little good. Let us seek him now, with humility and sincerity.
exp.41:4:
This verse presents God in all his power. He is the Creator who made the heavens and stretched them out, and who spread out the earth along with its offspring (the plants and vegetation that grow from the ground). He is also the one who gives breath to the people on the earth and life to those who walk in it. "Creator" means the same as Maker, and the "life" he gives here is the breath of life that sustains every living person.

God speaks here about his Servant, who was described in the verses before: someone gentle, who does not break a bruised reed. Before saying what he will do with him, God reminds us who he himself is. Many Christians see in this Servant Jesus, and the New Testament applies this passage to him (Matthew 12:18-21). Others also emphasize its meaning for Israel.

For today: the God who gives you breath can also sustain you when you are weak. Trust in him, even if you feel like a bruised reed.
exp.9:3:
He says that nothing will remain for the unjust but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain. Their rescue will not come from God, and they will be left with only these two outcomes. The phrase "nothing will remain but" describes this lack of any other option. Even so, God's anger has not turned away: his hand is still upraised, that is, still ready to bring judgment. "Anger" here refers to his righteous indignation.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just accused the leaders of Judah and Israel of making unjust laws, taking away the rights of the poor, and robbing widows and orphans. He warns that a disaster will come from far away, and the following text mentions Assyria as the instrument of judgment.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the weak. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are just and generous toward those who have less power, and act on their behalf with honesty and mercy.
exp.12:18:
Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms and the glory of the Chaldeans' pride, was the most admired city of its time, the showpiece and ornament of the Chaldeans. Yet the verse says it will be overthrown by God, just as Sodom and Gomorrah were, cities that God destroyed because of their wickedness. The word "overthrown" means that they were completely brought down.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces this message on God's behalf against Babylon. God says he will raise up the Medes to bring it down. Babylon was then a power that dominated other peoples, and the prophet shows that no empire stands above God. Scholars often connect this with the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians, although some also see a broader meaning, as a symbol of human pride.

Today we can remember that fame, success, and wealth do not protect us if we live with arrogance. It is wise to trust God and to live with humility.
exp.58:13:
The verse says that among the people there was no longer any uprightness or justice. Justice has been turned away, and righteousness stands at a distance, as if it had been pushed out of reach. The public square was the open place where trials and the affairs of the city were handled, and there truth "stumbled," meaning it fell down. Honesty could not even enter.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and confesses their sins: lies, slander, and rebellion against God. He explains that injustice in society is born from a heart that has drifted away from God. Then the text shows that God sees this situation, is displeased, and promises to act himself to bring salvation.

Today we can begin by being people of our word and of fair dealing in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in the community. Let us speak the truth with love, not repeat gossip, and stand up for those who are treated unjustly, trusting that God upholds justice.
exp.41:16:
Those who trust in idols and say to molten images, "You are our gods!" will be turned back in utter shame. Idols are figures carved from wood or stone or cast in shaped metal. Those who call such images their gods will be humiliated when they discover that these things cannot help them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will lead the blind, turn darkness into light, and not forsake his people. By contrast, the verse shows the fate of those who place their hope in things made by human hands. God is faithful; idols are not.

For today: an idol is not always a statue. It can be money, success, or the approval of others, anything we look to for security in place of God. Today, ask yourself what you trust most and surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.7:16:
Isaiah says that he will wait for the LORD and put his trust in Him, even though the LORD is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. The phrase "hiding His face" means that God has withdrawn His favor and His visible help. To "wait" means to hope with patience and confidence.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. The people of Judah lived under the threat of enemies and, instead of trusting in God, many sought security in human alliances and in fortune-tellers. God had announced judgment, and Isaiah decides to remain faithful, keeping God's word with his disciples while others stumbled.

There are moments when we feel God is silent or distant. This verse invites us not to run after easy solutions or doubtful voices, but to keep trusting, praying, and obeying His Word while we wait. Faith does not always see, but it keeps waiting.
exp.42:26:
Israel's sin goes back a long way. "Your first father" could refer to Adam, Abraham or Jacob, or to the nation's first leaders; scholars understand it in several ways. "Your spokesmen" were God's representatives or interpreters, such as priests and prophets. "Rebelled" means they betrayed their duty and turned against God.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just offered free forgiveness: "I, even I, am the one who blots out your transgressions for my own sake." Then he invites the people to present their defense, and he answers that they have no argument: the sin goes back through generations, and even their guides rebelled. The next verse shows the consequences of judgment.

For today: do not defend yourself or make excuses based on your past, your family or your leaders. Acknowledge your wrong sincerely and receive the forgiveness that God gives by his grace.
exp.55:0:
God speaks and calls his people to "maintain justice" and "do what is right," that is, to live uprightly and to treat others with honesty and fairness. The reason is that his salvation is coming soon, and his righteousness will soon be revealed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The verses that follow say that those who obey will be blessed, and that neither the foreigner nor the eunuch, who might feel shut out, should think that God rejects them. Many scholars place this message at the time of the return from exile, though not all agree.

For today: if we are waiting for God's work, we should not sit with our arms folded. Today you can choose to be just in a concrete matter, such as paying what is owed, speaking the truth, or standing up for someone who is being treated with contempt.
exp.18:4:
The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty. In this verse, the river is the Nile, which is the great river of Egypt. The image is one of complete drought, with the water gone and the channel left bare.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, in a message of judgment against Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile for its harvests, its food, and its economy. It also trusted in its idols, magicians, and fortune-tellers. God shows that none of these could save it. Scholars debate which exact historical event is meant, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work, or plans. All of these can dry up like a river. God, however, remains faithful, and we can trust in Him first.
exp.39:12:
It says that no one has given instruction or advice to the Spirit of the LORD. It is a rhetorical question: the answer is "no one." The word "or" here is simply the ordinary word for "or," and "informed Him as His counselor" means that no one advised Him to make Him wiser.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who feel that God does not see their situation. Just before this, God appears as a tender shepherd and as a powerful Creator who measures the seas and the heavens. With these questions, Isaiah shows that God has perfect wisdom and needs no one's help. For this reason his care can be trusted.

When you do not understand what God allows in your life, do not give him orders or judge him from your limited view. Pray with sincerity, tell him your doubts, and rest in the knowledge that his wisdom is greater than yours. He cares for you as a shepherd cares for his lambs.
exp.39:21:
He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth, and its people look as small to him as grasshoppers. The phrase "circle of the earth" can mean a round shape or a rounded horizon, so it is not certain that the prophet had a sphere in mind. God stretches out the heavens like a curtain and spreads them out like a tent to live in.

Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people living in exile, surrounded by powerful nations and idols. He contrasts the true God with the wooden images that people make. Before and after this verse, he shows that nothing and no one, not kings or rulers, can be compared with the Creator.

For today: when problems or authorities seem enormous, remember who is truly great. Bring your worry to God in prayer, trusting that he is still in control.
exp.64:6:
God says he will hold the people accountable for their sins, both their own and those of their ancestors. The words "burned incense" mean they offered smoke to idols on the mountains and hills, and in doing so they provoked him. To "scorn" him means to speak of him with contempt and dishonor him.

"I will measure their former deeds into their laps" is an expression meaning that he will repay them in full for what they deserve. "Their former deeds" refers to the sin they had practiced for many years.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. He rebukes a rebellious people who practiced idolatry and, at the same time, considered themselves holier than others. God does not overlook that sin, but he promptly promises to save a faithful remnant.

For today: let us not keep repeating inherited mistakes without examining them. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our sins, to leave behind every false refuge, and not to look down on others. His justice is serious, but his mercy is too.
exp.34:8:
On the Highway of Holiness there will be no lions or vicious beasts to threaten those who travel it. A "vicious beast" is a wild and dangerous animal. The "redeemed" are those whom God has rescued. The way will be safe for them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who lived in fear and under threat. Before this, he announces that the desert will bloom. Here he promises a safe return to Zion, with joy. Many see it as a promise for the exiles of Israel, and Christians also read it as a greater hope of final restoration.

For today: if God has rescued you, you can walk with confidence even when the path seems dangerous. Bring your fears to Him in prayer and take the next step of obedience, remembering that He cares for His own.
exp.59:4:
Then you will look and be radiant, and your heart will tremble and swell with joy. The phrase "your heart will tremble and swell" means that your heart will be filled with joy and wonder. "The riches of the sea" refers to the wealth of distant lands, and "the wealth of the nations" means the goods and resources of the peoples. All of this will be brought to you.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, after announcing that the glory of God rises upon her. It is a promise of restoration: God will bring the people back from afar and draw the nations to her. Some see this fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and others also in Christ and the Church. Interpreters understand it in various ways.

For today: when you feel small or without hope, remember that God can restore what seems lost. Trust in Him and keep your heart open to joy and gratitude.
exp.61:8:
The people who harvest the grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather the grapes will drink the wine in the courts of his holy place. They will enjoy the fruit of their own labor, and they will do it with thanks and praise to God.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who had suffered invasions, when enemies carried off their crops. God promises that this will not happen again. The promise announces restoration for Jerusalem. Interpreters see it fulfilled in part with the return from exile, and also pointing to a greater restoration, announced in the following verse with the coming of the Savior.

For today: God watches over the fruit of our efforts. When you enjoy what you have earned through your work, give thanks and praise him, recognizing that everything comes from his hand.
exp.50:20:
Here God calls Jerusalem "afflicted," meaning suffering and worn down, and "drunk, but not with wine." This drunkenness does not come from liquor, but from having drunk the cup of God's punishment, which left her dazed, staggering, and without strength.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. The people suffered invasion, hunger, and the loss of their children because of their disobedience. No one seemed able to comfort them. But this call to listen prepares a good word: in the verses that follow, God, who defends his people, says that he takes away that cup and that they will no longer drink it.

For today: if you are stunned by pain, or by the consequences of your mistakes, do not stay alone in your sadness. Listen to the voice of God, who not only names your wound, but also promises comfort and restoration.
exp.39:6:
The grass withers and the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them. In other words, human life is fragile and fleeting, and God is in control. The words "indeed, the people are grass" confirm this: we are weak and temporary.

A voice asks the prophet to proclaim a message, and he asks what he should say. The answer is this: every human being is like grass, but the word of God endures forever. Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, and this contrast gives them comfort: what is human passes away, but God does what he says. Some scholars see the "wind" as a dry desert wind; others see it as the breath of God himself.

Today we can stop placing our security in success, fame, or our own strength, and rely on the Word of God, which does not fail and never ends.
exp.9:13:
The king of Assyria is boasting about his conquests. He says he took the wealth of the nations as easily as someone reaches into a nest and gathers abandoned eggs. No one resisted him: no wing fluttered, and no beak opened or chirped, meaning no one cried out to sound the alarm or protested against what was happening. The "wealth" he takes is what the verse describes as the riches of the nations, and "seize" means to take hold of by force.

The one speaking is the king of Assyria, quoted by Isaiah. God had used Assyria to correct his people, but the king became full of pride and claimed all the credit for himself. For this reason God announces that he will judge him, and then compares the king to an axe that thinks itself greater than the one who wields it.

For today: what we achieve comes from God, who gives us strength and opportunities. Let us give thanks to him, and use our successes with humility and service, without boasting.
exp.25:7:
Isaiah 26:8 says that God's people have waited for him while he carries out his judgments, meaning his just decisions and his work to correct and govern. The verse speaks of walking in the path of those judgments and of longing for his name and renown. Their deepest desire is for God himself, for who he is and for what he has done.

The people of Judah sing this as a song of confidence within Isaiah 24–27. They live between hardship and waiting, and they affirm that the LORD is righteous and that his ways are just. Scholars differ on the exact historical setting, but the tone is one of trust in the middle of difficulty.

For today: when justice seems slow in coming, do not let the waiting turn into bitterness. Let it become a time to long for God more and to remember who he is. Pray with a calm heart, read his Word, and trust that he is good and just.
exp.12:14:
It says that, on the day of judgment against Babylon, no one who is caught will escape. "Stabbed" means pierced with a sharp weapon. The phrase "captured" means taken prisoner, and "die by the sword" means they will be killed in battle.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon, and God himself speaks of its judgment. The verses before this one speak of the day of the Lord, with the heavens and the earth trembling. The verses that follow announce that God will stir up the Medes. It is harsh language, typical of ancient warfare. Interpreters see here the historical fall of Babylon, and some also see an image of God's final judgment against human pride.

For today: God takes injustice and arrogance seriously, and no human power lasts forever. Trust that He judges with justice. And examine your heart: do not join yourself to what God condemns, but seek his mercy.
exp.4:7:
It says that God mourns over and condemns those who keep buying house after house and field after field, until they have taken up all the space. "Add" means to pile up and accumulate; "land" refers to the family property; "no place is left" means leaving nothing for anyone else. The closing words sound like a rebuke: will you be the only ones living in the land?

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. It comes from the song of the vineyard, where Israel is the vineyard that was meant to produce justice and produced injustice. This is the first "woe" against specific sins. In Israel the land was divided among the families as an inheritance, so hoarding property left others without a livelihood. What follows announces empty houses and poor harvests.

For today: check whether your desire to gain more is leading you to forget your neighbor. Strive to be just and generous, and share what God has given you.
exp.34:7:
God promises to build a special road, a raised and well-marked highway called "The Way of Holiness." The "unclean" are those who are not clean before God, and the verse says they will not travel it. Only those who walk in this Way may use it, and fools will not stray onto it. So the passage promises that those who walk this road will be guided, and that even the simple-minded will not lose their way.

Isaiah speaks to a people facing threats and exile. In this chapter, the prophet announces restoration in poetic form: the desert blooms, the weak are healed, and the redeemed return to Zion with joy. Many see it as a hope for the return of Israel, and Christians also read it as pointing to the work of Christ. There are different ways of interpreting it.

For today: you do not have to find the way alone. If you feel lost or weak, ask God to guide you, and walk alongside other believers who can accompany you.
exp.47:5:
The explanation says that the people had already heard and seen God's promises come true, and so they ought now to tell others about them. The words "you have heard these things" and "look at them all" are the verse's own wording, so no further comment is needed. "New things, hidden things unknown to you" refers to new announcements that were previously unknown to them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people who were stubborn and doubted Him. He had announced events before they happened, so that they would not credit them to their idols. Now He promises new things, probably the deliverance from Babylon, though some also see a broader scope.

For today: God has been faithful to you in the past. Recall one specific occasion when He was, and share it with someone this week. In this way your faith grows, and you do not attribute to chance what God has done.
exp.59:1:
This verse says that deep darkness will cover the earth and the nations. But upon God's people, addressed here as "you," the Lord will rise, and his glory will appear over them. The image is of the sun coming up over the horizon: God appears like a light dawning over the darkness. The phrase "the LORD will rise" describes him as the source of that light.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, especially to Jerusalem (Zion). He announces hope after difficult times: God will restore them, and his light will draw other nations. Many Christians also see in this verse a sign of Christ, the light of the world, although this is interpreted in several ways.

Even when there is dark news around you or moments of pain, God can be your light. Today, ask him to guide you, and try to reflect his goodness in the way you treat others.
exp.36:37:
One day, while Sennacherib was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword and fled to the land of Ararat. Another son, Esar-haddon, became king in his place. It is not known with certainty who Nisroch was.

The writer of the book of Isaiah tells how the Assyrian king who had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel came to his end. This ending fulfills what God had announced earlier: that Sennacherib would fall by the sword in his own land (Isaiah 37:7). It happened years after his withdrawal.

Today we can trust that God keeps his word, even when it takes time. Human powers may seem enormous, but they pass away. A false god could not protect even his own worshiper, so let us place our trust in the living God.
exp.25:2:
It says that God watches over and keeps in "perfect peace" the person whose mind stays fixed on Him. "Keep" here means to protect, like someone guarding a house. "Steadfast" means to remain firm and steady, not letting go. In the original language, the phrase "perfect peace" repeats the word for peace, as if to say complete peace. The reason the verse gives is simple: that person trusts in God.

It is part of a song that Judah will sing "in that day," meaning a future time of salvation. Isaiah writes it for a people living under threat, and he contrasts the city of God, strong because of His protection, with the proud city that God brings low (v. 5). Scholars debate which exact city is meant.

For today: when worry comes, go back to prayer and remember God's promises, instead of repeating your fears. Trusting is a daily decision, and God promises to sustain your heart.
exp.13:13:
This verse shows what this figure was saying in his heart: "I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High." The word "ascend" expresses the wish to rise to the heights and to take the place of God.

Isaiah gives this message as a mockery against the king of Babylon, who thought himself very great and was brought down (Isaiah 14:4). Many Christians have long read this passage as also referring to Satan, but others believe it speaks only of the human king. For that reason it is wise to be careful: the text clearly points to pride that ends in a fall.

For today: examine your desires with sincerity. When success or recognition tempts you to believe you are sufficient without God, pray and choose humility, for He lifts up the humble in His time.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. It says that what Isaiah is about to share is a "vision," meaning a message God showed him, and that it concerns Judah and Jerusalem. Isaiah was the son of Amoz. It names four kings of Judah: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

Here Isaiah himself is the one who saw the vision, though the message comes from God. The kings mentioned reigned for many years, so his ministry covered a long and difficult time for the people. The following verses show that God rebukes his people for rebelling, and at the same time calls them to return to him.

For today: God speaks in real situations and at specific times. You can read the Bible knowing that its message is not a distant idea, but a word addressed to real people, and to you as well.
exp.15:6:
This verse says that all the people of Moab will wail and cry out in pain together. The sound of their grief is strong, and the word "wail" in the verse above carries that idea. The verse then calls out to them to moan over the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, the city they trusted, and to recognize that they have been utterly struck down. Scholars understand the raisin cakes in different ways, some reading them as a literal food and others as a picture of the city's strength and support.

Isaiah, speaking on behalf of God, announces judgment on Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. The cause is their pride and their lies, mentioned just before. But the passage also shows hope: it speaks of a just throne in the tent of David, and even the prophet laments over Moab.

For today: pride may seem strong, but it does not hold up. We can examine what we place our security in, and ask God for a humble heart that also grieves for those who suffer.
exp.49:8:
He says that the Lord God is the one who helps the speaker, and so no one can truly condemn him. He asks, "Who is there to condemn Me?" and claims that his opponents will all wear out like a garment, with the moths devouring them.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, in the third Servant Song of Isaiah. He endures mockery and blows, but he trusts God. Many Christians see here an anticipation of Jesus; others also connect it to Israel or to the prophet himself. His confidence does not come from himself but from God's backing.

When you are accused unjustly, or feel guilty without reason, rest in the fact that the Lord God helps you. Human criticism passes away like worn-out clothing; the faithfulness of God remains.
exp.29:12:
This verse compares the people's sin to a high wall with a crack or a bulging, bent part. That wall looks solid, but its collapse will come suddenly, in an instant, without warning. The phrase "this iniquity of yours" makes clear that their sin will come back on them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. They rejected his word, would not listen to the prophets, and put their trust in violence, deceit, and human alliances instead of trusting in God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are relying on for our security. What is built on lies or pride may look firm for a while, but it cannot hold. God invites us to return to him and rest in his word.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that Israel will sing a song of contempt against the king of Babylon, mocking his downfall. The song celebrates how the oppressor has ceased and his fury has ended. Babylon was famous for its wealth and power, and the king was a tyrant who forced others to hand over what they owned.

Isaiah speaks of a future day when God will give rest to his people after their suffering. The verses just before this one promise that God will have compassion on Israel. He speaks to a people who would endure oppression, giving them hope that no empire lasts forever.

For today: if you feel oppressed or see injustice, trust that God has the last word. Rest in Him and avoid bitterness, waiting for his justice.
exp.6:14:
The verse says that the child promised, Immanuel, will be eating curds and honey. Curds are a simple food, something like cottage cheese. This simple diet continues while the child grows until he knows enough to reject evil and choose good, that is, until he reaches the point of discernment.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz and the house of David. Ahaz was afraid of two enemy kings and did not want to trust God. Then God gives him a sign: a child will be born, and before he grows up, those two kings will be removed. The simple food suggests hard times, since the land would be poor. Scholars debate whether the sign was first fulfilled in the time of Ahaz and then in Christ, as Matthew understands it.

For today: even in times of scarcity, God is with us. Ask him for wisdom to choose good, and trust him when you are afraid.
exp.4:4:
God announces what he is about to do with his vineyard. He will take away its hedge, the protection that surrounded it, and so it will be consumed by animals. He will also tear down its wall, the stone fence, and so it will be trampled underfoot by people. "Tear down" means to pull a wall apart so that it falls. "Trampled" means stepped on and crushed under foot.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf, in a song that uses the image of a disappointed vinedresser. God cared for his vineyard and expected good grapes, but it produced wild, bitter grapes. Verse 7 explains that the vineyard is Israel and Judah, and that God expected justice but found violence. Here the people themselves are called to judge the case.

God cares for us and looks for fruits of justice and mercy, not merely a religion of appearances. Today we can ask ourselves, with humility, what fruit we are bearing in how we treat others, and not take his protection for granted.
exp.7:1:
Isaiah says that he appointed two men to serve as trustworthy witnesses: Uriah, who was a priest, and Zechariah, son of Jeberekiah. The word rendered here as "appointed" means to choose or set someone in a role. A trustworthy witness was someone whose word could be believed whenever it was challenged.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, following God's command to write a message on a large scroll. That message announced that Syria and Israel would soon be defeated by Assyria. By appointing witnesses, Isaiah made it on record that he had said this before it happened. That way, when it came to pass, no one could claim he had made it up afterward. Scholars are not certain about the exact identity of these two men.

God is not afraid of being checked. If something in your life today depends on your word, make sure it is true and reliable, and do not fear that someone will examine it.
exp.28:9:
Here Isaiah says that God himself poured out on the people a spirit of deep sleep, like a very heavy sleep. He shut their eyes, that is, he took away their ability to understand. The prophets and the seers (those who received visions from God) were left as if a covering lay over their heads, unable to see clearly.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Jerusalem, also called Zion. The people practiced a religion of lips, but their hearts were far from God. For that reason they did not understand his message. Some scholars see here a judgment from God; others see it as the result of the people's hardness.

For today: if we hear the Word of God but do not want to obey it, it can become difficult for us to understand. Let us ask God for a humble and willing heart, and let us read the Bible with prayer.
exp.39:24:
God asks a question: "To whom will you liken Me, or who is My equal?" The one asking is "the Holy One," that is, God himself. The word "or" introduces a second way of asking the same thing, and "equal" means someone who matches Him, so the question is really asking, "What can you compare Me to?"

God has just said that powerful rulers are like plants that wither when He blows on them. Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who feel that God does not see their suffering. So God reminds them that no one can be compared to Him, and He invites them to look at the stars, which He calls by name.

Today we may be tempted to trust in money, in leaders, or in our own strength. When something worries you, look up at the sky and remember who God is: nothing is greater than He is, and you can rest in His care.
exp.41:21:
It says that the people of Israel were plundered, looted, and humiliated. Many were trapped in caves and locked up in dungeons. To be "plundered and looted" means being stripped of everything they had. No one came to rescue them, and no one said, "Send them back!" They were like helpless plunder.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, describing the condition of Israel, the blind and deaf servant he had spoken of before. The verses that follow explain that this ruin was not an accident: God himself allowed it because the people sinned and refused to walk in his ways or listen to his law. Many understand this to refer to the exile in Babylon, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when we suffer the consequences of ignoring God, we are not without hope. We can listen to his voice, return to him with humility, and trust that he does rescue those who seek him.
exp.43:27:
God says that Cyrus, king of Persia, is "my shepherd," meaning someone who will carry out His will. Cyrus will bring it about that Jerusalem is rebuilt and the temple's foundation is laid.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah at a time when Jerusalem had not yet been destroyed and the people were not yet in exile. He wants to comfort Israel and show that He is in control of history. He names Cyrus long before Cyrus ruled. Some believe Isaiah announced this in advance; others think this part was written during the exile. Either way, the message is that God can use a foreign king to fulfill His promises.

For today: when your situation seems to be in ruins, trust that God can work even through unexpected means. Pray, wait patiently, and watch for how He sustains you.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that the righteous person should be encouraged: it will go well with them, because they will enjoy the fruit of their labor. The phrase "they will enjoy the fruit of their labor" is a way of saying that they will receive the good result of their work and of how they live. The righteous person is one who lives uprightly before God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, on behalf of the LORD, to Jerusalem and Judah, who were in decline because of their open sin and their wicked leaders. In the midst of that judgment, God leaves a word of comfort for the faithful. The following verse shows the contrast: the wicked will reap their evil.

For today: do not lose heart if doing what is right seems to bring no reward. Remain honest and faithful even in small things, trusting that God sees and cares for those who obey him, even when we do not always understand the manner and timing.
exp.58:6:
They run toward evil without a second thought, and they are quick to kill innocent people. Their thoughts are sinful, and wherever they go, ruin and destruction follow in their wake. Their path is marked by harm to others.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He shows them that their sins, such as violence, deceit, and injustice, are the reason God seems far away and why there is no justice among them. Isaiah speaks on behalf of everyone and includes himself in the people's confession.

For today: evil almost always begins in the thoughts. Ask God to examine your mind, and reject resentment, envy, or the desire to harm others. Take care what you think, because from there your steps are born.
exp.36:12:
This verse is a question that does not seek an answer but aims to mock. It asks where the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah are, that is, of cities that had already been conquered. It means: "They no longer exist, and neither will you be saved."

The speaker is the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, speaking through messengers and letters addressed to King Hezekiah of Judah. He wanted to frighten him into surrendering, telling him that the gods of other nations had not rescued them and that the God of Judah would not rescue him either. Hezekiah did not answer with fear, but took the letter to the temple and spread it out before God.

For today: when threats or bad news overwhelm you, do not keep turning them over in your mind. Bring them to God in prayer, honestly, and trust that He is different from everything that seems powerful in this world.
exp.35:0:
This verse tells us that in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah's reign, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. The "fortified cities" were the ones that had walls and defenses.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, introducing a new section of Isaiah (chapters 36 to 39). It shows the crisis Judah faced before the powerful Assyrian empire. Hezekiah was known as a king who sought to honor God, and yet he faced this threat. Scholars debate how exactly to fit the date together with other chronologies of the period, so it is best to take it with caution.

Even faithful people can go through great trials. When everything that seemed secure falls apart, it is time to turn to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did, and not to trust only in our own defenses.
exp.62:4:
I looked around, and there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one came to my aid. So I acted myself: "My arm brought Me salvation" means that God's own power won the victory, and "My own wrath upheld Me" means that his righteous anger kept him steady.

The Lord speaks, pictured as a warrior who treads the winepress, that is, the place where grapes are trodden. That image of judgment against the nations contrasts with the year of his redeemed. Then the prophet recalls God's mercies toward Israel. Some Christians see here a shadow of Christ, but the text speaks directly of the Lord and his people.

For today: God does not depend on our strength to save. He rests in his work and responds with gratitude, remembering his mercies.
exp.46:2:
Babylon will be stripped bare and disgraced in full view of others. The words "shame" and "exposed" describe her public fall, with no place left to hide. God declares that he will take vengeance, meaning he will carry out justice. The line "I will spare no one" is clearer in the Berean wording, and it shows that no one will be left untouched by his judgment. Some readers take this to mean that no one will be able to stop God or plead for her, while others understand it to mean that God will accept no intermediary between himself and Babylon.

God speaks through Isaiah, addressing Babylon as a proud woman who goes from queen to slave. She had been harsh with God's people (v. 6), and she considered herself secure forever. God judges her and, at the same time, presents himself as the Redeemer of Israel.

For today: pride and cruelty do not last, because God sees and does justice. Instead of trusting in your power or your reputation, live with humility and treat others with compassion.
exp.7:12:
The verse tells us to regard God as holy and to let him hold first place in our hearts. "Regard as holy" means treating him as unique and set apart, worthy of our deepest respect. The words "feared" and "dreaded" here do not mean terror. They describe a deep, reverent awe toward God, the kind that orders our priorities and keeps us from bowing to lesser powers.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The kingdom of Judah was threatened by neighboring powers, and the people lived frightened, seeing conspiracies everywhere. God warns Isaiah not to be carried away by that panic. The verses that follow show that God would be a sanctuary for whoever trusts in him, but a stone of stumbling for whoever rejects him.

When fear of people, of news, or of the future overwhelms us, we can stop and pray: "Lord, you are greater than this." Putting God first brings back our calm and our perspective.
exp.29:17:
He says that God does not hurry to punish, but longs to show mercy to his people and waits for the right moment to do so. The word "therefore" links his patience to his desire to be gracious, and "rises to show you compassion" means that he will act in kindness and honor. "A just God" means that he acts with righteousness and fairness. "Blessed" means happy or fortunate. Those who wait for him are those who trust in him.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. They rejected God's help and sought to save themselves with horses and military alliances, probably with Egypt. Isaiah warns them that they would flee in defeat. Even so, this verse shows that God does not abandon them: he is willing to forgive them and restore them.

When you feel anxious, do not rush to hasty solutions that leave God out. Pray, ask him for direction, and wait with confidence. His timing may seem slow, but his mercy is certain.
exp.39:7:
It says that everything human is temporary, like the grass that withers and the flowers that fall. By contrast, what God says lasts forever. The wording here is "withers" and "fall," the verse's own words. "Stands forever" means it stays firm and does not change.

The passage comes from Isaiah 40, a message of comfort for the people of Judah, who faced exile or its consequences. A voice commands that someone cry out, and the prophet asks what to proclaim. The answer is that human strength is fragile, but God's promise is certain. Then comes the announcement: God comes to his people with power and care.

For today: when you feel weak or see that everything is changing, rely on the Word of God. Read a passage each day and trust his promises more than what passes quickly, such as success, fame, or worries.
exp.33:12:
It says that the towers and fortresses of this place will be left abandoned. Where the powerful once lived, thorns and thistles and briers will grow. In their place will come wild animals: jackals, which are dog-like creatures of the wild, and ostriches.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God on the nations, and in this passage in particular on Edom, mentioned in verse 5. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and appears in the Bible as an opponent of God's people. The picture of total ruin shows that no human power can withstand God. Some scholars also see in it a general picture of the final judgment.

Everything people build with pride is temporary. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our security: in our riches and achievements, or in God, who endures forever.
exp.37:15:
The explanation says that true life depends on the mercy of God, meaning his compassion and goodness. Hezekiah affirms that his spirit finds life in them, and that he will tell this to others. The word "rests on" captures the sense of what the verse describes. It ends with confidence: God has restored Hezekiah to health and let him live.

King Hezekiah of Judah is the one speaking. He had fallen gravely ill and received word that he would die. He prayed with tears, and God granted him more years of life. He wrote this song after he recovered, looking back with pain and now with gratitude, as the following verses show, where he speaks of the forgiveness of his sins.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not keep silent about what God has done for you. Write down how he sustained you and tell someone. In this way your gratitude can encourage others to trust in his mercy.
exp.13:7:
The explanation says that even the trees rejoiced when this tyrant fell. The "cypresses and cedars" are the trees named in this version, and scholars are not sure exactly which plants are meant. The word "exult" simply means that they were glad. The cedars of Lebanon, famous for their wood, speak as if they were saying: since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us anymore.

Isaiah announces a mocking song against the king of Babylon (v. 4). He was a cruel ruler who oppressed peoples and laid waste to nature for his building projects and wars. The trees appear in poetic language, as if all creation were breathing a sigh of relief. Afterward, the world of the dead also receives him with astonishment.

For today: oppressive power does not last forever, and God sees the harm done to people and to creation. We can use whatever authority we have, at home, at work, or in our community, to care for and not to destroy.
exp.13:14:
It says that the one who dreamed of rising up to heaven ends up "brought down," that is, thrown down, into the grave. The phrase "to the lowest depths of the Pit" in this verse points to the deepest part of the place of the dead.

Isaiah directs this mocking song against the king of Babylon, a proud and cruel ruler who oppressed many nations. His ambitious words, "I will be like the Most High," stand in sharp contrast with his end. Some Christians see here also an echo of Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of the human king; there are different interpretations.

For today: pride promises to rise, but it ends in falling. Let us ask God for a humble heart, for He Himself "gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6).
exp.37:0:
Hezekiah the king became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, came to him with a message from God: "Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover." In other words, the king should put his affairs in order and leave instructions, because his death was near.

Here Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, carries God's word to the king of Judah. This happens at a time of threats, when Assyria was pressing on the kingdom. The verses that follow show that Hezekiah prayed and wept, and the story continues with God's response. For that reason, the statement is not to be understood as final, but as the beginning of a dialogue with God.

For today: do not wait until you are sick or in crisis to put your life in order. Speak with God honestly, take care of important unfinished matters, and look after your family. And if hard news arrives, you can bring it to God in prayer.
exp.54:0:
God says he invites everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters. Even those who have no money may come, and they can buy and eat. Wine and milk are offered for free, without money and without cost. The word "come" carries the sense of "come along," and fullness means abundance, being well satisfied.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. This message is addressed to a weary people, probably in exile or near it, who are seeking comfort. The verses that follow show that God calls them to stop spending their strength on what does not satisfy, and he promises them an everlasting covenant, tied to the promises made to David.

Today, this invitation reminds us that we cannot earn God's favor through effort. If you feel emptiness or weariness, you can draw near to him just as you are, and receive his grace with open hands.
exp.21:24:
In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, God announces that the peg driven into a firm place will give way. It will be sheared off and fall, and the load hanging on it will be cut down. The peg seemed secure, yet it will be pulled out and broken, and everything hanging from it will be destroyed. "Driven into a firm place" means it was fixed solidly, and "give way" means it will fail and come loose.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah, in a message about the officials of the palace of Judah. The peg represents a trusted man, on whom his family hung all their honor. Scholars disagree about who he is: some think it is Eliakim, others see a reference to Shebna. What is clear is that no human support lasts forever, and that what was said will come to pass, for the LORD has spoken.

For today: value the strong people who hold you up, but do not hang all your security on them. Place your ultimate trust in God, who never fails and never breaks.
exp.29:21:
It says that when God restores them, the people will treat their idols with complete contempt. "Defile" here means to declare impure something that was once revered. The idols were covered in silver and gold, and they will strip off that covering and throw it away like a soiled cloth, something unclean and worthless, and say to the idols: "Be gone!"

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was seeking help in Egypt and in idols instead of trusting the Lord. Although suffering would come, Isaiah says God promises to guide them with his voice and lead them to repentance. Then comes the blessing of rain and abundant harvests.

For today: ask yourself what thing has taken God's place in your heart. When you recognize it, do not adorn or justify it: surrender it to God and cast it out with determination.
exp.9:20:
It says that a small group of the people of Israel, those who survive, will return to God. "Remnant" means those who are left over, the survivors. "Will return" means they will turn back and come home. "The Mighty God" is a title of the Lord that highlights his power.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the kingdom of Judah, at a time when the Assyrian empire threatened to destroy nations. God warns that judgment will come because of the people's injustice, but he promises that he will not wipe them out completely. A remnant will stop trusting in the power that had wounded them, which was Assyria, and will lean on God. The name of Isaiah's son, Shear-jashub, means "a remnant shall return" (Isaiah 7:3), although some connect it to this passage in different ways.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, God can still raise up a new life from what little remains. Return to him and lean on him, not on what has hurt you.
exp.32:18:
The explanation says that the people of Jerusalem will no longer see that insolent foreign people who inspired fear, whose speech sounded strange and impossible to follow. The word "insolent" describes a people who cause dread. The phrase "a people whose speech is unintelligible" and the comment about a "language you cannot understand" describe speech that cannot be understood. The promise is that this threat will disappear.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah when Assyria, a foreign power, was oppressing them and collecting tribute. The officials who counted and weighed the spoil were a symbol of that domination. The prophet announces that God will deliver his people, and that they will see the King in his beauty. Scholars debate whether that King is God himself, or King Hezekiah, or a future hope.

Today, God can give us peace in the face of what intimidates us and what we do not understand. When fear speaks loudly, let us remember the King who cares for his own, and trust that He has the last word.
exp.49:4:
God has opened my ears, so to speak, giving his servant the ability to truly listen and obey. In response, the servant has not been rebellious (he has not resisted God) and has not turned back (he has not drawn back or withdrawn).

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, in the third Servant Song in Isaiah. Each morning he receives God's teaching so that he can sustain the weary. What follows shows that obeying cost him suffering: blows, mockery, and spitting. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus; others first connect it to the prophet or to Israel, and it can be read on more than one level.

For today: begin the day by listening to God before the rush of your schedule. Read a passage, be quiet, and ask him for a heart willing to obey, even when it costs you.
exp.20:10:
This is a message from God that Isaiah calls a burden, concerning Dumah. A voice calls out to the prophet from Seir, a region of Edom: "Watchman, what is left of the night?" In other words, "Watchman, how much longer until this darkness ends?" The question is repeated because of the distress behind it.

The prophet stands like a watchman, waiting for the word of God. Dumah may refer to Edom or to a place in Arabia; it is not known for certain. The one asking lives in a time of oppression and wants to know whether relief will come. The watchman's answer is ambiguous: morning is coming, but so is the night. Many read it as an invitation to keep seeking God.

For today: when you go through a difficult night, do not keep the question locked inside. Bring it to God, stay attentive to his word, and return to him with patience, even when the answer is not immediate or complete.
exp.62:13:
Isaiah 63:14 says that the Spirit of the LORD guided Israel with care, the way cattle are led down into a valley: calmly and safely, so that they could rest. The word "cattle" here refers to livestock, and "led" means to care for and guide. God did this "to make for Yourself a glorious name": to show who He is.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, in a prayer that recalls the exodus. He looks back to the crossing of the sea and the desert, with Moses as the guide. He does this because the people feel far from God and ask Him to show His love and His power again, as the verses that follow say.

For today: when you feel lost or tired, remember how God has guided you before. That remembrance can become prayer and hope, because the Shepherd does not change.
exp.25:16:
The verse compares the people to a woman about to give birth, who writhes and cries out in intense pain. The words "in Your presence" mean that their suffering was fully visible to God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel (Judah). It is part of a song of trust after times of punishment and distress. The people acknowledge that they sought God in their trouble. But the verses that follow say that this pain did not bring the deliverance they hoped for. Then the hope appears that the dead will live. Interpreters debate whether this speaks of the restoration of the nation, of the final resurrection, or of both.

For today: when you suffer and see no results, bring your pain to God honestly. He sees your suffering and hears your cries, and He can give hope beyond what you see today.
exp.0:19:
It says that God sets two paths before his people. If they choose to resist and rebel, they will be "devoured by the sword", that is, destroyed by war at the hands of their enemies. The phrase "if you resist" in the verse refers to the people, and the verse ends with a statement of authority: "For the mouth of the LORD has spoken", meaning God himself declared it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he offers them complete forgiveness: their sins, red as crimson, would become white as snow. He asks them to decide. Then the text describes a city that was once faithful and is now full of injustice and violence.

For today: God's forgiveness is real and generous, but it also invites us to respond. Today you can identify one area where you have hardened your heart, speak with God about it honestly, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.63:6:
No one calls on your name or makes an effort to take hold of God. That is why he seemed to hide his face from them, and why they were left to the power of their own wrongdoing, like a dry plant crushed under its own weight.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people in a prayer of repentance. Many understand that he looks toward the time of exile or later, when Israel felt God's distance. He confesses sin honestly, and then, in verse 8, he holds on to God as Father and potter.

For today: if you feel spiritual coldness, do not stay in complaint. Wake up, pray sincerely, and confess whatever is pulling you away. God is still a Father, and he receives those who return to him.
exp.36:15:
Here King Hezekiah begins his prayer by calling God "LORD of Hosts," that is, the LORD who commands all the powers of heaven and earth. "Enthroned above the cherubim" refers to God's presence above the ark of the covenant, where there were figures of cherubim (angelic beings). Hezekiah declares that the LORD alone is God over all the kingdoms of the earth and that He made the heavens and the earth.

Hezekiah speaks in the temple, after receiving a threatening letter from Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who mocked God and wanted Jerusalem to surrender. The king does not respond with fear or with pride, but spreads the letter out before God and prays.

When you face a threat or a piece of news that troubles you, before doing anything else, bring it to God. Remind Him, and remind yourself, who He is: the Creator, greater than any problem.
exp.39:10:
He will care for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. The word translated "tends" describes a shepherd who guides, feeds, and watches over the flock. He will gather the lambs in his arms and carry them close to his heart. The nursing ewes are the ones he will lead with gentleness.

Isaiah announces comfort to Judah, a people beaten down and discouraged. The messenger is to shout without fear: "Here is your God!" The verse before this one shows God arriving with power and strength. This verse shows the other side: that same strong arm, which rules, also carries the weak with gentleness. The text then goes on to speak of God's incomparable greatness.

For today: if you feel tired or fragile, you do not have to pretend to be strong. God knows your limit and cares for you with patience. And if you have strength, you can treat those who are weaker with the same gentleness.
exp.63:11:
Here the people ask God whether he will hold himself back and stay silent in the face of so much suffering. The words "will You restrain Yourself" and "keep silent" carry the same sense as the verse: to refrain from acting, to stay quiet. The phrase "afflict us beyond measure" means to bring great hardship upon us, far beyond what is fair. It is an honest cry: "How long, Lord? Will You do nothing?"

The prophet speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of lament. The cities are deserted and the temple was burned, something many understand as the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. Some think Isaiah looks ahead to that future in advance; others think he speaks from the perspective of the exile. Scholars explain this in different ways. The people acknowledge their sin, yet still ask for mercy.

For today: when you feel that God is silent in the midst of your pain, do not hide your complaint. Bring it to him honestly, as this people did, and trust that God hears and is compassionate, even when his answer is slow in coming.
exp.1:0:
This verse works like a kind of title. It says that what follows is a message revealed to Isaiah, a message from God. Isaiah was the son of Amoz, and his message concerns Judah and Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, introducing the prophet. Isaiah prophesied in Judah, the southern kingdom, and the book itself mentions several kings of his time. What follows in the chapter is a vision of hope: one day the nations will seek God in Jerusalem. Some understand this as something still in the future, and others see a partial fulfillment in history.

For today: before hearing a message from God, it is good to remember that it comes from Him, not from human ideas. Read the Bible with attention and humility, ready to receive what God reveals.
exp.29:32:
It says that God has long had a place of judgment prepared, called Topheth, made ready for the king. The phrase "has been made ready" means it has been arranged and prepared. It is a deep and wide place, with a great fire and plenty of wood. The breath of the LORD, his breath, sets it ablaze like a torrent of burning sulfur.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was looking for help in Egypt out of fear of Assyria. He assures them that the LORD himself will break Assyria. Topheth was a place near Jerusalem, later associated with terrible sacrifices. Many believe the "king" is the king of Assyria; others see a more general picture of God's judgment on the proud. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: you do not need to fear the powerful or rely on your own resources. God is just and has the last word. Give your fears to him in prayer and trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.37:2:
Hezekiah asks God to remember how he has lived. To "walk before you faithfully" means to live faithfully before God, and "wholehearted devotion" means a devotion that is complete and undivided. He says he has done what is "good" in God's sight, that is, what is good in God's eyes. Then he "wept bitterly," meaning he wept with deep grief.

King Hezekiah is speaking while he is very ill. The prophet Isaiah has just told him that he is going to die. He turns his face toward the wall, perhaps to pray in private, and cries out to God. Scholars do not agree on every detail of his request, but God heard his prayer and his tears, and added fifteen years to his life.

For today: you can be completely honest with God in your moments of pain, fear, or distress. Bring Him your tears and your requests with sincerity, trusting that He hears you and cares about you.
exp.1:13:
This verse follows a list of proud and lofty things over which the "day of the LORD" will come. Here the tall mountains and the high hills are named. It is a poetic image: what looks great and secure on the earth will be brought low by God.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks in God's name. The cedars, the mountains, the towers and the ships represent people's pride and their trust in their power and wealth. Many understand these images as speaking of proud people, though some also see a judgment on nature and on human works. The central point is that only God is exalted (v. 17).

For today: examine what you trust in, whether your success, your money, or your position. Ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on him and not on what seems high and secure.
exp.33:15:
Isaiah invites readers to search the scroll of the Lord and confirm that nothing of what has been announced is missing. The word "search" in the verse is the same invitation to look closely and read carefully, and the phrase about the creatures each having a mate matches the verse's wording that not one will lack her mate. The birds and animals of the desert come in pairs because God has ordered it by His mouth, and He gathers them by His Spirit.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The whole chapter announces judgment on the nations, and Edom is named in a special way. The land will be left desolate and inhabited by wild animals. Scholars debate whether "the scroll" is Isaiah's own written book or a broader divine record. In either case, the message is that the word of God is fulfilled.

For today: you can trust that what God says is firm. Read the Bible carefully, compare passages, and rest in the fact that He keeps what He promises, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.8:7:
The verse says that the Lord sent a message against Jacob, that is, against his people Israel, and that it fell upon them. "Jacob" and "Israel" name the same people here.
