The word "fallen" suggests a message that arrives with force and cannot be ignored; some read it as a message of judgment that would come to pass.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Just before, he announced the promise of a child who would bring peace and everlasting justice. Now the tone changes: the northern kingdom, Israel, with Ephraim and Samaria, responded with pride, declaring they would rebuild better what had been destroyed, without turning back to God. The message had arrived, but they did not take it seriously.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, let us not brush it aside with pride or with confidence in our own strength. Let us listen with humility and allow it to correct us in time.
exp.28:10:
The explanation says that, for the people, the whole vision of God had become like a scroll sealed shut. If it is handed to someone who can read, he answers: "I cannot, because it is sealed." The word "vision" refers to the message God gave through the prophets. "Sealed" means closed, impossible to open.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for the LORD to Jerusalem. God says that he has poured out on them a deep sleep: his people were spiritually dull and did not understand. The problem was not that the message was missing, but that their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow explain this: they honored him with their lips, but their hearts were far away, and their religion had become merely human custom.

For today: owning a Bible or talking about God is not enough. Before reading it, ask God for a humble heart willing to obey. In this way his Word stops being a closed book and becomes a light for your life.
exp.43:13:
This verse describes a man who gets wood to make an idol. He cuts down cedars, takes a cypress or an oak, and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He also plants a laurel, which grows because the rain makes it grow.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, who lived surrounded by nations with idols. With a touch of irony, he points out the absurdity of idolatry: the man uses the same wood to warm himself and to cook, and also to make a god. Moreover, the laurel grows because of the rain that God sends, not because of the man.

For today: check which things, jobs or achievements have taken God's place. Everything we have comes from Him. Let us give Him first place and thank Him for what He gives us.
exp.34:3:
Explanation:
It says that anxious and discouraged people (those with anxious hearts) should be encouraged: "Be strong, do not fear!" God himself is coming. "Vengeance" and "divine retribution" mean that God will do justice and set right the wrong; "to save you" means rescuing his people.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to God's people, who lived in fear before enemies and judgments. After describing the desert that blossoms, he asks them to strengthen the weak. Then it is announced that the blind will see and the lame will leap: signs that God restores. Some see here also a promise that points to Christ; others read it mainly as hope for Israel.

Today, when someone close to you is discouraged, do not give them only advice: tell them gently that God is faithful and that they are not alone. And you, remember that promise when you feel fear.
exp.53:4:
This verse says that God himself is like a husband to his people. "Maker" means the one who created you; "Redeemer" is the one who rescues you and gives you back your freedom; "Holy One of Israel" speaks of a God who is pure and set apart. Although he has a powerful name, "LORD of Hosts," he also draws near with tenderness. And he is called the God of all the earth.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from God to Jerusalem, which feels like an abandoned woman without children. Before this verse, God promises growth and that there will be no more shame. Afterward, he explains that he left her for "a little moment" and that he will gather her back with great mercy. It is a poetic picture of God's love.

For today: if you feel lonely or ashamed of your past, bring that pain to God in prayer. He not only made you, he also redeems you and cares for you.
exp.51:3:
It says that God's people went down to Egypt long ago, not to stay there, but to live there as foreigners. Afterward, Assyria oppressed them without any just reason. The verse does not spell out the details of how they were treated, but it makes clear that their suffering was unjust.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, and comforts a people who are suffering. He recalls two oppressions: Egypt and Assyria. There are several ways to interpret which exact moment the verse points to, but the idea is clear: Israel was mistreated unjustly. That is why God promises to rescue them and to show himself present.

For today: when you feel you are suffering without reason, or feel bound and held back, remember that God sees injustice and does not forget you. Bring your pain to him in prayer, trust that he is at work, and shake off discouragement, because his rescue does not depend on what you are able to pay.
exp.5:6:
In this verse, the seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with the burning coal from the altar. Then he declares that Isaiah's guilt has been removed and his sin atoned for. "Iniquity" is the guilt that weighs on a person, and "atoned for" here means that the sin has been dealt with and forgiven.

Isaiah has seen God in his glory in the temple and feels lost, because he recognizes that his lips and those of his people are unclean. The seraph, a heavenly being, speaks on behalf of God. The forgiveness comes by divine initiative, from the altar, and not through any effort of Isaiah's own. After this, Isaiah hears God's call and responds. Scholars interpret the symbolism of the coal in various ways, but all agree that it shows the purification that God gives.

Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, acknowledging our faults without hiding them. He forgives and cleanses, and from that forgiveness he invites us to serve him with gratitude.
exp.54:7:
It says that God thinks and acts in a way that is different from ours. The words "My thoughts" and "your ways" show that the contrast is between God and the people He is speaking to, and the phrase "declares the LORD" shows that it is God Himself who is speaking. This does not mean that God is beyond understanding, but that His plans are greater than ours.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were living in exile and felt far from Him. Just before this, He invites them to seek Him, to leave the wicked way, and to return, because He pardons generously. This verse explains why they can trust Him: His forgiveness is greater than they imagine.

For today: when it is hard for you to forgive yourself or to believe that God welcomes you, remember that His mercy does not work the way ours does. Return to Him with confidence, even if you do not understand everything.
exp.37:18:
Only the living can truly give thanks to God. To "confess" here means to praise God or openly acknowledge what he has done. To be "made known" means to be made widely known and passed on. Parents, then, will teach their children that God is faithful and keeps his promises.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks in a song after being very ill, almost at the point of death. God healed him and forgave his sins. For him, death would end the opportunity to praise God in this life. So, grateful, he promises to sing and tell of his deliverance.

For today: if God has helped you through a difficulty, tell it out loud. Share with your children, nephews, nieces, or young friends how you have seen his faithfulness. Your testimony can strengthen their faith.
exp.22:2:
The verse says that Tyre grew rich from the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile, which came to her over the great waters. The phrase "grain of Shihor" refers to the crops sent from Egypt, and "harvest of the Nile" refers to the produce of the river's fertile lands. "Merchant of the nations" means that Tyre was a center where many peoples came together to trade.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Tyre, a great trading city by the sea. The ships and the merchants mourn because their harbor will be destroyed. The verse recalls where her wealth came from: trade with other peoples. Scholars debate at what historical moment this prophecy was fulfilled.

Today we can be thankful for the work and the goods we have, but without trusting in them as if they were our security. What seems firm today can change soon. It is wise to place our trust in God and to use what we have with generosity.
exp.31:9:
It says that women who live at ease and feel secure will tremble, "in a little more than a year." The reason is that the grape harvest will fail and the fruit harvest will not arrive. "Secure" here means feeling safe without good reason.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. Earlier he announced a righteous king (ch. 32:1), and now he warns the comfortable women who do not take the warning seriously. Many understand it to refer to a judgment that would come upon the land; scholars do not agree on the exact date.

For today: do not confuse comfort with security. Check whether your peace rests on your possessions or on God, and heed his voice before the crisis arrives.
exp.18:1:
Here God says that he will incite the Egyptians against one another. There will be fighting between brothers, neighbors, cities, and even kingdoms. "Incite" means to stir up conflict and disorder. A "neighbor" is the person who lives nearby or is close to us.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, in what is called a "burden," that is, a message of judgment against Egypt. This country trusted in its idols, its fortune-tellers, and its own wisdom. God shows that none of these will protect it. It is not known with certainty which specific historical event is meant; scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: when a society, a family, or a church is divided and filled with conflict, it is good to ask ourselves whether we have placed our trust in passing things instead of in God. Let us seek peace and humility before him.
exp.45:11:
God calls the attention of people who are "stubborn," that is, unwilling to listen or to change. He says they are "far removed from righteousness": they live apart from what is right and from what God approves. "Listen to Me" is a serious invitation to pay attention.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to the people of Israel. He has just shown that his plans are fulfilled and that the idols of Babylon cannot save anyone. Even so, the people were doubting. That is why God confronts them, but right away he promises to bring his righteousness and his salvation near to Zion.

For today: if you notice that your heart becomes stubborn in the face of God's correction, stop and listen. Read his Word with humility and ask him for a heart willing to respond. He does not call you in order to condemn you, but to bring you near to his salvation.
exp.45:0:
Bel crouches and Nebo cowers. The images of these Babylonian gods are carried on beasts and cattle, and they weigh the animals down. The idols you carry are a burden, a heavy load for the tired animal.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Bel (another name for Marduk) and Nebo were important gods of Babylon. The text announces that Babylon will fall and that its idols will be carried away. Then God contrasts this with how he treats Israel: he has carried them from the womb.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up weighing on us and cannot save us. God, on the other hand, carries us. Today you can hand him a specific worry and rest in his care.
exp.47:7:
God tells his people that he has never heard or understood these new things before, and that their ears have long been closed to him. God already knew how deceitful they were, and that they would be unfaithful and would disobey him. That is why he called them "rebels from birth," a way of saying that this tendency went back to the very beginning of their history.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel. He announces new things so that they cannot say, "We already knew it," nor credit them to their idols. Even so, the next verse shows that God, for the sake of his name, holds back his anger and does not destroy them.

For today: humbly recognize that at times your heart resists God, and yet he does not reject you. Ask him to open your ears to listen to him and obey him, trusting in his patience and his mercy.
exp.65:5:
Hear the uproar from the city, and listen to the voice from the temple. This is the voice of the LORD, repaying his enemies what they deserve. The word "uproar" here describes a loud, roaring commotion, the kind of noise that fills a whole place at once.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he rebuked those who did evil and did not answer his call. He also encouraged the faithful who were despised for their faith. Here he announces that he himself will act. Scholars debate which city and temple are meant: it may be Jerusalem, or it may be a picture of God's judgment.

For today: if you feel rejected for following God, do not seek revenge or despair. Trust that God sees everything and will bring justice in his time. In the meantime, remain faithful and respond when he speaks to you.
exp.62:3:
God says that he has held a day of justice in his heart to bring judgment against evil. "Vengeance" here means justice that sets crooked things straight, not an uncontrolled anger. The verse also says that the year of his "redemption" has arrived, that is, the time when he rescues his people. "Had come" simply means that the time had already arrived.

The Lord speaks, presented as a warrior coming from Edom with his clothes stained, like someone who has trodden grapes in the winepress. He does this alone, because no one else could save. Isaiah shows God judging the oppressors and freeing his people. Some Christians also see in this a look toward Christ; others read it mainly as historical judgment.

For today: if you have suffered injustice, do not take revenge with your own hands. Hand the matter over to God, trust that he will do justice in his time, and keep doing good with patience.
exp.20:0:
Isaiah announces a "burden," that is, a heavy message of judgment. He compares the arrival of an invader to whirlwinds, strong winds that sweep through the Negev, the southern desert. A "land of terror" is a frightening land, from which something dreadful comes. "The Desert by the Sea" is a hard phrase; many understand it as Babylon, but not everyone is certain.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks and recounts a vision that God shows him. In the verses that follow, which mention the Medes and the Persians, many believe it foretells the fall of Babylon. Isaiah does not rejoice: the vision fills him with anguish and dread.

Today we can remember that no empire or human power escapes the sight of God. When the world seems like a storm, trust that God governs history. And, like Isaiah, learn to feel pain for the suffering of others, without mocking it.
exp.39:20:
God asks four questions in a row to wake up his people. He reminds them that they already know the truth about him: they have been taught it from the very beginning, and creation itself shows it. The phrase "since the foundation of the earth" simply means since the world was created.

The prophet's message brings comfort to a tired and discouraged people. Earlier he speaks of idols that a craftsman shapes with wood and metal, and that must be fastened in place so they do not fall. Then he shows God ruling over the whole earth. The questions are meant to help the people remember who their God is.

For today: when you feel small or worried, take time to recall what you already know about God. Remember what you have heard about him and what you have seen of him in your life, and trust him again.
exp.46:4:
God tells Babylon, called "Daughter of the Chaldeans," to sit in silence and go into darkness. This is a picture of someone humbled, stripped of her seat of honor and her voice. Going into darkness suggests shame, loss of power, and gloom in place of glory. She will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms, the great power that ruled over other nations.

God himself speaks here through Isaiah. Babylon had dominated Judah, but it treated the people cruelly, and God judges it for its pride and lack of compassion. Some understand this as a prophecy about the historical fall of Babylon; others also see in it an example of human pride in general.

For today: power, success, and fame are not permanent. If God gives us authority, let us use it with humility and mercy, and not think that our position will be secure forever.
exp.39:8:
This verse calls a bearer of good news to climb up onto a high mountain and call out without fear. The message is for Zion, Jerusalem, and all the cities of Judah: "Here is your God!" The phrase "herald of good news" refers to the one who carries the news and announces it. "Raise your voice loudly" refers to the voice of the messenger.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who are weary and discouraged, probably in or near the time of exile. Earlier he said that all human things are fragile like grass, but that the word of God endures. Now God comes with power, and also as a tender shepherd who carries his lambs. Some scholars see Jerusalem herself as the messenger; others see a group of messengers.

For today: do not keep quiet the hope you have received. With humility and without fear, encourage someone who is tired, reminding them that God is strong and also cares with tenderness.
exp.32:2:
It says that when God acts with power, there is a great thunder of his voice, and the peoples flee in fear. "When You rise" means that God rises up to act, and then the nations scatter.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. He has just pronounced a "woe" against a cruel and treacherous plunderer, and then he prays to God asking for help. Many think it refers to Assyria, but the text does not name it here, and some see it as a broader message. What is clear is that God does not leave violence and treachery unanswered.

For today: when you feel that evil or injustice seems stronger, pray as Isaiah did: "be gracious to us; we have waited for You." Trust that God will rise up in his time, and in the meantime, do not repay evil with evil.
exp.47:1:
The explanation says that the people take their identity from Jerusalem, the holy city, and say they lean on the God of Israel. That God has a weighty name: the LORD of Hosts, meaning the LORD who rules over all the powers of heaven and earth. "Who call yourselves after the holy city" means they describe themselves as belonging to the holy city and claim it as their own.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Judah, who take the name of Israel and invoke the LORD, but not in truth or in righteousness. God reminds them that their words and their religious identity do not match their lives. Next he will tell them that he knows them as a stubborn people.

For today: it is not enough to say "I am a Christian" or to belong to a church. Ask God that your trust in him be sincere and that it shows in the way you live, speak, and treat others.
exp.25:20:
God says he is coming out of his dwelling, that is, out of the heavens where he rules, to hold the people of the earth accountable for their wrongdoing. The earth will reveal the bloodshed that was done on it and will no longer conceal those who were slain.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. This passage belongs to the section often called the "Little Apocalypse of Isaiah" (chapters 24 to 27), which speaks of God's judgment on the world and of hope for his people. Just before it, God invites his people to hide for a moment while his anger passes. Scholars interpret these images in different ways, but all see here the promise of justice.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that God sees every injustice, even the one no one else knows about. Hand over your pain, leave vengeance in his hands, and keep practicing justice and mercy.
exp.29:31:
God promises that every blow of punishment he brings down on Assyria will be accompanied by the sound of tambourines and lyres. The tambourines are hand drums, and the lyres are stringed instruments, similar to harps. The "rod of punishment" is the instrument God uses to strike, and the verse pictures him fighting against his enemies with weapons held high.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah. Assyria had oppressed the nations with violence, and Judah was seeking help from Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. God announces that Assyria, which struck others with the rod, will be broken by his voice.

For today: you can trust that God brings about justice in his own time. You do not need to take revenge or rely on human powers. Entrust your injustices to God and rest in the knowledge that he cares for you.
exp.65:13:
When you see this, you will rejoice, and you will flourish like grass. It says that God's people will see their promises fulfilled and their hearts will fill with joy. "You will flourish like grass" is an image of renewed strength and life, like grass that springs back to life after the rain. "The hand of the LORD will be revealed to His servants" means that God's care for his servants will be made clear. "His wrath will be shown to His enemies" means that he will show his anger against those who oppose him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. Earlier he has promised to comfort Jerusalem as a mother comforts her child. Then he announces judgment by fire. Thus the comfort for the faithful and the justice against the rebels go together.

For today: if you are tired or discouraged, rest in the knowledge that God cares for you as a mother cares for her child. Keep serving him with confidence, because he renews strength and will do justice in his time.
exp.64:10:
God speaks to those who abandon him and forget his holy mountain, that is, Jerusalem and its temple, the place where he is worshiped. Instead of seeking him, they set a table for Fortune and fill bowls of mixed wine for Destiny. These names seem to refer to gods of luck, although scholars are not completely certain about them. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and the bowls of mixed wine were offered as drinks in worship.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he promises to save a faithful remnant who will inherit the land. Here he marks the contrast with those among the same people who rejected his call and gave themselves over to idolatry. Then he announces the consequences of that choice.

Today we too can put our trust in luck, money, or success instead of God. Ask yourself: where do I place my confidence when I am afraid of the future? Return to God with simple prayer and trust in his care.
exp.62:6:
The explanation says that the one speaking will make known the Lord's loving devotion and recount his praiseworthy deeds. Its words for "loving devotion" refer to his steadfast love and compassion; "praiseworthy acts" refers to deeds worthy of being celebrated; "good things" refers to his generosity; and "great compassion" refers to his tenderness toward his people. All of this he did for the house of Israel, and it was a great deal.

The one speaking seems to be the prophet, who, on behalf of the people, begins a prayer that recalls the past. It comes after a passage about God's judgment against the enemies. Here the tone shifts: from justice to recalling his faithfulness. What follows shows that God had compassion on his people and rescued them.

For today: take stock of what God has done for you. Write down three concrete things and give thanks for them. Remembering strengthens faith when difficult times come.
exp.24:11:
God will bring down the high-walled fortress. The words "brought down" mean to level something, to knock it flat. The high walls were the walls that gave security. Being cast to the ground and into the dust describes a total fall, ending with the fortress lying flat on the earth.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a song of praise (chapters 24 to 27), where he celebrates that God will reign and save his people on this mountain. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears as an example of human pride. Many understand that it represents everyone who trusts in their own power. Some think that "your" refers to Moab, although the shift of person in the text is explained in several ways.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, fame, or your own strength. The walls we build out of pride fall, but whoever trusts in God rests safe.
exp.9:11:
God says that He will first finish what He intends to do with Jerusalem and Mount Zion, that is, His correction of His people. Then He will call the king of Assyria to account and punish him for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria was the nation God used as a tool to discipline His people, but the king believed he was the master of his own power and boasted of his conquests, as the verses that follow show. God makes clear that He does not overlook that pride.

For today: everything we achieve comes from God's hand. It is worth examining whether we are boasting of our successes, and asking Him for a humble and grateful heart.
exp.4:22:
The explanation says that God condemns those who take payment to declare the guilty person innocent, and who deprive the innocent person of justice. A "bribe" is a payoff. To acquit the guilty for a bribe means to clear them of wrongdoing in exchange for money, and to deprive the innocent of justice is to deny them fair treatment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. In this chapter, after the song of the vineyard, he pronounces six woes against injustices. Here he points to corrupt judges who, along with the proud and the drunkards, no longer respect the Lord's law. For that reason he announces judgment.

For today: God cares about justice in small things and in great ones. We can refuse to give or take bribes, even when they are common "favors," and honestly defend someone who is treated unfairly at work, at school, or in the community.
exp.13:11:
It says that someone very powerful and proud fell from a great height. "Day star, son of the dawn" is a brilliant title, like the star that shines before sunrise. The phrase "cut down to the ground" means struck down and thrown to the earth. The words "destroyer of nations" mean that he ruled over and oppressed the peoples.

Isaiah directs this prophetic taunt against the king of Babylon (see Isaiah 14:4). The dead receive him in the grave and are astonished that he too is mortal. Some Christians, since ancient times, see here also a reference to Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of a human king. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: pride promises to rise, but it ends in a fall. Ask God for a humble heart, and do not seek your worth in power or success, but in serving Him and others.
exp.46:7:
God speaks to Babylon, pictured as a luxurious and self-assured woman. The phrase "lover of luxury" describes someone who is used to comfort and indulgence. She feels so secure that she says, "I am, and there is none besides me," as if no one were greater than she is. She believes she will never be a widow or lose her children, that is, that she will never suffer ruin or loss.

God himself is the one speaking, through Isaiah. He used Babylon to discipline his people, but she was cruel and believed herself eternal. For this reason God announces that her fall will come suddenly.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in money, success, or our own intelligence. All of these can fail. Let us live with humility, remembering that we depend on God and that our firmest confidence rests in him.
exp.0:13:
God says he hates the religious festivals of his people. The new moon celebrations marked the start of each month, and the appointed feasts were the sacred festivals and gatherings. "I hate" means that he rejects them outright. "They have become a burden" means they are something heavy to carry. God says he is weary of bearing them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. God himself had commanded those feasts, so the problem was not the feasts. The serious issue was that the people kept them while practicing injustice, and the text says their hands were full of blood. God was asking for a change of life, not just rituals.

For today: going to church, singing, or praying is not enough if during the week we treat others badly or ignore the person in need. Ask God to show you something specific that you need to correct, and do it as part of your worship.
exp.22:16:
After the seventy years of being forgotten have passed, the Lord will restore Tyre, meaning he will attend to it and care for it. The city will return to its trade and its profits.

The picture of a city that trades with all the nations is drawn in the language of a prostitute. It describes a city that sells itself to anyone and is loyal to none of them.

The phrase "on the face of the earth" means across the surface of the whole world.

Isaiah prophesies against Tyre, a great trading city of Phoenicia. It is part of a message of judgment against several nations. The seventy years are understood in different ways: some see them as a literal period of time, and others as a symbolic period. What follows is surprising: its profits would be dedicated to the Lord and would serve to feed and clothe those who serve him.

For today: money and work can be either a trap or a blessing. We can ask ourselves whether what we earn serves only us, or whether we also put it at the service of God and of those in need.
exp.36:3:
This verse is part of the message that King Hezekiah sends to the prophet Isaiah. It says that perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, the officer sent by the king of Assyria to defy the living God. The "remnant" is the part of the people who still survive, and to "rebuke" here means to answer and correct those insults. Hezekiah asks Isaiah to lift up a prayer for them.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks through his servants. Jerusalem is threatened by the Assyrian army, and the Rabshakeh has scorned the people's trust in God. Hezekiah, distressed and dressed in mourning, does not rely on his own strength but seeks the prophet's prayer. God answers with the words, "Fear not."

For today: when you feel powerless before a problem, do not face it alone. Pray to God sincerely and also ask for the prayers of people of faith. He hears those who trust in Him.
exp.2:11:
The explanation says that those who rule over or collect payments from God's people are called "youths," and that "women" hold power over them. The word "oppress" refers to those who demand payments or tribute. Also, the guides of the people mislead them and turn them from their paths. Scholars understand "youths" in several ways: immature or weak rulers, or even actual young people. The meaning of "women" is also interpreted differently, perhaps as weak or easily influenced leaders.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God, in Judah. God announces that he will take away good leadership as a consequence of injustice. The verses that follow show that God will judge the elders and princes who took advantage of the poor.

For today: do not follow blindly whoever guides you. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and pray for your leaders, that they may act with justice and wisdom.
exp.52:8:
The passage says that the Servant of the Lord was assigned a grave with the wicked, yet in his death he was with a rich man. The reason given is that he had never done violence and no deceit was found in his mouth. The Berean wording "was assigned" reflects the idea of something decided or appointed, and "wicked" refers to those who live without reverence for God.

The passage is part of the fourth Servant song in Isaiah. The prophet speaks, and in other verses God also speaks, about a righteous servant who suffers because of the rebellion of the people. Christians see Jesus here, who was crucified with criminals and buried in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man (Matthew 27:57-60). Some Jews have understood it in another way, for example, as Israel.

For today: Jesus suffered while innocent, for us. When you feel unjustly judged, trust in him and seek to respond with truth and gentleness.
exp.8:12:
But the people did not return to the one who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts. This verse says that Israel, the northern kingdom, did not turn back to God even though He was disciplining them. "The one who struck them" is the Lord, who allowed the suffering to wake them up. "Return" means to turn around, to repent. "Seek the LORD" means to come to Him sincerely. They felt the blow, but they did not seek God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here in the name of God. He explains why the punishments keep coming: attacks by the Syrians and Philistines, and a judgment that continues. The leaders and the false prophets had led the people astray, and no one was changing course. Some understand these blows as God's discipline, not as simple bad luck.

When difficulties come, it is not enough to complain or to look only for relief. Let us ask ourselves with humility: "Lord, what do you want to teach me?" And let us return to Him in prayer and obedience.
exp.27:10:
He says God will speak to his people with mocking lips and foreign tongues. The phrase "mocking lips" refers to speech that scoffs and jeers, and "foreign tongues" refers to languages that the people cannot understand. The phrase "to this people" refers to Judah.

Isaiah speaks to the leaders of Jerusalem who were mocking his messages and treating them as if they were meant for children. God answers that, since they will not listen to his clear word, he will speak to them through foreign invaders, the Assyrians, whose language they will not understand. Paul quotes a related idea in 1 Corinthians 14:21 when speaking about tongues. It is a judgment for having rejected the rest that God was offering them.

When God speaks to us clearly and we ignore him, he may later speak to us through difficult circumstances. Let us listen to his Word today with humility, before correction becomes harder.
exp.40:20:
Here God invites the idols and those who worship them to present their defense. "Present your case" is like saying: "Lay out your argument, as in a trial." "Submit your arguments" means: "Show your proofs and solid reasons." God calls himself "the King of Jacob," that is, the King of Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is a courtroom scene before the nations and their false gods. The verses that follow ask the idols to declare the past and the future. God has just shown his power by transforming the desert, and now he challenges the idols to demonstrate something similar. They cannot.

For today: God does not fear questions or tests. We can examine where we have placed our trust, whether in money, success, or people, and return to trust in the God who does what he says.
exp.61:3:
God tells Jerusalem that she will no longer be called "Forsaken," and her land will no longer be called "Desolate," a word for being left in ruin. Her new name will be Hephzibah, and her land will be called Beulah. The reason is that the LORD will take delight in her, and her land will be His bride.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were suffering the consequences of exile and a city in ruins. God promises restoration and a new name, one that expresses a close, loving relationship, like that of a bride and her husband. Christian interpreters also see here a promise of God's love for his people in general.

For today: if you feel abandoned, or believe your past defines you, remember that God can give you a new identity. When you doubt it, repeat what He says about you, not what others have said.
exp.23:5:
A curse has consumed the earth, and those who live on it must bear the guilt. The phrase "must bear the guilt" means they are held responsible for the wrong that has been done. "Burned" here means consumed or reduced to very little, and in the end only a few survive.

Isaiah speaks as a prophet of God in a passage that many call the apocalypse of Isaiah, chapters 24 to 27. It describes a judgment that reaches the whole earth. The previous verse gives the reason: the people have broken the laws and the everlasting covenant. Scholars debate which covenant is meant. It could be Noah's, Moses', or the moral law in general.

For today: our decisions have consequences that go beyond ourselves. Today you can choose to be honest and just in small things, trusting that God cares for the earth and for those who obey him.
exp.29:29:
He says God will make everyone hear his majestic voice and see his mighty arm revealed when he acts. His anger appears as a consuming fire, and also as a storm: a cloudburst, wind, and hailstones. "Angry wrath" describes very strong judgment. A "cloudburst" is a sudden, heavy downpour. A "storm" is a violent wind that sweeps everything away.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who were afraid of the Assyrian empire. God promises that Assyria, which had struck down many nations, will be broken by his voice. For those who trust in him, that judgment brings relief and song, as at a festival.

Today we can remember that no human power is final. When you feel fear before something that seems bigger than you, pray and entrust that situation to God, trusting that he does justice in his own time.
exp.22:5:
The explanation says that the people of Tyre must flee toward Tarshish, a distant place across the sea. The first phrase in the verse is a call to cross over, to go away. "Wail" means to cry out loud in grief or pain. The "inhabitants of the coastland" are the people of Tyre and its coastal area.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Tyre, a city very rich from sea trade. The fall of Tyre would be so great that its inhabitants would seek refuge far away. Scholars do not agree on where Tarshish was; many think of the western Mediterranean, but this is not certain.

For today: wealth and success do not give us true security. Everything can change suddenly. It is wise to place our trust in God, not in what we have, and to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.59:5:
It says that Jerusalem will be visited so heavily that caravans of camels will cover the land, like a great procession of travelers. They come from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba, regions to the south and east of Israel known for trade. They bring gold and frankincense, valuable gifts, and they proclaim the praises of the LORD. "Proclaim" means they will announce them and make them known. The "young camels" named here are the animals that make up these caravans.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, who had passed through judgment and discouragement. He promises restoration: their light will come, and the nations will come. Interpreters differ about the fulfillment: some see the return from exile, others the Church, others a future time. Many Christians also connect this with the wise men who bring gold and frankincense to Jesus (Matthew 2), although the text does not say so directly.

For today: when you feel small or without hope, remember that God can change your situation. And the best we can offer him is our life and our praise.
exp.39:30:
This verse says that those who wait on the Lord will receive new strength. Their life is compared to eagles that rise high, and to someone who runs or walks without growing exhausted. The word "wait" here means trusting and expecting with faith, and the verse's words "will renew their strength" and "not grow weary" and "not faint" show that people lose their strength when they grow tired.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a tired and discouraged people of Israel, who felt that God had forgotten them. Earlier in the passage, the text shows that even the strongest young people grow exhausted, but God never grows weary and gives strength to the one who is weak. Many scholars connect this to the time of the exile in Babylon, though the exact period is debated.

When you feel you have no strength left, do not rely only on your own energy. Take a moment each day to pray, read the Bible, and hand your burdens over to God. He renews you step by step.
exp.41:20:
God was pleased, because of His righteousness, to make His law great and glorious. "Was pleased" means He did it with delight. "Magnify" and "make it glorious" mean to exalt the law and give it great worth and honor.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Israel, the servant who was meant to be a light, but who did not see or hear what God was showing him. Before and after the verse, the text describes a people who are blind and deaf, and also plundered and punished. God does not change His law because of the people's disobedience; His justice remains firm. Some understand that the verse also points to the perfect Servant, Christ, although this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: value God's Word as He values it. Read it with attention and ask Him for open ears to obey it, not only to know it.
exp.43:10:
It says that all who join themselves to idols will be put to shame. The makers of those gods are only human beings. Even if they assemble, present themselves side by side, and try to defend their idols, they will be brought to terror and, all together, they will be put to shame.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people Israel. Shortly before this, he told them that only he is the true God. Now he mocks idolatry with seriousness: an object made by human hands cannot see, understand, or save. The verses that follow show the blacksmith and the carpenter growing tired as they make their "god."

For today: examine what things you treat as your own source of security, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If you build it and hold it up, it cannot hold you up. Trust today in the God who created you.
exp.21:13:
God told the prophet Isaiah directly, and the message was very serious: the people's sin would not be atoned for as long as they were still alive. The verse says the message was heard in Isaiah's hearing, meaning he heard it from God. The title "the LORD of Hosts" speaks of God's power over all things. The words "until your dying day" show that the consequences would last until the end of their lives.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Jerusalem when the city was under threat. God called them to weep and to repent, but they held a feast, saying, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Their sin was ignoring God and failing to trust in Him. Some understand this as a punishment that would no longer be lifted; others see it as a hardening of the heart.

Today it invites us not to take lightly God's call to repentance. When He speaks to us, it is wise to answer Him with humility and not with indifference.
exp.23:15:
From the ends of the earth we hear singing: "Glory to the Righteous One." But the prophet, instead of joining in with joy, cries out. "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." He repeats that the treacherous keep betraying; to deal in treachery means acting with deceit and disloyalty.

Isaiah speaks within a long announcement of God's judgment on the earth (chapters 24 to 27). Before this, voices of praise are heard from a faithful remnant, but the prophet looks at the wickedness and the judgment that is coming, as the following verses show with their terror, pit, and snare. Scholars debate exactly who "the righteous" refers to.

For today: we can praise God and, at the same time, take seriously the sin and pain of the world. Pray with sincerity, without pretending, and ask for faithfulness for yourself.
exp.52:1:
It says the Servant of the LORD would grow up like a tender shoot, like a root coming up out of dry ground, where almost nothing lives. He would have no stately form or majesty, and no beauty that would draw people to Him; when others looked at Him, they would find nothing that made them want Him. The word "stately" here points to an impressive presence, and the word "shoot" means a new young growth.

It is a group speaking with "we," probably the people admitting their mistake. This follows the question of who believed the message. Christians see Jesus here, and the New Testament quotes this chapter in that sense. Some Jewish scholars understand the servant to be Israel; there are different interpretations.

Today it invites us not to measure the worth of people, or of God, by outward appearance, success, or what is eye-catching. God often works through what is humble and simple. We can learn to value what He values.
exp.22:6:
Isaiah asks Tyre: "Is this your jubilant city, whose origin is from antiquity?" Now its own feet will take it far away to settle, like someone forced into exile or made a refugee. "Settle far away" here means going to live in foreign lands, not a religious journey. The phrase about origins from antiquity speaks of a city with a long history.

Isaiah speaks in God's name against Tyre, a great trading city on the Phoenician coast. Its fall is announced with astonishment: even Egypt will grieve at the news. The following verses say that God decreed this to humble the pride of those who thought themselves glorious. Scholars debate exactly how and when it was fulfilled.

For today: wealth, reputation, or years of success are not a secure foundation. We can thank God for what He gives us, but without placing our trust in it. Let us put our security in Him, who endures when everything else changes.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that on God's holy mountain there will no longer be harm or destruction. The reason is that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD, as completely as the sea is full of water. "Neither harm nor destroy" means to do injury or to ruin. "Holy mountain" refers to the place where God reigns.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf and describes the king who would come from the family of Jesse, the father of David. Just before this, the prophet describes wild animals living in peace with the weakest ones. Many understand this as a picture of God's kingdom; others also see it as a literal picture of the renewed creation. Christians often see it fulfilled in Christ, but with a fullness that is still to come.

For today: if true peace is born from knowing God, we can seek him every day in his Word and in prayer, and let that knowledge soften the way we treat others.
exp.8:1:
The verse says that a people who had been living in darkness has now seen a great light. The words "darkness" and "the shadow of death" describe distress, oppression, and danger. "Living" means dwelling in a place. "Seen" is the plain word for perceiving with the eyes. The light that "has dawned" on them is an image of hope and rescue that arrives without them producing it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, in a time of threat from Assyria. The regions of Zebulun and Naphtali, in Galilee, were among the first to suffer invasion. Isaiah announces that God will end that oppression by breaking the yoke of the oppressor. Matthew 4:12-16 quotes this passage and applies it to Jesus, who began his ministry in Galilee.

For today: if you are going through a dark season, you do not have to create the light yourself. Ask God to show you his presence, draw near to Jesus in the Gospels, and share that hope with someone who is walking in darkness today.
exp.35:11:
Here Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, answers the officials of Judah harshly. He says that his master did not send him only to the leaders, but also to the men sitting on the wall. The crude words in this verse describe what those men will be reduced to: he warns that if the city stays under siege, they will face such hunger and thirst that they will be forced to eat their own waste and drink their own urine.

Rabshakeh speaks during the siege of Jerusalem, in the time of King Hezekiah. The officials asked him to speak in Aramaic so that the people would not understand. He refuses and wants everyone to hear, in order to spread fear and push them toward surrender. It is psychological pressure.

For today: when someone tries to frighten you with threats or exaggerations, do not let fear carry you away. Stop, pray, and seek the truth in God. He sustains those who trust in Him, even when the voices around them shout loudly.
exp.23:18:
The explanation says that the earth will be completely broken apart, split open, and shaken violently. These three phrases repeat the same idea for emphasis: the judgment will be total. The phrase "utterly broken apart" means the earth will be fully broken, and "split open" means it will be torn into pieces, like something cracked wide.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf in chapters 24 to 27, sometimes called "the apocalypse of Isaiah." Before this verse, the prophet describes judgment on the earth because its inhabitants broke God's laws and his covenant (v. 5). Some believe he is speaking of a final judgment; others also see it as a warning to the nations of that time. Both readings have been held.

For today: do not place your security in what can be shaken. Today you can entrust your life to God, who remains steadfast, and live with humility and obedience.
exp.39:5:
A voice says, "Cry out!" And the prophet asks, "What should I cry out?" The answer is that all people are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field, which bloom only briefly. "Flesh" here means weak and mortal humanity. "Cry out" means to call out loudly.

We are in the comforting part of Isaiah, where God announces that he is coming to rescue his people. A voice, not clearly identified, gives the command to proclaim. The prophet answers with humility, and the message contrasts human frailty with the faithfulness of God, whose word stands forever, as the following verses say.

For today: do not place your security in success, fame, or strength, which pass away. Rely on the word of God, which does not change. That trust gives you peace when everything around you seems unstable.
exp.57:3:
God says that his people fast, yet at the same time they quarrel, argue, and strike out viciously. "Contention and strife" are fights and arguments; "strike viciously with your fist" means to hit others unjustly. He warns them that fasting in this way will not let their prayer be heard on high, that is, by God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people complain that they fast and God does not answer. But on those days of fasting they were pursuing their own advantage and treating their workers badly. God shows them that their fasting was only outward religion, without justice or compassion.

For today: before you pray or fast, examine how you treat others. If you have an unresolved dispute or have been harsh with someone, seek peace and do what is right. In this way your devotion will be sincere.
exp.65:12:
God says that he will comfort his people the way a mother comforts her son. The image is of close, tender care, of an embrace and relief. The promise is personal: "I will comfort you." And the words that follow announce that this comfort will be experienced over Jerusalem, the restored city.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the end of the book. The people have gone through pain and ruin, and God promises restoration, peace flowing like a river, and joy. The text then adds that God will also act with justice against his enemies. Some understand this promise for the restored Israel, and others also see a foretaste of the final comfort in Christ.

For today: when you are weary or wounded, do not stay alone with your pain. Come to God in prayer, as a child runs to his mother, and let him comfort you.
exp.23:9:
It says that the city is broken and destroyed. It is called "the city of chaos," which is the wording your version uses, and its houses are closed to entry. The city has no firm foundation, and no one can come in: there are no more visitors, no feasts, no life in the streets. It is a picture of fear and loneliness.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's judgment on the earth (chapters 24 to 27). Joy disappears because humanity broke its covenant with God (v. 5). It is not stated with certainty which city is meant; some think of a specific city, and others of a symbol of all human pride without God.

For today: what we build without God, whether success, pleasure or security, can end up empty. Today you can ask yourself where you are placing your trust, and hand it over to God in prayer.
exp.8:14:
The explanation says that in Israel the respected elders and honorable leaders are "the head," that is, those who give direction. But the prophet who teaches lies is "the tail," in other words, the lowest part. The phrase "honorable man" refers to someone of dignity who commands respect. The verse shows that bad teaching dishonors the one who gives it, no matter what position he holds.

The passage is spoken by the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's judgment on the northern kingdom, Israel. The people did not return to God even after being punished. Their leaders and false prophets were leading them down the wrong path, and so the judgment would reach everyone, from top to bottom.

Today it invites us not to be impressed only by the position or reputation of someone who teaches. It is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible and to ask God for wisdom to distinguish the truth.
exp.44:13:
This is what the Lord says: the wealth that comes from Egypt, the goods of Cush, and the Sabeans, a tall and impressive people, will come over to Israel and become theirs. They will follow behind them, coming over in chains, and bow down to them. They will confess, "God is truly with you, and there is no other; there is no other God."

The Lord speaks to Israel through the prophet Isaiah while the people are living in exile, or are about to be. Just before this, God names Cyrus as the one who will set the captives free. Interpreters disagree about whether the chains point to forced submission or to a willing acknowledgment. Either way, the main point is that the nations will come to see that the Lord alone is God.

When you feel small or short on resources, remember that your worth does not depend on what you own, but on the fact that God is with you. Trust that He can show his power through your life.
exp.28:17:
He says that a time will come when God will change the condition of his people: the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and the blind will see even out of the deep darkness. The "deep darkness" is a picture of people who did not understand and who now do.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem. Before, the people had a faith of lip service only and did not understand God's ways, and for that reason they are compared to clay that does not recognize the potter. "The scroll" may refer to the words of the prophecy or to Scripture; some see here an announcement of times of restoration and others a promise that points to the Messiah. Interpreters understand it in several ways.

For today: ask God to open your ears and your eyes when you read the Bible. Read it with humility, hoping that He will give you light and understanding.
exp.65:1:
God says that He Himself made all these things, the heavens and the earth, and that they came into being by His hand. Therefore, the one He esteems is the person who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at His word. Trembling here does not speak of a fear that runs away, but of a deep reverence that takes seriously what God says. Looking here means paying careful attention with kindness.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people were very interested in the temple and the sacrifices, but their hearts were far from God. The verses that follow show that their offerings, without obedience, were offensive to Him. God does not seek buildings to dwell in, but hearts willing to listen to Him.

For today: before fulfilling religious duties, open the Bible with humility and ask yourself, "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" Then obey what you understand.
exp.53:9:
God says that even the most solid things in nature, such as the mountains and the hills, may be moved or shaken, but his loving devotion will not leave his people. His covenant of peace, that is, his promise of well-being and reconciliation, will not be broken either. The Lord says this, the one who has compassion on you.

God, called the Redeemer, speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as an abandoned and suffering woman. She had gone through judgment and exile, and God acknowledges that he hid his face from her "for a moment." Now he comforts her and compares his promise to the one he made after Noah's flood: just as he swore never again to cover the earth with water, he swears never again to be angry with her like that.

For today: when you feel that everything is being shaken, in your family, your health, or your work, remember that God's love does not depend on your circumstances. Rest in his promise and pray with confidence.
exp.52:4:
This verse says that the servant of God was pierced and crushed, but not because of his own wrongs, but because of ours. "Transgressions" are the times we turn away from God; "crushed" means broken under a heavy weight; "pierced" means wounded deeply. "The punishment that brought us peace" means the punishment that makes peace with God possible for us. By his wounds, we receive healing.

This passage is part of the prophecy of Isaiah, written to a people who were suffering the consequences of their turning away from God. It speaks of a servant who suffers for others. At first, people thought God was punishing him for his own faults; then they recognize that he was suffering for them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament applies it to Him (1 Peter 2:24). Jews often interpret the servant differently, for example as Israel.

For today: if you carry guilt or shame, come to God with confidence. Christ has already carried that weight, so you can receive forgiveness and begin again with gratitude.
exp.0:15:
This verse is a call from God to his people: "Wash and cleanse yourselves" is an invitation to wash away the dirt of sin. "Remove your evil deeds from My sight" means setting aside the wickedness in their actions, and "from My sight" shows that God sees everything. "Stop doing evil!" asks for a real change in conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. They kept festivals, brought offerings, and prayed, but their hands were full of blood, meaning there was violence and injustice. For this reason God rejects their empty religion. Even so, he immediately offers them forgiveness: their sins, red as crimson, can become white as snow.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or pray if we mistreat others. Ask God to forgive you and to show you an attitude or habit you need to leave behind, and change it this week with concrete actions.
exp.46:6:
Here Babylon boasted: "I will be queen forever." The phrase about what she did not consider refers to the final outcome, what comes afterward, the consequences. She believed her power would never end, and she did not think about how her actions would turn out.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon, called the daughter of the Chaldeans, was used to discipline Israel, but she treated the elderly with cruelty and showed no mercy. God judges her for her pride and her false sense of security.

For today: do not trust that what you have, your success or your strength, will last forever. Think about the outcome of your decisions, treat others with mercy, and live with humility before God.
exp.32:4:
The verse says that the LORD will be exalted, meaning acknowledged and raised up, because He dwells on high, in a place far above everything. He has also filled Zion, which is Jerusalem, with justice and righteousness, with decisions that are fair and with doing what is right.

This chapter is a prophecy by Isaiah addressed to Judah. First it speaks of a destroyer and asks God for help (vv. 1-4). Then, in this verse, the prophet declares that God will act and will be honored. The preceding verses show enemy nations fleeing and being stripped of their goods. The following verses promise stability: wisdom, salvation, and the fear of the Lord. Scholars debate which exact historical moment is in view.

For today: when the world seems unjust or disordered, remember that God remains above all. Ask Him to fill your home and your work with uprightness, and begin yourself by acting justly in small things.
exp.56:7:
The verse says that the people set up their symbols of idolatry hidden behind the door and the doorpost of their house. The word "memorial" may refer to pagan signs or emblems; some scholars understand it this way, while others question it. Then, using the image of a bed, it describes Israel as an unfaithful wife: she forsook God, opened her bed, climbed up and opened it wide, made a pact with others, and gazed upon their nakedness. "Forsaking Me, you uncovered your bed" suggests stripping oneself bare before others.

God speaks through Isaiah. He accuses Judah of abandoning him to follow idols and alliances with other nations. He presents their sin as spiritual adultery, because God had made a covenant of faithfulness with them.

For today: examine what things you hide and love more than God, even if it is in secret. God does not ask for a faith of appearance, but for a faithful heart. If you have given your loyalty to other things, return to Him with sincerity; He continues to invite repentance.
exp.62:9:
The explanation says that the people of Israel rebelled and grieved the Holy Spirit of God. Because of this, God, who had cared for them before, stopped acting as their protector and became their enemy, opposing them directly. The phrase "and he fought against them" means that God himself took action against them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, prayerfully recalling what God did for his people. Before this verse he tells of God's love and compassion; after it he recalls the exodus with Moses. Isaiah shows that Israel's suffering came from their rebellion, not because God stopped loving them.

For today: God is not indifferent to our attitudes. When we resist his guidance, we move away from his care. Today you can examine your heart, recognize where you have resisted God, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.27:0:
It says that a harsh warning is coming, a "woe," against Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel. Its "majestic crown" is its pride and its capital, probably Samaria, which sat on a summit above a fertile valley. The "drunkards" who were "overcome by wine" were its leaders, dazed by wine and luxury. Their glorious splendor is "a fading flower": it wilts quickly.

The prophet Isaiah, sent by God, speaks a few years before Assyria conquered the northern kingdom (around 722 B.C.). The people lived confident in their wealth and power, and forgot God. The verses that follow announce that God will bring a strong invader, like a storm and a flood, who will trample that crown.

For today: whatever fills us with pride or lulls us to sleep, whether success, pleasure, or comfort, fades away. Let us ask God for humility and an awake heart to listen to him.
exp.1:9:
It says that people should go into the rocks and hide in the dust to get away from the Lord. The "terror of the LORD" is his presence that causes fear, and the "splendor of His majesty" is the shining glory of his greatness. It is a command given with both irony and seriousness: before God, no one can stand proud.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah. The people were full of idols and worshiped what their own hands had made. For this reason he announces "the day of the LORD," a time when God would judge human pride. Scholars debate whether it refers to a judgment near in history, to a final one, or to both.

For today: do not place your trust in things made by human hands, such as money, success, or your own strength. Instead, humble yourself before God today with sincerity, so that you will not have to hide from him later.
exp.16:13:
In the evening, sudden terror comes, and before morning the enemy is gone. This is what awaits those who loot and plunder God's people: a swift and unexpected end to their power.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God. Just before this verse, he describes many nations surging like the sea against Judah. Many scholars think this refers to the Assyrian threat of his time, though not all agree. The verse brings comfort to the people: God rebukes the attack, and the enemy's power scatters like chaff before the wind.

When you feel overwhelmed by problems or injustices that seem enormous, remember that God has the last word. You can rest in Him, pray with confidence, and keep doing good, without letting fear defeat you.
exp.13:9:
The verse says that the dead, the ancient kings who are already in the grave, will all respond to the king who arrives. They will ask him in astonishment whether he too has become weak, just as they are, and whether he has become like them. Being "weak" here means that he has lost his power. The place of the dead is called Sheol, the realm where the dead are.

Isaiah presents a mockery against the king of Babylon, famous for his pride and violence. The prophet imagines his arrival in the world of the dead, where the kings he once ruled rise to receive him. It is poetic and figurative language. Some see here only the Babylonian king; others also see a broader reference to pride and its fall.

For today: power, money and fame do not make us different in the face of death. Live with humility, use what you have to serve others, and remember that your worth comes from God, not from your position.
exp.39:2:
A voice is calling out: prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness, and make a straight highway for our God in the desert. The first key idea is to clear a path, removing whatever blocks the way, and the second is a straight, firm road. The wilderness and the desert are empty, difficult places, yet it is there that God chooses to travel. It is like making the route ready so that a king can arrive.

God comforts Jerusalem: her punishment has ended and her sin has been forgiven. The one speaking is an unnamed voice in this passage, and the prophecy announces that God himself will come to his people. The Gospels (Matthew 3:3) apply this voice to John the Baptist, who prepared people for Jesus.

Today we can ask ourselves what obstacles are in our hearts: pride, resentment, or carelessness. Acknowledging them honestly and asking for forgiveness is a way of making a straight highway so that God can work in us.
exp.53:12:
This verse promises that the children of Jerusalem will be taught directly by God. As a result, they will enjoy great prosperity. The phrase "will be taught by the LORD" means that God himself will guide them and give them understanding. The phrase "great will be their prosperity" means that their well-being will grow and fill their lives.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, pictured as a grieving woman, battered by the storm and without comfort. After the suffering and exile, God promises her restoration, beauty, righteousness, and security. Jesus quoted the first part of this verse in John 6:45, and many Christians see it as a reference to those who are drawn to God and learn from him.

For today: it is not enough to give our children good habits; let us pray that God will teach their hearts. And let us also seek his daily guidance in the Bible, trusting that his teaching brings a full and flourishing life.
exp.20:16:
It says that of the archers of Kedar, the warriors of that desert tribe, only a few will remain, and those few will be very few. The word "remaining" refers to what is left over after the rest are gone. The wording of your verse makes plain that this is a firm statement, and it ends by saying that the Lord, the God of Israel, has spoken it, so this is no guess.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, passing on what the Lord told him. Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert, known for its archers and descended from Ishmael. This message closes a prophecy about Arabia, where people are fleeing from war. God announces that within a year their glory will come to an end. The Bible does not say here which army brings this about. Some think of Assyrian invasions, but this is not certain.

For today: no human power, however strong it may seem, is final. If you trust in your strength, your money, or your reputation, remember that God has the last word. Rest in Him.
exp.37:19:
The LORD will save me, and so we will play our songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD. In plain terms, the speaker is confident that God will rescue him, and he and his people commit to praising God with music in the temple for as long as they live.

The speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, who had been very sick and close to death. In the verses before, he says that the dead can no longer praise God, but the living can. This song gives thanks for his healing. The text then tells of the remedy with figs and the sign Hezekiah asked for.

For today: when God helps you in a crisis, do not let it be forgotten. Write down what he did for you, give him thanks out loud, and look for a community where you can praise him faithfully, not only in emergencies.
exp.43:19:
The verse says that whoever worships an idol feeds on ashes, that is, on something that gives neither life nor nourishment. His deluded heart has led him astray, and so he cannot rescue himself. He does not even stop to ask, "Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?" The right hand speaks of what a person takes hold of and what he trusts in.

God speaks through Isaiah. He mocks idolatry with sorrow: the man uses part of a tree to cook with, and with the rest he makes a god. This prepares the call that follows, where God tells Israel to remember Him and return, because He has redeemed them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we hold on to as if they could save us: money, success, approval. Let us ask God to show us honestly what we trust in, and let us return to Him, who truly forgives and sustains.
exp.17:6:
It says that when the time God has set arrives, gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts, to Mount Zion, from a people who are tall and smooth-skinned, widely feared from their beginnings until now, from a powerful nation whose speech is strange, and whose land is divided by rivers. The verse pictures a people honored by bringing their offerings to the place where God's name dwells.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, in a message against Cush (the region south of Egypt), whose messengers were going about seeking alliances. God says that He will act in His own time, like someone who prunes before the harvest. Scholars disagree about who this people is: some think of Cush, others of Israel.

For today: God does not hurry or forget, even when we feel weary of waiting. Instead of looking for human ways out, we can trust that He knows when to act, and bring Him our waiting and our wounds with patience.
exp.19:2:
Here God explains the meaning of something unusual that Isaiah had been doing. For three years, the prophet went about naked and barefoot, and this was a sign and omen, that is, a visible message about what would come upon Egypt and Cush. The word for "naked" probably means without the outer cloak, wearing only his inner garment, though this is not certain.

The Lord speaks, and his servant Isaiah obeys. Assyria had just conquered Ashdod, and some nations were thinking of seeking protection in Egypt and Cush. God uses this act to warn that such hope would fail: Assyria would lead them away captive, in shame.

For today: trusting in what seems strong, such as money, power, or influence, can leave us disappointed. Ask yourself where you have placed your security, and give it over to God, who never fails.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that a day of great upheaval had come, a time of crushing and of confusion, and that it comes from the Lord GOD of Hosts. It happens in the Valley of Vision, which is Jerusalem. The words "tumult," "trampling," and "confusion" describe noise, violent trampling, and bewilderment. The phrase "crying to the mountains" can be understood as cries of panic or a shout that echoes across the hills. Breaking down the walls speaks of the city being left defenseless.

Isaiah speaks in chapter 22 about Jerusalem, and it is not known for certain which siege he has in mind; many think of the Assyrian threat or the later fall of the city. The leaders fled, the people were in ruin, and the prophet wept for them. The text affirms that God allowed that judgment.

For today: do not place your security only in your "walls," such as your money, your job, or your own strength. Trust God first, and when you see ruin, weep and pray instead of ignoring it.
exp.25:18:
He says that God will give life again to those who died in him. The promise "Your dead will live; their bodies will rise" is a promise of resurrection. Those who dwell in the dust are the buried, and they are called to wake up and sing for joy. The "dew of the morning" is an image of the life God brings forth, like the dew that refreshes the plants at dawn. The phrase "the earth will bring forth her dead" means that the earth will give them back.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a song of God's people. Before this, the people confess that their efforts were like labor pains that brought no fruit: they could not save anything by themselves. Here God answers with hope: He himself will bring life. Many see in this one of the first clear hopes of resurrection in the Old Testament, although it is debated how Israel understood it at that time.

When your own efforts seem empty, remember that God has the last word. You can face grief and weariness with a real hope, and begin to sing with gratitude today.
exp.45:1:
The verse says that the idols of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, cower and crouch down together. They cannot relieve the burden of those who carry them, and they themselves end up going into captivity. The idols are the images or statues of the gods, and the word "together" describes how they crouch down side by side.

God speaks through Isaiah. Bel and Nebo were important gods of Babylon. Here they are described as statues loaded onto animals, that is, as a weight, while the enemy advances. Then God contrasts that picture with his own: he does not need to be carried, but carries his people from birth to old age.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, success, or approval, ends up weighing us down and cannot sustain us. Today you can hand God a specific burden and rest in the knowledge that he carries you.
exp.9:6:
God says that Assyria will be used as his instrument, but the Assyrian king does not see it that way. He has no intention of carrying out a plan of God; in his heart he only wants to destroy and wipe out many nations. To "cut off" means to put an end to them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was full of injustice, and God announces that he will send Assyria as discipline against his people. But Assyria acts with pride and ambition, and for that reason God later says that he will also judge Assyria. God uses this king, but he does not approve of his wickedness.

For today: God can work even through situations and people who do not acknowledge him, and that does not excuse evil. Trust that God governs history, and examine your own motives so that you act with humility and justice.
exp.40:22:
God challenges the idols and those who worship them. "Tell us the things that are to come" means: let them announce what will happen in the future. If they can do this, we will know that they are gods. "Yes, do something good or evil" is a simpler challenge: do something, anything, that can be seen. "That we may look on together in dismay" means that we would stand and watch in amazement.

The LORD speaks as a kind of public trial against the false gods of the nations. Israel lived surrounded by peoples who trusted in idols. God shows that only He knows the future and announces it before it happens. The verses that follow say the idols are "nothing," and announce someone whom God will raise up. Many think this refers to Cyrus, although the text here does not name him.

Today, in what do you place your trust: money, fame, your own plans? None of these can guarantee tomorrow for you. Rest in the God who truly holds your future.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that Aram (Syria), together with Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and the son of Remaliah, made a plot to ruin Ahaz, king of Judah. Aram here stands for the king of Syria, and a plot to ruin someone is a wicked scheme. The sentence ends with a colon because what they said continues in verse 6.

God speaks through Isaiah. Ahaz was terrified because two allied kings were coming to attack Jerusalem. God sends Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub (a name that means "a remnant will return") to tell the king not to be afraid. Here God reminds Ahaz what his enemies are planning, but he also shows him that their plan will not succeed.

For today: when someone plans something harmful against us, or when fear seems enormous, we can remember that God knows every plan and still governs. Let us speak to Him with confidence before we act out of panic.
exp.36:20:
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to King Hezekiah. The prophet tells him that the LORD, the God of Israel, has heard his prayer about Sennacherib, king of Assyria. The phrase "sent a message" means Isaiah passed word along to the king.

Hezekiah was in great distress. Assyria had conquered many cities and threatened Jerusalem. Sennacherib mocked God. Hezekiah brought his problem to the LORD in prayer, and now God responds through the prophet Isaiah. The one speaking in the message is God himself, and Isaiah only passes it on.

For today: God hears the sincere prayers of those who trust him. When you face a situation that is beyond you, bring it to God honestly and wait for his answer, even if it does not come in the way you had imagined.
exp.9:22:
For this verse, God, the Lord of Hosts, will carry out a complete and decided destruction across the whole land. The destruction is not partial or half-finished. It is the full outcome of what God has determined, a sentence carried through to the end.

Isaiah speaks for God to Judah while Assyria was threatening the region. The prophet explains that the judgment would be severe but just. Even so, only a remnant of the people would return to God. Right after this comes comfort: God asks His people not to fear Assyria, because the punishment would have a limit.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but He also cares for those who turn back to Him. If you feel under pressure or correction right now, do not run from God. Return to Him with humility, trusting that His justice is always joined with His mercy.
exp.40:23:
