Isaiah 41:24 says that idols and false gods are worth nothing, and that what they do is empty. Here "of no value" describes something hollow, without power. "Detestable" describes something repugnant. So whoever chooses to trust in those gods becomes like them: they cling to something empty.

God speaks, through Isaiah, in a kind of trial before the nations. He challenges the idols to tell what has happened and what will happen, or to do something, good or bad. They cannot. With this God shows that only He knows and directs history. Then He announces that He will raise up someone from the east, whom many understand to be Cyrus, although the text here does not name him.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we place our trust in that cannot answer: money, success, the opinion of others. Let us hand that trust today to the God who does speak and does fulfill what He says.
exp.36:5:
Isaiah answers the messengers of King Hezekiah with a word from God: do not be afraid. The mockery they heard from the servants of the king of Assyria is blasphemy, that is, insults against God.

The phrase "Tell your master" refers to Hezekiah, and "who replied" simply means that Isaiah spoke to the messengers.

Hezekiah was in a desperate situation, since the Assyrian army threatened Jerusalem. Rabshakeh, a senior Assyrian spokesman, mocked the people's trust in God. Hezekiah asked the prophet for prayer, and God answered him through him. What follows in the text shows that God took the matter into his own hands.

For today: when the words of others frighten us or mock our faith, we can bring the matter to God in prayer. He listens, and we need not defend ourselves in fear, because our confidence rests in his care.
exp.39:26:
The explanation says that God's people are complaining: "God does not see my path, and He does not care that justice is done for me." "My way is hidden from the LORD" means they feel their life is hidden from God's sight. "My claim is ignored by my God" means their just cause has been overlooked. God asks them, with a certain tenderness, why they speak this way.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Israel, who was suffering and felt forgotten, probably in a time of exile or under the threat of it (scholars place it in different ways). Earlier in the chapter, God is shown as the Creator who calls each star by name. If not one star escapes Him, neither does His people. Later, He promises strength to the weary.

When you feel forgotten or ignored by God, do not silence your complaint, but remember what you know of Him: He cares for the stars and also for you. Pray, telling Him honestly what you feel, and ask Him for strength for today.
exp.42:17:
God tells his people not to stay looking back. "Do not call to mind" and "pay no attention to" here mean fixating on what has already passed, turning it over and over. "The former things" are events from the past, such as the exodus from Egypt, which the earlier verses recall with the sea and the army that fell.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, who was in exile in Babylon. He reminds them of what he did at the Red Sea, but tells them not to live only on the memory of it, because he is going to do something new: open a way in the wilderness and give water to his people. Some understand that he is not asking them to forget, but not to limit God to what they have already seen.

For today: do not let old failures, pains, or even past successes keep you from trusting that God can do something new in your life. Give him what has already passed, and take the next step with hope.
exp.9:4:
God speaks and calls Assyria the rod of his anger and the staff in their hands his wrath. That is, he uses it like a stick to correct. The words "anger" and "wrath" speak of his righteous response against evil. He says he places that anger in its hands, meaning that Assyria would be the instrument.

God speaks through Isaiah to the people of Judah and Israel, who had fallen into injustice and disobedience (see the preceding verses). He warns them that a punishment is coming from far away and that no one will be able to save them without him. Assyria does not know that God is using it; its plans are of conquest and pride. That is why later God will also judge it.

For today: God governs even the nations and the difficult situations. If we go through a correction, we can humbly ask what he wants to teach us, and trust that he remains in control and is just.
exp.50:9:
This verse is a question that calls to mind what God has already done. The dried-up sea and the road made through its depths point back to the people's crossing of the Red Sea during the Exodus. The "redeemed" are those who were rescued, and the word here means those who were bought back and set free.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and asks God to act again as he did in the past. Israel was discouraged, probably because of the exile in Babylon. Remembering the Exodus gave them hope that God would bring them home to Zion, as the next verse says. The sea monsters and the dragon are poetic images of chaos and hostile power; some connect them to Egypt, and scholars do not explain them in just one way.

For today: when you face a "sea" that seems to block your path, remember what God has done before for his people and for you. Pray with confidence, knowing that he can open a way where no one else sees one.
exp.62:8:
God did not stay far away when his people suffered: he felt their pain along with them. "The angel of his presence" refers to a messenger or to God's own presence, and readers understand it in several ways. He saved them, and he redeemed them (rescued them) out of love and compassion, and he lifted them up and carried them through "all the days of old," that is, from long ago.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people and gratefully recalls what God did in the past, such as the exodus from Egypt. He does this because Israel is in a difficult moment. The verses that follow admit that the people rebelled, yet he still remembers God's faithfulness.

Today, when you go through distress, remember how God has cared for you before. Write it down and give thanks; that strengthens trust.
exp.32:1:
The people ask God to show them mercy. They say they have waited for him, and they ask that he be their strength every morning, and their salvation in times of trouble.

The people of Judah speak here, praying in the midst of danger. Earlier, Isaiah announced judgment against a cruel invader who plundered and betrayed; scholars often connect him with Assyria, though the text does not give the name. Faced with that power, the people do not trust in their own strength but cry out to God. Their prayer rests on waiting for him and depending on him alone.

For today: begin each morning by asking God for strength for that day, and trust that he will also sustain you when a difficulty comes that you did not expect. Waiting on him is not standing still, but resting in his help while you do what is yours to do.
exp.15:0:
Isaiah 16:1 says that tribute lambs should be sent to the ruler of the land. The verse describes the sending as going from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. Some believe the ruler is the king of Judah; others hold that it refers to the Messiah who is to come.

Isaiah prophesies against Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. Moab lies in ruin, and its women flee like frightened birds. Moab is advised to seek refuge and help in Judah, sending the tribute it once gave. Scholars debate the exact historical details.

For today: when everything falls apart, let us not rely only on our own strength or our pride. Humbly seeking the help of God and of his people is wisdom. Asking for help in time is not weakness; it is a step toward hope.
exp.21:22:
He says that God will set his servant like a peg driven firmly into a secure place, and that he will become a throne of glory for his father's household, that is, a source of respect and dignity. The word for "I will drive" refers to fastening him firmly in place, and "throne of glory" describes a seat of honor.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He removes Shebna, a proud administrator of the palace, and puts in his place Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, to take care of the king's house. The verses that follow show that the people will lean on him, but also that this burden has limits. Some Christians see here a shadow of Christ (Revelation 3:7); others read only the historical moment.

For today: if God gives you a responsibility, serve it with humility and faithfulness, remembering that your steadiness depends on Him, not on your position.
exp.18:7:
The fishermen will mourn, and everyone who casts a hook into the Nile will lament. Those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. The word "pine away" describes wasting away from grief and loss of strength. "Mourn" means to weep and grieve deeply.

Isaiah speaks against Egypt, within a message about God's judgment on that nation. The Nile was the source of life, food, and work for the Egyptians. If the river failed, fishing, farming, and the trades that depended on it would also come to an end. Scholars do not agree on how or when this was fulfilled; some read it as a general warning that Egypt could not rely on its resources.

For today: examine what your security depends on. Work, money, or plans can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else runs dry.
exp.7:21:
He says that when these people look toward the earth, they will see only distress, darkness and the gloom of anguish, and they will be driven into utter darkness. "Distress" means great affliction or serious trouble. "Driven into utter darkness" means pushed completely into a place with no light at all.

Isaiah speaks in a time of crisis for Judah, threatened by neighboring kingdoms. Many, instead of trusting God, sought answers from mediums and spiritists (verse 19). The prophet calls them to return to "the law and to the testimony," that is, to God's Word. Whoever rejects that light ends up angry, hungry and without direction. The text is followed by a promise of light (Isaiah 9:1-2), which the New Testament connects with Jesus.

For today: when distress comes, do not look for answers in just any voice. Open the Bible, pray, and let God's light guide you, even when the path seems dark.
exp.53:15:
He says that God is the maker of everyone: of the craftsman who fans the coals into flame and forges a tool fit for his work, and also of the destroyer who wreaks havoc. The word "created" in the verse means "made." Coals are glowing embers. Weapons and the people who use them exist under God's power.

God speaks to Jerusalem, the people of Israel, who felt abandoned and vulnerable after the exile. He promises them protection and a secure future. The verses that follow say that no weapon formed against them will prevail. Some understand that God allows the enemy but limits him; the text does not explain how this happens.

When you feel fear for people or situations that threaten you, remember that nothing is outside God's control. You can pray with confidence, do what is right, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for his own, even when you do not always understand how.
exp.40:5:
The explanation says that the people of the nations helped one another. Each one supported the other and said to his brother, "Be strong!" That is, they called on one another to take heart and stand firm.

Here God speaks through Isaiah. He presents himself as the Lord of history, who calls the generations from the beginning. The nations see his work and become afraid. Then they encourage one another to make idols, as the following verses show. Contrast this with Israel, whom God calls his chosen servant. Many understand that this mutual encouragement is in vain, because it rests on idols made by hand.

Encouraging others is a good thing, but it depends on where we place our trust. Today we can comfort someone who is weak, but we can also point him to the living God, who does not move or fall like an idol. Look for someone discouraged this week, offer him concrete help, and remind him that God sustains him.
exp.31:8:
God, speaking through the prophet, calls out to certain women who live at ease and without worry. He tells them to stand up, to listen to him, and to pay attention to his words. The verse's "complacent" means they are satisfied with how things are and feel comfortable. "Overconfident" means they feel secure and see no need for concern. "Word" here refers to what is said, the message.

The one speaking is Isaiah, who passes on the message of God. Earlier he spoke about people who took advantage of the poor and others who acted with generosity. Afterward he warns that the comfort of these women will end, because years of scarcity are coming. Some think he means the women of Jerusalem in particular; others think he means the whole people, and the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not confuse comfort with security. Take a moment this week to listen to God and ask him whether there is something in your life you have stopped attending to because you feel settled.
exp.43:20:
God tells his people to remember what he has just said: that they are his servant and that he made them. "Jacob" and "Israel" name the same people. The promise that he will never forget them is an invitation to stay close to God and not turn away from him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he mocks the person who uses half of a log to warm himself and cook food, and with the other half makes an idol to worship. That kind of deception leaves the person without understanding. In contrast, God reminds Israel who its Creator is. Next he promises to forgive its sins and redeem it.

For today: when something takes the place of God, such as money, success, or the opinion of others, stop and remember that he made you and will never forget you. Return to him with confidence, because he already offers forgiveness.
exp.37:16:
Here the explanation says that Hezekiah suffered great anguish just when he expected his welfare to be secure. But God, in love, rescued him from the pit of oblivion. "Pit of oblivion" refers to the grave, the place of the dead, and "cast all my sins behind your back" means that God forgave them and no longer holds them in view.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks in a song after recovering from a deadly illness. Isaiah had told him he would die, but he prayed and God granted him more years of life. Some understand "for my own welfare" as a time of calm that became anguish because of the sickness; the text does not give more detail. Here he gives thanks for having been rescued.

For today: when you remember a failure or a painful season, do not stay bound by guilt. If you ask God for forgiveness, he has already cast your sins behind his back. Answer him with gratitude and tell others what he has done for you.
exp.64:8:
God promises that he will bring forth descendants from Jacob and heirs from Judah, and that his chosen ones will possess his mountains and his servants will live there. The people he chooses are those he has selected, and the servants are those who serve him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people had turned to idols, burning incense on the hills and turning away from God. For this they deserved judgment. But God compares his people to a cluster of grapes with good juice: he will not destroy everything, because there is still blessing in them. So he preserves a faithful remnant. Scholars understand this promise in several ways: as the return from exile, as something still future, or as fulfilled in Christ.

For today: God is just, but he also cares for those who seek him. If you feel small or weak in faith, trust that he knows how to keep what belongs to him.
exp.63:7:
Here the people acknowledge that God is their Father and their Creator. They use the image of the potter: they are the clay, and God is the one who formed them with his hands. The word "clay" refers to the soft material the potter shapes. Being "the work of his hand" means that they belong to him and that he made them.

The one speaking is the prophet, on behalf of the people of Israel. After confessing their sin and acknowledging that they deserve nothing, they ask for mercy. It is a prayer of repentance, probably reflecting on the ruin of Jerusalem and its cities, as the following verses show. Scholars debate the exact date, but the tone is one of humility.

For today: when you feel weak or have failed, do not run away from God. Come to him as a child comes to a father, and surrender yourself again into his hands. He can keep shaping your life with patience and love.
exp.41:13:
God says that he has kept silent from ages past and has remained quiet and restrained. But now he will groan like a woman in labor, gasping and panting, and he will act all at once.

The phrase "from ages past" means that he has been silent for a very long time. The image of a woman in labor shows strain and intensity, as God's coming action will be felt with force.

The Lord himself speaks, in the prophecy about the Servant and the deliverance of his people. His silence may have looked like indifference, but it was patience. Now he announces that he will act against evil and idolatry. The verses that follow show that his action also brings hope: he will guide the blind and will not forsake them.

For today: when God seems silent in the face of injustice or your pain, do not conclude that he is absent. Keep trusting that his patience has a purpose, and that the time to act will come. In the meantime, let him guide you.
exp.1:8:
It says that the ordinary person and the important person have both been brought low and humbled, but before idols. The word "humbled" here corresponds to the word "brought low" in the verse. The final phrase, "do not forgive them," is understood in several ways: as a statement that judgment will come, or as a question or plea from the prophet. The text is not entirely clear.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. The land was full of wealth, horses and idols, and they trusted in these more than in God. The verses that follow announce that God will bring low all pride and that he alone will be exalted.

Today we all bow down before something. Ask yourself honestly: what holds first place in my heart, money, success, or the opinion of others? Give that place to God, who alone is worthy of it.
exp.20:11:
The explanation says that the watchman, the sentinel, answers someone who asks him about the night. He replies that the morning has come, but that the night is still there as well. Then he invites them: the words "If you would inquire, then inquire" mean that if you wish to ask, then go ahead and ask, and "Come back yet again" is an invitation to turn back and draw near once more.

Someone from Seir, a region of Edom, asks the watchman how long the night will last, that is, the time of distress. Isaiah presents the watchman as a spokesman for God. His answer is not entirely clear, and scholars interpret it in several ways: it may speak of a brief relief followed by more trials. What is certain is that the invitation to come back remains open.

For today: when you go through dark moments, do not settle for quick answers. Keep asking God, come back to Him again and again, and trust that He always receives you.
exp.56:4:
God asks the people of Judah whether they are not ashamed of what they do. Their burning with lust for idols is described in the verse, and the "luxuriant" tree they worshipped under was a dense, full-leaved tree where pagan rites were performed. They also sacrificed their children in the valleys and under the clefts of the rocks, the rough rock formations where they hid such acts.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He is accusing the people of unfaithfulness, and for this reason he calls them "children of the sorceress," meaning the children of a witch. These practices were common among the neighboring peoples, and the people copied them. Scholars debate the exact period when this happened, but the accusation is clear.

For today: we no longer worship under trees, but we can give our hearts to things that are not God, such as money or success. Ask yourself what thing you are more passionate about than God, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.34:9:
The explanation says that the redeemed of the Lord will return and enter Zion singing with happiness. A joy that never ends will crown them like a garland, and sorrow and sighing will run far away. The "redeemed" are those whom God has bought back and set free. Gladness and joy will overtake them, meaning they will be surrounded by that happiness and will not lose it.

Isaiah, a prophet of the eighth century B.C., speaks to the people of Judah, who faced threats and later exile. This chapter describes the restoration in poetic images: the desert blossoms and God comes to save. Scholars understand this as a promise of return from captivity and also as an announcement of a still greater, final hope.

Today, when you are tired or sad, remember that God promises you an ending of joy, not of weeping. Walk with that hope, give thanks for what He has already given you, and help others trust that He will bring them home.
exp.0:22:
It says that the leaders of Jerusalem have become corrupt. Those who are "rebels" are the ones who betray justice, and "friends of thieves" are those who join with unjust people. They love bribes and chase after rewards, and for that reason they do not defend the fatherless, and the plea of the widow never comes before them. In other words, they neglect the most defenseless.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, who denounces Judah and Jerusalem. The city that was once faithful and just is now full of injustice. God does not only condemn: the verses that follow announce that he will remove the impurity, like someone who melts metal to draw off its dross.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot pay or defend themselves. We can ask ourselves whether, at work, in church, or in our community, we give fair attention to everyone, without favoring only the person who benefits us.
exp.25:15:
When the people went through distress, they turned to God. "Distress" means suffering or a tight spot. "They poured out a quiet prayer" means they prayed sincerely, with their hearts open, even if they said very little. "When You disciplined them" refers to God's correction of them.

The people of Judah speak in a song of trust within Isaiah 24 to 27. They acknowledge that God had allowed the judgment, and that in that pain they sought Him. The verses that follow compare their suffering to the pains of childbirth: they felt they could accomplish nothing. Some understand the discipline as God's correction for their sins; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you are going through a difficult moment, do not hold back your prayer. Speak to God honestly, even with few words or with tears. Difficulty can draw you closer to Him rather than push you away.
exp.56:5:
God tells his people that their "portion" and their "lot," meaning what they count on as their inheritance and their security, lies among the smooth stones of the valley. To those stones they have poured out a drink offering and offered a grain offering. At the end God asks: "Should I relent because of these?" In other words, will I not respond with judgment?

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Judah of idolatry: worshiping in the valleys and under the trees, and on high places. Some believe the smooth stones were objects of Canaanite worship, but scholars are not completely certain. God speaks like a husband wounded by unfaithfulness.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your security. Anything we treat as a source of life, whether money, success, or approval, can take the place of God. Return to Him with sincerity, for He forgives those who repent.
exp.40:24:
God says he has stirred up a man from the north, and that this man is coming. From the east, the rising of the sun, one will come who calls on God's name. He will march over rulers as if they were mortar, the way a potter treads the clay to work it.

God speaks, challenging the idols of the nations to declare the future, and they cannot. God shows that he alone directs history. Many understand this man to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who conquered Babylon and allowed the Jews to return. Others also see a broader announcement of God's plan. The text does not give the name here.

For today: God governs history, even when the powerful seem to have no limits. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and the world are not adrift. Trust him with your worries.
exp.6:6:
God declares that the plan of Judah's enemies will fail. The words "It will not arise; it will not happen" mean that it will not take hold and will never be carried out. This refers to the "evil counsel," that is, the wicked plan to invade Judah, divide it up, and set up a puppet king, the son of Tabeel.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Ahaz, who was very afraid because Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) had allied against him. God sends him a message to calm him: those kings appear strong, but their power is limited. Verse 9 ends with a challenge to believe: if they do not believe, they will not remain.

For today: when plans or pressures threaten you and seem bigger than you are, remember that God rules above them. Trusting Him does not remove the problem at once, but it allows you to face it with firmness and peace, instead of acting out of fear.
exp.4:14:
The explanation says that human pride has an expiration date. "Mankind" and "each man" refer to people in general, both the ordinary and the important: everyone will be brought low. "Brought low" means knocked down or lowered. "The arrogant" are the proud, the ones who look down on others, and they will lower their eyes, meaning they will have to drop their gaze in shame.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. He has just described injustice, luxury, and indifference toward God in the nation, and he announces that punishment is coming, including exile. The verse that follows shows the outcome of all this: God will be recognized as just and holy.

For today: ask God to show you the areas where you feel superior or self-sufficient. It is better to humble yourself willingly, asking forgiveness and serving others, than to wait for life to humble you by force.
exp.0:9:
Here God calls the rulers and the people of Jerusalem "rulers of Sodom" and "people of Gomorrah." "Listen" means pay close attention, and "instruction" means God's teaching. He asks them to take seriously what he is about to say.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the previous verse it was said that, without God's mercy, Judah would have ended like Sodom. Now God uses those names as a strong rebuke: they were behaving like those cities. What follows shows that they had a religion of rituals and sacrifices, but without a sincere heart or justice.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious practices if we do not truly listen to God. Before we pray, sing, or serve, we can ask ourselves humbly, "Lord, what do you want to tell me?" And then we can obey in concrete ways, such as treating others with justice and kindness.
exp.62:5:
It says that God, in his anger, trampled the nations like someone crushing grapes, made them stagger like drunkards in his wrath, and poured their blood out on the ground.

The word "trample" here means to step on something and crush it.

The Lord speaks in a vision in Isaiah about God as a warrior who comes to judge the enemy nations and to rescue his people. The verses before speak of "the day of vengeance" and "the year of my redeemed": judgment for some, deliverance for others. Some see here an image of Edom; others, a broader picture of the final judgment. Christian interpreters often also connect it with the work of Christ.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not leave it without a response. This allows us to leave vengeance in his hands, trust that he will do justice and, in the meantime, live with humility and mercy toward others.
exp.21:14:
God tells the prophet Isaiah to go and speak to Shebna, a high official in charge of the palace. The phrase "the steward in charge of the palace" points to a man who managed the king's household and property. "Go, say to Shebna" means "go, stand before this official and deliver what follows." What comes next is a message from God to him.

This is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says, meaning the Lord of all power. Before this, the people had lived in feasting and carelessness, without turning back to God. Now God confronts one particular leader. The verses that follow show that Shebna was carving himself a luxurious tomb, a sign of pride. Information about his life outside this passage is scarce.

For today: God sees those who have power and calls them to account. Examine whether you use your work, money, or influence to serve others or to exalt yourself. Ask Him for humility.
exp.6:20:
It says that on that day a man will raise a young cow and two sheep. That is very little livestock. The word "raise" means that he will feed and care for them. The verse does not say this is a great blessing, but something small and simple.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, when the kingdom was threatened by enemies and Ahaz did not trust God. Isaiah announces that judgment will come through Assyria. The land will be nearly empty, and the people will live on the bare minimum. The verses that follow show that there will be milk and honey, but in a desolate land. Some understand this as survival, and others as a sign that God sustains a remnant.

Even when we lose much, God can sustain us with what we need. We can learn to be thankful for little and to trust in Him, without seeking security in human powers.
exp.36:4:
The servants of King Hezekiah went to the prophet Isaiah. They went to bring him a message from the king and to ask him to pray.

The king of Assyria had surrounded Judah, and his spokesman mocked the God of Israel. Hezekiah, distressed, did not rely on his own army. He sent his servants to the prophet to seek the word of God and to ask for prayer for the people who remained. Isaiah answered with comfort: "Do not be afraid."

When fear grips us, we do not have to carry it alone. We can pray, and we can also seek out someone of mature faith who will pray with us and remind us of God's promises.
exp.0:12:
God tells the people of Judah to stop bringing worthless offerings. Their incense is detestable to him. The new moons, the Sabbaths, and the solemn assemblies were festivals God himself had commanded, yet now he says he cannot endure them, because they are joined with iniquity, that is, with wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people kept the rituals, but they lived in injustice, and so their hands were full of blood, as verse 15 says. God is not rejecting worship itself, but a religion that is only outward show and does not change the heart or conduct.

For today: before you sing, pray, or give an offering, ask yourself whether your daily life matches it. God looks for a sincere heart that also deals justly and compassionately with others.
exp.29:10:
Here the people of Judah tell the prophets to get out of their way. The phrases "get out of the way" and "turn off the road" are ways of asking them to leave them alone. "Rid us of the Holy One of Israel" means that they no longer want to hear about God or his commands.

Isaiah denounces a rebellious people who preferred pleasant words to the truth. Judah sought political help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. That is why God, through Isaiah, warns them that this sin will be like a crooked wall that suddenly collapses.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only want to hear what comforts us. A good practice is to read the Bible letting it correct us, and to listen with humility to someone who tells us the truth with love.
exp.29:14:
God tells his people how they could be saved: by turning back to him and resting in him, in quiet and in trust. "Rest" and "quiet" describe calm, and not acting out of desperation. "Strength" is the true power that holds us up. But the verse ends in sorrow: "you were not willing." God offered the way, and they turned it down.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah was threatened by Assyria and sought protection in an alliance with Egypt, which God had not asked for. So the people say, "We will flee on horses," trusting in military force. God warns them that this plan would collapse like a cracked wall or a broken vessel.

Today, when fear arrives, we often rush to solve everything with our own strength. Before acting, stop to pray, hand your worry over to God, and trust him. Resting in God is not passivity, but choosing his guidance over panic.
exp.54:2:
God invites his people to come close and listen carefully. "Incline your ear" means paying attention with a humble heart. He promises that whoever listens will "live," meaning they will have true life. He also promises an everlasting covenant, a bond that does not end, and describes it as "My loving devotion promised to David," that is, the faithful love he pledged to David.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, probably to a people in exile or weary and thirsty. He offers freely what money and effort cannot provide. The verses that follow speak of one who will be a witness and a leader for the nations. Many Christians see here a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David; others first emphasize the promise to Israel.

For today: set aside a moment each day to listen to God, reading his Word calmly. Trust that his love sustains you, even though you have not earned it.
exp.30:2:
The explanation says that the Egyptians are simply human beings, not God, and that their horses are flesh, not spirit. That is, they are strong in appearance, but limited. When the LORD stretches out His hand, the helper and the one being helped will both stumble and fall; both will perish together. "Both will perish together" means that they will all fail at the same time.

Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C., when Judah, threatened by Assyria, was seeking a military alliance with Egypt. The prophet warns them that trusting in chariots and horses, and not in the Holy One of Israel, is a mistake. The verses that follow show that God will indeed protect Jerusalem.

For today: it is good to use resources, plans, and human help, but let us not place our ultimate security in them. Before rushing to look for solutions, we can stop to pray and ask God to guide us.
exp.44:17:
He says that the Lord is the Creator of the heavens and of the earth. He formed the earth, fashioned it, and established it, that is, He set it in order and firmly in place. He did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited. And he concludes by affirming that there is no other God besides Him.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier He mocked those who make idols, who will be put to shame, and He promised salvation to Israel. Here He presents himself as the only true God, who does not speak in secret or deceive those who seek Him, unlike the idols that cannot save.

For today: your life is not an accident. The same God who made the world with purpose also has a purpose for you. Seek Him, and not things that cannot save.
exp.26:2:
He says that God himself takes care of his vineyard, which represents his people. He waters it continually and guards it night and day so that no one can disturb it.

The Lord speaks, and the song about the vineyard comes after he announces his judgment against Leviathan, an image of evil powers or oppressors (interpreters apply it to different kingdoms or forces). When Isaiah speaks of the vineyard, he means Israel, to whom God promises protection and constant care, without anger toward her.

For today: if your life is in God's hands, you do not depend only on your own strength. When you face what worries you, pray and give it to him, remembering that he cares for you at every moment.
exp.31:2:
When the righteous reign comes, it says, people will be able to see and hear clearly. "Will no longer be closed" means their eyes will no longer be shut. "Will listen" means their ears will attend closely and truly understand.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah, who lived among injustice and spiritual blindness. He first announces a just king who will be a refuge and relief, like shade in the heat. Many Christians see here a promise fulfilled in Jesus; others connect it first to King Hezekiah. Both readings are possible. He then says that the foolish will understand.

For today: ask God for eyes and ears that are attentive. Before you give an opinion or pass judgment, take a moment to read God's Word and to listen with humility, both to God and to those who speak to you.
exp.23:21:
This verse says that the powerful will be gathered together like prisoners and locked away in a dark jail. The word "pit" in the verse refers to an underground cell, a dungeon where prisoners are kept out of sight. The phrase "punished after many days" means that God will call them to account, that is, he will judge them, and this will happen after a long time.

Isaiah speaks in God's name within a prophecy about judgment on the whole earth. The "host on high" is understood in several ways: some see rebellious spiritual powers, others see proud rulers. Then comes the promise that the LORD will reign in Zion with glory.

For today: no human power escapes God, and his justice arrives in its time. If something troubles you because of injustice, trust that God sees it. Better still, live today with humility, without relying on your own strength.
exp.59:9:
It says that people from other nations will help rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and that their kings will serve her. God explains the reason: although he once struck her in anger, he now shows her mercy out of his favor. The word "struck" here refers to punishment that God brought on her.

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem, his people. The chapter announces a glorious restoration after the punishment. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as the return from exile and the rebuilding; others see it as a promise fulfilled in Christ or at the end of time.

For today: God disciplines, but his discipline is not his final word. If you are going through a correction or a failure, do not shut yourself in guilt. Return to God with humility, trusting that his mercy can rebuild what has fallen, and that he often uses unexpected people to help you.
exp.44:21:
God invites all people, even those farthest away, to turn toward him and be saved. "Turn to me" means "turn your attention to me," "be saved" means "let yourselves be saved," and "all the ends of the earth" refers to the most distant corners of the world. The reason is clear: there is no other God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses those who have survived from the nations, people from other peoples who continue to worship wooden idols that cannot save. God shows them that he alone announced what would happen, and that he is a righteous God and Savior. His invitation is universal.

For today: when you feel lost, burdened, or guilty, do not look first to other ways out. Pause, pray, and turn toward God with confidence. He invites and receives everyone.
exp.10:6:
The verse describes animals that are normally enemies or dangers living together in peace. In the Berean Standard Bible, the cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. The image is of grazing animals and predators sharing the same peaceful ground, so even violent nature will be transformed.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah, who lived among injustice and threats. He first announces a righteous king, a descendant of Jesse, the father of David. Many Christians see in him Jesus. Some understand these images literally, and others as a picture of peace among the nations. The Bible allows room for both ideas.

For today: if God promises such peace, we can practice it now. Seek to be reconciled with someone with whom you have tension, and treat with gentleness those who think differently.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that the promised king will take delight in fearing the Lord, that is, in revering and honoring him. The phrase "quick understanding" means that he will be very sharp, quick to perceive. He will not decide by what his eyes see or by what his ears hear, so he will not be fooled by surface appearances or by what people merely say.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, threatened by powerful kingdoms and poorly governed by their leaders. He announces a descendant of Jesse, father of King David, on whom the Spirit of God will rest. Christians see in this branch Jesus; the text describes him as a perfect judge, just toward the poor.

For today: before forming an opinion about someone, do not settle for what you see or for what is being said. Ask, listen calmly, and ask God for wisdom to judge with justice and mercy.
exp.51:14:
Here the servant of the Lord is said to sprinkle many nations. Sprinkling was a gesture of purification in Israel's worship. Kings will shut their mouths, meaning they will fall silent out of amazement and respect. The verse says "because of Him," so the silence is a response to the servant himself. They will see and understand something they had never been told or heard before.

God speaks here, presenting his servant, and the passage continues into Isaiah 53. Before this, the servant is disfigured and suffers, but later he is exalted. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes this verse in Romans 15:21. Some Jews have understood the servant to be Israel; there are various interpretations.

For today: do not be discouraged if the gospel seems small or despised. God can open the eyes of powerful and humble people alike. Share the good news with humility, trusting that God makes understood what no one had understood before.
exp.17:1:
It speaks of a nation south of Egypt, beyond the rivers of Cush, that sends couriers by sea in boats made of papyrus reed on the waters. God calls them "swift messengers" and sends them to a people described as tall and smooth-skinned, widely feared, and a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of Assyrian threat. Cush was probably seeking allies, and Judah could be tempted to trust in them. Isaiah announces that God watches calmly and will act in his own time. The details about the people are interpreted in several ways.

For today: before rushing after alliances or human solutions, pause and trust that God sees everything and works in his own time.
exp.41:15:
This verse says that God will lead the blind by a way they did not know and guide them on paths that are unfamiliar to them. The "darkness" will become light before them, and the "rough places" (twisted and difficult roads) will become level ground. In the end, God promises: "I will not forsake them," that is, he will not abandon them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, he announces that he will act with power after a long time of silence. Then he speaks against those who trust in idols. Many understand the "blind" to be his people, who could not see their situation or God's way clearly. Others also see it as a promise for everyone who is lost.

For today: when you do not know which way to take, hand your confusion over to God and take the step you can already see. He promises to go with you and not leave you alone.
exp.0:4:
What it says: God asks why he should keep striking his people if they keep rebelling. Here "stricken" means beaten or corrected. Then he describes the nation as a wounded body: the head, which thinks and directs, has a serious wound, and the whole heart, the center of life and desire, is suffering and weak.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, at the beginning of his book. He has just said that even an ox knows its owner, yet Israel does not recognize God. The punishments that had already come, such as the land laid waste, did not lead them back to him. Many understand that the image of the wounded body shows that sin had already damaged the whole people.

For today: If we repeat the same mistakes and only feel the pain, we do not heal. This week, ask God to show you something you keep repeating, and take one concrete step of repentance, turning back to him with sincerity.
exp.23:3:
The explanation says the whole earth falls into ruin. The verse's wording "mourns and withers" means the earth is worn down and dries up, like something that loses its life. The "exalted of the earth" are also left weakened: the leaders and the powerful waste away too. No one escapes, not even the most important.

The prophet Isaiah, a messenger of God, speaks within a section (chapters 24 to 27) that announces a judgment on the whole earth. The text itself gives the reason: the people broke God's laws and covenant. Scholars debate whether it refers to a near event, to the end of time, or to both, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: sin has consequences that reach everyone, not just a few. We can examine our own lives, return to obeying God with humility, and trust that He remains our refuge.
exp.0:18:
It says that if the people are willing and obedient, they will enjoy the best of the land. The phrase "if you are willing" means willing to do what God asks, and "obedient" means listening and doing what is commanded. "You will eat the best of the land" speaks of enjoying its fruits and its abundance.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah. He had just invited them to leave injustice, care for the orphan and the widow, and return to Him to be forgiven. Then he warns of the opposite: rebellion brings destruction. God does not force anyone; He sets out two paths and asks them to choose. The people had fallen into violence and injustice, though they still kept their religious rituals.

God offers forgiveness and blessing, but He expects a response from the heart. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God is asking of me that I have been putting off? Obeying Him, even when it costs us, is the path to His good.
exp.9:15:
He says that the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria's stout warriors, that is, its strong soldiers and its proud leaders. A wasting disease is a sickness that slowly consumes strength. And under its pomp, that is its splendor and its power, God will kindle a fire that will burn like a flame.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Assyria had conquered peoples, and God used it to discipline Israel and Judah. But the Assyrian king became full of pride, like an axe that boasts against the one who wields it. That is why God announces that he will judge that arrogance. Some understand the fire as a plague or a military disaster; the text gives no further details.

For today: everything we have comes from God, so there is no reason to boast. Ask him to give you a humble and thankful heart.
exp.41:18:
Here God asks who is more blind and deaf than his own servant. He calls the one he sends a "messenger," and the one who is "perfect" in his eyes, and yet he says that this servant does not see or hear well. "Perfect" can be understood as someone who is at peace with God, or who has been placed in a complete relationship with Him.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked those who trust in idols, and now he turns his gaze to his people, Israel, the servant who sees many things but does not take them seriously. Some believe it refers only to Israel; others also see a contrast with the faithful Servant announced earlier in the chapter.

For today: it is not enough to know the Word or to have heard it many times. Ask God for an attentive heart, and take time today to read a passage slowly, asking what it is asking you to do.
exp.33:7:
This verse says that God has an appointed time to act with justice. "Vengeance" here does not mean human anger or resentment; God is setting right what is wrong. "A year of recompense" means paying back what is due, and "the cause of Zion" refers to the cause of his people, who had been mistreated.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the nations, and especially on Edom, Israel's neighbor, which often treated Israel with hostility. The images of sword, blood and sacrifice are very strong poetic language meant to show how serious this judgment is. Some believe it refers to a historical event, and others believe it also announces a final judgment.

For today: do not take justice into your own hands. If someone has harmed you, hand your pain over to God and trust that he sees everything and judges with justice. That helps you let go of bitterness and act with mercy.
exp.27:22:
It says that God asks for complete attention. He repeats the call to listen, as if to say: "Listen truly, not just with your ears." The Berean Standard Bible uses the words "Listen and hear my voice" and "Pay attention and hear what I say," so the verse calls for both listening and paying attention. The phrase "what I say" points to God's words and his message.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he warned the proud leaders of Judah who mocked his warnings, and he spoke of a judgment that would come. Now the tone changes: he calls people to listen to a teaching. Right after, he uses the example of the farmer, who does not plow all the time but does each task in its season. Many understand that in this way God works with wisdom, and his discipline has a purpose.

For today: before you react or doubt God, stop for a moment and listen to his Word with humility. Read a passage slowly and ask: "Lord, what do you want to teach me?"
exp.65:14:
It says that the LORD will come with fire, and that his chariots will be like a whirlwind, sweeping in with great speed and force. The phrase "execute His anger" means that his anger will be carried out in full: it will fall with its complete force. "Rebuke" is his correction or judgment, which here is compared to flames.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, near the end of the book. Shortly before, he promises comfort to his faithful servants, as a mother comforts her child. Then he announces judgment against his enemies and against those who practice a false religion, mixed with customs that God calls detestable. Thus the same God who comforts also does justice.

For today: do not take God lightly or use religion as a facade. Live with sincerity, trust that he will do justice, and rest in his comfort.
exp.18:13:
It says God allowed the leaders of Egypt to become confused. "A spirit of confusion" means a spirit of disorientation and unsteadiness, as if the mind were thrown off balance. So Egypt's leaders led the whole country to stagger in everything it undertook, like a drunken man who staggers through his own vomit.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf within a prophecy against Egypt. Pharaoh's counselors, like the princes of Zoan and Noph, prided themselves on their wisdom, but they could not understand what God had determined. Some believe this is a judgment on their pride; the text does not give an exact date.

Today we can remember that human wisdom, without God, can easily be lost. Before deciding something important, it is wise to pray, ask for humility, and seek sound counsel in God's Word.
exp.42:6:
He says God calls everyone who bears his name "my sons and daughters," that is, those who belong to him. He created them for his glory, meaning to display who he is. The verse also says God formed and made them, which stresses that he shaped them with care, like a potter.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, which was scattered and going through trials. He promises them, "Do not fear, I am with you," and that he will gather his children from the east, the west, the north, and the south. Then he presents them as witnesses that he alone is God.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements, because God made you with purpose. Today you can live without fear and do something simple, such as your work, the way you treat others, or your prayer, to honor him.
exp.14:8:
The waters of Dimon are full of blood, and God says he will bring still more disaster upon Dimon. A lion will come against those who flee from Moab and against those who remain in the land. The explanation of "more" is that God is adding further punishments to those already described, and "remnant" refers to those who survive, the people left behind.

This is part of a prophecy of Isaiah against Moab, Israel's neighbor. God himself speaks ("I will bring"). The Moabites flee weeping and carry their riches to the brook of the willows. Dimon was probably a Moabite town, and its name sounds like the Hebrew word for "blood"; some believe Isaiah is playing on that similarity. Not even fleeing saves them. The "lion" may be a real animal or a symbol of new invaders; it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: let us not trust in riches or in human escapes, but in God, who is just and governs the nations. Let us seek refuge in him in time.
exp.2:25:
The explanation says that the gates of the city, which were the place of gathering and justice, will be filled with sadness and mourning. Zion, pictured as a woman, will be left alone and without comfort, sitting on the ground. "Sit" in the verse means to take a seat or settle down, and "destitute" means stripped of everything, without help. Sitting on the ground was a sign of deep mourning.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. Earlier in this chapter, he describes the women of Zion, proud of their luxury and their beauty, while in the city there was injustice toward the poor. The message announces a judgment: what they admired will be lost. This verse uses the image of a widow to show the fall of the city after the war.

For today: let us not place our security in what looks good or in what we possess. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that seeks justice and cares for the needy.
exp.54:4:
It says that someone will summon nations he does not know, and nations who do not know him will come running to him. They will not come on their own merit, but because of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who has bestowed glory on him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the verse before, he mentions the covenant with David and someone set up as a witness and teacher to the nations. Many understand the "you" to be the people of Israel, others see the ideal king who comes from David, and Christians usually see Christ. God invites everyone to come and live.

For today: God can draw people we would never have imagined. Live in such a way that others see God in you, and do not hesitate to kindly invite those who seem far away.
exp.27:19:
The bed is too short for a person to stretch out on, and the blanket is too small to wrap yourself in. The word translated "blanket" refers to a bedspread or covering, and "wrap" here means to pull it around yourself. It is a saying about a discomfort with no remedy.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the leaders of Jerusalem. They trusted in political alliances, and perhaps in agreements with foreign powers, to save themselves from judgment, and they called these a covenant with death. Many understand the bed and the blanket as an image of that false security: it looks like a shelter, but it is not enough to protect them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we seek rest apart from God: money, influence, our own plans. If that "bed" leaves us short, it is better to trust the Lord again, who alone gives true rest.
exp.41:6:
This verse says that God's servant has the mission of opening the eyes of the blind and bringing prisoners out of the dungeon. It also speaks of those sitting in darkness, that is, those who live in darkness, with no way out, shut away from the light.

God himself, the LORD, the Creator of all things, speaks. He addresses his servant, whom he called, holds by the hand, and sets as a light to the nations. Christians see Jesus here; others also understand it as a reference to Israel. The blindness and the prison may be literal or spiritual.

For today: if God has given us light, we can be instruments of that light. This week, approach someone who feels trapped or hopeless with patience and kindness, listen to them, and pray for them.
exp.20:8:
The explanation says that the watchman sees riders coming in pairs. Then one of them announces, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon!" and that all the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground. Here "riders" means horsemen, and "shattered" means smashed to pieces.

The prophet Isaiah speaks like a sentinel who keeps watch at night from a tower. God shows him, in a vision, the fall of Babylon, the great power that oppressed the nations. Some think it refers to the conquest in 539 B.C. by the Medes and Persians, but the text gives no further details. The message encouraged God's people: no empire lasts forever.

For today: when evil and injustice seem very strong, remember that God still rules. Watch with patience, pray, and trust that no power or idol can stand before Him.
exp.61:9:
God commands that the way be prepared. "Go out through the gates" means to leave the city. "Clear away the stones" means to take away whatever is in the way. "Build up the highway" means to make the main road level and ready for travel. "Prepare the way for the people" means to make the road open for them. A "banner" is a flag raised high so that everyone can see it and draw near.

God speaks to Jerusalem after promising her that she will no longer be plundered. The verses that follow announce that her Savior is coming. Many understand that the return of the exiles is being prepared. Christians also see in this an image of the coming of Christ. Both readings have been held for a long time.

For today: ask God which "stones" are standing in the way in your life or in your church, such as resentment, laziness, or pride. Remove one this week. In this way you help others draw near to Jesus more easily.
exp.9:30:
The explanation says that the people of Madmenah are in flight and that the people of Gebim take refuge, perhaps running for safety or saving what they can carry. "Flees" means that the town is running away in fear and alarm; those who live there are the ones who dwell in that place.

Isaiah speaks to Judah about the advance of an Assyrian army, which in his description comes down from the north toward Jerusalem. The towns named lie along that route, and the fear runs from place to place. It is not known with certainty where all these places were, but the meaning is clear. The prophet wants the people to feel the threat, so that he can then show that God will bring down the proud invader.

For today: when fear advances like a wave in your life, remember that no threat has the last word. God reigns and can humble what seems invincible. Trust in Him.
exp.0:2:
It says that even the simplest animals, like the ox and the donkey, know who takes care of them and where they are fed. In contrast, Israel, God's people, does not know the one who has cared for them. The word "manger" is the feeding trough where the animal eats, and "do not understand" means that they do not reflect or pay attention.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he raised and exalted his children, but they rebelled. With this comparison, God expresses pain and reproach: his people forgot where all good things came from.

For today: let us not take daily blessings for granted. Today you can stop and thank God for something specific, such as food, health, or family, recognizing him as the one who cares for you, instead of living distracted.
exp.20:2:
It says that the prophet feels a very strong pain in his body, and an anguish like the pains of a woman in labor. The phrase "I am bewildered to hear" means that he was overcome with sorrow by what he heard, and "I am dismayed to see" means that he was filled with fear because of what he saw.

Isaiah speaks, and the passage is a "burden," that is, a message of judgment against Babylon, called "the wilderness of the sea." God shows him a harsh vision: the Persians and the Medes will come to destroy. Many understand that Isaiah suffers because of what he sees, though some think it also expresses the terror of the people before that fall.

For today: God does not ask us to be indifferent to the suffering of the world. We can bring to prayer the tragedies we see, feel compassion, and trust that God is just and in control.
exp.42:7:
God commands that his people be brought out, people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf. The phrase "bring out" means "make come out" or "bring to the front." This does not speak of blindness of the body, but of failing to recognize what God has done and said.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, who was in exile. He has just promised to bring his children back from far away. Then he calls them forward as witnesses before the nations, to show that he alone is God and that he does what he announces. His people had seen much, but they did not understand.

For today: it is not enough to have seen and heard of God many times. Ask him to open your eyes and your ears, and think about how he has cared for you. That will help you trust him and speak of him to others.
exp.13:12:
He says that someone was thinking in his heart: "I will ascend to the heavens, I will raise my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of assembly, in the far reaches of the north." "Throne" is the word for the seat of a king. "The mount of assembly" is the mountain of gathering, where the gods were thought to meet. "The far reaches of the north" is the direction of the verse's final phrase.

The prophet Isaiah speaks. It is a mocking song aimed at the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), who oppressed many nations. His fall from power to the grave is described. Some early Christians have also applied this passage to Satan, but others believe the text speaks only of the human king. This is debated. In both cases, the center is the pride that wants to take the place of God.

Today, when we want to control everything or to be admired without limit, let us remember that God resists the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and serve others without seeking applause.
exp.25:13:
The verse says that Israel's former oppressors are dead and will not live again. The departed spirits will not rise. The Berean wording "You have punished and destroyed them" explains that God acted to judge them, and "You have wiped out all memory of them" means that their power and their name were erased.

The people of God speak in a song of confidence. Earlier they say that other lords ruled over them, but now they say that only the Lord's name is remembered. The "dead" are those masters, probably powers that oppressed Israel. Some scholars see specific kings here, and others see a general image. Afterward, the text speaks of God making his people grow.

Today we can remember that no unjust power lasts forever. If something oppresses you, such as fear, an injustice, or a difficult situation, hand it over to God and trust that he has the last word. In the meantime, try to remember his name and seek him in prayer.
exp.65:4:
God speaks to those who take his word seriously, those who tremble at it. He tells them that their own brothers hate them and push them out because of his name. Those brothers mock them, saying, "Let the LORD be glorified that we may see your joy!" as though they were the devout ones. But God promises to act, and those who mocked will be put to shame.

The word "ashamed" points to people who are put to shame or left disappointed.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah. At the end of the book, the people are divided: some worship in an empty way and mix their religion with practices that God rejects, while others are faithful to him from the heart. God comforts the faithful who are pushed aside by their own people, and he assures them that he will do justice.

If you are rejected or mocked for obeying God, do not lose heart. Keep going with humility, trusting that God sees everything and that he himself will make the truth clear in his time.
exp.13:19:
He says this king will not be joined with the other kings in burial. The reason is that he destroyed his own land and slaughtered his own people. "Offspring" means descendants, and "the wicked" means evildoers. His family line will not be remembered.

The prophet Isaiah is delivering a mocking song against the king of Babylon, and the text presents it in poetic form. Dead kings receive a dignified tomb, but this tyrant is cast out like a trampled corpse. God himself then announces that he will wipe out the name of Babylon. Some apply this to one particular king, and others also see a broader picture of human pride.

For today: power used to harm others does not leave a good memory behind. Ask God to help you use your influence, even if it is small, to care for people and not to take advantage of them.
exp.16:7:
In that day, the people will stop placing their trust in the altars they have built with their own hands and in the things they have made with their fingers. The verse names the Asherahs, the sacred poles connected with pagan worship, and the incense altars they had set up. Those objects, made by human hands, were given a place that belonged to God alone.

God speaks through Isaiah. The message is about judgment on Damascus and the kingdom of Israel, called Ephraim here, which had turned away from Him. After the punishment, only a small remnant will be left, like a few olives left on a tree after the harvest. That remnant will again look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel.

For today: ask yourself what things you have made with your own hands, such as your work, your money or your public image, that have taken the place of God. Honestly, look again to Him, who is your true security.
exp.47:17:
God says with sorrow, "If only you had paid attention to my commandments!" If you had, your peace would have been like a river, flowing steadily, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, arriving one after another without end. Here "paid attention" means to obey.

The LORD, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, speaks to his people who were in exile or about to leave Babylon. He reminds them that he taught and guided them, but they did not listen. It is a lament from God, not only a rebuke: it shows what he longed to give them. Then he invites them to leave Babylon and to rejoice in their redemption.

For today: true peace grows when we listen to God and follow him. Today, before deciding something, take a moment to ask him what his Word says about it.
exp.17:0:
It speaks of a "woe," a warning from God, against a distant land. The land is described as one of "whirring wings," and this may be understood as a place full of winged insects, of armies, or of ships with sails. It also lies along the rivers of Cush, which at that time was the kingdom south of Egypt. Scholars are not sure exactly what that image means.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, sent by God to Judah. Judah probably faced the threat of Assyria, and some were thinking of seeking help through alliances with Cush. Many believe the message reminds them that God rules over all nations, though this is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. Before rushing to seek human support, it is good to pray and to trust first in God, who has control of history.
exp.40:10:
Isaiah 41:11 says that those who rage against God's people will be ashamed and disgraced, and that those who contend with them will be reduced to nothing and will perish. "Rage" means they are full of fury; "contend" means they argue or struggle against others with hostility. "Ashamed and disgraced" here refers to being defeated and left humiliated. To be "reduced to nothing" is to lose all strength and importance.

God, through the prophet Isaiah, speaks to Israel, whom he calls "my servant." The people were surrounded by powerful nations and felt afraid. God reminds them that he chose them and did not abandon them, and for that reason he promises to be with them and to uphold them.

For today: when you feel attacked or afraid, do not respond with resentment. Pray, trust that God sustains you, and leave justice in his hands while you keep doing good.
exp.48:13:
Here the text says that Zion, that is, the people of God in Jerusalem, complains and thinks that God has abandoned her. The words "The LORD has forsaken me" and "the Lord has forgotten me" express the pain of feeling forgotten. It is not a fact, but what she feels.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of exile, when Israel was suffering far from its land. Just before, God promises comfort and the return of people from far away. But Zion says that God has forgotten her. Immediately God answers with the image of a mother who does not forget the child she nurses, and says that even if she could, He will not forget His people.

For today: when you feel forgotten by God, do not keep that pain silent. Bring it to Him honestly, as Zion did, and rest on what He has promised, not only on what you feel.
exp.9:1:
Isaiah says that some rulers made unjust laws so that the poor would be left without protection in the courts. They denied the oppressed among God's people their rights, preyed on widows, and robbed the fatherless. The phrase "to deprive the poor of fair treatment" means refusing them fair treatment, and to take away what they had is to rob them of what was rightfully theirs.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the people of Judah, especially to their leaders. He warns them with "Woe!" because they were abusing their power. The verses that follow announce that God will call them to account, and neither their wealth nor their position will save them.

For today: God cares for the weakest and expects the same from us. We can ask ourselves whom we might defend or help, and treat everyone with justice and honesty, above all those who have no one to speak for them.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that God himself will judge between the nations and settle disputes for many peoples. As a result, people will turn their weapons into tools for work: the swords into plowshares (the iron blade that breaks open the ground) and the spears into pruning hooks (for trimming vines and cutting branches). Nations will no longer take up the sword against one another, and no one will train anymore for war.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, describes a vision of "the last days." The nations stream up to God's mountain, to Jerusalem, to learn his ways. Then the prophet calls his own people, the house of Jacob, to walk now in the light of the LORD, because at that time they were relying on fortune-tellers and foreign customs.

For today: the peace God promises begins where I live. I can ask myself what "sword" I carry at home, at work, or in church, such as a harsh word or a grudge, and turn it into something that serves and builds up.
exp.44:14:
This verse says that God, though at times he cannot be seen or understood, is the God who saves. The phrase "who hides Himself" means that he conceals himself, that his purposes and the way he acts are not always clear to us.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks. God has just announced that he will use Cyrus to free his people held in captivity, and that the nations will acknowledge that he alone is God. Isaiah responds with wonder: God works in unexpected ways. Some understand this to mean that God works behind the events of history; others see it as an expression of reverence before a mystery.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, do not conclude that he is absent. Trust that he works and saves, even in silence. Tell him honestly what you feel, and wait on him.
exp.44:12:
God says that he himself raised up a man to carry out a just purpose. This man will rebuild God's city, Jerusalem, and will set free God's exiles, that is, his people who were carried away from their land. The phrase "I will make all his ways straight" means that God will clear the road ahead of him. And he will do this "but not for payment or reward": without taking payment or a bribe.

The Lord speaks, the LORD of Hosts, the Creator of all things. From the context, the verse before it and the name of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, many understand this to refer to the Persian king Cyrus, who allowed the Jews to return from exile in Babylon. Some also see in this a shadow of the deliverance that Christ brings, though that is an interpretation. God wants to show that he directs history.

For today: if God could use a pagan king to carry out his plan, he can also work in your difficult circumstances. Trust that he is still guiding, even when you cannot see how.
exp.47:14:
He says that God himself has spoken, has called a certain person, and has brought him, and for that reason that person will succeed in his mission. The word "succeed" means that things will go well for him in the task God gave him. The repetition "I, even I" stresses that everything depends on God and not on human strength.

The Lord speaks to Israel, who was about to live in exile in Babylon. He reminds them that he is the Creator and that he announced things before they happened. The "he" is not named here, but many understand it to be Cyrus, king of Persia, whom Isaiah mentioned earlier (44:28; 45:1). Others see it in a broader way, as God's plan to deliver his people.

For today: when God calls you to something, trust that he also sustains the path. Obey step by step, without relying only on your own strength.
exp.64:12:
God says he will make a clear difference between two groups. Those who serve him will have food, drink, and joy. Those who reject him will have hunger, thirst, and shame. The word "ashamed" here means they will be disappointed and humiliated when they see that their hopes have failed.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses those who had abandoned him and who set out tables of offerings to Luck and Fate, which were false gods of fortune. God had spoken to them, and they refused to listen. That is why he announces this contrast between the faithful and those who turned away.

For today: do not place your trust in luck, money, or anything else that promises security. Respond when God speaks to you, and seek in him your provision and your joy.
exp.8:11:
The explanation says that Israel would be attacked from two sides: Aram from the east and Philistia from the west. Both would devour Israel with open mouths, meaning they would do it easily and without resistance. Even so, God's anger had not turned away, and his hand was still upraised, ready to strike again.

Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom, Israel. They had suffered blows, yet they proudly said they would rebuild stronger, with dressed stone and cedar. Instead of turning to God, they trusted in themselves. For this reason God allowed their enemies to keep pressing them.

For today: when crises come, it is not enough to rebuild with our own strength. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but every difficulty is a good moment to stop, pray, and ask what God wants to teach us. Let us return to him with humility.
exp.47:13:
Come together, all of you, and listen. God invites everyone to gather and pay attention. He asks, with a note of challenge: which of the idols or the nations was ever able to foretell these things? Then he says that the one he has chosen is his ally, and that this ally will carry out God's desire against Babylon and the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). "His arm" refers to God's power at work.

God himself is speaking, addressing Israel, a people surrounded by idols and filled with doubt. Many understand the chosen ally to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who would later defeat Babylon and set the people free. Some scholars debate the exact identity, but the central message is clear: only God knows and directs the future.

For today: when the future fills you with fear, remember that the God who announced everything in advance still governs history. Trust in him and rest.
exp.57:7:
Then the explanation says that when people live out the kind of fasting God desires, their lives will be filled with light, like the coming of dawn. "Your healing" here means restoration and wholeness, and "will come quickly" means it will arrive soon. The righteousness that goes before you is an upright life that opens the way ahead, and the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard, the one who watches over your back and protects you.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who fasted and carried out religious acts, but who mistreated their workers and neglected the poor. God tells them that true fasting includes freeing the oppressed, sharing bread, and clothing the naked. The promise of the verse is God's response to that obedience.

For today: join your prayer with a concrete act of kindness. This week, share a meal, help someone in need, or deal justly with the people you work alongside.
exp.42:11:
God says that he alone decreed what would happen, saved his people, and proclaimed it to them. No foreign god was there with him to do these things. Because of this, Israel is a witness that the LORD is God. Here "proclaimed" means announced publicly, a "foreign god" is a false or other god, and "witnesses" are people who can tell what they have seen.

Here God speaks himself through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, surrounded by peoples who worshiped idols. God reminds them that he had decreed, had rescued, and had spoken clearly, something the idols never did. The verses that follow call him the Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel.

For today: think about the times God helped you, held you up, or kept his word in your life. This week, tell someone one of those experiences in simple words. Your story can be a witness that God is faithful.
exp.47:9:
God tells Israel that he has tested and cleansed them, but not as silver is refined, that is, not in the same way silver is refined, or not to the level of complete purification. This phrase is understood in several ways. The verse says "I have tested you," and the "furnace of affliction" is the suffering God used to test his people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a stubborn and rebellious people. Soon they will live in exile in Babylon. God makes clear that he does not spare them because of their own merit, but for the sake of his own name. Even the punishment seeks to cleanse them and not to destroy them.

For today: when you go through a hard time, do not assume right away that God has abandoned you. He may use the trial to remove pride and strengthen your trust in him. Ask him to show you what he wants to form in you, and keep walking in faith.
exp.12:0:
This verse is the heading of a prophetic message. "Burden" does not refer to a physical weight but to a serious message of judgment, a sentence that God places upon a nation. The verse says this is a message against Babylon that Isaiah the son of Amoz received.
