Here God does not speak directly; the one who introduces the message is Isaiah, the son of Amoz, a prophet in Judah. The following verses do show God summoning armies to carry out his judgment. Babylon was then a power that would later be an enemy of Judah. Scholars debate exactly when this message was fulfilled, but the text presents it as the word of God.

For today: God sees and governs over all nations, even the most powerful. You can trust that injustice will not have the last word, and that God cares for his people.
exp.47:3:
God tells his people that he knows how stubborn they are. He uses strong images. The "neck" stands for the throat and the back of the neck, and calling it "iron" means it is rigid and will not bend. The "forehead of bronze" speaks of a hard face, one that is not ashamed and will not let itself be corrected.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel. He reminds them that he announced things before they happened, so that they could not credit them to their idols. Their hardness made such clear warnings necessary.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for a spirit willing to listen, to acknowledge our mistakes, and to change course, trusting that his correction comes from his love and faithfulness.
exp.63:10:
The passage speaks of the temple in Jerusalem, the holy and beautiful place where our ancestors gave praise to God and which was the pride of the people. It was burned, and everything that was precious to them was left in ruins. The phrase "has been burned with fire" means the temple was destroyed, and "lies in ruins" expresses the same loss.

The speaker is the prophet, praying on behalf of the whole people. These words seem to come from a time after the temple was destroyed, probably by the Babylonians in 586 BC, although some scholars believe the prophet sees it in advance. The people confess their sin, ask for mercy, and remind God that they are his.

For today: when you lose something very dear, do not keep silent or shut yourself away. Speak with God honestly, acknowledge your failures if there are any, and remind him that you belong to him. He listens to honest pain.
exp.13:18:
He says that the king of Babylon, whom Isaiah addresses as "you," will not receive a dignified burial. He will be cast out of his grave like a rejected branch. The word "rejected" describes a branch that is thrown away as worthless. The phrase "covered by those slain with the sword" describes the bodies of men who died in battle. His corpse will lie like theirs, and like a carcass trampled underfoot.

Isaiah pronounces this poetic mockery against a proud and cruel king. Earlier the text says that the other kings rest with honor in their tombs, but he does not. Many identify him with the king of Babylon; others also see a broader background about pride. God denounces that he destroyed his land and killed his people.

For today: power and fame do not guarantee a good ending. God sees how we use the authority we have, whether in the home, at work, or in the church. Let us ask him for humility to serve and not to crush others.
exp.6:5:
Here the plan of Judah's enemies is spelled out. Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) say: "Let us invade Judah, terrorize it, and divide it among ourselves." Their goal is to frighten and conquer the land, split it between them, and then install the son of Tabeal as its king. We do not know for certain who this man was; he was probably not of David's line.

God speaks through Isaiah to King Ahaz, who was afraid. Kings Rezin and Pekah were threatening him, and God calls them "two smoldering stubs of firewood," sticks that are nearly burned out. With this, God asks Ahaz for calm and trust, because the enemy's plan would not come to pass.

Today, many threats seem enormous and make us afraid. Before acting in panic, we can pray and remember that God still governs. The plans that frighten us do not have the last word.
exp.59:13:
The sons of those who oppressed you will come and bow down before you. Those who once mocked you will fall facedown at your feet, and they will call you the City of the LORD and Zion of the Holy One of Israel. The mockery is scornful ridicule, and the facedown bow is a deep sign of respect and submission.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who had endured exile and contempt. He promises to restore Zion and to show that she belongs to him. Many believers see here a hope for Israel, and others also see an image of the Church. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

For today: if you have been hurt or looked down upon, do not carry the burden of revenge. Trust that God defends his own and knows how to restore your dignity in his time.
exp.50:16:
Isaiah calls Jerusalem to wake up and rise up. She has drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his fury, and she has drained it to the dregs, the thick residue left at the bottom. That cup is the kind that makes people stagger. Staggering means stumbling and losing your balance, unable to think or act clearly. To have drained the goblet to the dregs means she held nothing back, not even the last drop.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. The people had suffered greatly because of their disobedience, and they were left like someone reeling from sorrow, without strength and without anyone to guide them. But God has just reminded them that he is their God and that he called them "my people." The call to rise is the beginning of a promise of comfort.

For today: if you are worn down by the consequences of past mistakes or pain, do not stay on the ground. God calls you to rise, not to condemn you, but to restore you. Today you can return to him with sincerity.
exp.40:6:
They say the craftsmen encourage one another to make an idol. The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and the one who wields the hammer cheers on the one who strikes the anvil. Someone checks the welding and says, "It is good." Then they nail the figure down so that it will not be toppled.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just called the nations to judgment, and they, frightened, respond by making gods and encouraging one another. God lets the absurdity show: an idol needs nails to keep it from falling over. Right away He contrasts this with Israel, His chosen servant, whom He Himself upholds.

For today: when you feel afraid, do not look for security in things you hold up with your own hands. Rest in God, who holds you up.
exp.7:19:
To the law and to the testimony! The explanation says we should return to God's law and his testimony, that is, to what he has said in his Word. If someone speaks and does not agree with that, the verse says they have no light of dawn, that they are like someone still walking in the darkness of night. The "pythones," the spirits or mediums who claimed to speak with the dead, are also mentioned here.

Isaiah speaks in a time of fear, when Judah was threatened by enemy kings. Some were suggesting that the people seek answers from mediums and fortune-tellers. The prophet replies that the people should consult their God, not the dead. The verses that follow show the distress of those who reject that guidance.

For today: when you hear opinions, advice, or teaching, compare them with the Bible. Before you decide out of fear or confusion, read Scripture and pray; there you will find firm light to walk by.
exp.20:5:
God tells the prophet to post a lookout, that is, someone who pays close attention and reports at once what he sees. The instruction is simple: keep watch and report what you see.

Isaiah speaks within a prophecy about a message of judgment that many connect with the fall of Babylon, though not all agree. The prophet is troubled by the vision, while the city seems to carry on with feasting. God tells him to keep watching, and the lookout then sees chariots and riders approaching.

For today: do not live distracted or indifferent. Set aside time to pray and to listen carefully to God, and humbly share what you learn from his Word to help others stay prepared.
exp.32:15:
This verse speaks of the righteous person described earlier: the one who walks in uprightness. That person will dwell on the heights, protected as if in a mountain fortress. A "refuge" is a place of safety. Also, their food will be provided, and their water assured, meaning secure and never failing.

The prophet Isaiah writes to Judah when Assyria was threatening and the people trembled before the judgment of God. Sinners grow afraid before the consuming fire, which probably points to the holiness of God. Then the question is asked: who will be able to stand in his presence? This verse answers with a promise of care for the one who lives with integrity.

For today: God cares for the one who seeks to live honestly, even when there is fear or scarcity. Today you can choose one concrete step of integrity, such as turning down an unfair advantage, and trust that God sustains your life.
exp.36:31:
It says that from Jerusalem a group of survivors will come out, and that deliverance will come from Mount Zion. A "remnant" means those who are left, a part that is saved. "Deliverance" is rescue or salvation. And "zeal" here is God's burning commitment to his people and to his word: he himself will bring it about.

It is part of God's answer to King Hezekiah through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Assyria, and the people were afraid. God gives a sign: although now it is not possible to sow normally, the land will again bear fruit. Then he promises that the Assyrian king will not enter the city.

For today: when you feel surrounded by a great problem, remember that your hope does not depend on your own strength, but on God's faithful commitment. Rest in him and keep taking simple steps of obedience.
exp.8:17:
The verse says that wickedness burns like a fire. It starts by consuming the thorns and briers, the small and easily caught things, but it then spreads into the thickets of the forest, and the whole mass rolls upward in billows of smoke. The thickets are dense growths of brush and trees, and the image shows how evil starts small, spreads, and destroys.

Isaiah speaks to the northern kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. Its leaders misled the people, the people followed them, and no one was left untouched by the corruption. Isaiah explains that this wickedness was already consuming the nation from within, and the verses that follow describe violence even between brothers. Some scholars also see here a reference to the internal conflicts of that time.

For today: do not dismiss the "small" sins, such as dishonesty or resentment, because they can grow beyond your control. Today, confess to God something you tend to tolerate, and ask him for help to put it out before it spreads.
exp.65:22:
In the time God promises, people from every nation will come to worship him, at every new moon and every Sabbath. "From one New Moon to another" refers to the new moon, the start of each month. "All mankind" means all people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah near the close of the book. God promises new heavens and a new earth, and that his people will remain. It includes people from other nations, since he will also take priests from among them. The passage contrasts those who worship with those who rebelled. Christians interpret it in different ways: some see it as a picture of the future kingdom, others as symbolic language of universal worship.

For today: make worship a constant habit, not only an occasional one. Set aside a regular time, whether weekly or daily, to give thanks to God, pray, and listen to his Word.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that those who rebel against God and keep on sinning will be destroyed together. The explanation of an older phrase is not needed here, since the verse itself says "together" and "perish" directly. The words "shattered" and "perish" are likewise made clear by the verse's own wording, so they are not explained here. Those who "forsake the LORD" are those who turn away from God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Earlier, He promises to cleanse the city, restore righteous judges, and redeem Zion with justice. But here He makes clear that not everyone will be restored: those who refuse to return to Him will face the consequences. The verses that follow speak of the shame of having trusted in places of worship dedicated to idols.

For today: God offers forgiveness and a fresh start, but it must be accepted. Today you can ask yourself whether there is anything in which you have drifted away from God and, with humility, return to Him in prayer, before pride hardens your heart.
exp.57:4:
Is this the kind of fast God really wants? Is it only about spending a day denying yourself, bowing your head like a reed, and lying down in sackcloth and ashes? God asks whether such a day can truly be called a fast and a day acceptable to the LORD. The implied answer is no. To deny yourself means to give up something for a time, and bowing the head like a reed pictures humility. Sackcloth and ashes were rough, plain cloth and dust worn as signs of grief and repentance. Here God questions whether outward displays like these are enough.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people complain that they fast and God does not respond. But God shows them that while they were fasting, they were also seeking their own gain, mistreating others, and quarreling. Their religious practice looked good on the outside, but their hearts were not with God or with their neighbor.

For today: before practicing something spiritual, such as prayer, fasting, or serving, ask yourself whether the way you treat others matches it. Today, concretely help someone in need or correct a small injustice you have been ignoring.
exp.27:13:
God calls the leaders of Jerusalem "scoffers," that is, men who mock the warning God has given. They "rule" (hold authority over) the people. God asks them to hear his word, even though until now they have refused to listen.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. The rulers of Judah mocked the prophet's message and trusted in political alliances, which the following verse calls a "covenant with death" and a refuge in lies. Some scholars think this refers to pacts with foreign powers, but the text does not say so with complete clarity. God responds by announcing a firm stone in Zion, where trust can truly be placed.

For today: when a word from God makes us uncomfortable, let us not mock it or seek false refuges. Let us stop to listen to it with humility and trust in the foundation that God offers.
exp.7:17:
Isaiah says that he and the children God gave him are "signs and symbols" in Israel. A "sign" is something that points to a greater truth, and a "symbol" is something that stands for a larger meaning. All of this comes from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of fear and political pressure in Judah. Many people were looking for help from mediums and spirits. Isaiah's children had names that carried a message (Isaiah 7:3; 8:3), and their lives reminded the people of what God was saying. In this way, his family was a living message for the people.

For today: our lives also speak. Let your way of living and of trusting God, even in difficult times, be a clear witness to those around you, one that rests on his Word.
exp.57:9:
If you give yourself fully to the hungry, and truly satisfy the one who is suffering, then God promises that your light will shine even in the darkness, and your night will be as bright as midday.

"Giving yourself" means offering yourself wholeheartedly, not just handing over what you have left over. To "satisfy" someone is to leave them well fed and at peace. "Noonday" is the hour of brightest light in the day.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted and carried out religious practices, yet still treated others unjustly. He explains that the fasting that pleases him is joined to compassion and justice. The promises of light, guidance, and restoration come after that change.

Today you can help someone concretely: share food, stay with a person who is suffering, or give them your real time. Do it with kindness, without seeking applause. God cares for those who give themselves in this way.
exp.9:23:
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: He speaks to his people who live in Zion, that is, Jerusalem. He tells them not to fear Assyria. Although Assyria will strike them with a rod and lift its staff against them, as the Egyptians did in the past, God does not want them to live gripped by fear. "Rod" and "staff" are instruments of punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah had lived in disobedience, and God allowed Assyria, a feared power, to be a rod of correction. But the verse that follows says that his anger will soon pass, and that God himself will judge Assyria. The punishment therefore has a limit, and God still calls them "My people."

For today: when you face a trial or correction, do not see it as abandonment. God remains your Father and has control. Come to him with humility and trust, without letting fear dominate you.
exp.51:12:
It says that God's servant will prosper and will be raised and lifted up to a very high place. The words "raised," "lifted up" and "highly exalted" repeat the same idea: great honor and elevation. "Prosper" here means that he will succeed and accomplish what God purposes for him.

God is speaking, presenting his servant. Earlier, he called his people to leave Babylon with confidence, knowing that he would go before them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes it about him. Other Jewish readers have understood the servant to be Israel. What follows shows that before being exalted he will go through great suffering.

For today: when the path of obedience costs you or seems to bear no fruit, trust that God knows how to finish what he begins. Keep doing good with patience, without rushing or looking for shortcuts.
exp.42:20:
This verse says that God formed his people with a purpose: that they would speak of his praises and make known how good he is. The word "formed" means that he shaped them and brought them into existence as a people. The idea of declaring his praise means that they will speak of it openly, so that others will know.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, who was living in the midst of hardship and exile. He promises to do something new: to make a way in the wilderness and give water to his chosen people. Then, in the verses that follow, he rebukes them because they have neglected him. Even so, his purpose for them does not change, and his grace goes forward.

For today: God made us to know him and to speak of his goodness. Today you can tell someone, simply, how God has sustained you in a difficult moment, and thank him out loud.
exp.65:18:
God promises to set a sign among his people and to send some of those who survive to distant nations: Tarshish, Put, and the archers of Lud, Tubal, Javan, and the islands far away. Those peoples had never heard of God or seen his glory. They will proclaim his glory among the nations. The word "nations" here is the same idea the verse expresses as the nations as a whole.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah near the close of the book. First he warns those who practice a false and hidden religion, and then he announces that he will gather all the nations to see his glory. It is not known for certain what the "sign" was or who the survivors are; there are several interpretations. The exact locations of all these places are also uncertain.

God wants his glory to reach all peoples, even the most distant. We can take part by praying for missionaries, supporting them, and speaking of God with those around us, with humility and joy.
exp.60:8:
Their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. Their descendants are their children and the generations that follow, and their offspring are the young shoots that spring up from them, like new branches on a tree. Everyone who sees them will recognize that the Lord has blessed them.

The one speaking is the prophet Isaiah, announcing God's promise to a people who were humbled and wounded. God tells them that he will turn their shame into honor and make an everlasting covenant with them. Many believe this refers to a restored Israel; Christians also see in the passage Christ (Isaiah 61:1-3 is quoted by Jesus in Luke 4) and those who belong to him.

Today we can live in such a way that others notice God's goodness in us: with honesty, kindness, and hope, trusting that he restores what seemed lost.
exp.52:5:
We all, like sheep, have gone astray. Each one has turned to his own way. But the LORD has laid upon the Servant the guilt of us all. "Gone astray" means wandering away from the right path. "Laid upon" means that God placed the weight of our sin on him.

Here the prophet Isaiah is speaking, and the "we" is a people who recognize their own error. Before, they thought the Servant was suffering because of his own fault, but now they understand that he was suffering for them. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament applies it to him (1 Peter 2:24-25). Other Jewish readings see the people of Israel.

Today we can honestly admit that we sometimes go our own way. And instead of hiding it, we can return to God with confidence, because he himself took responsibility for our guilt.
exp.49:7:
The One who vindicates me is near; who will dare to contend with me? Let us confront each other! Who has a case against me? Let him approach me! The speaker says that God is very close to him and is the one who vindicates him. For this reason he is bold enough to challenge anyone who brings an accusation against him. "Let us confront each other" means let us face one another in a formal setting, as in a court. "Who has a case against me?" means who wants to argue the matter. "Let him approach me" means let my accuser step forward to face me in the trial.

The speaker is the Servant of the LORD, who endures blows, mockery, and spitting without giving up. Christians see in this an image of Jesus, although the original text also speaks of a faithful servant who trusts in God. His confidence does not come from being perfect in himself, but from God's support.

For today: when you are falsely accused or feel guilty without reason, do not live in fear. Pray, do what is right, and rest in the knowledge that God knows the truth and sustains you.
exp.53:6:
God tells his people that he forsook them for a brief moment, but that with great compassion he will bring them back. "I will bring you back" means gathering together those who had been scattered and returning them home. "Compassion" means acts of kindness and mercy that they did not deserve.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His people, Israel, had suffered the punishment of exile because of their unfaithfulness, and they felt like an abandoned wife. God presents himself as their husband and redeemer. He compares his promise to the one he made to Noah: just as he swore never again to flood the earth, he swears never again to be so angry with them.

For today: if you go through a season when you feel that God is far away, do not conclude that he has abandoned you forever. Tell him honestly what you feel, and trust that his compassion lasts longer than any trial.
exp.30:6:
This verse says that when God acts to save his people, people will reject the idols of silver and gold they made. "Reject" here means to throw away decisively, with nothing kept back. The phrase "sinfully made" shows that making idols was itself a sin, not just a mistake.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Judah was looking for help in Egypt against the threat of Assyria, instead of trusting the Lord. Before this verse, God promises to protect Jerusalem like a bird that shelters its young, and he calls the people to return to him. Afterward, he announces the fall of Assyria. When God's deliverance is seen, the idols will be exposed as worthless.

For today: ask yourself where you place your security, such as money, success, or your own plans, and hand it over to God with confidence.
exp.58:20:
God makes a covenant promise: his Spirit and his words will stay in the mouths of his people, and in the mouths of their children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore. The phrase "will not depart" means that they will not be lost or taken away.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah. Earlier, the people had been accused of sin, but God promises that the Redeemer will come to Zion for those who turn from their wickedness. This verse is part of that promise of restoration. Some understand "you" to refer to the Redeemer, others to the faithful people or to Isaiah as a representative; the text does not fully clarify this here. Many Christians see a fulfillment in Christ and in the Spirit given to his people.

For today: if you want your faith to reach your children, do it through example and through words. Read the Bible at home and speak about God naturally, trusting that he sustains his work.
exp.4:9:
Isaiah 5:10 says that a large vineyard, ten acres in size, would produce only a small amount of wine, just a bath, which is roughly 20 to 40 liters, though the exact measure is debated. And a homer of seed, a large quantity sown, would yield only an ephah of grain, a far smaller amount. In other words, the harvest would be wretched, far less than what was planted.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD to Judah. He has just condemned the wealthy who piled up houses and land without thinking of others. God announces that this greed will bring punishment: fields that yield almost nothing and houses left empty.

For today: accumulating more and more does not bring security or peace. Ask yourself whether you use what you have with generosity and justice, and trust that God is the one who gives true fruit.
exp.6:13:
God himself will give a sign: a virgin will become pregnant, give birth to a son, and name him Immanuel, which means "God with us." The verb "will be with child" means "will give birth." The Hebrew word for "virgin" can also be translated "young woman," which is why scholars differ about its original meaning.

Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz, of the house of David. Judah was threatened by two enemy kings, and Ahaz, instead of trusting God, refused to ask for a sign while pretending to be humble. God gives one anyway. The child would be a sign that those two kings would soon fall. Christians also see in this passage a greater fulfillment in Jesus, as Matthew 1:22-23 says.

When you are afraid, remember that God is with you. Trust his promise instead of looking for ways out on your own.
exp.43:2:
God promises to pour water on dry ground, and with that image he announces that he will pour out his Spirit and his blessing on the descendants of his people. A thirsty, parched land is what the picture describes, and the new growth that springs up stands for the children and grandchildren.

The Lord speaks to Israel, here called Jacob and Jeshurun (an affectionate name meaning something like "the upright one"). The people were discouraged, and God comforts them with the words "Do not fear." The verses that follow show the result: the descendants will grow like willows beside the water and will gladly say that they belong to God.

For today: if you worry about your children or about loved ones who seem spiritually dry, pray with hope. God is the one who gives life, and you can entrust them to him while you live out your faith and set a good example.
exp.49:6:
He says that the Lord GOD is the one who helps the servant, so he has not been disgraced. "I have set My face like flint" means he stayed firm and determined, like a very hard stone. "I will not be put to shame" means he will not be defeated or left in disgrace. He trusts that God will not leave him that way.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, in the third Servant Song in Isaiah. He is obedient, though he suffers blows, mockery, and spitting. Many Christians see here a prophecy of Jesus, who also set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Others read it first as the voice of the prophet himself, and there are also those who see the faithful people. It can be understood in several ways.

For today: when obeying God brings you criticism or mockery, do not depend on the approval of people. Pray asking God for help, and keep going with firmness and gentleness, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.20:9:
He says the prophet speaks to his people, whom he calls "my people, crushed on the threshing floor." These are images of grain beaten on the threshing floor, the place where the wheat was separated out. Isaiah affirms that he invents nothing: he tells them faithfully what he has heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel.

Isaiah speaks after seeing in vision the fall of Babylon. That news was hard for God's people, who were suffering under the empires. Many understand that the people would be crushed, that is, tested and broken, though the phrase can be interpreted in other ways. What is clear is that the prophet insists the message comes from God.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, even if it is hard to hear, let us receive it with humility. And if we share anything of him, let us do so faithfully, without adding or taking away anything.
exp.35:15:
The messenger of the king of Assyria speaks to the people of Jerusalem and tells them not to listen to Hezekiah. He offers them terms to "make peace" with him, that is, to surrender, and to "come out" to him, meaning to give themselves up. In return he promises that each of them will be able to keep eating from his own vine and his own fig tree and drinking water from his own cistern. The "cistern" here is the well or water source of each household.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a senior Assyrian officer, when Sennacherib threatens Jerusalem. He wants to sow fear and distrust toward King Hezekiah and toward God. His offer sounds calm, but later he speaks of being carried away to another land, that is, exile.

For today: be wary of easy offers that ask you to abandon your faith in exchange for comfort. Before accepting anything, ask yourself what it will really cost you and what God says about it.
exp.22:15:
Isaiah 23:16 tells Tyre, pictured as a forgotten prostitute, to take up a harp and walk through the city. She is to play a good tune and sing song after song, so that people will remember her once more. The word "harlot" here is an image for a city that lives by trade and looks for customers. The phrase "so you will be remembered" means to be brought back to people's minds again.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah within his message about Tyre, the great trading city. After seventy years of being forgotten, Tyre would return to its business. Scholars debate how exactly to understand those seventy years. The tone is mocking: Tyre tries to attract customers once more. Even so, the text that follows says that her profits would end up serving God and his people.

For today: let us take care that our success is not based only on earning and being remembered. Let us put what we have at the service of God and of others.
exp.33:4:
God's sword, which has drunk its fill in the heavens, will now come down to punish Edom. God calls this people "the people I have devoted to destruction," meaning a condemned people, set apart for destruction because of their wickedness. The phrase "then it will come down" points to a sentence that follows once God's judgment in the heavens is complete.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Chapter 34 announces judgment on the nations, and Edom appears as an example of those who oppose God and his people. Scholars debate whether all of this describes a historical event close at hand, a final judgment, or both. The language is poetic and very strong.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook it. We can trust that he will judge with justice, and so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. In the meantime, let us live with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.42:2:
God presents himself as the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, and your Savior. He says that he gives Egypt, Cush, and Seba for your ransom, that is, as the price of your deliverance. The word "ransom" speaks of a payment to set someone free.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to his people, Israel, who were suffering in exile and were afraid. The LORD reminds them that he created them, redeemed them, and calls them his own. Scholars understand the mention of those nations in several ways; what is certain is that it expresses how much God values his people.

For today: when fear overwhelms you, remember that you belong to God and that he values you deeply. Say to him in prayer: "Lord, you are my Savior; in you I trust."
exp.21:2:
Verse 3 says that the city's leaders ran away together, yet they were captured without using a bow. The people who had fled to a distant place were also caught together. The point is that the leaders were taken prisoner even though they never fought back with weapons, and that those who had gone far away were not safe either.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from God about "the valley of vision," which almost everyone understands to be Jerusalem. The city was festive and confident, but it did not see the danger. Scholars disagree about which historical moment is meant: some think of the invasion of Sennacherib, others of the fall before Babylon. The text does not make this clear. Isaiah weeps for his people.

For today: let us not place our security in leaders, money, or our own plans, because they can fail. Let us seek God first, listen to his warning in time, and live with humility, not with false calm.
exp.9:9:
The king of Assyria boasts that he has conquered kingdoms that worshiped idols. Those kingdoms had more images than Jerusalem and Samaria, which means they seemed stronger in religious matters. The phrase "my hand seized" is a way of saying "my power reached," so this part can be read directly as "as my hand seized the idolatrous kingdoms." "Images" refers to the statues of their gods.

The one speaking is the king of Assyria, in a proud tone, within a prophecy of Isaiah. God had used Assyria to discipline his people, but this king thought all the credit was his. Therefore, afterward, God says he will judge him for his arrogance. Some understand that the king compares Jerusalem with the peoples he defeated, believing it will fall the same way.

For today: when we succeed, let us remember that everything we achieve depends on God. Humility protects us from believing we are owners of what He has allowed us to have.
exp.42:25:
It says that God invites his people to an open trial. "Remind me, let us argue the matter together" means: remind me, present your case. "Let us argue the matter together" means: let us talk it through face to face. "State your case, so that you may be vindicated" means: state your reasons to clear yourself, and see whether you have any.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel. He has just told them that he blots out their rebellions for his own sake, not because of their merits. His people had grown weary of God with their sins and their empty sacrifices. Then he reminds them that from their ancestors on they have failed, so they have no defense. It is a challenge that shows salvation is a gift and not something earned.

For today: instead of defending ourselves before God, we can honestly confess our faults and trust in his forgiveness, which does not depend on what we do, but on his grace.
exp.17:3:
The explanation says that the Lord spoke to the prophet and told him that he would stay still and calm, as if resting, watching everything from his dwelling, that is, from his place in heaven. This stillness is compared to shimmering heat in the sunshine and to a cloud of dew in the heat of the harvest. "I will quietly look on" means "I will stay calm and still while I watch."

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, who tells what God said to him. The chapter mentions a distant nation, which many believe is Cush (Ethiopia), though this is not certain. God does not act in a hurry; he observes quietly and waits for the right moment, which the following verses compare to pruning before the harvest.

For today: when it seems that God is slow or silent, this does not mean he is absent. He sees everything and works in the right time. You can rest and wait patiently, trusting that He is in control.
exp.22:3:
Isaiah 23:4 tells Sidon, the great city by the sea, to be ashamed. The sea itself, called "the stronghold of the sea," speaks like a woman who has never given birth: she has not been in labor, has not raised young men, and has not brought up young women. It is a picture of total loss: the city is left empty, without people or a future.

This verse belongs to Isaiah's prophecy against Tyre, the Phoenician city known for sea trade. Sidon, its neighbor, appears here alongside it. Interpreters explain in various ways who is speaking and what the image means, but all agree on the message: the commercial power of these cities would fall, and even the sea would seem to mourn the ruin of its children.

For today: the riches, success and security we build can disappear. It is wise to place our trust in God, who does not change, and not in what seems strong today.
exp.37:4:
God tells Isaiah to go to King Hezekiah and give him this message: "I am the LORD, the God of your father David. I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. I will add fifteen years to your life." The phrase "add fifteen years" means that God gives him more time than he had.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and shortly before this Isaiah had told him he would die. The king turned to God, remembered that he had tried to live with sincerity, and wept bitterly. Then God speaks through Isaiah. God also promises to deliver Jerusalem from the king of Assyria, who was threatening it.

For today: God hears sincere prayers and sees our pain. We can speak to him honestly, even in tears, and trust that he listens. He will not always answer as he answered Hezekiah, but he is always attentive to us.
exp.29:25:
He says that when God heals his people, there will be an extraordinary light: the moon will be as bright as the sun, and the sun will be seven times brighter. The phrase "binds up" means to join back together what has been broken, and "brokenness" describes something cracked or fractured, like a broken bone. A "wound" is an open sore. God promises to repair the damage his people have suffered.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah, which was trusting in alliances with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. Before this verse, the prophet announces judgment and "the great slaughter," and also blessing: water, food, and rest. Many understand the light as poetic language for complete restoration; others see it as a promise for the final future. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: if you are wounded by your mistakes or by pain, do not hide the wound. Bring it to God with humility, because he knows how to heal what seems impossible to repair.
exp.40:7:
God speaks to his people and says, "You are my servant." Israel and Jacob are two names for the same people. God chose them, and he describes them as the descendants of Abraham, whom he calls "my friend."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the neighboring nations would encourage one another to make idols, out of fear and with a great deal of human effort. Here God contrasts that with how he treats Israel: they do not need idols fastened with nails, because God himself chose them and sustains them. The verses that follow say, "Fear not, for I am with you."

Today we can remember that our security does not depend on what we build or on our own strength, but on the fact that God calls us and walks with us. When you feel afraid, rest in his faithfulness and speak to him as you would to a friend.
exp.11:4:
This verse calls us to sing to the LORD, because He has done glorious things. It also asks that this be made known throughout the whole earth. Here the praise is a song offered to God, and the LORD is the God of Israel.

Isaiah 12 is a brief hymn of thanksgiving. The prophet speaks, or the people he leads speak, of "that day," a future time of salvation and comfort after the judgment announced in the earlier chapters. God had been angry with His people, but now He comforts and saves them. That is why the song bursts forth. The mention of "all the earth" shows that this joy was not only for Israel, but was to be shared with the nations.

For today: when you remember something good that God has done for you, do not keep it to yourself. Tell someone about it this week, or sing a song of praise out loud as a way of making His works known.
exp.2:16:
God will punish the women of Jerusalem for their pride. The phrase "will make their foreheads bare" means stripping away what covers the head or leaving it exposed, something that brought humiliation. The reference to making them bare speaks of being exposed to public shame. Some think it points to the nakedness of captives, and others to humiliation in a more general sense.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was living in luxury while the powerful oppressed the poor. The daughters of Zion represent the women of the upper class, who showed themselves proud and vain. God announces that they will lose what made them proud.

For today: examine what you boast about, whether money, appearance, or position. Ask God for a humble heart, and use it to care for those in need instead of showing off.
exp.48:17:
God tells Zion, who feels abandoned, to lift up her eyes and look around, because her children are coming back to her. They are like jewelry she will wear and like the adornment a bride puts on. "As surely as I live" is an oath from God himself.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to the people of Jerusalem, who were living in exile or in ruins. She had said that God had forgotten her (v. 14), and he answers that he has her engraved on the palms of his hands. This promise refers to the restoration of the people. Some also see a broader fulfillment in God's people of all times.

For today: when you feel alone or abandoned, remember that God does not forget you. Lift up your eyes, trust in his faithfulness, and wait for him to restore what seems lost.
exp.56:14:
This verse says that God is great, eternal, and holy, and yet he lives near those who are oppressed and humble. "High and lifted up" speaks of his greatness. The phrase about inhabiting eternity means that he is not limited by time. Someone who is oppressed is a person who is burdened or crushed by hardship. To restore and revive means to give life and courage again.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he had condemned idolatry and trust in human helpers that the wind would carry away. Now he promises that whoever waits on him will receive the inheritance. Then he explains that he will not be angry forever, because the human being would faint before his discipline.

For today: if you feel tired, guilty, or hurt, do not think that God is far away. Come before him with humility and sincerity, and trust that he can give you new strength and hope.
exp.12:12:
Therefore God says that he will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken from its place. This will happen at the wrath of the LORD of Hosts, on the day of his burning anger. "The LORD of Hosts" is a title that shows his power over all things. "The day of his burning anger" speaks of a moment of judgment.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The chapter announces judgment against Babylon, and the verses before it speak of punishing wickedness and humbling the proud. Many believe that the images of trembling heavens and a shaken earth are poetic language for a very great judgment. Some also see an announcement of the final judgment; interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God does not ignore injustice or pride. We can live with humility, trust that he is a just judge, and seek his mercy today.
exp.11:5:
This verse calls on the people of Jerusalem to cry out and sing. The reason is that the Holy One of Israel, God, is great and is among them. "Citizen of Zion" refers to the people who live in Jerusalem, pictured as one city.

The prophet Isaiah ends this song with a section about the promise of rescue for God's people. After speaking of judgment, he announces that on that day, a future time of restoration, the people will praise God for his salvation. Interpreters apply it to the return from exile, and many Christians also see it fulfilled in Christ. The speaker is the prophet, calling the people to sing.

Today you can rejoice because God is not far away. Before asking him for anything, take a few minutes to sing to him or thank him aloud for what he has already done in your life.
exp.62:15:
Here the people say that God is their true Father. "Does not know us" and "does not acknowledge us" mean that Abraham and Israel (Jacob), the ancestors, cannot help them and do not know their situation. "Redeemer" describes the one who rescues and frees someone; "from everlasting" means he has been so from the beginning and forever.

The passage is spoken by the people of Israel, or by a prophet on their behalf, in a prayer of lament. It seems they are in a time of suffering, with the sanctuary trampled by enemies. They remember how God cared for them before and ask where his compassion is now. Many believe it is a prayer from the exile, though the text does not give all the details.

For today: when you feel alone or without support, do not depend only on your family, your history, or your merits. You can come to God honestly, even with your doubts, because he is Father and Redeemer.
exp.7:0:
God told Isaiah to take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus, so that the words would be plain and easy for anyone to read. What he was to write was a name, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, which is usually understood to mean "swift to the spoil, quick to the prey."

The Lord spoke to his prophet in a time of threat to Judah, when neighboring kingdoms were pressing King Ahaz. According to the verses that follow, Isaiah calls witnesses, and then his son is born with that name. It was a public sign: the power that now frightens Judah would soon be taken away. Scholars debate some details, such as exactly who "the prophetess" is, but it is commonly understood to be Isaiah's wife.

For today: God keeps what he says, and so we can trust his word even when fear seems stronger. Write down God's promises and remember them when distress comes.
exp.39:18:
This verse describes how an idol is made. The craftsman shapes a figure by hand or casts it into form. Then the metalworker covers it with a layer of gold and fits it with silver chains, which were probably ornaments to decorate the figure. Some scholars think that last phrase is difficult to translate exactly.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to comfort a people who live among nations full of idols. He has just said that the nations are like nothing before the Lord. With a pointed question, he shows how absurd it is to compare God with something that human hands make.

Today we have other "idols": money, success, image. Everything we build and then expect to save us is far too small. Today, place your trust in the God who created everything, not in what you can make for yourself.
exp.48:3:
The explanation says that the servant of the Lord feels his effort was wasted. The words "I have labored in vain" and "I have spent My strength in futility and vanity" express that he worked hard and gave all his strength. Even so, he trusts: "yet My vindication is with the LORD" means that God is the one who judges his work and proves it right, and "My reward is with My God" indicates that his reward is in God's hands.

The one speaking is the Servant of the Lord, who is called Israel. Some see him as the people of Israel, others as a faithful servant within the people, and many Christians see Jesus here. He expresses his weariness because it seems there is no fruit, but God answers him that his mission is even greater: to be a light to the nations.

For today: when you serve while weary and do not see results, do not measure your work only by what you can see. Entrust it to God, who sees everything and rewards with justice.
exp.9:7:
He says in this verse that the king of Assyria is boasting: "Are all my commanders not kings?" That is, his leaders and officers have as much authority as a king, and that is why his power seems so vast to him.

Here God speaks through Isaiah and quotes the proud words of the Assyrian king. God uses him as an instrument to discipline his people, but the king does not know this and thinks everything is due to his own strength. That is why God exposes his arrogance, and later in the chapter announces that he will judge him.

For today: when we have success, power or good results, let us not claim all the credit for ourselves. Let us give thanks to God, for he gives and sustains what we have. Humility keeps us grounded.
exp.4:19:
Woe to those who call evil good and good evil. In this verse God laments and warns, pronouncing judgment on people who reverse the values: they call evil good, and good evil. Light and darkness, and bitter and sweet, are images of what is right and wrong, of what heals and what harms.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks in God's name within the song of the vineyard (chapter 5). He denounces a people who mock God's judgment, pride themselves on their wisdom, and live in excess and injustice. The problem is not only doing wrong, but justifying it and changing its name.

Today we can honestly ask ourselves: am I excusing something the Bible calls sin, or criticizing something that is good? Measuring everything by God's Word, and not by fashion or by my own desires, protects my conscience.
exp.20:1:
Isaiah says he has received a very harsh vision. A traitor keeps betraying, and a destroyer keeps destroying. Then Elam and Media are told to go up and lay siege, that is, to surround a city in order to attack it. The word "treacherous" here describes someone who acts with deceit and betrayal. At the end, God says that he will put an end to all the groaning, that is, the suffering caused by that oppression.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, and in the last sentence it seems that God is speaking. The message is a heavy burden, a weighty warning, concerning the wilderness of the sea, a phrase that many connect with Babylon. The text does not name it here, so there are different opinions. Many understand that the groaning that ends is that of the peoples oppressed by Babylon. Isaiah trembles at what is coming.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it forever. If you find yourself suffering or witnessing abuse, you can pray and trust that He governs history, while you choose to act with truth and justice.
exp.23:22:
It says that the sun and the moon, which seem so bright and powerful, will be put to shame before the glory of God. "Lord of hosts" means the LORD who commands all power. The word "reign" means that he will rule, and "elders" refers to the leaders of his people.

Isaiah speaks in a passage where he announces God's judgment on the earth and on the powers that rise up against him. The verse before speaks of "that day," a time in which God acts. Some understand this as the end of time, while others also see a broader meaning in history. What is clear is that it ends with hope: God reigns.

Today we can remember that nothing we admire or fear stands above God. When something seems too great to us, let us offer it to him in prayer and trust in his rule.
exp.1:21:
Isaiah says: stop trusting in human beings. The phrase "put no more trust in man" means "keep away from him," that is, do not place your confidence in him. "Breath" is the air we breathe, the breath that is "in his nostrils": human life depends on a fragile puff of air. The question "of what account is he?" means: what value does he have that you should trust him instead of God?

Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. He has just described the day when God will rise up in majesty, the idols will fall, and the people will flee to hide. Earlier in the chapter he showed a nation full of pride, riches, and false securities. The prophet calls them not to lean on what cannot save them.

For today: when you feel pressure, check where you truly rest. Value and respect people, but do not make them your ultimate security. Place your trust first in God, who does not vanish like a breath.
exp.60:0:
The explanation says that the Spirit of the Lord God is upon the one who speaks, because the Lord has anointed him, that is, set him apart and equipped him for a mission. He was sent to bring good news to the poor, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and freedom to the prisoners. The word "sent" in this verse is the one that "He has sent Me" expresses.

The one speaking is not named here. Many believe he is the prophet Isaiah, and others see the Servant of God who would bring comfort to a people in distress. Jesus read this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in Him (Luke 4:16-21). For that reason Christians see it fulfilled in Christ.

For today: God draws near to those who suffer. We can accompany someone who is hurt through a visit, a prayer, or a word of encouragement, trusting that God also heals our own heart.
exp.47:8:
God says that, for the sake of his own name, he will delay his wrath and hold back his anger. He does this for the sake of his praise, so that you will not be cut off. The explanation of the word "delay" is what the reader needs here: it means to hold off or put off, and God's patience is that he gives time and waits, as one who is patient, and that he does not cut them down, as one would cut down a tree.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel (Judah), a people whom he had known as stubborn and rebellious from the beginning. Even so, he does not abandon them because of what the people deserve, but because of his own faithfulness and glory. The verses that follow show that he refines them in the furnace of affliction.

For today: if God has been patient with you despite your failures, do not take that lightly. His patience is mercy that invites repentance. Respond with gratitude and return to him today.
exp.18:15:
In that day, the Egyptians will be left without strength and full of fear, "like women." This was a common expression of the time for speaking of people who were frightened and helpless. They will tremble before the "uplifted hand" of God, that is, his power raised and ready to act against them.

Isaiah, as a prophet, speaks to Judah in the name of God. Egypt was a power in which many trusted instead of trusting in the Lord. Earlier, the text says that God confused their plans. Scholars discuss which historical moment the phrase "in that day" refers to, and it may have a broader scope.

For today: no human strength, money, power, or plans gives us ultimate security. Today you can hand your fears over to God and trust in Him rather than in your own resources.
exp.46:11:
Here, the prophet says Babylon should keep relying on her spells and her many sorceries, the practices she has worn herself out with since her youth. The words "Perhaps you will succeed; perhaps you will inspire terror!" are spoken with irony. God is mocking her, because these practices will do her no good at all.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon believed herself secure, wise, and unbeatable. God judges her for her pride and for trusting in magic and astrology. The verses that follow show that her counselors will be unable to save her: they will fall like straw into the fire.

For today: examine where you place your security. It may be horoscopes, money, your own intelligence, or your pride. None of that will sustain you in a crisis. Trust instead in God, who truly knows the future and cares for those who seek him with humility.
exp.59:21:
The explanation says that the least of the people will grow into a thousand, and the smallest will become a mighty nation. God promises that he will bring this about quickly, at the time he has chosen. The phrase "in its time" is the verse's own wording, so it stays as it is in the reader's version, and no separate word needs explaining.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem and its people. Earlier he spoke to them of mourning and ruin, and now he promises light, justice, and restoration. Interpreters read it in different ways: some apply it to Israel's return from exile, others to the Church, and others to a future fulfillment. In every case, the center is God's faithfulness.

For today: if you feel small or have little, do not despise your beginning. Remain faithful, and trust that God works on his own schedule, which is not always ours, and that he keeps what he promises.
exp.42:1:
He says that God promises to be with his people in the midst of trials. The waters, the rivers, and the fire stand for dangers and hard moments. The promise does not say there will be no trials, but that God will be present and you will not be destroyed. The verse says the waters will not overwhelm you, meaning they will not sweep over you and carry you away.

The LORD speaks to Israel, the people he created and redeemed. Before this, the people had suffered because of their disobedience, and for that reason he had sent them into exile. God reminds them that they belong to him, that he called them by name and loves them. For this reason he says to them: "Do not be afraid." His companionship is based on that covenant relationship.

For today: when you face an illness, a loss, or a crisis, remember that you are not alone. Pray and rest in the presence of God, even if you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.62:11:
This verse recalls how God led Israel through Moses. With the phrases "the right hand of Moses" and "his glorious arm," the text speaks of God's power working through his servant. The phrase "who divided the waters before them" refers to the Red Sea, which opened so the people could pass through. In this way God gained for himself everlasting renown, that is, a name that is not forgotten.

The speaker is the prophet, in a prayer of remembrance. The people are in difficulty and look back to the past. They remember that Israel was rebellious and that God had nevertheless rescued them. The questions in the passage express longing and ask that God act again as he did before.

For today: when you feel lost or weak, remember the times God has sustained you. That memory can become a prayer and renew your confidence that he remains faithful.
exp.44:23:
This verse says that the day is coming when people will recognize that true righteousness and strength are found in the Lord alone. In the Berean Standard wording, people will say this of God himself. Those who rage against him will come to him, and they will be put to shame, while those who turn to him will find refuge.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel and all the nations. He has just invited all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved, and he has declared that every knee will bow before him. The verses that follow say that Israel will be justified in the Lord and will glory in him.

For today: instead of relying on your own strength or your own righteousness, come to God with humility. Tell him honestly that in him are your strength and your hope.
exp.47:19:
The explanation says that God's people must leave Babylon and get away from the Chaldeans. They must announce this with a shout of joy and proclaim it so that it goes out to the ends of the earth. The message is: "The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!" "Redeemed" means that God rescued and freed him. "The ends of the earth" means the most distant places.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces in advance that Israel would be freed from exile in Babylon. Earlier, God laments that his people did not obey, for they would have had peace that way. Even so, he promises to rescue them. Some also see here an image of leaving sin, although the text speaks first of a real liberation.

For today: if God has rescued you, do not stay silent or tied to what was enslaving you. Take a concrete step to leave it behind, and share with joy with someone what God has done for you.
exp.53:1:
It says that God tells Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, to make the site of her tent bigger. She must stretch out the curtains of her dwellings, not hold back, lengthen her ropes, and drive her stakes in deep. The words "tent" and "curtains" refer to field tents. "Do not hold back" means do not be stingy with the space. The "stakes" are the pegs that hold the tent up.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, seen as a barren and abandoned woman, probably during a time of exile or great desolation. God promises her a large family, and so she must prepare for a growth she does not yet see.

For today: if God has given you a promise or a calling, prepare with faith before you see the results. You can pray, organize your time, learn, or make room in your life and in your church, trusting that God keeps what he says.
exp.9:26:
He says that a day is coming when God will lift the burden and the yoke that Assyria had placed on the people, just as a load is lifted from the shoulders or the neck of an animal. The yoke will be broken because the neck will be too large for it to fit anymore. "Neck" is the part of the body the yoke rests on.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing the word of God to Judah, which was threatened by Assyria. God allowed that oppression to correct his people, but he promises that the oppressor will come to an end, as in the victory over Midian and the deliverance from Egypt.

For today: if you carry a weight that seems endless, remember that God can break any yoke in his time. In the meantime, trust in him, pray, and keep doing what is right, knowing that he has not forgotten you.
exp.27:18:
It says that when God's punishment begins to pass through, it will not be a matter of a single moment: it will come again and again, every morning, by day and by night, and it will carry off those who trusted in themselves. The word for "carry off" means to take away by force. The understanding of this message will bring sheer terror; only when the fear arrives will people grasp the warning they heard earlier and ignored.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The leaders of Judah mocked his warnings and believed they were safe because of their political alliances, which the text describes as a covenant with death. God warns them that this false security will not withstand judgment.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to arrive before we take God's voice seriously. If He speaks to us today through His Word, let us respond with humility and trust in Him, not in false refuges.
exp.46:0:
It says that Babylon, pictured as a noble and pampered young woman, must come down from her high place and sit in the dust. "Virgin daughter" is a poetic way of speaking about the city and its people. "Without a throne" means she no longer rules. "Not called tender or delicate" describes a life of luxury and comfort, which will come to an end.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Babylon was a powerful and proud empire. God announces its fall and the humiliation of those who believed they could not be touched. Isaiah wrote this long before Babylon reached its greatest power, so many read it as a prophecy.

For today: power, money, or success can make us feel secure and proud. This text invites us to live with humility, remembering that everything comes from God and that nothing we have is eternal.
exp.65:23:
It says that the redeemed will go out and see the dead bodies of those who rebelled against God. Their worm will never die and their fire will never be quenched, meaning their ruin does not come to an end. The word "horror" describes something that causes fear and disgust, and "all mankind" refers to all of humanity.

The words are spoken by the LORD through the prophet Isaiah, as the book closes. Before this, he promises new heavens, a new earth, and worship from all the nations. This ending contrasts the faithful with the rebels. Interpreters disagree: some see it as a picture of the final judgment, others as a symbolic scene. Jesus used similar words in Mark 9:48 to warn about judgment.

For today: let us take God's warning seriously, but also his invitation. If there is rebellion in your heart, come to him in humility and trust in his forgiveness, while there is still time.
exp.34:5:
It says that when God comes to save, those who cannot walk today will leap for joy like a deer, and those who cannot speak will shout for joy. It also promises that waters will gush forth in the wilderness and streams will flow in the desert. Here the word "streams" means flowing water, and a wilderness is an empty, dry place where few people live.

Isaiah writes to the people of Judah, who are tired and afraid. Earlier, the prophet tells them to be strong, because God is coming to save them. The verses that follow speak of a "Way of Holiness." Many see it as a promise of restoration for the people; Christians often see in it also an announcement of the work of Christ and of the final restoration. There are several ways of understanding it.

For today: when you feel dry or without strength, do not just stare at the desert. Speak to God honestly, remember his promises, and encourage another person who is discouraged.
exp.36:33:
God says that the king of Assyria will go back by the same road he came, and that he will not manage to enter Jerusalem. The verse states this plainly, so no further explanation of a word is needed. The words "declares the LORD" stress that this promise comes directly from God.

God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to King Hezekiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah and was threatening Jerusalem with his powerful army. The people were afraid, but Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. God responds by assuring that he will protect the city for the sake of his own name and because of the promise made to David.

For today: when you face a problem that seems bigger than you, do as Hezekiah did and bring it to God in prayer. He does not always act as we expect, but he is faithful to his promises and can change the course of what seems impossible.
exp.40:18:
God promises to fill the wilderness with trees: cedars, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees, which are trees valued for good timber, fruit, or fragrance, along with cypresses, elms, and boxwood. The trees named here are the ones in the verse, and the phrase "together" means that they grow side by side. Some of these trees are identified in several ways, so the exact names may vary from one translation to another.

The Lord speaks to his people Israel, who are tired and distressed, probably during the time of exile. He promises that he will hear them and will not abandon them. The flourishing desert is an image of God's care, and the text that follows says that everyone will see that his hand has done it.

For today: when you find yourself in a dry season or a situation with no way out, pray with confidence. God can bring life and hope where you see only emptiness, and his timing and his way of doing it may surprise you.
exp.0:5:
It says the people are wounded from the sole of the foot to the top of the head, with no healthy part left. They have open wounds, welts, and festering sores. Nobody has cleaned them, bandaged them, or soothed them with oil. The phrase "no soundness" means there is no part without harm, and "festering sores" are sores that have become infected and are spreading decay.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. He describes Judah as a body mistreated because of its rebellion and its abandonment of God. Many understand this as an image of their spiritual ruin and of the consequences they were already suffering, such as the devastation of the land described next. Scholars debate which exact moment in history it refers to.

For today: let us not hide our spiritual wounds or assume they will heal on their own. Let us acknowledge our sin honestly, return to God, and let Him heal what we cannot heal ourselves.
exp.57:2:
The people complain to God: they say they fasted and humbled themselves, but God did not notice. God answers that, on the very day of their fast, they do as they please and oppress all their workers.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He tells Isaiah to denounce the sin of his people, who seem to seek God every day but live in injustice. Their religion was a matter of appearances: they fasted, but did not change the way they treated others. The verses that follow show quarreling and mistreatment in the midst of the fast.

For today: it is not enough to practice religious acts if the heart remains selfish. Before you pray, fast, or serve, ask yourself whether you are treating with justice and kindness those who depend on you or live with you.
exp.46:5:
God says he was angry with his people, Israel, and let them be treated as if they had no value. ("I profaned My heritage" means he allowed his own people to be humiliated.) He placed them under the control of Babylon. But Babylon showed them no mercy: even the elderly were burdened with a most heavy yoke.

God himself speaks, the Redeemer of Israel, addressing Babylon, called the daughter of the Chaldeans. God used her to discipline his people, but she went too far in cruelty and believed herself unconquerable. For this reason God now announces her fall.

For today: God can correct his own, but he does not approve of abuse by those who hold power. If you have authority over others today, treat them with mercy, especially the weakest, and remember that one day you will give an account to God.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that God, who created and shaped his people, speaks to them with tenderness. "Creator" and "Former" mean that God made them and formed them. To "redeem" is to rescue by paying a price. The phrase "I have called you by your name" shows that God knows them personally, and "you are Mine" expresses that they belong to him.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel (Jacob), a people suffering the consequences of their disobedience and facing exile. The opening words "But now" mark a turn: after judgment comes comfort. The verses that follow promise that God will be with them in the waters and in the fire.

For today: when fear reaches you, remember that you are not a stranger to God. Christians see in Christ the fullest redemption. Pray, "Lord, I am yours," and take the next step with confidence.
exp.40:1:
Isaiah 41:2 asks a question: who has stirred up someone from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness? It says that God hands nations over to him and subdues kings before him, turning them to dust with his sword and to windblown chaff with his bow. "Subdues" means to bring under control.

God himself is speaking, and in verse 4 he identifies himself as the LORD. He calls the nations to a trial, as in a courtroom, to show that he directs history. Many believe the one raised up is Cyrus, king of Persia, although some connect him with Abraham. It is a debate among interpreters. God reminds his people that they should not fear empires.

For today: when the news or powerful people frighten you, remember that God still governs. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.30:5:
The explanation says that the people should return to God, the one they had rebelled against with such blatant defiance. The word "return" means to come back. "Blatantly rebelled" means that their rebellion was open, obvious, and deliberate.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah sought protection in Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. A few verses earlier, God promises to defend Jerusalem like a lion guarding its prey and like birds covering their nest. So this call comes with tenderness: God cares for those who had turned away, and He invites them to come back. Then He announces that they will abandon their idols and that Assyria will fall.

For today: if at any time we trust our own plans, money, or human help more than God, we can stop and return to Him sincerely. He still welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.32:6:
Isaiah 33:7 says that the brave men of the people cry aloud in the streets, and that the envoys of peace weep bitterly. The "envoys of peace" were the people sent out to carry proposals meant to avoid war. Their weeping shows that their efforts had failed.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah at a time when Assyria was threatening Jerusalem. Many scholars think this refers to the envoys of King Hezekiah, who paid tribute to Assyria but were betrayed when Assyria broke the agreement (see the verses that follow). Others read it more generally. What is clear is that the passage contrasts the failure of human diplomacy with the promise that God will be exalted and will give security to Zion.

When human plans fail and hope runs out, we can weep honestly before God. But we can also trust that He is our true refuge and treasure.
exp.14:6:
In this verse, the Moabites are shown fleeing with everything they have been able to gain and keep. They carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows, a stream that many believe lay on the border of Moab. Some think it may be the Zered brook, but this is not known for certain.

God speaks through Isaiah in a prophecy against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. He announces a destruction that sends the people fleeing, weeping. The prophet himself grieves for them (v. 5), which shows that God does not take pleasure in human suffering.

Today we can remember that possessions cannot save us in times of crisis. It is wise to trust God more than what we have piled up, and to have compassion for those who suffer.
exp.27:2:
The verse says that the majestic crown of Ephraim's drunkards will be trampled underfoot. "Trampled" means walked on, crushed beneath the feet. The crown represents the pride and glory of Ephraim's leaders, who gave themselves over to wine and vanity. What they considered so splendid will end up on the ground.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf, probably before the fall of the northern kingdom (Israel, called Ephraim here), which fell to Assyria. Its leaders trusted in their wealth and their strength, and lived in excess. God announces that he will send a powerful force, like a storm and a flood, that will bring them down. But the passage ends with hope: God will be a crown for those who remain faithful to him.

Today we can ask ourselves what we take pride in, or where we place our security. Anything that does not rest on God is fragile. He wants to be our true crown.
exp.33:11:
It says that in that land there will be no one left to proclaim a king, and the nobles will come to nothing. Their great ones will be reduced to nothing, with no kingdom left for them to rule. "Palaces" are the royal houses, and "without a kingdom" means without power or territory.

Isaiah announces here God's judgment on the nations, and in this chapter Edom is mentioned in a special way. He speaks as a prophet, in the name of the Lord. His message is that no human power can stand when God judges. The images of smoke, wild animals and ruins paint a total desolation. Some see poetic and symbolic language; others take it more literally.

For today: do not place your security in titles, money or position, since all of that can disappear. Trust in God, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.21:0:
This verse opens a message of judgment, or "burden," which means a heavy warning from God. It is aimed at the "Valley of Vision," and then asks what is wrong with the people, that they have all gone up to the rooftops.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Almost everyone understands that the "Valley of Vision" is Jerusalem, although the text does not name it here. The verses that follow show a city in uproar and celebration, while its leaders flee. Some think of an invasion; the exact details are debated.

For today: when a crisis comes, let us not settle for noise, celebration, or distractions. Let us stop and ask what God is trying to tell us, and return to trusting Him with humility.
exp.44:5:
This verse says that God wants all people, from where the sun rises to where it sets, that is, from east to west, to recognize that there is no other God. "The LORD" is the name of God, and "there is none but Me" means that no one else shares his place.

God speaks to Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he called by name to help free Israel from exile, although Cyrus did not know the true God. Out of love for his chosen people, God uses a foreign king. In this way he shows that he rules over all nations and that his plans are carried out.

For today: when you feel that everything is out of control, remember that God still reigns. Rest in him and pray with confidence, knowing that he can work even through people who do not know him.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the Lord will wash away the moral filth of the women of Zion and remove the bloodstains left by violence in Jerusalem. "Filth" means impurity; to wash and to cleanse mean to make clean. The "spirit of judgment" and the "spirit of fire" describe a cleansing that corrects and burns away what is bad, the way metal is refined by fire.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. In chapter 3 he denounced the pride and injustice of Jerusalem. Here he promises that, after the punishment, a clean people will remain, called "holy." Some see in this a promise for the future of Israel, and others see a broader picture of God's work.

For today: God not only forgives, he also transforms. We can ask him to cleanse us without fear, even when correcting something in our lives hurts, because his goal is to heal and care for us.
exp.59:15:
It says that Zion will be nourished with the riches of the nations and their kings, like a baby who drinks at the breast. Drinking milk and nursing are images of care and abundant provision. The result is that she will know that the LORD is her Savior and her Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob, that is, the powerful God of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem, a people who had suffered contempt and destruction. He promises them restoration, honor, and peace. Scholars understand this in different ways: as the return from exile, as something fulfilled in Christ and the church, or as a hope still to come.

For today: when you feel abandoned or lacking, remember that your provision comes from God, not only from your own strength. Ask Him to care for you, and trust that He is your Savior and your strength.
exp.50:21:
God tells his people that he has already taken the cup of punishment out of their hand. The cup of staggering is a cup that makes a person reel, and the cup of his fury is the one filled with his anger. God is their defender, the one who takes up their cause, like a lawyer. He promises: "you will never drink from it again."
