The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Jerusalem had suffered greatly for its sin and was like someone staggering with sorrow, without strength. Now God presents himself as their defender and passes that cup to the oppressors who mistreated them. Scholars debate how this relates to the exile and to the future, but the comfort is clear.

If you feel you carry guilt or suffering with no way out, remember that God can be your defender. Trust in his forgiveness, rest in his care, and rise again with hope.
exp.5:10:
Isaiah, after receiving his call, asks: "Lord, how long?" God answers that the judgment will last until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, the houses are left unoccupied, and the land is desolate and ravaged.

The prophet Isaiah speaks with God, in the vision where he is sent. God entrusts him with a message for a people who do not want to listen, and Isaiah asks how long that hardness will last. The verses that follow say that, even so, a remnant will remain, like the stump of a felled tree, called the holy seed. Many see judgment here, but also hope.

For today: when you see someone rejecting the truth, or when you face difficult consequences, remember that God does not abandon completely. Trust that He can bring forth new life even where it seems that only a stump is left.
exp.30:1:
He also is wise, and not only the counselors of Judah or the Egyptians. If He decides to bring disaster, He will do it, and He does not take back His words. Disaster here means calamity or judgment, not wrongdoing on God's part. The "wicked" and "evildoers" are those who do wrong, and their "allies" are the help they offer. The phrase "rise up" here means that God will rise up.

Isaiah speaks to Judah in a time of military threat. The people sought an alliance with Egypt, trusting in its horses and chariots instead of trusting in God. The prophet warns them that this human help will not save them, and that God would act against those who leaned on it.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, connections, plans. Planning is not wrong, but above all we must seek God, ask Him for direction, and trust Him more than any human resource.
exp.4:5:
It says God will leave his vineyard turned into abandoned ground. No one will prune it (cut back the branches so they bear more fruit) or cultivate it (work and loosen the soil). Instead, thorns and briers will grow up in it. God will also command the clouds that no rain fall on it.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a song about his vineyard. God cared for that vineyard with great care, but he expected good grapes and received wild, sour grapes. The following verses explain that the vineyard is Israel and Judah. God expected justice, and found violence and abuse. For that reason he announces judgment.

For today: God cares for us and expects fruits of justice and compassion. Today you can ask yourself honestly: what fruit is my life bearing, and how do I treat others?
exp.48:5:
God speaks to his servant and tells him that merely restoring the tribes of Israel is not enough. His mission will be greater: to be a light for the nations, that is, for peoples beyond Israel. The phrase "my salvation" points to God's rescue and deliverance, and God says this salvation will reach to the ends of the earth, meaning the most distant places in the world.

The one speaking is the servant of the LORD, who felt tired and that his work bore no fruit. God responds by widening his calling. Christians see Jesus in this passage, and the New Testament quotes this text with reference to him (Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47). Others also understand it as a reference to Israel as a people. The passage allows both readings.

For today: when you feel that your effort was in vain, remember that God sees further than you do. Remain faithful and share his light with those near you, trusting that he can do far more with your life.
exp.55:1:
He says that the person who puts into practice what God has just asked is happy and blessed: keeping justice and doing what is right. "Blessed" here means happy. "Holds it fast" means clinging to something with devotion. "Profaning it" means treating it as something ordinary. "Keeping his hand from doing any evil" means not using his hands to do wrong.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. His salvation is near, and so he calls his people to live righteously. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant with God. In the verses that follow, God opens his arms to foreigners and eunuchs, who felt excluded, and promises them a place in his house.

For today: set aside time to rest and to remember that God is your provision. Ask him to care for your hands as well, so that you treat others with justice and kindness in your work and in your home.
exp.58:3:
No one calls for justice, and no one pleads his case honestly. The people rely on empty pleas, which have no real substance or truth, and they tell lies. Their plans are harmful, and what they plan ends up producing wickedness. The image is one of conceiving and giving birth: they plan evil and bring it into the world.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He explains that their sin, and not any weakness on God's part, is what separates them from Him. He describes a corrupt society marked by violence, lies, and injustice in the courts. Then he compares their works to spider webs: they look like something substantial, but they neither serve nor protect anyone.

For today: before you speak or decide, ask yourself whether what you say is true and whether it is just. Be encouraged to speak honestly for the one who is being treated unjustly, even when no one else will.
exp.25:6:
The life of the one who does what is right goes along a level road, without bends. God, who is perfectly upright, clears a straight path for such a person, meaning he examines the road with justice and keeps it smooth, like someone preparing a path for a traveler. The word "righteous" refers to a person who lives according to the will of God.

These words belong to a song of trust in Judah, in the book of Isaiah. Before this, the text speaks of God bringing down the proud city, and the poor trampling it. Afterward, the people say they wait for God and seek him from the early morning. Interpreters disagree about which city is meant, but the message is clear: God corrects the arrogant and cares for the humble.

For today: when your path feels hard, keep doing what is right and trust that God sees your life with justice. Ask him to guide you each morning.
exp.3:2:
It says that, after God's judgment, the few who remain in Jerusalem will be called "holy." The phrase about those "recorded among the living" refers to people God has kept alive, as if their names were written in a list of the living. "Holy" means set apart for God.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks this after describing a harsh judgment on Jerusalem, with war and great loss of life (chapter 3). Then he promises a future of restoration. The "branch of the LORD" has been understood in several ways: as God's blessing on the land, or as a sign pointing to the Messiah. Interpreters do not fully agree. What is clear is that God purifies his people and preserves a faithful remnant.

For today: God does not stop at punishment, but cleanses his people so that they may live close to him. If you are going through correction today, trust that his aim is to restore you. Ask him to cleanse you and set you apart for himself.
exp.18:23:
In that day, Israel will join a three-party alliance with Egypt and Assyria, and it will be a blessing upon the earth. The verse describes a union among three nations living together in peace, and Israel is pictured as a source of blessing for the whole world. The word describing this alliance points to a partnership among equals, not to a ranking of one nation above the others.

Isaiah, God's prophet, speaks in a message about Egypt. First he announces judgment, but then he promises healing and conversion. Egypt and Assyria were powerful enemies of Israel, and yet God calls them "my people" and "the work of my hands." Scholars disagree about whether the fulfillment is still future, spiritual, or both.

For today: God loves peoples who seem like enemies to us and wants to reconcile them. Ask him to help you be someone who builds bridges and blesses those who think or live differently from you.
exp.29:0:
He says God grieves over the situation of his rebellious children. "Woe" is an expression of sorrow and warning. They turn away from God to seek advice from others, and not from him. "Covering with an alliance" means seeking protection and shelter in plans that are not God's. In this way they keep adding sin to sin, that is, one wrong after another.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. At that time they were threatened by neighboring powers, and instead of trusting in God, they made plans to ally themselves with Egypt. The verses that follow make this clear: they went down to Egypt without consulting God. He warns them that this help would leave them ashamed.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we turn first when we are afraid or facing difficult decisions. Praying and seeking God's guidance in his Word before we act protects us from trusting only in human resources.
exp.62:18:
The explanation says the people feel as though God had never been their Lord and had never called them his own. Your verse reads "We have become like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name," so the comment on that wording uses your text: "Ruling over" means governing or having authority over someone. "Called by Your name" means belonging to God. "We have become" describes how the people now see themselves.

Here the prophet speaks on behalf of the people of Israel, in a prayer of lament. Enemies have trampled the sanctuary, and the people feel that God is far away. Some scholars think it refers to the time of the exile or to the period after Jerusalem fell, but there is not full agreement. Their complaint is that they seem just like the nations that do not know God.

For today: when you feel far from God or abandoned, do not hide that pain. Bring it to him honestly, as the prophet did, and rely on what God has promised concerning you, not only on what you feel.
exp.12:3:
Isaiah 13:4 describes a loud tumult in the mountains, like the sound of a huge crowd. It is the sound of kingdoms and nations gathering together. Here "tumult" means a loud roar, not a quiet whisper. The LORD of Hosts is the Lord in command of all the forces, and it is he who mobilizes the army for war.

Isaiah prophesies against Babylon. God himself speaks in the verses nearby and calls his "consecrated ones," that is, those he has set apart for this task. Scholars understand this to refer to armies that God would use to judge Babylon's pride and violence. Some also see here an image of the final judgment of the whole earth.

For today: even when the world seems like a chaos of nations and conflicts, God remains sovereign. You can rest in the fact that he governs history and is just, and live with humility and confidence.
exp.44:0:
This is what the LORD says to Cyrus, his anointed, the one whose right hand he has grasped. The LORD says he will help Cyrus subdue nations, disarm kings, and open the doors before him, so that the gates will not be shut. Anointing marks someone chosen for a mission, and grasping the right hand signals strength and support.

The LORD is the one speaking, through the prophet Isaiah. Cyrus was king of Persia, and the Bible presents him as the LORD's instrument for letting the people of Israel, who had been exiled in Babylon, return to their land. Cyrus did not know the LORD, yet the LORD uses him all the same. When exactly this prophecy was written is something scholars debate.

For today: God governs history, even through people who do not know him. You can trust that doors which seem closed are no obstacle for him, and that he accomplishes his purposes.
exp.18:12:
The leaders of Egypt, those of Zoan and those of Memphis, are described here as having lost their way. They thought they were wise, but they were mistaken and led the whole country down the wrong path. The "cornerstones of her tribes" refers to the chiefs or pillars of the tribes and clans, the ones who held the nation up.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing a message from the LORD against Egypt. The Egyptians boasted of their wisdom and their royal lineage, and Judah sometimes sought their help. God shows that their counselors cannot understand or stop what He has determined.

For today: let us not place our final trust in leaders, titles, or the opinion of people who call themselves "experts." Let us seek God's wisdom first in His Word and in prayer, and weigh every piece of advice in its light.
exp.23:14:
Isaiah calls the people to praise the Lord and honor him. He tells them to do this "in the east" and "in the islands of the sea," meaning in distant places. To glorify the Lord means to honor him and to recognize his greatness.

Isaiah speaks in the middle of a judgment that reaches the whole earth. There will be destruction, and only a small remnant will be left, like the few olives that remain after the tree is shaken. That remnant, scattered in faraway lands, sings to God. Scholars do not always agree on exactly who that remnant is, but the text shows that God is praised even in times of judgment.

For today: praise God also in difficult moments, wherever you are. Your situation does not change the fact that he is worthy of honor.
exp.14:4:
Here the pain of Moab after its destruction is described. Those who escape flee as far as Zoar and as far as Eglath-shelishiyah, and they climb the slope of Luhith weeping, lamenting their destruction on the road to Horonaim. The image of a young cow in the verse is one of strong, loud crying; some explain it in another way.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces a judgment of God upon Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. What is striking is that the prophet says "My heart cries out over Moab": he speaks not with mockery but with sorrow. The verses before show whole cities weeping in the streets and on the rooftops.

For today: even when someone suffers the consequences of their own actions, let us not celebrate their fall. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, one that prays and helps with mercy.
exp.62:7:
He says that when God chose Israel, he declared, "They are surely My people," that is, "truly they are My people." He calls them "sons who will not be disloyal," meaning sons who would not be unfaithful to him or betray him. And he concludes: "So He became their Savior."

The writer is the prophet Isaiah, who gratefully recalls God's mercies toward Israel. He describes what God hoped for from his people when he rescued them. The following verses show the painful contrast: even so, they rebelled. Some see here God's hope, and others see an expression of his confidence in choosing them. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God saved us, hoping for a sincere relationship with us. Today we can answer him with honesty, without pretending, and trust that his mercy lifts us up when we fail.
exp.47:20:
It says that when God led his people through dry places, they lacked no water. He made water flow from a rock: he split the great rock and water gushed out. "They did not thirst" means they did not go thirsty; "the rock" is a large stone; "led them" refers to his guiding them through the deserts.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just invited the people to leave Babylon with joy and to announce that God has redeemed them. To give them confidence, he reminds them how he cared for their ancestors in the desert after they left Egypt (Exodus 17; Numbers 20). If he cared for them then, he can care for them now. The following verse warns that there is no peace for the wicked.

For today: if God calls you to leave something behind and move forward with him, you can trust that he will also provide what you need along the way. Remember how he has sustained you before, and take the next step in faith.
exp.27:8:
Whom do they think they are teaching? To whom are they explaining their message? To infants just weaned, just taken from their mother's breast? Here the words "knowledge" and "message" point to understanding and teaching, and the phrase "just weaned" refers to children who have already stopped nursing.

Isaiah speaks to the priests and prophets of Judah, who were drunk and confused. Many understand these words as mockery of them: they felt insulted because Isaiah was correcting them as if they were children. Others think it is the prophet's own irony. The text does not make this entirely clear. In any case, it revealed a proud heart that did not want to listen to God.

Today: when the Word of God corrects us, let us not become defensive. Let us learn with humility, like someone who always has something more to learn.
exp.36:24:
Here the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, boasts about what he has achieved. He says that he dug wells in foreign lands and drank their waters, and that with the soles of his feet he dried up all the streams of Egypt. He presents his conquests as proof that nothing can stand in his way, and he feels unstoppable.

God speaks through Isaiah, and God himself quotes the proud words of the king. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel, and King Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. God answers by saying that this king has really only been an instrument in his hands, and that his arrogance is an offense against the Holy One of Israel.

For today: when you accomplish something, do not take all the glory for yourself. What you have and what you are able to do comes from God, so use your strength with humility and gratitude, and remember that whoever boasts of his power falls, but God upholds the one who trusts in him.
exp.39:9:
This verse announces that God himself is coming. The phrase "comes with might" means that he arrives in power. The words "his arm establishes his rule" mean that his arm secures and maintains his authority. His reward is with him, and his recompense accompanies him; both come along with him.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who faced punishment and discouragement. The message of comfort begins in this chapter. Messengers are told to cry out with courage: "Behold your God!" Interpreters debate whether the "reward" refers to the recompense for his people or to judgment, and perhaps it includes both. Right after this, the text shows this powerful God as a tender shepherd.

For today: when you feel weak or weary, remember that God is not distant. He is strong and he is near. Give him one specific worry today and trust that he cares for you.
exp.64:4:
They say, "Keep to yourself; do not come near me, for I am holier than you!" The text describes people who separate themselves from others and claim to be more holy than those around them. God answers that such people are smoke in his nostrils, an irritation that does not go away, like a fire that burns all day long.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He complains about a people who provoked him with practices of false worship: sacrifices in gardens, rites among the graves, and foods forbidden by the law. The serious thing is that, while they did this, they considered themselves superior to others. God overlooks neither their idolatry nor their pride.

For today: check whether you ever look down on others because you think you are more spiritual. True holiness is not presumed upon and does not push people away; it makes us humble and compassionate, and it brings us closer to God and to others.
exp.52:2:
He is described as the Servant of the Lord, rejected and brought low by the people. He is a man of sorrows, one who came to know suffering up close. Grief here means deep pain. The phrase "like one from whom men hide their faces" means the people turned their eyes away, the way someone avoids a person who makes them uncomfortable. "Despised" means treated as having little worth.

Here a group speaks in the first person plural, "we," probably the people admitting their mistake. They recognize that they did not value the Servant, and in the verses that follow they understand that he was carrying their sins. Christians see in this a prophecy about Jesus; others have also read it as referring to Israel.

Today, do not turn your eyes away from the one who suffers, and do not judge by appearances. Jesus knows your pain and drew near to those who were hurting; seek to draw near to the wounded as well.
exp.15:7:
The verse says that the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah. The rulers of the nations have trampled its choicest vines. Those vines had once reached as far as Jazer, spread toward the desert, and passed over the sea. The shoots of the vine are its branches, so the picture is of a vineyard that once spread very far and now lies broken.

Isaiah announces a judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. The prophet speaks on God's behalf and points to Moab's pride as the cause of its fall. The vineyards were its pride and its wealth. Scholars do not agree on who the invader was exactly, so it is better not to state it. Even so, the prophet shows sorrow for Moab, not satisfaction.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or achievements. All of that can be lost. Trust in God, who gives what truly endures, and ask for humility so that you do not live in pride.
exp.43:4:
This verse describes several people who, one after another, identify themselves with God. One will say, "I belong to the LORD." Another will call himself by the name of Jacob. Still another will write on his hand, "The LORD's," and will take the name of Israel. "Take the name" means that he adopts that name as his own, and writing on the hand seems to be a way of marking oneself as belonging to the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will pour out his Spirit on the descendants of Israel, like water on dry ground. This comes at a time of discouragement for the people. As a result, many will openly declare themselves his.

For today: when God renews the heart, faith becomes something a person confesses without shame. We can ask him to fill us with his Spirit and dare to say, simply, at home and at work, "I belong to the LORD."
exp.29:8:
It says that the people of Israel are rebellious. It calls them "deceitful children," that is, people who say one thing and live another. They are unwilling to obey the LORD's instruction, that is, God's teaching and guidance. Here "obey" means to hear and act on what is said.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. At that time, Judah was seeking the protection of Egypt against its enemies, instead of trusting in God. He had told them that their strength would be found in waiting quietly. That is why he commands this message to be written down, so that it would serve as a witness in the future. The verses that follow show that they did not want to hear truths, but pleasant words.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we listen to God only when it suits us. A good practice is to read the Bible with humility, willing to accept what corrects us, not only what comforts us.
exp.32:9:
Here the text says that God himself steps in. After describing a ruined land, the LORD announces that he will now act. He repeats "now" three times to mark that the moment has come. The words "arise," "lift Myself up," and "exalted" mean that God will rise and be raised high, and his greatness will be recognized by all.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Before this, the text shows a devastated land: empty roads, broken treaties, and fertile places like Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel withered away. This is often connected to the Assyrian threat during the time of Judah, although scholars debate the details. Then God warns that the plans of the proud will be consumed like straw in the fire.

When everything seems lost and no one else can help, God is not absent. You can hand him your difficult situation and trust that he will act in his own time and in his own way.
exp.40:9:
God tells his people not to be afraid or lose heart, because he is with them. He says, "I am your God," and promises, "I will strengthen you." He will help them and support them with his powerful, righteous hand, a picture of his strength acting with justice and faithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, whom he calls his servant, chosen and descended from Abraham, "my friend." The people were surrounded by hostile nations and felt weak. God reminds them that he chose them and did not abandon them. Then he promises that their enemies will be put to shame and left powerless.

Today, when you feel fear or weariness, do not lean only on your own strength. Pray and repeat this promise, remembering that God is with you and sustains you. Then take the next step with confidence, even if you do not yet see the solution.
exp.53:5:
God says that he calls his people like a wife who has been deserted and whose spirit is wounded, like a wife rejected in the years of her youth. "Deserted" means left behind, "wounded in spirit" means hurt deeply in the heart, and "rejected" means turned away. But the verse speaks of a calling: God is calling her back.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Jerusalem, or Israel, which has lived through punishment and exile and felt abandoned. God uses the image of marriage to say that he has not forgotten her. The verses that follow explain that the abandonment was brief, and that he returns to her with everlasting mercy. Some see here also a promise for the Church, but the text speaks first to Israel.

If you feel rejected or have a broken heart, God does not leave you in that place. He calls you back. Speak honestly with him about your pain, and trust that his compassion is greater than your wound.
exp.4:8:
Here Isaiah says that the LORD of Hosts himself made this known to him: many houses will be destroyed and left empty. The word translated as "desolate" means laid waste, reduced to ruins. The phrase "great mansions left unoccupied" means that no one will live in them, not even the grand and beautiful homes. The phrase "I heard" indicates that Isaiah received this message directly from God.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. Shortly before, he compares Israel to a vineyard that God tended, but which produced bad fruit: injustice instead of justice. He condemns those who were accumulating houses and lands, taking space away from others. For this reason he announces that such wealth will not last.

For today: the ambition to have more and more can make us forget about others. Today you might ask yourself whether you use what you have with generosity and justice, or only to secure more and more for yourself.
exp.30:4:
This verse compares God's care to that of birds hovering over their young. It says that the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem, meaning he will shield it and watch over it. Then it uses four actions: protect, deliver, pass over, and preserve. "Passing over" seems to recall Passover, when God passed over the houses of Israel in Egypt, although some understand it simply as passing over the city to protect it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Judah was tempted to seek help from Egypt, with its horses and chariots, in the face of the threat from Assyria. Isaiah reminds them that Egypt is only human, but God is the one who truly protects his people. Then he calls them to turn back to him.

For today: when you are afraid or in need, do not place your trust first in human resources. Use your wisdom, but turn to God in prayer and rest in the knowledge that he cares for you with tenderness and power.
exp.23:16:
God's judgment will come upon all the people of the earth in a way that cannot be escaped. "Terror" is a sudden dread; "the pit" is a deep hole; "the snare" is a trap for catching animals. These are three images of danger that close in on people without leaving them any way out.

Isaiah 24 speaks of God's judgment upon the whole earth, not only upon one nation. The prophet speaks in God's name and explains that humanity has broken His laws and His covenant. In the verses before, some praise God, but Isaiah grieves over so much betrayal. Interpreters debate whether it describes a historical judgment, a future one, or both.

Today it invites us to take God seriously and not to trust in our own security. We can ask ourselves: what am I trusting in? God calls us to return to Him, who is the only true refuge.
exp.64:14:
It says that the rebels will leave their name as a curse for God's chosen people. That is, when someone wants to curse, they will say, "May it happen to you as it did to them." The Lord will slay you, but to His servants He will give another name.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He contrasts two groups: the faithful servants, who receive blessing, and those who abandoned Him and followed other practices, who suffer the consequences. It does not say with certainty what the new name is, but it points to a renewed identity. The passage moves toward the promise of new heavens and a new earth.

For today: God sees the difference between living for Him and living far from Him. If you are faithful to Him, your identity rests on what He says about you, not on your failures. Ask Him today to remind you who you are in Him.
exp.55:2:
Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the Lord think, "The Lord will utterly exclude me from His people." Nor should the eunuch say, "I am but a dry tree," meaning someone without fruit or future. The verse's word "joined" means united or drawn near.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. There were people who could feel shut out: foreigners and eunuchs, whom the law restricted in certain aspects of life among the people (Deuteronomy 23:1-8). God assures them that, if they keep his covenant, they will have a place in his house and an enduring name, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel lesser, without value, or out of place, do not define your future by that label. If you have drawn near to God in faith, he receives you. Learn to trust his word more than your fears, and welcome also those who feel excluded.
exp.1:11:
It says there will be a "day of the Lord," a time when God will come against everyone who is proud and lofty, against all that is exalted, and that this will bring it low. To be "exalted" means to be lifted up or placed very high; to be "humbled" means to be brought down. No one who makes himself great will remain standing.

Isaiah, a prophet in Judah, speaks to a people who trusted in their wealth, their armies, and their idols (vv. 6-8). The cedars, the mountains, and the hills in the verses that follow represent everything that seems great and secure. Many understand this day as a specific judgment of God in history and also as a sign of the final judgment; there are different interpretations.

Today we can examine where we place our trust, in our success, our money, or our image. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on Him and treats others with respect.
exp.15:5:
We have heard of the pride of Moab. It is an enormous pride: pomposity, arrogance, and self-importance, that is, thinking oneself superior to others. "Arrogance" here means excessive pride. But the verse says of Moab's boasting that it is empty, that is, his confidence will not hold up.

Isaiah announces a message of judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Shortly before, the prophet speaks of refuge for displaced Moabites and of a future just king on David's throne. After this, the text shows Moab's lament because its cities and its vineyards will be destroyed. Scholars discuss which exact historical moment is meant, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: pride seems strong, but it is fragile. Today we can ask God for humility and rest our security in his truth, not in boasting about what we have or who we are.
exp.64:16:
God says that he is going to create new heavens and a new earth. The word "create" here is the same word the verse uses, so no further explanation is needed. The former things, that is, the pain and anguish of the past, will not be remembered or come to mind. God promises a renewal so complete that the old suffering will be forgotten.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a people who have suffered because of their sin and rebellion. He promises to restore his faithful servants. Christians often see here an announcement of the new creation that Revelation 21 takes up again. Some scholars think the text also speaks of a near renewal of Jerusalem, and others of a final fulfillment. Both readings have been held.

For today: if you carry wounds or sorrows, this promise invites you to wait in hope. God not only comforts, he also renews. Bring your pain to him with confidence.
exp.0:3:
God speaks with both grief and firmness. He calls Israel a "sinful nation" and a "people laden with iniquity," because their guilt weighs on them like a heavy load. "Evildoers" and "corrupters" describe a life that has gone crooked and rotten. Then he says three things: they have forsaken the Lord, they have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just called the heavens and the earth as witnesses. He complains that he raised his children and they rebelled. Even the ox and the donkey recognize their owner, but his people do not. Then he describes the consequences as a body wounded from head to foot.

For today: do not ignore God's calls to return to him. Today, acknowledge in prayer where you have drifted away, and come back to him with humility. He remains a Father ready to heal.
exp.64:18:
God himself says he will rejoice over Jerusalem and take delight in his people. The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in the city.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a people who had suffered greatly. He promises a new heaven and a new earth, where past pain will no longer weigh on them. The verses that follow describe long life and houses and vineyards enjoyed. Some believers see here a restoration of Israel, others the final fulfillment in eternity, and others both.

For today: when pain wears you down, remember that God is not indifferent; he delights in his people and promises final comfort. That hope can give you strength to keep going and to comfort others.
exp.63:0:
Here the prophet cries out to God with great urgency: "If only you would tear open the heavens and come down!" He asks that God act in a powerful and visible way. "So that mountains would quake at your presence" means that the mountains would shake and tremble before him.

The one speaking is the prophet, on behalf of the people of Israel. It comes from a prayer that remembers God's past deeds and feels that now he seems far away. Many understand that the people live in a time of ruin or exile, though scholars debate the exact moment. The people acknowledge their sin and plead for help.

Today we can pray sincerely when we feel God is far away. There is no need to pretend: we can ask him to act, confess our faults, and remember how he has helped us before.
exp.6:8:
Isaiah says that Ephraim, meaning the northern kingdom, has only Samaria as its head, and Samaria has only a human king, the son of Remaliah. Then he warns: "If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all," meaning that if they do not put their confidence in God, they will not remain steady.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to King Ahaz of Judah. Syria and Ephraim had joined forces against Judah, and Ahaz was terrified. God tells him that these enemies are only men with limited power. In Hebrew, the words for "trust" and "stand firm" sound alike, and that resemblance reinforces the message.

For today: when fear makes you feel that everything is falling apart, remember who is truly greater. Trusting in God, and not only in your own calculations, is what gives you firmness.
exp.48:23:
This verse asks two questions that seem to have an obvious answer: can plunder be snatched from a mighty warrior? Can the captives of a tyrant be set free? The word "plunder" refers to what a conqueror has seized. "Captives of a tyrant" points to people held by a cruel ruler who has taken them by force.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, who in exile felt abandoned and without a way out. The question expresses the people's doubt: it seemed impossible that Babylon would let its captives go. The following verses give the answer: God himself will deliver them.

For today: when a situation seems impossible to change, do not measure the problem by its strength, but measure God by his power. Bring him your doubt honestly, and trust that he is able to set you free.
exp.18:14:
It says that Egypt will get no benefit from anything its people do, whether they are the most important or the most humble. The words "head or tail" refer to those at the top and those at the bottom, and "palm or reed" refers to the top of the palm tree and the reed of the marsh, another way of saying the same thing. The phrase "there is nothing Egypt can do" means that no effort will serve a purpose or produce a result.

Isaiah speaks in the name of God and directs a prophecy against Egypt. The counselors of Zoan and of Noph (Memphis) had led the nation down a wrong path, and the text says that the LORD allowed that confusion, like a drunkard who staggers. Scholars debate exactly which historical moment the passage refers to.

For today: human wisdom, without God, can become confused. Before deciding, whether at home, at work, or in church, ask God for direction and listen to humble counsel.
exp.57:12:
If you hold back your steps from breaking the Sabbath, from doing as you please on My holy day, and you call the Sabbath a delight, the LORD's holy day honorable, and you honor it by not going your own way, not seeking your own pleasure, and not speaking idle words, then a promise will come.

Holding back your steps means refraining from what you would normally do. To honor something means to show it respect.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked a false fast, one that looked religious but ignored justice and compassion toward the needy. Now he shows that the Sabbath was meant to be joy and communion with God, not a burden. The blessings that follow speak of restoration and of delight in the LORD.

For today: set aside time each week to rest and seek God without rush or distraction. Quiet the noise, pray, give thanks, and enjoy his presence as a gift, not as an obligation.
exp.48:16:
Isaiah 49:17 says that the people who will rebuild Zion are coming back soon, and that those who ruined her are leaving. The "builders" are those who raise her up again; the "destroyers" are those who leave a place in ruins.

God speaks through Isaiah to Zion, the people of Israel, who felt forgotten in exile. He has just told her that he has not forgotten her: she is engraved on his palms, and he always keeps her ruined walls in mind. This verse promises restoration, return, and new life for the community.

For today: if you feel that your life is in ruins, remember that God has not forgotten you. Trust that he can rebuild what is damaged and drive away what was tearing you down, even though it may take time.
exp.40:26:
God says that he was the first to tell Zion about these things, long before they happened. He promises to give Jerusalem a herald who brings good news. The messenger is the one who carries the good news, and the news itself is the good news. The word "Zion" here refers to God's people and to their city.

The Lord speaks in an imaginary trial against the idols of the nations. He asks who announced beforehand what was going to happen, and no one answers. Only God announces the future and then fulfills it. Many understand that the one who comes from the north and the east is Cyrus, king of Persia, although some interpret it differently. The herald of good news points to the deliverance of Jerusalem, and Christians also see it fulfilled in Christ.

Today we can trust that God keeps what he says. When everything seems uncertain, we can return to his Word and rest in his faithfulness.
exp.31:14:
It says that the desolation will last until God pours out his Spirit from on high. The Spirit being poured out is the Spirit who comes from God. Then the dry and empty land will become an orchard, a place of fruit and growth. And that orchard will be so abundant that it will seem like a forest, a land full of life.

Isaiah speaks to Judah. He announces that, because of their pride and their spiritual neglect, the city will lie in ruins, with thorns and empty palaces. But the desolation does not have the last word: this verse marks the turning point, and the verses that follow say that justice, peace, and security will come. Some see it partly fulfilled in the restoration of the people, and others also at Pentecost or in the future; Christians have understood it in several ways.

For today: if there are dry areas in your life, do not rely only on your own effort. Ask God to fill you with his Spirit, and wait patiently for his renewing work.
exp.33:8:
It says that the land of Edom, the enemy of God, will be turned into a landscape of judgment. Its streams will become tar, its soil will become sulfur, and the whole land will become a blazing pitch, a fire that never stops burning.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing the judgment of the LORD upon the nations, represented in this case by Edom. The passage describes a time of repayment, when God defends his people and corrects injustice. Many understand the images as poetic and symbolic language for total destruction.

For today: God takes evil and injustice seriously, and he does not leave them without an answer. We can trust that he will do justice, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves. In the meantime, let us live with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.40:12:
It says that the Lord, the God of his people, takes hold of his right hand, like a father who guides his child, and tells him, "Do not fear." To take hold means to grasp someone firmly. The words "I will help you" are a promise about what God will do, and they are spoken with certainty.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, his servant, probably at a time of threat from powerful nations. The verses before this one promise that those who oppose them will vanish. God wants to encourage a small and frightened people, reminding them that they are not alone.

For today: when you feel afraid or small before a problem, imagine that God is holding your hand. Pray simply: "Lord, hold me up today." You do not depend on your own strength, but on the one who holds you.
exp.0:16:
This verse is an invitation to change how you live. "Learn to do right" means that doing good is something you learn and practice. "Seek justice" means working for what is fair. "Correct the oppressor" means stopping the one who is doing the harm, and "defend the fatherless" and "plead the case of the widow" mean standing up for those who have no one to speak for them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Judah and Jerusalem. They practiced religion with prayers and offerings, but they lived with injustice and violence. That is why God says he does not hear their prayers. He does not reject prayer itself, but religion without obedience. And right away he offers them forgiveness if they repent.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we might help or defend: someone alone, in need, or ignored. A concrete step is to visit, accompany, or support that person this week, so that our faith shows in actions.
exp.25:11:
The explanation says that the people trust God to give them peace. In the Berean Standard Bible, the phrase "You will establish peace for us" means that God will set peace firmly in place for them. Also, they acknowledge that everything they have accomplished, God has done for them. Peace is not presented as a human achievement, but as a gift from God.

Here the people of Judah speak in a song of trust within Isaiah's prophecy. Before this, there is talk of a wicked man who does not learn even when shown kindness, and of enemies who do not see the hand of God. Afterward, the believers confess that other masters had ruled over them, but that only to God do they call. Some understand "all that we have accomplished" as the people's victories and achievements; the central idea is the same: God is the one who sustains.

Today, before struggling to achieve tranquility, ask God for his peace. And when something good comes from your effort, thank him, because he gave you the strength to do it.
exp.25:3:
Trust in the LORD always, without growing weary, because he is firm and does not change. The phrase "forever" in the verse conveys the idea of lasting through all times. The name "GOD the LORD" and the image of him as "the Rock eternal" point to a secure refuge that endures through every age.

It is part of a song that the prophet Isaiah announces for the people of Judah, directed toward a future time of restoration. The song contrasts the righteous who trust in God with the proud city that he humbles, as the following verses say. Scholars debate which city is meant; the text does not name it clearly here.

Today, when everything seems unstable, you can choose to trust God one day at a time. Speak to him honestly about your worries, and remember that he remains firm even when your circumstances change.
exp.7:7:
It says that the army of Assyria, like a river that has burst its banks, will pour into Judah, sweeping over it and rising up to the neck (almost covering the people, like water that reaches the throat), and then spread across the whole land, like a bird that spreads its wings. The image of "swirling and sweeping over" means the force will pass beyond every boundary, flooding everything in its path. The land is addressed as Immanuel ("God with us").

God speaks through Isaiah, around 730 BC. The people turned away from the gentle waters of Shiloah, which many understand as a sign of trusting God, and placed their hope in human alliances. God says that Assyria will come as judgment. Even so, the name Immanuel shows that God does not abandon his people.

For today: when difficulties seem to flood over you, do not look for security only in human resources. Trust in God, who remains with you even in the middle of the trial.
exp.46:8:
These two things will overtake you in a moment, in a single day: the loss of children, and widowhood. They will come upon you in full measure, despite your many sorceries and the power of your spells. The phrase "in full measure" stresses that the blow will be complete, with nothing held back, and the sorceries and spells that you relied on to protect yourself will not stop it.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Babylon, pictured as a proud woman who believed she would remain a lady forever. She trusted in her power and her magic, and she did not expect to be held accountable. God announces that her fall will come suddenly and that her resources will not save her.

For today: do not place your security in your success, your intelligence, or any practice meant to control the future. Trust God with humility, because He is the one who sustains our lives.
exp.22:0:
Tyre, the great trading city by the sea, is said here to have been destroyed completely, left with no houses and no harbor to enter. The word "burden" means a heavy message of judgment. The "ships of Tarshish" were large trading vessels, and they are told to wail, that is, to cry out loudly in grief. The verse says word has reached them from Cyprus, so the news comes to the sailors from that island, where they learn of the destruction when they return.

The speaker is the prophet Isaiah, announcing a message from God against Tyre, a wealthy and proud city. Interpreters disagree about which conquest is meant: some think of Babylon, others of Alexander the Great, and others see several stages. The text does not make this clear.

For today: wealth and success are not a safe refuge. Place your trust in God, and use all you have with humility and generosity.
exp.34:0:
It says that the wilderness, the dry land and the desert will be glad and rejoice. The "wilderness" is abandoned ground where nothing grows. The desert will "blossom like a rose." Some translators think the Hebrew word may refer to a different flower, perhaps the saffron or crocus, but this is not known with complete certainty.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah, after announcements of judgment in the earlier chapters. It is a promise of restoration: God will bring renewal, and his glory will be seen. The verses that follow encourage the weary and fearful to take heart, because God is coming to save.

For today: if you are going through a dry or exhausting season, do not think that God has forgotten you. You can wait on him with hope, and encourage someone who is tired with a kind word or a simple act of help.
exp.50:3:
God calls on his people to pay attention and listen to him. He tells them that a law will go out from him, that is, his teaching and his guidance. He also says that his justice will become a light to the nations, and that he will bring it about quickly.

The Lord is speaking to Israel, a discouraged people in difficulties. He has just reminded them of Abraham, whom he called alone and then multiplied, and he promises them comfort for Zion. God assures them that his teaching and his justice will not remain only in Israel, but will reach the other nations. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, the light of the world.

When our spirits sink, let us turn again to listen carefully to God. His word not only comforts us; it also guides us and makes us a light for others.
exp.24:1:
God has made the city a heap of rubble, and the fortified town a ruin. The strong city, with its walls, has been left in shambles. In this verse, the fortress is described as a place of strangers, meaning outsiders who are enemies of God's people, and the fortress is said to be a city no more. The statement that it will never be rebuilt means that this stronghold will never be raised up again.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, praising God for His just and faithful works. It is not stated clearly which city is meant; some think of a real city, and others of a symbol of human pride and power that opposes God. What matters is that God brings down the proud and protects the poor, as the following verses say.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever, but God is faithful. When you see injustice or powerful people who seem untouchable, do not lose hope: trust in God and praise Him, because He cares for the weak.
exp.36:30:
The explanation says that the people of Judah who survive will once again take root below and bear fruit above. It is an image of a plant: first it becomes firm beneath the soil, and afterward the fruit can be seen. The word "remnant" means those who are left, and "again" means they will return.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. The army of Assyria, under King Sennacherib, had invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem. God promises to stop the invader and gives a sign: two years of eating what grows on its own, and in the third year, sowing and reaping as usual. It is a promise of restoration.

For today: when we go through a crisis, let us not expect quick results. God often heals what is hidden first, such as faith, prayer, and character, and in his time visible fruit comes. Let us cultivate those roots today.
exp.30:7:
The passage says that Assyria, the great enemy power, will fall by a sword that no human warrior wields. The word for "sword" appears in the verse as the same term throughout, so the sword and the one who destroys are presented as one divine action. The verb meaning "devour" is the same verb used for what will happen to Assyria. The young men are the ones who will be put under forced labor, made to work and serve.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, which was seeking military help in Egypt instead of trusting in God. He calls them to return to God and to set aside their idols. The text does not say precisely how Assyria will fall; many connect it with the defeat of Sennacherib at Jerusalem (Isaiah 37:36), although this is an interpretation.

For today: when a problem feels too big, do not place your security only in human resources or in things that take the place of God. Return to him sincerely, because he can act in ways we do not expect.
exp.42:27:
He says that God himself disgraced the leaders of the temple and gave his people over to destruction and reproach. "Disgrace" means removing honor and holiness from what was set apart. "Devote to destruction" refers to handing something over to ruin or judgment. "Reproach" is public shame and scorn. "Princes of your sanctuary" are those in charge of worship, the priests and officials.

God speaks through Isaiah, in a kind of legal case where he invites Israel to defend itself. He reminds them that their history was marked by sin, including the sin of their teachers. Many understand this verse as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, though the text gives no further details. Just before this, God says he blots out their rebellions for his own sake (v. 25).

For today: do not minimize sin or your need for forgiveness. If God corrects, it is to call you back to him. Confess to him sincerely and receive his grace, without excuses or pride.
exp.37:17:
The explanation says that the dead cannot praise God the way the living do. The word "Sheol" refers to the grave, the place of the dead, and "the Pit" refers to the burial pit, the tomb. "Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness" means that those who have died can no longer trust in God's faithfulness. The text expresses that, from the tomb, one can no longer proclaim God's faithfulness.

The speaker is King Hezekiah, who was gravely ill, and God granted him more years of life. This is his song of gratitude. His words reflect a limited view of what lies beyond death; the Bible reveals more about that in other passages.

Today, every day of life is an opportunity to give thanks to God and to tell others, especially our children, what He has done for us. Do not leave it for later: praise Him today.
exp.43:15:
He takes a single piece of wood and uses it for two very different things. He burns half of it in the fire, roasts meat on that half, eats the roast until he is satisfied, and warms himself. He is content and says, "Ah! I am warm; I see the fire." With the other half, as the following verses say, he makes a god.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people tempted by idolatry. With irony, he shows how absurd it is to worship something a person makes himself out of ordinary wood, the same wood he uses to cook.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things, even good ones such as money, work, or success, we have placed in the place of God. What we do or control cannot save us. Today we can thank God for his gifts and trust in him, not in them.
exp.51:5:
God says that his people will come to know his name, that is, to truly know who he is. This will happen "on that day," when God himself, the one who now speaks through the prophet, makes his presence known. "Here I am" means "I am here, I have arrived."

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to a people who are humbled and held captive, whose name was mocked by the nations. God shows that he is not indifferent to that situation. The verses that follow announce to the messenger who proclaims: "Your God reigns." Christians often see here a promise that is fully fulfilled in Christ, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

When you feel forgotten or are in the middle of a trial, remember that God is not far away. His promise is to be present, and knowing him better is the greatest comfort.
exp.59:11:
This verse says that any people or kingdom that refuses to serve Zion, that is, Jerusalem and God's restored people, will be destroyed. "Will perish" means it will come to an end, and "utterly destroyed" means it will be reduced to ruin.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who had suffered punishment and exile. God promises to restore Jerusalem, and that nations will come to it. Many understand that serving Zion means recognizing God's work among his people. Some see this fulfilled in the return of Israel, and others in Christ and his kingdom. Not everyone interprets it the same way.

For today: no human power can stand firm by opposing God. We can rest in the knowledge that his justice and his mercy will prevail, and also live with humility, seeking to be on the side of his work rather than against it.
exp.22:11:
God announces to Sidon, the Phoenician city that was proud and joyful, that its celebrating is over. He calls it "virgin" because it thought itself untouched and secure, but now it is "oppressed." Even if it tries to escape across the sea to Cyprus, it will find no rest there either. "Rest" means peace and calm.

Isaiah speaks for the LORD against Tyre and Sidon, cities made rich by sea trade. The Lord is the one who stretches out his hand over the sea and weakens its power. Scholars debate which exact historical event the prophet has in mind, but the message is clear: no power stands above God.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or our own plans, because they can fall. Let us rest in God, for only in him is there a rest that cannot be lost.
exp.5:1:
These verses describe beings called seraphim, who stood above God. Each one had six wings: with two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. The word "seraphim" probably means "burning ones," and they appear only here in the Bible.

Isaiah tells what he saw in a vision, in the year King Uzziah died. The seraphim do not speak yet; in the next verse they proclaim the holiness of God. Many understand that covering the face and the feet shows reverence and humility before God. The feet may be a gentle way of referring to the body, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if even the seraphim cover themselves before God, we too can approach Him with respect and gratitude. Before you pray, pause and remember who God is.
exp.44:7:
It says that God calls on the heavens to "drip down" and pour out righteousness like rain, and calls on the earth to open up so that salvation may sprout and righteousness may spring up with it. The two grow together, like a seed that breaks through the soil. At the end, God declares, "I, the LORD, have created it," meaning that He is the one who makes this happen.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel and the Persian king Cyrus, whom He would use to free His people from exile. God insists that there is no other God and that He governs everything, the light and the darkness. Many understand "evil" as calamity or judgment, not moral wickedness. Some see here also a promise of the Messiah.

For today: when the world seems dark, trust that God is still at work and causing salvation to sprout. Pray in patience, without trying to control everything.
exp.2:5:
In times of crisis, the text says, people will be so desperate that a man will seize his brother within his father's house and say to him: "You have a cloak, you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble."

The phrase "seize his brother" describes grabbing hold of someone. "You have a cloak" points to having something, even a little, to offer. The reader should note that the one who is grabbed and called on is someone who appears to have some small means, and the call is to lead over a city in ruins.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. He announces that God will remove the provision and the capable leaders, and disorder will come. The poverty will be so great that no one will want to govern, and whoever has a cloak will be seen as a candidate. The verses that follow explain why: the people had turned against God with words and deeds.

For today: let us not seek leadership for comfort or by pretending to be sufficient, and let us pray for honest and wise leaders. When a society turns away from God, it needs to return to Him before seeking only human saviors.
exp.9:24:
It says that the time of God's anger against his people is very nearly over. "Fury" and "anger" speak of his discipline. "Destruction" means an end or ruin, and here it refers to the enemies, that is, Assyria, not Judah. Some understand that the anger turns against Assyria; the context that follows suggests this.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had been used as a tool to correct Judah for its sin, but Assyria was proud and cruel. God comforts "my people who dwell in Zion" and tells them not to fear. He recalls past deliverances, such as the one from Egypt and the one from Midian, to show that he will rescue them again.

For today: when you go through a trial or a correction, remember that God sets limits on the time of suffering. Trust that he cares for you, and do not let fear control you.
exp.20:3:
Here the prophet says that his heart is faltering and that fear makes him tremble. The "twilight I desired" is an evening he had looked forward to with gladness, perhaps for rest or celebration, but it has become horror to him.

Isaiah speaks here, having just seen a difficult vision about the fall of Babylon to the Persians and Medes. He does not celebrate the fall; he feels it in his body, with pain and anguish. The text refers to an evening that was meant to be peaceful, and scholars connect it with the feast and the sudden fall of the city, though not all agree on the details. Soon after, God tells him to set a watchman.

For today: when God shows you a painful reality, do not harden yourself or ignore it. Feel its weight, and then remain alert and attentive to his voice.
exp.33:10:
The passage says that Edom will be left empty, with only wild desert birds living there, such as the desert owl, the screech owl, the great owl, and the raven. The exact birds are hard to be sure of, but the picture is clear: the land will be abandoned and silent. The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction. These were tools used for measuring and building, but here God uses the image of measuring to show that he is marking out the land for ruin, not for rebuilding. The words "chaos" and "destruction" mean total ruin.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces God's judgment on the nations, and here Edom is especially named (v. 5). The chapter shows that God is just and that violence and pride do not go unanswered. Many read the language as a poetic and exaggerated picture of judgment, not only as a literal description.

For today: do not trust in your strength, your success, or your pride; only what God builds endures. Ask him today to give you humility and to teach you to build your life on his truth.
exp.37:13:
The explanation says that the king was in such distress that his cries sounded like the cries of birds: the chirping of the crane, the sad song of the swallow, and the moaning of the dove. He lifted his eyes toward heaven, and he cried out, "O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security." In other words, he felt crushed and weighed down, and he asked God to be his protection and his strength.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks in a writing of his own after he fell gravely ill. Isaiah had told him he would die, and he felt his life being cut off like cloth that the weaver pulls from the loom. Here he has no clear words, only moaning, and yet he still looks toward God.

For today: when pain leaves you without words, you do not have to speak beautifully to pray. You can bring God your sighs, your weariness, and your fear, and simply ask him to be your security. He hears even the moans.
exp.1:2:
This verse describes many peoples who call out to one another to go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob. They want Him to teach them His ways so that they may walk in His paths. "Zion" and "Jerusalem" refer to the same city, and from there the law will go forth, along with the word of the LORD. "Law" here means instruction, not only rules.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking to Judah and Jerusalem. He announces what will happen "in the latter days," that is, in a future that God will bring about. After the verse comes peace among the nations. Christians often see it fulfilled in Christ and his Church, while others expect it at a future time; it is understood in several ways.

For today: before deciding something important, ask God what He thinks and seek His teaching in the Bible. Coming to Him with humility and a willingness to obey is the first step toward walking in His paths.
exp.31:16:
It says that righteousness produces good fruit. "The service of righteousness" is the result, and "the work of righteousness" is the labor or fruit of righteousness. That fruit is peace, quiet confidence (a calm, restful state, marked by trust without fear), and it will last forever.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived with injustice, fear and threats from other nations. Earlier he announces a righteous king (32:1) and a time when God will pour out his Spirit from on high. Then the dry land would bear fruit, and justice would dwell in it. Christians often see here an announcement of Christ's reign, though it also speaks of a restoration for Israel.

Today, do not seek peace only by avoiding problems. Strive to live uprightly: be honest, treat others well and trust God. True calm is born from living in what is right with the help of his Spirit.
exp.36:8:
The explanation tells us that Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, received a piece of news: Tirhakah, king of Cush, had set out to fight against him. After hearing this, he sent messengers to Hezekiah with another message. The phrase "on hearing this" marks the moment the news reached him, and the report itself is the turning point of the sentence.

Here the account from Isaiah describes the Assyrian invasion of Judah. God had already announced that Sennacherib would hear a rumor and return to his own land. That rumor seems to be this news. Under pressure, Sennacherib tries to make Hezekiah surrender with threats and mockery aimed at his trust in God. The exact military details are debated by scholars, but the text shows how God directs events.

For today: when someone threatens you or makes you doubt God, remember that He governs circumstances, even those you cannot see. Trust and pray, as Hezekiah did.
exp.28:19:
It says that the end will come for those who harm others. The "ruthless" are the abusers; the "mockers" are those who scorn what is good and scorn God. The verse's image of those who "look for evil" describes people who keep watching for chances to do wrong, eager to carry it out. "Cut down" means cut off, as a tree is cut down.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah. Their leaders oppressed the weak, bent justice, and silenced anyone who corrected them. Earlier, God promises that the humble and the poor will rejoice in Him. This verse shows the other side: injustice will not last forever.

For today: if you suffer injustice, trust that God sees and will act. And examine your own heart: do you spend your energy thinking about blessing others or about taking advantage of them? Ask God to make you humble and just.
exp.33:6:
God's judgment on Edom will be complete. The word "wild oxen" in this verse is a term (re'em) that most likely refers to powerful wild oxen or large buffalo, not a legendary creature. The "young bulls with the strong ones," along with the images of the land drenched with blood and the soil soaked with fat, describe a massive slaughter, pictured as a sacrifice.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing what the LORD will do. Edom, a neighbor of Israel, stands as an example of the nations that oppose God and his people. The language is poetic and exaggerated, and it speaks of divine justice and of God defending Zion, that is, his own people.

For today: God takes injustice seriously and does not overlook it. We can rest in the fact that he judges with justice, leave vengeance in his hands, and live with humility and mercy.
exp.9:5:
God says he will send Assyria against a godless nation, and he calls that nation "a people destined for My rage." Assyria will take the spoils, seize the plunder, and trample the people down like clay in the streets, showing them no respect at all.

God speaks through Isaiah. He addresses Judah and Israel, who had fallen into injustice and idolatry (see the beginning of the chapter). God uses Assyria as the instrument of his discipline. But the verses that follow show that Assyria acted out of pride, not obedience, and for that reason it too would be judged.

For today: God governs history and corrects his own people with justice. If he calls our attention, let us not harden our hearts; let us return to him in humility. And let us not forget that no human power escapes his judgment.
exp.42:10:
It says that the Lord is the only true God and the only one who can save. The phrase "I, yes I, am the LORD" repeats the pronoun for emphasis: there is no doubt about who is speaking. "No Savior but Me" means that no one else can rescue or deliver from danger and evil.

God himself speaks here, addressing Israel, his chosen people. It is like an imaginary trial: God invites the nations to bring forward their gods as witnesses, to see whether any of them announced what was going to happen. None can. Israel, however, has seen God announce and fulfill, and for that reason Israel is his witness.

For today: when you feel trapped by fears, guilt, or problems you cannot solve, do not look for your security in things or people who cannot fully save you. Go to God with confidence, and tell others how he has helped you.
exp.29:16:
It says the people will be so weak and so afraid that a thousand men will run away at the threat of one alone, and all of them will run away at the threat of five. In the end only a few will be left, alone like a pole on the top of a mountain or like a banner on a hill. A hill is a small rise or height of land.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. The people were looking for military protection in Egypt, with horses and chariots, instead of trusting the Lord, who offered them salvation in quietness and confidence. They said "No." So God warns that the flight they chose would turn against them. Even so, the passage that follows shows that God waits so that he may show mercy.

For today: when fear pushes us to look for quick escapes without prayer, we can stop and trust God. He remains patient and is ready to help anyone who turns back to him.
exp.41:8:
God says that the things he announced earlier have already happened. "The former things" are what he had said and then fulfilled. Now he announces "new things," and he tells them to you before they happen.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just introduced his Servant, who will open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of darkness. God declares that he will not give his glory to idols. His ability to announce the future sets him apart from them. Then comes a call to sing him a new song. Many believers see here a look toward Christ, although the text also speaks of what God would do in his own time.

For today: if God fulfilled what he promised before, you can trust that he will fulfill what you do not yet see. Today, bring your uncertainty to him in prayer and wait with patience.
exp.18:24:
The passage says that the LORD of Hosts will bless Egypt, Assyria and Israel. He gives each of them a warm title: Egypt is "My people," Assyria is "My handiwork," and Israel is "My inheritance," that is, his treasured possession.

Isaiah speaks to Judah at a time when neighboring powers threatened it. Egypt and Assyria were longtime enemies of Israel and of other peoples. Here God speaks of a future time, when these nations will worship him together. Interpreters differ on when and how this is fulfilled: some see a partial historical fulfillment, others see it in Christ and the church, and others see it in a time still to come.

For today: God loves and seeks people whom we see as enemies. We can pray for someone with whom we are in conflict and ask God to help us treat them with respect and a desire for peace.
exp.28:14:
The explanation says that God grieves over the situation of those who want to hide themselves from Him. "Dig deep to hide their plans" means trying to conceal what they intend, and "in darkness they do their works" refers to actions done in secret because they know they are wrong. They think, "Who sees us, and who will know?", as if God did not notice.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in Judah. Shortly before, He accuses the people of honoring Him only with their lips, while their hearts are far away. Many understand that here He is referring to leaders who made political plans in secret, seeking alliances without consulting God. Then He reminds them that the clay cannot say the potter has no understanding.

For today: do not live a faith that is only outward appearance. When you are tempted to hide something, remember that God already sees it and loves you. It is better to bring it to Him in prayer, confess it, and seek someone you trust who can help you walk in the light.
exp.56:13:
This verse is a command: someone must prepare the way. The reader's wording is "Build it up, build it up, prepare the way, take every obstacle out of the way of My people," so the preparation is described as building up the road and removing every obstacle from it. An obstacle is anything that could cause someone to stumble or be blocked. The road being prepared is the road of God's people.

God speaks here, having just shown that idols and human alliances do not save, since the wind carries them away. Instead, he promises refuge to whoever waits on him. Now he orders the removal of whatever stands in the way of his people's return. Some read this as an announcement of the return from exile, and others also see it as a picture of the work of Christ. Both readings are possible.

For today: God wants us to come back to him, and sometimes there are obstacles we ourselves can remove, such as a grudge, a habit, or a distraction. Ask him to help you remove that obstacle, and also to help others come near to him without stumbling.
exp.20:7:
The watchman cries out, and tells the Lord that he has stood on his post all day and all night, without leaving it. The watchtower is a high tower from which people kept watch. The phrase "my post" refers to the place where he was stationed to keep watch.

God had asked the prophet to set a watchman to report what he saw. Here the watchman answers that he has been faithful and steady, waiting. Shortly afterward he announces the fall of Babylon. Some scholars think the watchman is Isaiah himself; others think he is a symbolic figure. The original text is difficult and is translated in several ways.

For today: faith is sometimes waiting with steadiness. Stay alert and faithful in prayer and in your duty, even when God's answer is slow, trusting that He speaks in his own time.
exp.61:0:
He says that the speaker will not stay silent or keep still for the sake of Zion and Jerusalem. He will keep going until her righteousness shines like a bright light, and her salvation, that is, her deliverance, blazes like a torch. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "I will not keep still" means "I will not stop."

The context is a promise of restoration for God's people after punishment and exile. It is not entirely clear who is speaking: some think it is the prophet Isaiah, and others think it is the Servant of the Lord, whom Christians connect with Christ. The verses that follow show the purpose: that the nations would see God's glory in his people.

For today: do not give up praying or serving for your church, your family, or your city. Persevere with hope, trusting that God keeps what he promises.
exp.61:11:
It says God will give his people new names: "The Holy People" and "The Redeemed of the LORD." Holy means set apart for God. The redeemed are those who have been bought back by paying a price. Jerusalem will be called "Sought Out," meaning desired and cared for, and "A City Not Forsaken," meaning never abandoned again.

The prophet Isaiah announces a promise of restoration for Israel, probably addressed to a people who were suffering after the exile. They are invited to prepare the way, because the Savior is coming with his reward. Many Christians also see here an anticipation of Christ and his Church, although the text speaks first of Israel.

Today, you can remember that your identity does not depend on your failures or on what others say about you. If you trust God, he sees you as someone redeemed, set apart, and loved. Today you can live with that security.
exp.21:23:
He says that all the weight of honor of his father's house will be hung on this man, as objects are hung on a firm nail in the wall. The "vessels" were household utensils: from the bowls used for holding food to the jars used for storage. That is, everything will depend on him, from the most important relatives down to the smallest things.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He will replace Shebna, a proud administrator of the palace, with Eliakim, to whom He will give authority and the key of the house of David. The following verse makes clear that this "nail" will also fall: no man is an eternal support.

For today: if many depend on you, carry that responsibility with humility and do not think yourself indispensable. Only Christ, whom the New Testament connects with "the key of David" (Revelation 3:7), is a support that never fails.
exp.38:0:
It says that Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to King Hezekiah of Judah. He did this because he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery. "Recovery" means that Hezekiah got better from his sickness. A "gift" is a present.

Here the narrator of the book of Isaiah is speaking. This comes after God healed Hezekiah (chapter 38). Scholars think Babylon was also looking for allies against Assyria, although the text does not say so clearly. What follows shows that Hezekiah showed all his treasures to the visitors, and God corrected him through Isaiah.

For today: after receiving a blessing from God, we may be tempted to boast or to trust in people. Let us ask for wisdom to give the glory to God and to guard our hearts well in the face of flattery.
exp.18:8:
The verse says that those who work with fine flax, combing and preparing it to make cloth, and the weavers of fine linen, will be dismayed and turn pale. "Dismayed" means they will be shaken and their hopes and plans frustrated. Egypt was known for its flax and its fishing.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah in a message against Egypt. If the Nile River dries up, everything that depends on it fails: the plants, the fishing, and the flax industry. The verses that follow show that not even the wise counselors of the pharaoh will be able to solve it.
