Scholars debate the exact timing of this judgment, but the message is clear: no one stands without God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we depend on most: our work, our money, or our skill. All of that can fail. Let us work with diligence, but place our trust in God, who sustains all things.
exp.17:5:
It says that the bodies of those who are struck down will be left lying on the mountains, and the birds of prey and the wild animals will feed on them. The words "in summer" and "in winter" mean that the birds will feed on them in the warm season and the wild animals in the cold season, so the feeding goes on through the whole year.

God speaks through Isaiah about a powerful nation beyond the rivers of Ethiopia (Cush). It is not known for certain which nation this was. God watches calmly, and just when everything seems to be ripening, he steps in and cuts off the branches. Judgment comes at the least expected moment. Afterward, a people will come to bring an offering to God in Zion.

For today: do not despair when the powerful seem to have no restraint. God watches calmly, has his own timing, and governs history. Trust in him and live righteously.
exp.28:4:
It says that the great crowd of Jerusalem's foes will become like fine dust and like blowing chaff, the light straw that the wind carries away. And this will happen suddenly, in an instant.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Ariel is a name for Jerusalem. First he announces that the city would be humbled and besieged, and then he promises that the armies that attack it will disappear, like a dream. Scholars debate which historical event is in view, perhaps the siege of Sennacherib, though there is no full agreement.

For today: when a problem looks huge and threatening, remember that God can change the situation in a moment. Hand your fear over to Him in prayer and keep trusting in Him.
exp.26:7:
God disciplines his people with measure, meaning with moderation and never without limit. "His shoots" are the branches, an image of the people. God holds back his fierce wind, his harsh judgment, on the day of the scorching east wind, the hot, dry wind that blows in from the desert. Even when he disciplines, he sets a boundary.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, passing on God's word about Israel, which is pictured as a vineyard. The verse before it promises restoration, and the verse after it explains that the punishment aims to cleanse the people of idolatry. Some understand "it" to refer to the people and others to the city, and the Hebrew text is difficult, so it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you go through a correction or a trial, remember that God does not act with unrestrained fury. His discipline has a purpose and a limit, and it seeks to restore your life and your fruit.
exp.25:14:
Here the people of God tell the LORD that He has enlarged the nation, and they repeat it to stress the point. In doing so, God gained glory for Himself. The phrase "You have gained glory for Yourself" means that God showed Himself to be glorious. Also, "You have extended all the borders of the land" means that He enlarged the land's borders. Some understand this to refer to the territory, and others to the fame of God.

The faithful remnant of Judah speaks within a song of trust. They say that other lords ruled over them, but that they acknowledge only God. The oppressors have already fallen, and God restored His people. It is not clear whether Isaiah speaks of a past event or of a hope seen as already fulfilled.

For today: when God blesses you or lifts you up, do not claim the credit. Give Him thanks, and let your life show who He is.
exp.10:14:
God promises to destroy the gulf of the Sea of Egypt and to sweep His hand over the Euphrates with a scorching wind, splitting the river into seven streams so that people can cross it in dry sandals. The reader can see that the promise is about the great waters being made passable, and that the river is generally understood to be the Euphrates, though this is not certain.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Judah. He announces that God will gather the survivors of His people, scattered among the nations. He recalls the crossing of the Red Sea: what God did before, He will do again. Some see in this also a sign of the kingdom of the Messiah.

For today: if before you there is an obstacle that seems impossible, remember that God has opened paths before. Trust in Him, take the next step, and let Him take care of the rest.
exp.35:2:
The explanation says that three officials of King Hezekiah went out to meet the messenger from Assyria. Eliakim was the palace administrator, the one in charge of the royal household. Shebna was the scribe, the secretary who kept the records. Joah was the recorder, the official who kept track of the kingdom's history and important events. The phrase "went out to him" means that they went out to speak with Rabshakeh.

The account is told by the prophet Isaiah. Assyria had conquered many cities of Judah and now threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah sent these three men as his spokesmen, and immediately Rabshakeh uses them to intimidate the people and undermine their trust in God.

For today: when pressures come and voices try to discourage us, there is no need to respond with fear or to argue endlessly. We can act with calm and bring the situation to God, as Hezekiah later did.
exp.43:3:
It says that the descendants of Israel will grow with strength and life, like green grass and like willows that grow beside a flowing stream. "They will sprout" means they will come up and grow. The streams are the flowing water that the willows stand beside. The willow is a tree that grows quickly where water is plentiful.

God himself speaks, the Creator of Israel. His people were downcast, and He tells them: "Do not be afraid." He promises to pour out his Spirit and his blessing on their children, like water on dry ground. The growth the verse describes is the result of that water, that is, of God's work and not of human effort.

For today: if you feel dry or tired, seek God in prayer and in his Word. Just as the willow depends on water, our life grows when we remain close to Him, who gives his Spirit to those who trust in Him.
exp.62:14:
Here the people ask God to look down from his holy and glorious heaven. They ask where his zeal and might are, along with his yearning and compassion for them. The words "yearning" and "compassion" speak of his deep, tender care. The question "Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained" asks whether those expressions of his love toward us have been held back or stopped.

The people speaking are Israel, probably in a time of exile or hardship, though scholars place it in different settings. Before this verse they recall how God led them through the wilderness and the sea. Now they feel far from him and confess that he alone is their Father and Redeemer.

For today: when you feel God is distant, you can pray honestly, as they do. Remember what he has already done for you, and ask him with confidence to look on you and help you.
exp.2:1:
God continues the list of what he is going to take away from Jerusalem and Judah: the mighty man, the warrior, the judge, the prophet, the soothsayer, and the elder. These are the leaders who gave the people security, order, and direction. The word "soothsayer" here refers to someone who claimed to know the future; the Bible condemns this practice in other passages, so its mention alongside the prophet shows that there was a mixture of true and false guides.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Judah had turned away from God through injustice and idolatry, and the punishment would be the loss of firm leadership, which would bring disorder and weakness.

For today: let us not place our security only in leaders, institutions, or strong people. Let us pray for those who guide us, ask for wisdom for them, and trust first in God, who sustains all things.
exp.3:0:
It says that, in a future time, seven women will take hold of one man. They say they will provide their own bread and their own clothes, and they ask only to be called by his name and so have their disgrace taken away.

Isaiah speaks of the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem, described at the end of chapter 3. Many men would fall in war, and so many women would be left alone that social disgrace would be great. Some think the number seven is a way of saying "many." The following verse announces hope: God would cleanse and restore his people.

For today: when shame or loss comes, let us not seek just anything that gives us identity or acceptance. God offers us his name and his restoration, and that is what truly sustains us.
exp.2:14:
God asks the leaders of his people a sharp question: "Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor?" To "crush" means to strike or pound hard, and "grind the faces of the poor" is a picture of mistreatment and humiliation. It is an accusation, not a doubt on God's part.

The Lord, the God of hosts, speaks through the prophet Isaiah. It is like a trial against the elders and princes of Judah. They had the duty to care for the people, but they took advantage of the poor and kept for themselves what belonged to them. God takes the case of the weak as something personal: he calls them "my people."

For today: if I have any power, whether at work, at home, or in the church, I must use it to protect and not to abuse. God watches how we treat the most vulnerable.
exp.23:10:
In the streets they cry out for wine, because the drink that marked celebration is gone. All joy turns to gloom, as if night has fallen on it, and rejoicing is cast out of the land.

Isaiah, a prophet of God, speaks within a section (chapters 24 to 27) that describes a judgment upon the whole earth. Scholars debate which city is meant by the "city of confusion": some think of a particular city, and others of a symbol of humanity living without God. The message is that when the covenant with God is broken, the joys that do not rest on him come to an end.

Today we can ask ourselves what our joy is based on. Pleasures pass away, but God does not. Let us seek in him a gladness that does not depend on circumstances.
exp.48:21:
He says that God himself, the Lord GOD, will raise a mighty sign to the nations. The phrases "lifting up the hand" and "raising the banner" are gestures of calling, like a signal for people to gather together. As a result, the peoples will bring back the sons and daughters of Israel, carrying them in their arms and on their shoulders, with care. "The nations" here refers to the peoples beyond Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Zion, or Jerusalem, who felt abandoned, alone and without children during the exile. The people doubted that God remembered them. God answers by promising restoration. Some see here the return from Babylon; others also see a broader fulfillment in the future.

For today: when you feel forgotten or without hope, remember that God has not left you. He can work in unexpected ways, and his care is tender. Wait on him with confidence.
exp.64:0:
God says he revealed himself to people who did not ask for him, and he was found by people who did not seek him. To a nation that did not call on his name, he said, "Here I am! Here I am!"

Isaiah is the prophet through whom God speaks. The verses that follow describe a rebellious people, to whom God kept reaching out his hands all day long. Some understand the "nation that did not call on his name" to be the non-Jewish nations, and Paul applies it that way in Romans 10:20. Others see it as referring to Israel itself, since God kept offering himself even to those who did not seek him. Both readings show his initiative.

For today: God seeks us first, even when we are distracted. If you sense his call today, respond simply. And pray for someone far away, trusting that God can also go out to meet them.
exp.28:0:
A painful warning is coming to Ariel, a name given to Jerusalem, the city where King David camped. "Woe" expresses grief and a warning of judgment. "Year upon year let your festivals recur" describes the people continuing their yearly cycle of religious feasts, one after another.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. The exact meaning of "Ariel" is debated: it may point to the "lion of God" or to the altar where the sacrifices were burned. The people kept their rituals, but their hearts were far from God, and for that reason an enemy siege would come.

For today: keeping a religious routine is not enough if the heart is not with God. Today you can ask yourself whether your prayer, your church, and your customs come from a sincere love for Him, and ask Him to renew your heart.
exp.44:8:
Woe is coming to the one who argues with God, his Maker. A piece of clay is one of many clay pots on the earth, so a person who quarrels with God is like one ordinary clay pot trying to talk back to the potter who shaped it. The clay has no right to ask the potter, "What are you making?" Nor can the work say, "He has no hands," as if the potter does not know what he is doing.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He announces that he will use Cyrus, a foreign king, to free his people from exile. Some Israelites doubted or complained that God would act in this way. God reminds them that he is in control and that his plans have a purpose.

Today we can trust God even when we do not understand what he allows. We can bring our questions to him honestly, as the psalms do, without accusing him of not knowing what he is doing. His hand is wise and loving.
exp.47:0:
God calls the people's attention: "Listen to this, O house of Jacob." They bear the name of Israel and have descended from the line of Judah. They swear by the name of the LORD and invoke the God of Israel, but not in truth or righteousness, that is, without sincerity or an upright life.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses a people who took pride in their religious identity but lived with a divided heart. His rebuke seeks to awaken them, not to destroy them. The verses that follow show that they relied on their holy city and on their name.

For today: it is not enough to say that we believe in God or to use religious words. Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is sincere and whether it shows in how we treat others and in how we live each day.
exp.50:1:
God tells his people to look back, to Abraham and to Sarah, the ones who gave them their beginning. Sarah is the one who gave them birth as a nation. God reminds them that when he called Abraham, he was only one man, and yet he blessed him and multiplied him.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah to Israelites who are discouraged, probably in times of exile or great weakness. They are few and feel forsaken. God reminds them that their beginning was humble: one man alone and a woman who gave them birth. If God could do that then, he can fulfill the promises of comfort that still follow.

For today: when you feel small or alone, remember that God often begins with little. Trust that he can make grow what seems weak, and take the next step of obedience.
exp.26:10:
The branches of a tree dry out and snap off, and women gather them to make a fire. In the same way, this people will be judged: because they lacked understanding, meaning they did not want to know or obey God, their Maker will show them no compassion. The one who will show no compassion refers to the people, and the phrase "has no compassion" means he will not feel pity for them.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier, the text speaks of cleansing the sin of Jacob by removing the altars and the false idols, and of a strong city left deserted. Scholars debate which city is meant. Even so, the verse shows judgment on spiritual foolishness, and then God promises to gather those who have been scattered.

For today: let us not harden our hearts. Let us seek to understand God through his Word and prayer, obey him while there is still time, and trust in his mercy.
exp.1:17:
He says that God will completely remove the idols, meaning the images and the things people give the place that belongs to Him alone. "Will vanish completely" means that none will be left. The word "idols" here refers to figures made by human hands and worshiped as gods.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He describes a time when God will judge human pride. Earlier he mentions ships, riches, and valuable things in which people trusted. The message is that everything people lift up will fall, and only God will remain lifted up. Scholars understand this "day" in different ways: as historical judgments, as the end of time, or as both.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, success, reputation, or comfort. We can give that place to God and trust in Him, before those things fail us.
exp.16:5:
After the judgment, only a small remnant will be left. It is like an olive tree that has been beaten to gather its fruit: on the top of the tree only two or three olives remain, and on the fruitful branches, four or five. The gleanings are the few fruits left behind after the harvest. The olive tree is the tree itself.

Isaiah announces that God will leave Damascus and the northern kingdom, Israel (Jacob), without strength, since they had trusted in human alliances and in their idols. The Lord declares this through the prophet. The judgment is severe, but it is not total: a remnant remains. The verses that follow show that this remnant will turn its eyes back to its Maker.

For today: when life leaves you with little, do not lose hope. God can use those few olives to draw you closer to Him and teach you to trust in Him, not in your own securities.
exp.25:19:
God invites his people to go into their rooms, shut their doors behind them, and hide themselves for a little while, until his wrath has passed. The phrase about going into their rooms refers to the private rooms of the house. The word "wrath" refers to God's judgment against evil.

The prophet Isaiah speaks these words for God. Before this, the people confessed their helplessness and held to the hope of the resurrection of the dead. After this, God comes out to call to account the wickedness and violence on the earth. Interpreters differ: some see a picture of physical shelter, others a picture of trusting God during judgment. The text does not make this clear.

When everything feels uncertain or unjust, there is no need to respond with fear or haste. You can step aside for a moment, pray, and rest in God, trusting that he cares for his own and will bring about justice in his time.
exp.58:2:
This verse describes the people's sin using the image of a whole body: hands stained with blood, fingers full of wickedness, lips that speak lies, and a tongue that mutters injustice. "Stained" means dirty or soiled. "Wickedness" is injustice, doing what is not right.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. The verse before makes clear that God is able to save and able to hear. The problem is not His power, but that the people's sin had separated them from Him. That is why the prophet shows them plainly what they were doing: violence, deceit, and injustice. Scholars debate the exact date of this passage, but the message is clear.

For today: before we think that God is far away, it is wise to examine honestly our actions and our words. We can ask for forgiveness and begin to speak the truth and to treat others well.
exp.42:19:
It says that even the wild animals of the field, such as the jackals and the ostriches, will give honor to God. The reason is that He will provide water in dry and empty places. The word "wilderness" here refers to uninhabited, arid land. That water is for His people, whom He calls "My chosen people."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a discouraged people who were living, or would live, in exile. He asks them not to remain tied to the past, because He is doing something new. This promise of rivers in the desert is understood as an image of rescue and return, and many believers also see it as a sign of the renewal that God gives.

For today: if you are going through a dry season, do not conclude that God has forgotten you. Bring that area of your life to Him in prayer and wait with confidence, because He knows how to open a path where we see only desert.
exp.6:10:
God tells King Ahaz to ask for a sign, a proof that would confirm his promise. The sign can be as deep as Sheol or as high as the heavens. The word translated "ask" here means asking for it. God gives him complete freedom to ask.

The LORD speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to the king of Judah. Ahaz was afraid because Syria and Ephraim (Israel) had joined forces against him. God promises him that this threat will not succeed, but Ahaz does not trust. Then he answers with a false humility: "I will not ask." In reality, it seems he was already looking for another way out, and the Bible shows him to be distrustful.

God invites trust, not living in fear. When you doubt, you can speak to him honestly and ask him for strength to believe. But avoid hiding your distrust behind phrases that sound pious.
exp.40:2:
He pursues his enemies, going on safely and hardly touching the path with his feet. He moves forward without any stumble, secure and unharmed. He is walking along a road that is new to him, where his feet have never trodden before. The phrase "pursues them" means he goes after them, and "going on safely" means he gets through without being hurt.

God speaks, calling the nations to judgment as if in a courtroom. He asks who raised up that righteous man from the east. Many understand this as Cyrus, king of Persia, though others see it differently, even as Abraham. The point is that the LORD directs history, and so the nations should not trust in their idols.

For today: when you face an unfamiliar path, such as a change of job, city, or season of life, remember that God already knows that ground. Ask him for direction, take the next step with humility, and trust that he sustains you.
exp.35:16:
He says that the king of Assyria promises the people of Jerusalem that, after a while, he will take them to another land like their own, rich in grain and new wine and full of bread and vineyards. Grain refers to the harvested crops of the field, new wine is the fresh juice of the grape, and vineyards are the fields where grapes grow.

The one speaking is Rabshakeh, a spokesman for King Sennacherib, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants the people to surrender and stop trusting in Hezekiah and in God. It sounds kind, but it is an offer of exile: he asks them to leave their land in exchange for peace and comfort.

For today: sometimes temptations come with pretty, attractive promises. Before accepting an offer that pulls us away from trust in God, it is wise to ask where it really leads and what it asks us to leave behind in exchange.
exp.60:9:
The speaker says they will rejoice greatly in the Lord and that their soul will exult in their God. The reason is that God has clothed them with garments of salvation and wrapped them in a robe of righteousness. The verse compares this to a bridegroom who wears a priestly headdress and to a bride who adorns herself with her jewels. Adorning means dressing up and decorating oneself.

In this passage the speaker is the prophet, or the anointed servant described in Isaiah 61:1-3, and it can also be understood as the voice of the restored people. Some see here a reference to Jesus; others, to Israel. The surrounding context speaks of God's everlasting covenant and of his people being recognized as blessed. That is why this song is a response of gratitude.

For today: salvation and righteousness are not earned, they are received as a gift. When you feel unworthy, remember that God clothes you. Give thanks to him today with a song, a prayer, or a testimony.
exp.12:4:
They are coming from faraway lands, from the ends of the heavens. The LORD himself comes, together with the weapons of his wrath, to carry out his judgment. The phrase "to destroy the whole country" may refer to the whole territory of the empire being judged, although the language also anticipates a wider judgment.

Isaiah speaks against Babylon. God gathers nations and troops to judge its pride and its violence. Those who are set apart are the ones God has dedicated to that task. Many understand this to refer to the Medes, although the text also points to the final day of the LORD.

For today: God rules over the nations and does not overlook injustice. This invites us to live with humility, not to trust in human power, and to seek his mercy now, while there is still time.
exp.38:7:
Hezekiah answers Isaiah that the word of the LORD is "good," meaning he accepts it as right. He then says that at least there will be peace and security in his lifetime. Here the idea of "security" captures the stability he hopes to enjoy.

Isaiah had just announced that Babylon would carry off the treasures of the palace and some of the king's own descendants. Hezekiah had shown his riches to the Babylonian envoys. Scholars debate his attitude: some see humility and submission; others see a somewhat selfish relief because the punishment would not fall on him. The text does not make this clear.

We can learn to accept God's correction without arguing against it. But it is also wise to think beyond our own comfort: our decisions today affect those who come after us. Let us ask God to give us wisdom to care for the next generation.
exp.10:3:
He says that the King who is coming will not judge by favoritism. He will defend the poor with righteousness and decide fairly for the lowly of the earth. The word for "decide" refers to settling a case in their favor, so he will take up the cause of those who have no one else to speak for them. The rod of his mouth and the breath of his lips show that his word carries the authority to bring down wickedness. The wicked are the ones who do evil.

Isaiah prophesies in the name of God. He speaks of a descendant of Jesse, the father of David, on whom the Spirit of the Lord rests. Judah was living under unjust leaders, and the prophet promises a different ruler. Christians see Jesus in this announcement. What follows, with the wolf and the lamb, describes the peace that his reign will bring.

For today: trust that God sees those whom no one defends. And strive to treat everyone with justice, without judging only by appearances or by rumors.
exp.56:9:
They wore themselves out on many journeys, yet they never said, "There is no hope!" Admitting that would have meant recognizing that those roads led nowhere. Instead, they found renewal of their strength, and because of that they did not grow weak, and so they did not turn back to God.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, whom he describes as an unfaithful wife who seeks alliances and idols. Scholars debate whether this refers mainly to idolatry, to political alliances with other nations, or to both. God shows them that their stubbornness kept them from seeing their error.

For today: sometimes we grow weary seeking security in work, money, or people, and we tell ourselves, "one more effort." Today you can stop, admit that this does not save you, and return to God with humility.
exp.12:6:
This verse says that, when the day of the Lord comes, all hands will fall limp and every person's heart will melt with fear. "Will fall limp" means they will be left without strength, drained and hanging down. "Melt" means to dissolve or lose all firmness, like something that loses its solidity.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces judgment against Babylon and, in a broader sense, against the pride of the nations. The verses before this one describe God gathering an army to act. That is why verse 7 shows the human reaction: neither strength nor courage helps when divine judgment arrives. Some see this as already fulfilled in history, and others also read it as a warning of the final judgment.

For today: do not trust in your own strength or your own security. Live with humility and draw near to God now, for He offers forgiveness and rest to whoever turns to Him.
exp.21:1:
God speaks to Jerusalem, here called a "city of commotion" and a "town of revelry." He says the city is loud, restless, and given to celebration. But its dead did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. While danger draws near, the people celebrate on their rooftops without taking it seriously. The leaders flee and are captured, and the prophet weeps. It is not known with certainty which moment he has in mind; some scholars think of an Assyrian siege and others of a Babylonian one. It is also unclear how those dead died, perhaps of hunger or disease.

Today, let us not ignore God's warnings with distractions and false cheer. And when others suffer, let us imitate Isaiah: let us weep with them and truly help.
exp.59:6:
It says that the peoples of the desert will bring their best animals to Jerusalem. Kedar and Nebaioth were nomadic tribes, descendants of Ishmael, rich in flocks. "All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you" means they will be gathered and brought. "Go up on My altar with acceptance" means God will receive them gladly. "I will adorn My glorious house" refers to the temple, which God promises to honor and beautify.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Jerusalem. The chapter announces that, after times of sorrow, God's light will shine upon her and the nations will come to worship. Scholars understand it in several ways: as hope for the return from exile, or as an announcement of a greater future time. Many Christians see here an image of people from all nations coming to God.

For today: God gladly receives what is offered from the heart. Put your time or your talents at God's service today, with joy and without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.13:31:
When envoys from other nations come to ask what is happening, the answer is simple: the LORD has founded Zion, Jerusalem, and there His afflicted people will find refuge. The point of "find refuge" is that they will run to God for protection.

Isaiah speaks here in a message against Philistia, a neighboring nation that had oppressed Israel. He announces that judgment will come upon it, while God's afflicted people will be cared for. Some think the envoys come to ask about the fall of Philistia or to seek alliances, but the text does not spell this out, and readers have understood it in different ways.

For today: when you feel weak or afflicted, do not place your security in human alliances or in your own strength. Run to God, who remains a firm refuge for his people. And if someone asks you where your hope is, you can answer with the same simplicity: the LORD founded it.
exp.56:3:
God asks some of the people pointed questions: Whom are you mocking? At whom do you sneer and stick out your tongue? To "mock" is to make fun of someone, and sneering and sticking out the tongue are gestures of contempt. Then he calls them "children of transgression" and "offspring of deceit," that is, people who turn away from him and live in deception.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Shortly before, the righteous man dies and enters peace. Now God addresses those who practiced idolatry and mocked the faithful. His questions are meant to make them see their sin and realize that, at heart, they are mocking God himself.

For today: before we mock someone for their faith or for the way they live, let us remember that God sees the heart. Let us ask him for humility to correct ourselves and for respect to treat everyone with dignity.
exp.9:31:
The explanation says that the enemy army, advancing toward Jerusalem, will halt at Nob, a town very close to the city. From there it will shake a fist, a gesture of threat, at the mount of Daughter Zion, also called "the hill of Jerusalem." The word "today" points to the immediacy of the moment, as if the army has arrived within sight of its goal.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah. He describes the march of Assyria, naming towns along the road, as if the danger were drawing closer step by step. Many understand this as a prophetic picture rather than an exact itinerary. Right after, God shows that He Himself will bring down the pride of the invader, like someone cutting down a forest.

For today: when the problem seems to be at the gates, remember that God still rules over it. Bring your fear before God in prayer and trust that no power, however great it may seem, has the final word.
exp.42:4:
God speaks to his people and tells them not to be afraid, because he is with them. The word "offspring" here means descendants, that is, the children and descendants of Israel. God promises to gather them from the east and the west, that is, from faraway places. "I will bring" means to bring together those who had been scattered.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. His people lived under the threat of exile and scattering. God reminds them that they are precious to him: "you were precious in my eyes, and I have loved you." The promise rests on that love. Many understand it to point to the return from Babylon, and others also see a broader fulfillment in God's people gathered from everywhere.

Today, when you feel afraid or find yourself far from everything, remember that God loves you and is with you. Pray today and say to him: "Lord, I trust in your company."
exp.13:17:
The explanation says that all the kings of the nations, when they die, lie in state, each in his own tomb. "Lie in state" here means they are laid down in death with honor, and each is given a proper resting place.

Isaiah is delivering a prophetic taunt against the king of Babylon, whom the text names as the king of Babylon at the beginning of the chapter. The other kings receive an honorable burial, but this one does not. He will be cast out of his tomb and despised, because he was cruel: he destroyed cities, killed his people, and never released the prisoners. Some think he also speaks of a spiritual power behind that pride, but the text is clearly addressed to a human king.

For today: what we leave behind at the end of life depends on how we used the power we had. Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat with justice and compassion those who depend on us.
exp.29:20:
God says he will guide his people with a clear voice. That voice will be heard "behind you," like a guide who walks behind you and tells you which way to go. The message is: "This is the way. Walk in it." Whether you turn to the right or to the left, the command comes from behind, so you are not left to wander off to either side.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah, a people who sought help in Egypt instead of trusting God. Before this promise, he announces that God will be merciful and will answer their cry. Even though there will be days of hardship and suffering, God's guides will not disappear. Then the people will give up their idols.

For today: when you have to make a decision, do not rush or rely only on your own opinion. Read the Bible, pray, and listen to the advice of wise people. God usually guides step by step, and his direction never contradicts his Word.
exp.44:15:
They will all be put to shame and humiliated, and the makers of idols will depart together in disgrace. Those who make idols are the people who craft images to worship them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel. In the verses before this one, the nations acknowledge that the God of Israel is the only God, though at times he seems hidden, that is, he is not always seen acting. After verse 16, God promises lasting salvation to his people. The contrast is clear: idols fail, but God saves.

Today we can ask ourselves what takes the place of God in our hearts: money, fame, success, or approval. All of these end up disappointing us. Trusting in God gives us a firm hope that does not put us to shame.
exp.29:1:
Some of the people of Judah set out on the road to Egypt to seek help, but they did not ask God for his advice. "Without asking my advice" means they did not seek his direction. They wanted to lean on Pharaoh's power, the Egyptian king, and find shelter under Egypt's protection.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah faced the threat of Assyria, and its leaders looked for an alliance with Egypt instead of trusting the Lord. God calls this sin, because it was a way of setting him aside. The passage that follows warns that such help would end in shame.

For today: before making an important decision, whether about money, work, or family, pray first and seek God's guidance in his Word. You may ask for advice and use resources, but do not let them take the place of God.
exp.44:24:
The explanation says that all the people of Israel, that is, their descendants, will be declared righteous and will have reason to rejoice and be glad, but not because of their own merits, but because of what God does. To be declared righteous means to be accepted as right before God. To rejoice in him means to find joy and confident praise in him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just declared that every knee will bow before him and that those who oppose him will be put to shame. This verse is the other side of that: those who turn to him receive righteousness and joy. Some see here a future fulfillment for Israel; others also see a promise open to all the nations, since the context reaches out to "all the ends of the earth."

For today: do not look for your worth in what you achieve or in comparing yourself with others. Rest in the fact that God is the one who declares you righteous when you trust in him, and let that give you a quiet and humble joy.
exp.65:15:
God himself will judge all people, using fire and the sword as images of his judgment. "All flesh" means every human being. The ones who fall under that judgment are "slain by the LORD," and they will be many.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, passing on God's words at the end of the book. Earlier, God promises comfort and joy to his faithful servants. Then he points to those who practice a false religion, mixed with things he calls an abomination. Some scholars see here a judgment that is near, and others see a final one; the text allows both readings.

For today: God sees our deeds and thoughts. Examine your heart with honesty and trust in his mercy, seeking a genuine faith and not merely religious appearance.
exp.18:20:
It says that Egypt, which before did not know the God of Israel, will come to know him "on that day." Egypt will worship him with sacrifices and offerings. The Egyptians will also make vows to the LORD and keep them, that is, they will make solemn promises to God and follow through on them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. Earlier he announced judgment on Egypt, but here he promises something surprising: Egypt, a powerful nation and at times an enemy of Israel, will also call out to God and be healed. Some see here a future fulfillment, others see a foretaste of the gospel reaching all nations. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: no one is too far away for God to reach. Pray for people or peoples who seem distant from God, and if you have made God a promise, keep it with sincerity.
exp.39:29:
This verse says that even young people, who are the strongest and fullest of energy, become exhausted and worn down. The words "youths" and "young men" both refer to the young. The Hebrew words behind this verse, one meaning to lose strength and the other showing that they stumble or collapse, are rendered here as "grow tired and weary" and "stumble and fall."

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Israel, who were discouraged and felt that God did not see their situation. Many believe he addresses people in exile, though scholars explain this in different ways. Isaiah compares human strength, which runs out, with God, who never grows tired and gives strength to the weak.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. When you feel tired, whether from work, family, or life, acknowledge your limits and pray sincerely. Take a few minutes to wait on God, asking him to sustain you today.
exp.0:20:
It says that Jerusalem, the city that once was faithful to God, has now become like an unfaithful woman. The image of a prostitute is a strong way to describe unfaithfulness to God. The word "justice" here means fairness, equal and honest treatment for everyone. The verse says that where justice and righteousness once lived in the city, now only murderers are found, which shows how far things have fallen into violence and abuse.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to Judah and Jerusalem. God has just offered them a way out: obey and live well, or rebel and suffer the consequences. Here He grieves painfully over what they have become. The verses that follow explain the problem: corrupt leaders who love bribes and neglect the fatherless and the widow.

For today: examine whether your faith shows in how you treat the weak. God does not seek only religious words, but justice and compassion. Today you can help or defend someone who has no one else to do so.
exp.60:4:
It says that people from other nations, called "foreigners" and "strangers" here, will do the field work for Israel. They will tend the sheep and work the land and the vineyards. To "feed" the flocks means to lead the livestock out to graze on pasture, and the "plowmen" and "vinedressers" are those who cultivate the ground and the grapes.

The one speaking is the prophet, announcing God's message to a people who suffered destruction and exile. God promises comfort, restoration, and honor. The verses around it speak of ruined places being rebuilt and of a people called "priests of the LORD." Some see here the return of Israel; others see a wider promise that Christ fulfills (Luke 4:18-21 quotes the beginning of this chapter).

For today: when you feel ruined or without strength, remember that God knows how to restore what was lost and raise up those who have fallen. Trust in Him, and let His grace return hope to you.
exp.31:7:
It says that a noble person makes plans that honor others, and that by these worthy causes he stands up for what is right and holds his ground. The word "noble" here does not speak of politics, but of someone with a good, giving heart. Acts of generosity and integrity are what the verse points to. Standing up for worthy causes means that he stays steady and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In the verses before, he describes the foolish and the greedy, who oppress the poor with deceptive words. Now he sets them in contrast with the noble person. Then he warns the complacent, careless women of Jerusalem that their false sense of security will come to an end.

For today: our thoughts shape our actions. Before the opportunity comes, think about how you could help someone in need, and pray that God will give you a generous heart, determined to do good.
exp.41:3:
The explanation says that the Servant of God will not wear out or give up. Words like "grow weak" and "discouraged" describe losing strength or courage. He will remain steadfast until he has established justice on the earth. The distant lands, the islands, represent faraway peoples who put their hope in his teaching and guidance.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, presenting the Servant chosen by God. He is a gentle servant, who does not shout or crush the weak, like a bruised reed. Christians see Jesus here, and the New Testament quotes this passage in Matthew 12. God promises him strength to carry out his mission.

For today: when you feel weary of doing good, remember that Christ does not give up on you. Rest in his strength and keep serving with tenderness.
exp.26:4:
God asks whether anyone will lay claim to his protection. Then he invites them: let them make peace with him, yes, let them truly make peace with him.

Here "lay claim" means to take hold of something that is rightfully available, and "protection" can be understood as shelter or refuge. Some see this as an invitation to seek refuge in God.

The Lord speaks, and in this passage he cares for his people, whom he calls his vineyard. He says he has no anger toward her and that he will destroy the enemies, compared to thorns and briers. Even so, he leaves the door open: whoever opposes him may be reconciled and find peace. Scholars interpret this phrase in various ways.

For today: if there is something in your life that keeps you from God, do not put it off. Come to him with sincerity, for he offers peace and care to those who come to his protection.
exp.2:10:
It says that the one who lives in wickedness will have a bad end, because he will be repaid for what he has done. The word "wicked" refers to the person who lives without reverence for God. "Woe" is an expression of grief and warning. "Disaster is upon them" points to trouble that is already on its way. "They will be repaid with what their hands have done" means that people receive back according to their own deeds.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah and Jerusalem. The people had unjust leaders, and many sinned openly, without shame, as in Sodom. The verses around it contrast the wicked with the righteous, who will eat the fruit of their deeds. God appears as a judge who defends his people and calls to account those who deceive them.

Today it reminds us that our decisions have consequences. Before acting, ask yourself: "What am I sowing with this?" Ask God for help to sow honesty, justice and kindness, trusting that he sees everything.
exp.27:11:
It says that God offered his people a place of rest and repose: a way of life where the weary could rest and find true peace. That was the peace God wanted to give them. But they would not listen. The word "repose" means calm and restful stillness, the kind of relief a person finds when they have been worn down for a long time.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in Jerusalem to leaders and people who mocked his message. They treated him as if he were speaking only in endless repetition, "line upon line," as if to children. God says that if they will not hear his clear voice, he will speak to them through foreigners, and that will be judgment. There are different ways to understand who the "weary" is, but the general sense is clear.

Today, we can seek rest in God and also be rest for others. This week, help someone who is exhausted with a visit, a meal, or a kind word, and listen humbly to what God is saying to you.
exp.49:0:
Here God speaks to his people through questions. A "certificate of divorce" was the written paper that ended a marriage, and "creditors" are the people who lend money and collect debts. God asks: where is the certificate of divorce with which I sent away your mother? To which creditor did I sell you? There is none. God says they were sold because of their wrongdoing, and the mother was sent away because of their rebellion.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah to a people who were in exile and believed that God had abandoned them forever. God answers that the separation did not happen because of any lack of love or power on his part, but because of the people's sin.

For today: when you feel that God is far away, examine your heart honestly and do not assume that he has abandoned you. Return to him, because his hand has not been shortened to save.
exp.47:11:
God asks his people to listen to him. He reminds them that they belong to him, because he has called them. When he says "I am He; I am the first, and I am the last," he declares that he has always existed and will always exist. Nobody was before him, and nobody will come after him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people live through trials, and God says he chose them in the furnace of affliction. The verses that follow show his power as Creator and announce that he will act against Babylon. God wants Israel to trust in him and not in idols or human powers.

For today: when you go through a trial, remember that God did not begin with you and will not leave you unfinished. He is the first and the last, and your story is in his hands. Take a few minutes today to listen to him in prayer and in his Word, and rest in his care.
exp.41:17:
This verse is a direct call. God tells the deaf to listen and the blind to look closely so that they may truly see. Your verse says, "Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see!" It does not speak of a physical disability but of a spiritual condition.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised that he will lead the blind and will not forsake them, and has warned that those who trust in idols will be put to shame. Now he addresses his own people, Israel, who had seen and heard much of God but did not take him seriously. The verses that follow show this: the servant sees many things but does not observe them. Scholars discuss how this servant relates to the earlier passages about the servant of the LORD.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are truly attentive to God or only accustomed to what we already know. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible in silence and ask God to open your eyes and your ears.
exp.0:28:
It says the people will be ashamed of the sacred oaks they took pleasure in and embarrassed by the gardens they chose. The word for the oaks is one that some render as "great trees," and the word for the gardens refers to sacred gardens or orchards. To be embarrassed here means to be left in shame.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the people of Judah. They practiced idol worship under leafy trees, a common practice in Canaanite religion. God announces that he will judge the rebels, but that he will redeem Zion with justice. What today seems a source of security will later bring shame.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust, such as money, prestige, or success. If they are not God, sooner or later they will leave you disappointed. Return to the Lord, who is faithful and does not put to shame those who wait for him.
exp.47:18:
It says that if Israel had obeyed, their descendants would have been as countless as the sand of the sea, and their offspring as numerous as its grains. "Descendants" means the people who come after them, and "offspring" refers to the children born to them. God says that their name would never have been cut off or removed from his presence.

The Lord, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, speaks to a people who did not listen to him. With sorrow, he shows them what they would have received: peace like a river and a large family. Even so, he immediately invites them to leave Babylon, because he still redeems them.

For today: obedience to God is not a burden but the path to a life of peace. Before deciding something, ask yourself what God says, and trust that his correction seeks your good. If you have drifted away, he still calls you to return.
exp.0:1:
God calls the heavens and the earth to listen, as if they were witnesses at a trial. Then he says that he raised his children and brought them up, that is, he cared for them and helped them grow, but they rebelled against him. The words "listen" and "give ear" point to the same idea here, to pay attention and take in what is said.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, who received this vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of several kings. God brings a complaint like that of a wounded father. What follows shows that his people do not even recognize him, while an ox knows its owner.

For today: let us remember how much we have received from God and not take it for granted. One practical way is to thank him each day for something specific, and to ask him to help us obey him with a grateful heart.
exp.39:23:
This verse describes powerful rulers as plants that have barely had time to put down roots. As soon as they begin to grow, God blows on them and they wither. Then a whirlwind, or strong wind, sweeps them away like stubble, that is, like dry stalks and light straw.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people who live under the shadow of very strong empires. He wants to remind them that God is far greater than any king or nation. That is why, in what follows, God asks: "To whom then will you liken me?" No one is his equal.

For today: when you feel afraid before people or situations that seem enormous and unstoppable, remember that none of them is greater than God. You can bring your worry to him in prayer and trust that he still governs.
exp.22:8:
The LORD of Hosts planned this. He says that God himself decided what would happen to Tyre. His purpose was to defile all its glorious beauty, to strip away the pride that rests on human splendour. He also meant to disgrace the renowned people of the earth, those famous and respected figures, and bring them low.

Isaiah speaks in a prophecy against Tyre, a Phoenician city very rich from sea trade. Its merchants were treated like princes. The prophet answers the question "who decided this?": it was not chance or only the politics of empires, but God. Scholars debate which exact historical moment is meant, and that remains open.

For today: money, prestige, or achievements can give us a false sense of security. Today we can examine what we boast in and place our trust in God, who gives everything we have and sustains what truly lasts.
exp.14:2:
They say that the people of Moab will wear sackcloth in their streets. On the rooftops and in the public squares, they will all wail, falling down in weeping. The word "wail" means to cry out in anguish, and the phrase "falling down weeping" suggests grief so deep that they can barely stand.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, announces a message of judgment against Moab, a people neighboring Israel. Their cities fall in the night, suddenly, and mourning fills the whole land. Even so, the prophet shows his own sorrow: "My heart cries out for Moab" (v. 5). Scholars debate which exact invasion is meant; the text does not name it clearly.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, yet the prophet does not rejoice in another's fall. We can learn to weep with those who suffer, even with those far from us, and to pray for them with compassion rather than mockery.
exp.47:6:
God says that these new things "are created now", meaning that He is bringing them into being right now. You have not heard of them before today, so you cannot claim, "I already knew them!" "Created" means made or brought into existence.

God speaks through Isaiah to Israel, a stubborn people who credited events to their idols. God had already announced past events so that they would not attribute them to the idols. Now He reveals new and hidden things, so that they will recognize that only He governs history. Scholars disagree about exactly which new things are meant, but the context points to the deliverance from Babylon.

Today we can give God credit for the good we experience, without saying "I already knew that" or "it was my luck." Thank Him today for one specific blessing.
exp.31:10:
Isaiah says that the women who live at ease should shudder and be troubled, and that the careless ones should tremble. The phrase "ladies of leisure" describes women who live without worry. Stripping yourselves bare means taking off their fine clothing. Putting sackcloth around the waist means wearing rough cloth as a sign of mourning, sorrow, and repentance.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to well-off women of Judah. They lived secure while the people were turning away from God. The prophet announces that the harvest will fail and the land will be overrun with thorns. Many believe this refers to a near crisis, such as an invasion or famine, but the text gives no exact date.

Today, comfort can dull the heart. Ask yourself: what am I trusting in, my possessions or God? Set aside a few minutes this week to pray with humility, give thanks for what you have, and ask God to awaken you wherever you have become indifferent.
exp.53:11:
God promises his people a beautiful and secure city. Its pinnacles will be made of rubies, its gates of sparkling jewels, and all its walls of precious stones.

The LORD speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as a poor, weary, and comforted woman. He first assures her that his mercy and his covenant of peace will not change, even though the mountains may be moved. The image of jewels expresses restoration, care, and worth, more than a literal description.

For today: if you feel tired or discouraged, remember that God not only comforts you, but also rebuilds with care what is broken. You can hand over a difficult situation to him today and trust that his faithfulness does not depend on your circumstances.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that when God rises to judge the earth, people will flee to hide in caverns in the rocks and in crevices in the cliffs. The verse speaks of a terror so great that people will run to hide, and of a splendor of God's majesty so overwhelming that they cannot stand before it. The "splendor of His majesty" is the bright, radiant greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. He denounces the pride and idolatry of the people, who trusted in wealth and idols. He announces the day of judgment, when everything man exalts will be brought low and only God will be great. The verses that follow call people not to trust in human beings, who are as fragile as a breath.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, success, or people. All of that can fall. Trust in God, who alone is firm, and live with reverence toward Him.
exp.57:0:
God tells the prophet to speak out loudly and without fear. The words "Cry aloud" mean to shout with all your strength. "Do not hold back" means not to hold anything back or pull away. The voice should be raised like a ram's horn, a sound that wakes people up and warns them of danger. The message is clear: to declare to the people their rebellion and their sin.

Here God speaks to the prophet Isaiah. The people seemed very religious: they sought God every day and fasted. But, according to the verses that follow, their lives did not match their practice. God confronts them because their religion was only on the outside. Scholars debate the exact date, but the message is directed to Israel.

Today, it is worth asking ourselves honestly whether our faith shows in our daily life. And if we speak to others about their mistakes, let us do it with truth and with love, seeking that they return to God.
exp.50:18:
This verse speaks to Jerusalem and reminds her of her suffering. The reader's wording says these pairs have befallen her: devastation and destruction, famine and sword. "Devastation and destruction" names total ruin, and the two pairs describe disasters that came upon her in quick succession. The question "Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you?" shows that no one seemed to pity or console her.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here in God's name. The city had suffered God's judgment for its sin, and its children lay fallen and without guidance. The text probably looks to the fall of Jerusalem, though not every detail can be pinned down. But the passage does not end in punishment: what follows (v. 22) is that God himself will take up her cause and remove the cup of his wrath.

For today: when you feel alone in your pain, do not stay silent. God sees your affliction and can comfort you in ways no one else can. Bring your brokenness to him in prayer.
exp.65:8:
It says that God, who gives the ability to bring forth, will not leave unfinished what He has begun. "Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?" means that He brings things to the moment of life and then brings them through. "Or will I who deliver close the womb?" is the picture of God stopping a birth that He has already started. The expected answer is no: God completes what He starts.

The Lord speaks through Isaiah, at the end of the book. Zion, that is Jerusalem, appears as a mother who suddenly gives birth to a new people. It is an image of restoration that seems impossible. Scholars see it as a promise for the return from exile, and many also as a foreshadowing of something greater, still to be fulfilled.

For today: if God has started something in your life or in your family, even if it takes a long time or seems stuck, trust that He is faithful to complete it. Wait with prayer and patience.
exp.48:11:
God's people will return from very distant places. Some will come from far away, others from the north and the west, and others from the land of Aswan. The exact meaning of "Aswan" as a place name in this verse is not fully agreed upon. Some take it as a reference to a distant region to the south, linked with the city of Aswan in Egypt, but this is uncertain.

God speaks to Israel, who lives in exile and feels abandoned. He has already promised to guide them, give them water, and open paths for them. This verse shows that the promise is broad: God will gather his people from every direction. Shortly afterward, Zion says that God has forgotten her, and the Lord answers with tenderness.

For today: if you feel far away or forgotten, remember that God knows where you are and can bring you back. No distance, mistake, or loneliness is too great for his care. Trust his guidance and take the next step toward him.
exp.44:9:
It is a serious thing to bring a complaint against parents for having brought a child into the world. The words "fathered" and "gave birth" refer to the father who gives life and the mother who brings forth. The "Woe" is a serious warning: someone complains about their origin as if they had no right to question how they were formed.

God speaks through Isaiah, and the passage is addressed to a people in exile who doubted his plans. God had just announced that he would use Cyrus, a foreign king, to help his people. Some may have been troubled by that method. That is why God uses the image of clay and the potter, and now that of parents, to show that it is not fitting to call the one who gives life to account.

Today we can learn to trust God even when we do not understand the way he works. Instead of complaining bitterly, we can bring our questions to him honestly and rest in the knowledge that he knows what he is doing.
exp.6:15:
The explanation says that, before that boy is old enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings that Ahaz dreads will be laid waste. The word "dread" describes the fear and dislike that Ahaz felt toward that land. The idea behind the verse is to reject evil, meaning to refuse it and turn away from it.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz of Judah, who was frightened by the threat from the kings of Syria and Israel. God offers him a sign so that he will trust in Him and not in human alliances. Christians see in the child Emmanuel a final fulfillment in Jesus, as Matthew 1 says. Some scholars think there was also a nearer fulfillment in the time of Ahaz. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

When fear presses on you, remember that God keeps His promises in His own time. Before looking for hasty solutions, ask Him to increase your trust in Him.
exp.37:11:
He says his dwelling is being pulled up and carried away from him, like a shepherd's tent taken down and moved elsewhere. He also compares his life to cloth a weaver rolls up and cuts from the loom: it seems to be cut off before it is finished. The phrase "picked up and removed from me" means that his home, that is, his life, is being taken away from him. He feels that God is bringing it to an end between day and night, very quickly.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks here, when he was seriously ill. This song expresses his anguish at the thought that he would die young, in the middle of his days. After praying, God granted him more years of life (Isaiah 38:1-5).

For today: when you feel fragile or see that life is passing quickly, do not hide your pain. Speak with God honestly, as Hezekiah did, and place your days and your future in his hands.
exp.52:7:
He was arrested and condemned without justice, and his life was taken away. "Cut off from the land of the living" means that he died. No one thought about his descendants, or about his future. The question "who can recount his descendants?" can be understood in several ways. What is clear is that he suffered for the rebellion of the people.

In this passage, the prophet speaks of the Suffering Servant. Some believe the speakers are the people and the nations, admitting their guilt. Jews have understood it in different ways. Christians see Jesus here, as Philip did in Acts 8.

Today, this verse invites us not to see Christ's suffering as something distant. He bore what we deserved. We can respond to him with gratitude, confessing our wrongs and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.61:1:
It says that when God makes the righteousness of Jerusalem shine, the nations and their kings will see it. The word "nations" here means peoples or groups of people, and "righteousness" includes both the uprightness and the salvation that God gives to her. Also, God will give her a new name, one that the mouth of the LORD bestows. A new name speaks of a new identity.

The one speaking seems to be the prophet, though some understand it as a voice of the Messiah. He says he will not keep silent until Zion is restored. The people had lived through exile and ruin, and felt abandoned. The verses that follow explain the new name: no longer "Forsaken," but "Hephzibah," which means "my delight is in her."

For today: if you belong to God, your identity is not defined by your failures or by what others have said about you. God names you with love. Today you can live according to what He says about you, and not according to your wounds.
exp.6:9:
This is a brief introduction. It says that God spoke again to King Ahaz, that is, that he continued his message. "Spoke again" means "kept speaking" or "spoke once more." "Ahaz" is the spelling used in this translation.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Isaiah. Ahaz, king of Judah, was afraid because Syria and Ephraim (the northern kingdom) were threatening him. God had just told him to trust, and that if he did not believe, he would not remain firm. Now he gives him another opportunity: he offers him a sign to help him believe. Even so, Ahaz will reject it with an excuse that sounds pious.

For today: God keeps speaking to us with patience, even when we doubt. When you feel fear, do not shut yourself in or look only for human solutions; listen to his Word and respond with sincere faith, not with religious excuses.
exp.47:10:
He says that God will act for his own sake, so that his name will not be dishonored. "Defamed" means having one's good name damaged by false or harmful talk. "Glory" here refers to his honor. God states that he will not yield that glory to anyone else.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who had been rebellious and stubborn. Even so, God holds back his anger and does not destroy them completely. He has tested them in the furnace of affliction, that is, in suffering. Some understand this to refer to the exile in Babylon, though the text does not say so in those words. What matters is that God shows his faithfulness, not the merits of his people.

For today: when you fail or go through trials, remember that your hope rests on the faithful character of God, not on your perfection. Trust in him and live in a way that honors his name.
exp.12:16:
God himself says he will stir up the Medes against Babylon. The Medes are described as people who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold, so they cannot be bought off or stopped with bribes. The point is that wealth will mean nothing to them.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a message from God against Babylon, a proud and violent empire. The harsh scenes of war show judgment on a nation that oppressed others. Historically, the Medes were part of the alliance that later defeated Babylon. Some understand the passage as fulfilled in that event, and others also see a broader picture of God's judgment.

God rules over the nations and does not overlook injustice. Today we can trust that no human power lasts forever, and we can live with humility, seeking justice rather than pride or wealth.
exp.36:27:
God tells the king of Assyria that he knows him completely. "Sitting down" refers to where he settles and rests, "going out and coming in" is everything he does, his comings and goings, and "raging against Me" is his anger aimed at God. Nothing of his life or his pride is hidden from Him. God even knows that this rage is directed against Him.

Speaking through the prophet Isaiah, God addresses Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Hezekiah. God answers that He governs history and that Assyria has been only an instrument in His hands. Then He announces that He will stop the king and make him return the way he came.

For today: God sees everything that happens, including the injustices and abuses that make us suffer. You can rest in the knowledge that no human power is beyond His control. Bring your fears to Him with confidence, and do not take justice into your own hands.
exp.4:20:
This verse is a warning against self-satisfied pride. Those who are "wise in their own eyes" and "clever in their own sight" are people who count themselves clever simply because they think so themselves. The word "woe" expresses grief and a warning of judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. This is a series of six "woes" against injustice: greed, drunkenness, mocking God, and twisted justice. Those who asked God to hurry, as if mocking him, and who called evil good, considered themselves wiser than God. Isaiah shows that this pride lies behind their bad decisions.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I accept advice or correction? One practical way to live out humility is to read the Bible with a willingness to be corrected, and to ask the opinion of wise and sincere people before making important decisions.
exp.56:10:
God asks his people: "Whom have you dreaded and feared, so that you lied and failed to remember Me or take this to heart?" To lie here means to be unfaithful, to betray the trust God has placed in them. God's silence is a patient silence, a time when he did not punish right away. And because of that long silence, God says, the people stopped showing him reverence.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He accuses Israel of seeking help in alliances with kings and nations, and also in idolatrous practices, instead of trusting in him. Some understand the "king" as a foreign ruler or as a false god; the text does not fully clarify this. Even so, God ends by promising good to whoever waits on him.

For today: when you feel fear, do not rush first to your own solutions. Before you act, speak with God and remember that his patience is an invitation to return to him.
exp.23:13:
This verse says that a small group of survivors will raise their voices and sing with joy to honor the greatness of God. Their praise will be heard from the west, and they will proclaim the majesty of the LORD with shouts of joy.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the middle of a announcement of judgment on the earth. The cities are left empty and only a few remain, like the olives left over after the tree has been shaken. Even so, these few praise God. Scholars debate exactly who they are: some think of a faithful remnant of Israel, others of believers from all nations. Later on, the prophet himself laments the wickedness of the people.

For today: even when everything seems lost or in ruins, we can choose to praise God. Our joy does not depend on circumstances, but on who He is.
exp.57:5:
God asks what kind of fasting truly pleases him. It is not only giving up food, but setting others free: breaking the chains of wickedness, untying the cords of the yoke, freeing the oppressed, and tearing off every yoke.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who fasted with great devotion, yet still fought and mistreated others. He tells them their fasting had no value if their daily lives were unjust. He then adds that sharing bread and clothing the naked is also part of that fast.

Today, when we pray or fast, let us also ask ourselves whom we can help. We can pay a fair wage, forgive a debt, stand up for someone, or share food with those who need it.
exp.8:3:
He says that God has shattered the burden that weighed down his people. The "yoke" is the wooden frame placed across the shoulders of working animals, and here it stands for the load their oppressors forced on them. The "bar across their shoulders" and the "rod" of the oppressor point to the same kind of crushing weight and force. All of it was broken. The day of Midian recalls the victory God gave Gideon with a very small army (Judges 7).

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, addressing God. Judah lived under the threat of the Assyrian invasion, and the people were in anguish. Isaiah announces that God will bring freedom, and right away he connects it to the child who is promised, the Prince of Peace. Christians see in him Jesus.

For today: if you carry something that crushes you, such as fear, guilt, or pressure, remember that God knows how to break yokes. Bring that burden to him in prayer and trust that he acts, even when you feel weak.
exp.29:15:
Here God says that his people rejected the salvation he was offering them. They answered, "No, we will flee on horses," meaning they planned to seek escape through military strength and speed. The word "swift" in the verse is the one to note: it means fast. God answers them with irony: if they flee, they will indeed flee, and those who pursue them will be faster than they are.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. The verses just before offered them rest, quietness, and trust in God. Many understand that the people were seeking protection in military alliances, perhaps with Egypt, instead of trusting in God. For that reason the result would be defeat and fear.

When you face a problem, before rushing to your own solutions, stop and pray. Trusting God is not doing nothing, but seeking his direction first and resting in his care.
exp.45:7:
God asks his people to remember what they have just seen: the foolishness of worshiping idols. "Be brave" means facing the truth with courage, admitting that you were wrong. "Take it to heart" means coming back to your senses and reflecting. "Transgressors" are those who rebel and break faithfulness to God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just described how someone pays a silversmith to make a god that must be carried, that does not move and does not answer. Then God reminds them that he is the one who announced the future and carries out his plan. This contrasts the living God with powerless idols.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have put in the place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. If they cannot answer us or save us, it is time to come to our senses and return to God with sincerity.
exp.42:15:
Here God presents himself with a very well-known image: he is the one who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters. The word "surging" here describes waters that are strong and turbulent, moving with great force.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah to a people who would be taken captive to Babylon. He reminds them that he is their Redeemer, their Holy One, and their King. This image is often connected with the crossing of the Red Sea, and the following verse speaks of how God defeated the Egyptian army. In this way he gives them hope that he will again rescue them.

For today: if you face a situation that seems closed off, remember that God has already opened impossible ways before. Trust him and take the next step in faith, even though you cannot yet see the whole route.
exp.56:19:
This verse compares the wicked to the sea during a storm. Its waves never settle, and all they bring up onto the shore is mud and muck. The phrase "storm-tossed sea" describes a sea churned up by a storm, and the idea of being "still" simply means being at peace and calm.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just promised to heal, guide, and comfort his people, offering peace to both those who are far off and those who are near. Then he warns that whoever lives in rebellion and rejects God does not have that peace. Some understand "the wicked" as those who persist in turning away from God, rather than those who repent.

For today: if your heart is troubled by guilt, pride, or worry, do not keep struggling alone. Come to God with sincerity, acknowledge what you have done wrong, and receive his forgiveness and his peace.
exp.43:6:
God issues a challenge to all the false gods: "Who is like Me?" He asks who can do what He does. Let anyone step forward and state their case before Him, since He established the ancient people. Let them foretell what is to come, and what is to take place. To "declare" a matter means to make it known or announce it, and to lay out one's case before God means to present the evidence. Then He invites them to announce what is coming.

Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, who has just said: "I am the first and I am the last." His people were living under pressure and surrounded by religions with idols. God reminds them that He alone knows and directs the future, and that they are His witnesses.

For today: when the future frightens you, remember that God has already spoken and fulfilled His word throughout history. You can rest in Him, instead of seeking security in things that you cannot see and that know nothing.
exp.2:7:
Isaiah 3:8 says that Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen. The reason given is that the people spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence. The phrase "defying His glorious presence" means that they openly resisted God, who sees everything and whose glory is real.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah. The verses before it describe a society without leaders, so weakened that no one wants to rule. Isaiah explains that this collapse is not bad luck, but the result of turning away from God in words and conduct. The exact historical details are interpreted in several ways.

For today: let us examine whether our words and actions agree with what we say we believe. We can ask God to help us speak the truth and live with integrity, because He hears us and sees us with love.
exp.26:6:
This verse asks two questions about Israel. It asks whether the LORD struck Israel as severely as He struck those who oppressed her, or whether Israel was killed the way her enemies were killed. The implied answer is no: Israel's punishment was much milder.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, presenting God's words about His people, whom God compares to a vineyard. The context shows a God who corrects with measure, not with fury. His aim is to purge the sin of Jacob and restore him, so that he will bear fruit again. Some scholars understand "the one who struck him" as the enemy nations, and others read it differently; the general meaning remains the same.

For today: when God corrects us, He does not do it to destroy us, but to cleanse us and make us bear fruit. Receive His correction with confidence, knowing that His discipline is measured and comes from His love.
exp.32:5:
