The verse says that, in the days of Zion, God Himself will be the sure foundation for His people's times, a storehouse of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The most valuable thing for the people will be the fear of the LORD, that is, honoring God and living in reverence toward Him. The word "knowledge" here means understanding of what is true. The phrase "your times" refers to the era in which God sustains His people.

It is a prophecy from Isaiah to Judah, spoken in the midst of threats from invaders and distress. Before this, God is exalted and fills Zion with justice; afterward, messengers are described as weeping and roads as ruined. Many understand that this verse offers hope in the middle of that suffering, although scholars debate which exact moment it refers to.

For today: in times of fear or uncertainty, do not seek security only in money or human plans. Ask God for wisdom and cultivate a sincere respect for Him in everyday life. That reverence is a treasure that is not lost.
exp.37:12:
He says the man spent the night restless, counting the hours and waiting for morning to come. He feels that his suffering is like a lion that breaks all his bones. He believes God is bringing his life to an end, from day until night.

The words "breaks" and "make an end" show how completely he felt overwhelmed.

Here the speaker is King Hezekiah of Judah, after he recovered from a serious illness. Earlier, the prophet Isaiah had told him that he would die (Isaiah 38:1). Here he recalls his anguish, when he believed his life was ending before its time. His language is poetic and very honest.

For today: there is no need to hide pain and fear from God. Hezekiah put them into words and brought them to God, and the text then shows that God responded. When you go through a difficult night, speak to him with sincerity.
exp.18:6:
It says that the bulrushes growing along the Nile, at the river's mouth, and all the fields planted along the Nile will dry up. They will be blown away, and they will cease to exist. The bulrushes are the tall reeds that grow in the water, and the "fields sown along the Nile" are the ground where seed has been planted. The phrase "will be no more" means they will vanish completely.

Isaiah announces a message from God against Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile for its livelihood: food, fishing, flax, and trade. Here God shows that He has power over the very things that people trusted. Many think this refers to a drought or to a judgment on the land, although scholars do not agree on the exact time.

We can ask ourselves where we place our security: in work, money, or health. All of these can fail, but God remains. Today you can thank Him for what you have and trust Him first.
exp.16:2:
It says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel) will lose its stronghold, and that Damascus will lose its sovereignty and no longer rule as a kingdom. The word "fortress" refers to a place of protection or defense. What little remains of Aram (Syria) will be like the splendor of Israel, meaning it will share the same fate: a glory that fades away. "The LORD of Hosts" is the LORD, the one who commands all power.

Isaiah announces this message against Damascus. Israel and Syria had formed an alliance, perhaps seeking security against Assyria. God warns that this alliance would not save them. Many understand that the judgment came because they trusted in human alliances rather than in God, although the historical details are explained in several ways.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, connections, or plans. All of these can fail, but the LORD remains faithful. Trust in Him first and seek His guidance.
exp.24:10:
He says that God will spread out his hands within Moab, the way a swimmer spreads his arms to move through the water. In this way he will bring Moab's pride low, humbling the arrogance it has been holding onto. The reference to the skill of their hands is hard to pin down. Some read it as the skill Moab relies on, and others see Moab thrashing about in the water, unable to save itself.

The prophet Isaiah speaks within a song of praise for God's salvation. Moab, a neighbor of Israel, appears here as an example of a pride that rises up against God and his people. The message is that God brings down the proud and cares for those who wait on him.

Today we can examine our hearts and ask God to free us from pride. If we trust in him, we do not need to win by our own strength; we can wait with humility and patience for his justice.
exp.48:19:
This verse says that the children born in times of loss and sorrow have grown so many that the place has become too small for them. They say to Zion: "This place is too small for us; make room for us to live here." The phrase "too small" means narrow or cramped. The "children of your bereavement" are the children born when she felt alone and without children. "Make room" here means step aside so there is space for them.

God speaks through Isaiah to Jerusalem, called Zion, who felt forsaken during the exile. He promises to restore her and fill her with people. The picture is of a mother who believed she had no children and suddenly sees a huge family. Some also see here a broader promise for the people of God.

For today: when you go through a season of loss or loneliness, do not think that God has finished with you. He can bring fruit and companionship where you did not expect them. And when God gives you more, be ready to make room and receive with generosity.
exp.40:3:
God asks: who has done all this, raising up a conqueror and guiding history? He himself gives the answer: "I, the LORD." He calls forth the generations from the beginning. He is the first, and he is the same with the last, that is, the final ones.

God speaks through Isaiah and challenges the nations that trusted in idols. "The righteous one from the east" is often understood as Cyrus of Persia, though some think of Abraham. The central point is that God directs history, and idols do not.

For today: when the world seems out of control, remember that God was there at the beginning and will be there at the end. You can rest in the knowledge that your life and your time are in his hands, and pray with confidence.
exp.56:8:
God tells his people that they went to Molech with oil and multiplied their perfumes, and that they sent their envoys a great distance. The word "oil" refers to scented oil, the kind used for perfume and anointing. The verse ends by saying they descended even to Sheol, the realm of the dead, which may be a picture of the grave or of utter ruin. Some read "Molech" as the name of a false god, while others understand it as a foreign king with whom Judah sought alliances. The text does not settle the question for certain.

God speaks through Isaiah and accuses Judah of unfaithfulness, like a wife who abandons her husband. They sought security in idols and in foreign powers, instead of trusting God. They wore themselves out in that effort, but they did not repent.

Today we can ask ourselves where we seek security apart from God: money, influence or success. It is better to stop exhausting ourselves on what does not save, and to return to him with trust.
exp.63:3:
From ancient times, the verse says, no one has heard, no ear has perceived, and no eye has seen any God besides you, who acts on behalf of those who wait for him. The words "heard" and "perceived" here mean that people have not grasped or known anything like this.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, praying on behalf of the people of Israel. He asks that God act with power, as he did in the past, and he recalls his wonderful works. The people acknowledge their sin in the verses that follow, but still hold on to the hope that God will save them.

For today: when your situation feels hopeless, do not stop waiting on God. He acts on behalf of those who trust in him. Spend a few minutes in prayer, remembering something God has already done for you, and bring your waiting to him with confidence.
exp.50:8:
Here the people ask God to act. "Arm of the LORD" is a way of speaking about his power. They call on him to awake, to put on strength, and to act as he did in the past. "Rahab" and "the dragon" are figures of chaotic and hostile powers; many think they point to Egypt and its defeat in the Exodus. And the question "Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces, who pierced through the dragon?" reminds God, and the reader, that he has already won.

The one speaking seems to be the people of Israel, or the prophet speaking on their behalf, crying out in the midst of exile. Earlier, God had told them not to fear human beings, because his righteousness endures. Then the memory of the Red Sea becomes hope: the redeemed will return to Zion singing.

Today, when you feel weak or afraid, you can pray with sincerity and remember what God has already done for his people and for you. His faithful past feeds your hope.
exp.32:17:
In the end, when deliverance comes, the faithful person will look back in amazement at the time of terror. They will ask where the enemy's officials are: the one who kept the records, the one who weighed the tribute or the plunder, and the one who counted the towers or important houses in order to seize them.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who were threatened by the Assyrian invasion. Earlier in the chapter he announces that the one who lives in righteousness will be protected and will see the King. Many understand that this verse looks back at a fear already past, since the officials who caused it are no longer there. Some read it differently, but the overall sense is one of relief.

For today: when fear makes your problems seem enormous, remember that God can bring you to a day when they feel like things of the past. Trust in Him and keep doing what is right.
exp.14:1:
Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Moab wails over Nebo and over Medeba, that is, they cry out aloud in grief. Shaving the head and cutting off the beard were signs of deep mourning. "Shaved" means cut bare, and "cut off" means removed.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking. This message, called a "burden," is a warning of judgment against Moab, a neighboring nation of Israel. Moab wept at its high places, seeking help from its gods. Scholars debate when this destruction happened and who caused it; the text only shows that God sees the nations and that their fall would come suddenly.

For today: do not place your security in things that can fall in a single night, such as money, reputation, or plans. Seek God first; he remains, and he comforts those who weep.
exp.18:17:
In that day, the passage says, five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan, the language of Israel, and will swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. One of them will be called the City of the Sun. This name is a puzzle, and scholars read it in different ways.

Isaiah speaks for God within a prophecy about Egypt. First he announces judgment and fear for that nation, but then he shows that God does not abandon it. Egypt, the long-time enemy of Israel, will come to know the true God.

For today: God can change hearts that seem far away or out of reach. So do not give up on any person or any people; pray for them and treat them with hope.
exp.13:29:
It says that the poorest and most needy will find pasture and rest in safety, while God will bring Philistia to an end by famine. The phrase "the firstborn of the poor" means the very poorest among the poor. The needy are those in want. The "root" and the "remnant" refer to what is left of that people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah in the year King Ahaz died. The Philistines were rejoicing that a king who had struck them had fallen, but God warns them that something worse is coming. Scholars debate which king is meant by the "broken rod"; it is not entirely clear.

For today: God cares for the weak and judges pride. If you feel small or in need today, trust that he sees your situation. And if things are going well for you, do not become proud or mock the fall of others.
exp.5:5:
It says that one of the seraphim, heavenly beings who surround God's throne, flew toward Isaiah. In his hand was a glowing coal, a hot ember, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, a tool for gripping hot objects so as not to be burned.

Isaiah is speaking, recounting his vision of the temple. He has just seen the holy Lord and feels lost because of his sin and that of his people. The coal comes from the altar, a place tied to sacrifice and forgiveness. Many understand that it shows God himself cleansing and preparing the one he calls. The text does not explain every detail of the gesture.

For today: when you feel unworthy before God, do not hide. Bring your sin to him with sincerity, trust in his forgiveness, and let yourself be cleansed. Then you will be ready to say, "Here I am."
exp.48:7:
God tells his Servant that he will answer him in the time of favor, when God shows goodwill. In the day of salvation, God will help him. He promises to keep him and appoint him as a covenant for the people, meaning the means by which God renews his promise. He also sends him to restore the land and to apportion again the desolate inheritances, the places left in ruin.

The LORD speaks to the Servant, whom people despise. The context shows that his mission reaches Israel and also the nations. Many Christians see Jesus here, and Paul quotes the first part in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Others think first of Israel as the servant. Both readings recognize that God restores.

For today: even when you feel despised or in ruins, God hears you and sustains you. Today is a time to draw near to him with confidence.
exp.19:3:
This verse explains the meaning of Isaiah's sign. The king of Assyria would lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks bared, to Egypt's shame. Exiles are people taken from their homeland and forced to live in another land, and the bare buttocks describe a very severe public humiliation.

God speaks through Isaiah. Judah was tempted to trust in Egypt and Cush to defend them against Assyria. Isaiah, walking naked and barefoot as a sign, showed that those nations would fall and would be unable to save anyone. The text speaks of "three years," and it is not known for certain whether this refers to the whole length of that time or to a period of the sign.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, people, or plans. All of these can fail. Simply put, we place our trust first in God, and then use other resources with gratitude.
exp.8:13:
He says that God will cut off from Israel, in a single day, everyone: from the most important to the least important. The phrase "head and tail" refers to those above and those below. The "palm branch and reed" are similar images: the tall palm branch and the low reed. That is, no one will be left outside the judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had already suffered attacks from enemies such as Syria and the Philistines, but they did not return to God or seek him. The following verse explains the image: the head is the elders, and the tail is the prophets who teach falsehood. Interpreters agree that it speaks of a broad and sudden judgment.

For today: when difficulties come, let us not ignore them or blame others. Let us ask ourselves humbly whether God is calling us to return to him, and let us respond by seeking him wholeheartedly and sincerely.
exp.0:11:
God asks with sorrow, "Who has asked this of you?" He is speaking about the people who came to the temple to stand before him. The phrase "to trample" means to crush underfoot. "Courts" are the courtyards of the temple. God says that they only trample his courtyards, and their visit means nothing to him.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Judah, whom he calls "Sodom and Gomorrah" in order to rebuke them harshly. They kept on with sacrifices and feasts, but their lives were unjust, as becomes clear later in the chapter. God does not reject worship itself, which he himself had commanded, but empty religion, without obedience or justice.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our life in church, prayer, and giving is joined to an obedient heart. Before we sing or give, it is good to examine how we treat others and correct what is wrong.
exp.43:14:
He says that a man uses the same tree for two very different things. He burns one part to warm himself and to bake his bread. With another part he makes a god and bows down before it. The verse itself says the wood serves as fuel, that he takes some of it to warm himself, and that he kindles a fire and bakes his bread. The explanation simply tells the reader that the wood is used both for heat and for the bread.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people tempted by the idolatry of the neighboring nations. With irony, the prophet shows how absurd it is to worship something a person makes with his own hands. The same piece of wood serves for the fire and for the "god." This contrasts with the living God, who created the trees and human beings.

Today we may not carve statues, but we can give God's place to things we ourselves make or obtain: money, success, image. Ask yourself: what do I expect will save me or give me security? Hand that over to God and trust in him.
exp.9:29:
The verse is a cry of alarm. The people of that town, called here "Daughter of Gallim," are told to cry aloud to give warning. The warning must reach Laishah, and the prophet calls out to wretched Anathoth, a village that lies on the enemy's path. The word "wretched" here expresses pity.

Isaiah describes, in poetic tone, the march of the Assyrian army toward Jerusalem. He names northern villages one after another, which grow frightened as they see it advancing. These places were near Jerusalem, and the prophet thus announces the danger that was drawing close. Scholars are not sure whether it is a real march or a vision of the prophet, and the exact location of Gallim and Laishah is debated.

When a threat arrives, one should not stay silent or pretend that everything is fine. Warning in time, praying, and asking others for help is an act of love and wisdom, and God cares for those who cry out to Him.
exp.54:9:
It says that the rain and the snow fall from heaven and do not return there without doing their work. They water the earth, make it bud and sprout, and so there is seed for the one who sows and food for the one who eats. "Filled" means that it fills the earth and leaves it thoroughly soaked. "Seed" is what is sown.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a discouraged people, probably in exile. After inviting them to return to him and reminding them that his thoughts are higher than ours, he uses this image. The following verse explains it: so is his word, which does not return empty, but accomplishes what he wills.

For today: do not become discouraged if you do not see immediate results when you read, pray, or share the Bible. Like the rain, God's word works quietly. Keep sowing with patience and trust that he will make the fruit grow in its time.
exp.64:3:
He says this rebellious people sits among the graves and spends the nights in secret places. Furthermore, they eat the meat of pigs, which the law of Moses forbade, and in their bowls there is broth made from polluted things, that is, things the law declared unclean.

God speaks through Isaiah. He complains about a people he patiently called ("I spread out my hands all day long"), yet who followed their own paths. Many understand these practices to be pagan rituals, perhaps tied to consulting the dead, although scholars are not entirely certain of the details. What is serious is that they combined this with a religion of outward appearance, considering themselves "holier" than others.

For today: examine whether your faith is only appearance. God seeks a sincere heart that obeys him, not a religiosity that considers itself superior to others.
exp.65:17:
God says that he knows very well what people do and what they think in their hearts. For this reason he announces that the time is coming when he will gather all nations and tongues. They will come and see his glory, that is, his presence and his shining power. "Knowing" here means that God knows thoroughly.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah, near the close of the book. He has just said that he will judge those who practice a false and mixed religion, even though they appear to be holy. Then he shows that his plan goes beyond Israel: he will send survivors to distant peoples who have never heard of him, to proclaim his glory. Interpreters disagree on the details of how this is fulfilled.

Today we can remember that God looks at the heart, not only at appearances. And we can share with love what we know of him, because he desires that all peoples come to know him.
exp.40:25:
God asks the idols and those who follow them: who announced this from the beginning, so that we might know, and who foretold it long ago, so that we could say, "He was right"? And he answers: no one. No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard the words of the idols. Here "right" means that something is true or correct.

The Lord speaks as though in a courtroom case against the false gods of the nations. He challenges them to prove that they are gods by showing that they can announce the future. Shortly before, he mentions one who will rise up "from the north," which many connect with Cyrus, king of Persia, though the text here does not name him. Only the God of Israel declares what is coming and fulfills it.

Today too there are voices that promise security and answers, but they cannot sustain what they say. Before you place your trust in something, ask yourself whether it has proven itself worthy of that trust. Rest in the God who has spoken and has kept his word.
exp.51:4:
God says that his people were taken away without cause. There was no payment made for them and no just reason for their captivity. Those who rule over them taunt them, and God's name is blasphemed continually, all day long.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing Israel in captivity. He mentions Egypt and Assyria as examples of oppressors. The words "What have I here?" can be understood in several ways: as a question from God showing that he does not remain indifferent, or as a lament. In any case, God prepares the announcement of the deliverance that follows.

For today: when you suffer injustice or see people mocking the name of God, remember that he is not indifferent. Pray with confidence and wait for his rescue, without becoming bitter or responding with evil.
exp.13:6:
It says that after the oppressor fell, the whole earth was calm and at peace, and the people broke out in joyful song. The idea of "rest" and "peace" here speaks of a deep relief after much suffering. The "song" in this verse is a shout of celebration.

Isaiah speaks in a prophecy against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4). It is a mocking song about his fall. That king had oppressed many nations with cruelty, and God broke his power. Some think it refers to one particular king; others also see a broader message about pride and tyranny. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God sees injustice and does not let oppressors rule forever. If you are suffering abuse or the abuse of power today, trust that God is just. And if you have authority, use it with humility and with care for others.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that when that day comes, the splendor of Jacob, that is, the wealth and strength of the people of Israel, will fade. The phrase "will fade" means it will grow smaller and weaker. The "fat of his body" speaks of a full, healthy body, and "will waste away" means it will become thin and frail.

Isaiah speaks as God's messenger in the midst of a judgment against Damascus and Ephraim (the northern kingdom), which had joined forces against Judah. By trusting in human alliances instead of in God, Ephraim would lose its power. The harvest images that follow show that almost nothing would be left, although a remnant would survive.

For today: let us not place our security in riches, alliances, or our own strength, because all of these can fade. Let us trust in God, who cares for his own even in times of scarcity.
exp.10:12:
In the time of God's restoration, the long rivalry between the two main groups of his people will come to an end: Ephraim (the northern kingdom) and Judah (the southern kingdom). "Jealousy" here means envy and resentment. "Cut off" means cut down or removed. "Harass" means to trouble or pester. The enemies of Judah will be removed, and the two brothers will no longer fight among themselves.

Isaiah is the one writing, speaking on behalf of the LORD. After announcing the righteous king who would come from the root of Jesse (the father of David), the prophet describes how God will gather his people scattered among many nations. Israel had been divided into two kingdoms, and between them there was tension and war. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others see it already beginning in Christ.

For today: if God promises to heal divisions between brothers, we can move toward that now. Think of someone with whom you have jealousy or resentment, and take a step toward peace: a phone call, an apology, or a sincere prayer for that person.
exp.62:17:
The explanation says that God's people, described as "Your people" (the people set apart for God), possessed the holy place for only a short while. Now their enemies have trampled God's sanctuary, which means they walked all over it and treated it with contempt. The sanctuary, the holy place of worship, has been defiled.

The one speaking is the prophet, praying on behalf of the people. It is a prayer full of grief, probably offered after the destruction of the temple and the exile, although scholars debate the exact date. The people acknowledge God as Father and Redeemer, and ask him to return to them with mercy.

For today: when you feel that you have lost something sacred, or that everything is falling apart, do as this people did. Come to God honestly, without hiding your pain, and call him "Father" again. He listens to his children.
exp.54:10:
The explanation says that God's word is like a mission with a sure destination. When God speaks, that word does not come back without result. It accomplishes what God desires and achieves the purpose for which he sent it. In this verse, the idea of "not returning" means it will not come back empty, without having done its work.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the people of Israel, who were living in exile or coming out of it (scholars debate the exact date). God compares his word to the rain and the snow, which come down from heaven and make the earth produce. In the same way, his promise of forgiveness and restoration will be fulfilled, even though his ways may seem hard to understand.

For today: read the Bible with confidence, knowing that God works in you through his word, even when you do not see the fruit right away.
exp.45:8:
Isaiah 46:9 tells the people to remember what God did long ago. The reason is clear: God alone is God, and there is no other. The phrase "long ago" here refers to ancient times, or the distant past. The words "there is none like Me" mean no one is similar to him or equal to him.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he mocks idols: they are objects that must be carried on people's shoulders, that do not move and do not answer. God calls the rebellious to think it over and return to him. Then he shows that he does announce the future and fulfills what he says.

For today: when you feel fear or doubt, call to mind the times God helped you, or your family. Write them down and thank him. Remembering his faithfulness helps you trust in him and not in things that promise security but cannot answer.
exp.16:8:
The verse says that when God's judgment comes, the cities that seemed strong will be left almost empty, like the few fruits left on the branches after the harvest, or like thickets and hilltops abandoned to others. In the end it speaks of ruin and desolation.

Isaiah announces this message against Damascus and the northern kingdom of Israel, which trusted in alliances and fortresses. The verses that follow explain the cause: they forgot God, their rock.

For today: check where you place your security, whether in money, work or plans. All of these can fail, but God does not. Seek God first, and he will sustain the rest.
exp.53:8:
God compares his promise to Israel with the one he made after the flood. Just as he swore that the waters would never again cover the earth, he now swears that he will not be angry with his people or rebuke them. Here, "to be angry with" means to reprove or punish harshly.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Jerusalem, pictured as an abandoned and suffering woman. The people had gone through judgment and exile, and they felt forsaken. God assures them that that season of discipline was brief, and that now comes a restoration based on his mercy and his covenant of peace.

For today: when you feel guilt or fear that God has let you go, remember that his compassion is firmer than your failures. Rest in his word and return to him with confidence, without fear of rejection.
exp.22:13:
Isaiah 23:14 tells the great ships of Tarshish to wail, that is, to cry out loud in grief, because their harbor has been destroyed. Tarshish was a distant place across the sea, and its ships were trading vessels. The harbor here is the port of Tyre, where these ships came to trade.

It is part of Isaiah's prophecy against Tyre, a city rich from sea trade. God speaks through the prophet and announces that this power will fall. The sailors of Tarshish mourn because they lose their great trading partner. Scholars debate where Tarshish was located, and some think of Spain, but this is not certain.

For today: our security should not rest on money, success, or business, for all of that can fall suddenly. Today you can hand your plans over to God and trust Him more than your resources.
exp.51:0:
Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, also called Zion, and calls her to wake up and dress herself in her finest clothes, like someone getting ready for a festival. Strength means power, and splendid garments means fine, beautiful clothing. She is promised that the uncircumcised (someone outside the covenant people) and the unclean (someone ceremonially impure) will no longer enter her.

The prophet Isaiah passes on God's word to the people of Judah, who lived in humiliation and captivity. God encourages them to rise, because their deliverance is coming. The verses that follow speak of shaking off the dust and loosing the chains. Interpreters debate whether "no more" refers only to the return from exile or also to a future, spiritual restoration.

For today: if you feel fallen or discouraged, God calls you to rise up, trusting in his rescue. Today you can pray, remember his promises, and take one concrete step of faith.
exp.39:0:
God himself commands that his people be comforted. The repetition of the word "comfort" twice gives it emphasis, like a tender and urgent invitation. Furthermore, God calls them "My people" and presents himself as "your God," that is, he affirms that he remains bound to them.

Here God is speaking, and his message seems directed to those who will carry the news, perhaps the prophets. The verses that follow say that Jerusalem has completed her time of punishment and that her sin has been pardoned. The phrase about receiving "double" is understood in several ways, and it is not certain which is the correct one. What is clear is that God announces relief and a road of return toward him.

Today, if you are tired or burdened with guilt, remember that God speaks with tenderness. You can also be an instrument of comfort: this week, look for someone who is suffering and speak words of hope to them.
exp.32:22:
The verse describes a ship that is badly prepared: the ropes are slack, they cannot hold the mast firm, and the sail cannot be spread. Even so, an abundance of spoils will be divided, and even the lame will carry off plunder. The word "ropes" names the lines that hold the mast and sail in place, and "slack" means they have gone loose and are not pulled tight.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and distress. The verses before it present the LORD as judge, lawgiver, and King who saves. Many understand the weak ship to represent the enemies, who cannot control the situation. Others think it describes Jerusalem. The text does not make clear who the subject is, so it is wise to read it with caution.

For today: when you feel weak or poorly prepared, remember that your security does not depend on your own strength but on God, who can give you what you need.
exp.57:1:
The verse says that the people seek God day after day and seem eager to learn his ways. They look like a nation that does what is right and has not abandoned the justice of their God. They ask him for righteous judgments and appear to delight in drawing near to him. The phrase "righteous judgments" refers to fair decisions, and "does what is right" describes living out that fairness in practice.

God speaks here, telling the prophet Isaiah to confront the sin of his people. The verse describes their religious appearance, but the surrounding context shows that it was superficial. They fasted, yet they kept pursuing their own benefit, oppressed others, and lived in quarreling and violence. Many interpreters understand that God does not deny that they sought him, but that their religion was not matched by a just life.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our prayer, our attendance at church, or our fasting is reflected in how we treat family, coworkers, and those in need. Let us seek God with sincerity and obedience.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that all the people, specifically Ephraim and the dwellers of Samaria, the capital, will come to know or feel the judgment of God. The phrase "will know it" points to the message God has sent. They speak with pride and arrogance of heart, meaning a mindset that thinks itself superior and refuses to yield.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he announced hope through the eternal kingdom of David. Now he warns Israel, the northern kingdom, which had suffered blows and damage. Instead of turning back to God, they responded with confidence in themselves, as the following words show: they would rebuild better, with cut stone and cedars.

Today, when losses or failures come, we can react with pride and say, "I will rise up on my own." It is better to stop, listen to God, and humbly ask him for direction before rebuilding.
exp.22:9:
The explanation says that the "daughter of Tarshish" must work her land as freely as the Nile works its fields, because there is no longer a harbor to shelter her. The harbor is the safe place a city depends on for trade and protection. Once it is gone, she is left to manage on her own. The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain, and readers may notice that the wording can be understood in more than one way, so it is wise to read the verse closely in context.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God in a prophecy against Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. God himself decreed her fall to humble her pride. When Tyre fell, her trading partners, such as Tarshish, would be left without support.

For today: do not place your security in money, success, or your connections, because all of that can change suddenly. Trust God first, and use what you have with humility.
exp.7:4:
It says that the Lord spoke to Isaiah further. The words in the original that correspond to "further" and the connecting word are short phrases, and the verse itself simply reads "And the LORD spoke to me further:" It is a short sentence that introduces a new message from God to the prophet.

Isaiah writes here in the first person. He has just described the birth of his son, whose name was a sign that Assyria would soon defeat Damascus and Samaria. Now God gives him another message: the people of Judah had rejected trust in God, the gentle waters of Shiloah, and had sought security in human alliances. For this reason the power of Assyria would come upon them.

God does not remain silent when we turn away. He speaks to us again and again, through His Word and through His Spirit. Today we may ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to Him once more, even if it is to correct us, and to trust in Him more than in our own securities.
exp.32:11:
The explanation says that the enemy peoples of God will be completely destroyed. The "burning of lime" refers to limestone which, when burned, turns into white, crumbling ash. The "thorns cut down" are dry branches thrown into the fire, which burn quickly. Both images speak of a total and swift end.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah lived under the threat of Assyria, and God promises to act against those who oppress and betray. The verses before it say that their plans are like straw: they produce nothing, and their own fire consumes them. The verses that follow call everyone, far and near, to acknowledge the power of God, and they also make the hypocrites in Zion tremble.

For today: do not trust in violence or in plans made without God, because they do not last. Ask Him to examine your heart, and live with sincerity before Him.
exp.35:4:
Rabshakeh, the messenger of the king of Assyria, tells Judah that their talk of having a strategy and strength for war is only empty words, with no real value. Then he asks: "In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me?" He wants Judah to realize that they have no one to lean on.

The king's messenger is speaking before the walls of Jerusalem. Hezekiah's officials have come out to listen to him. His aim is to frighten the people and break their confidence so that they will surrender without a fight. He mixes half-truths with mockery, and he has not yet mentioned God, though he soon will.

For today: when the voices of fear question whom you trust, do not rely only on your own strength or on human plans. Examine honestly where your trust lies, and place it in God, who is faithful.
exp.0:23:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord GOD of Hosts and the Mighty One of Israel, is going to act. The words "Ah" and "I will be relieved" introduce his resolve to act at last. "I will be relieved of My foes" and "avenge Myself on My enemies" mean that God will do justice and will not leave evil without a response. "Foes" and "enemies" refer to those who oppose him.

God speaks through Isaiah. The leaders of Jerusalem had become corrupt: they accepted bribes and did not defend the fatherless or the widow. God's enemies here are his own unjust people. But what follows shows that his judgment seeks to cleanse and restore, not only to punish.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, especially against the weak. We can ask where we fail to be just and how we might help those who have no voice, trusting that God corrects in order to heal.
exp.1:10:
It says that human pride, that look of superiority with which someone thinks of himself as better than others, will be brought low. "The proud look of man" and "the loftiness of men" describe pride and arrogance. The proud look of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day, the day when He acts in judgment.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, speaks to the people who trusted in their wealth, their power and their idols. The verses nearby describe people hiding themselves before the majesty of the LORD. Then the day of the LORD is mentioned, along with tall trees like the cedars, images of everything people consider great. Some see here a historical judgment, and others also see the end of time.

Today we can examine what we take pride in: success, money or knowledge. It is better to recognize with humility that everything comes from God and to live grateful, without looking down on anyone.
exp.40:11:
The explanation says that Israel's enemies, those who fought and argued against them, will vanish so completely that even if people search for them, they will not be found. The phrase "will come to nothing" means that they will lose all their power and be left without any importance. To contend against someone means to dispute with them or to be in conflict with them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Israel, a small and frightened people surrounded by stronger nations. God wants to calm their fear by reminding them that he is with them, helps them, and sustains them. It is a promise to that people in their specific situation.

For today: when you feel pressure from conflicts or from people who make your life difficult, do not let fear take charge. Pray, trust that God sustains you, and avoid repaying evil with evil. He knows how to care for you.
exp.22:1:
Be silent, you who live along the coast. Here "coastland" refers to the seafaring region of Phoenicia. The merchants of Sidon, whose traders crossed the sea, once filled the city of Tyre with wealth and now have nothing to say.

Isaiah is the prophet speaking, announcing a judgment from God against Tyre, the great trading city. Its harbors and businesses depended on seaborne commerce, and its fall would affect all its partners, such as Sidon. Scholars debate exactly how and when this prophecy was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: no human riches are secure.

For today: it is easy to trust in money, work, or economic stability. This verse invites us to give thanks for what we have, but to place our security in God, who does not change or pass away.
exp.21:17:
He will surely roll you into a ball and sling you into a wide land. There you will die, and there your glorious chariots will remain, a disgrace to the house of your master. Explanation: It says God will throw this man hard, the way one flings a ball, into a wide and distant land. There he will die, and there his chariots, which stood for his prestige, will be left behind. The image of the ball means he will be rolled up and sent away, far from home. His pride turns into shame for the house of his master.

God speaks through Isaiah. He addresses Sebna, a high official of the king (v. 15), who had carved himself a luxurious tomb as though he would stay forever. His ambition and pride offended God, and for that reason he will be removed from his post. The text does not say which land he will go to; it only announces exile and death far from home.

For today: take care that your service does not become a pursuit of fame. Every position or achievement is a temporary assignment from God, and true security lies in living with humility before Him.
exp.44:19:
God invites the people of the nations who have managed to survive to gather together and come close. The word "fugitives" describes those who escaped, perhaps from wars or disasters. God points out that those who carry an idol made of wood and pray to it for help are ignorant: that god cannot save.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He has just said that he is the Creator, that he speaks plainly, and that he deceives no one. Now he calls the nations to come and compare. Right after, he challenges them to see who announced these things long ago. Many interpret this as referring to the return of the people from exile, but the text leaves it open.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. An idol can be money, fame, or control. If it cannot save us, let us return simply to God, who does listen.
exp.62:16:
Here the people ask God why he has let them stray from his ways and why their hearts have become hardened so that they no longer fear him. "To stray" means to turn aside from the right path, and "heritage" refers to the people God has claimed as his own. They ask God to return to them, for the sake of his servants.

The people of Israel are speaking, probably in a time of ruin and exile. They acknowledge that God is their Father and Redeemer, even though their ancestors can no longer help them. It is a painful and bold prayer. Some understand that God allowed their hardness as a consequence of their rebellion; others see a language of sincere complaint, not an accusation against God.

For today: when you feel far from God, do not hide. Bring him your confusion honestly, acknowledge your part, and ask him to draw you near again. He remains a Father.
exp.58:12:
This verse describes the sin of the people with several strong words. "Rebelling" means refusing to submit to authority and resisting what is right. "Denying the LORD" means refusing to acknowledge him, and "turning away from our God" means turning your back on him and no longer following him. "Oppression and revolt" are words that do harm and defy God. And sin does not come only from the mouth: the lies are conceived and formed in the heart, that is, they take shape in the mind before they are spoken.

Here Isaiah speaks on behalf of the people. He includes himself in the message and acknowledges the guilt. Before this verse, the people complain that salvation has not come, but the prophet explains that their own sins separate them from God. Afterward, we see how lying damages justice in society.

For today: before you speak, examine what is in your heart. Ask God for sincerity, and practice telling the truth with love, even when it is costly.
exp.2:8:
Their faces give them away: their guilt and their brazenness show. Like the people of Sodom, they flaunt their sin and do not conceal it. To conceal something means to hide it or act as if it is not there. Their own disaster has come upon them, so the prophet cries out: "Woe to them!"

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah and Jerusalem, who were in crisis. The verses before this one describe a fallen leadership, and the people no longer wanted to take responsibility. The prophet says their words and their deeds were against the Lord. Sodom appears as an example of shameless sin. But right away Isaiah affirms that it will go well for the righteous.

Today this invites us to be honest with God and not to grow used to sin. If something in our life no longer makes us ashamed, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer and seek his forgiveness and his help to change.
exp.21:20:
It says that God will clothe Eliakim with another man's robe of authority, tie his sash around him, and give him the power that man once had. Eliakim will be like a caring father to the people of Jerusalem and to the people of Judah.

God is speaking through the prophet Isaiah. The verses before this are addressed to Shebna, a high official of the palace, whom God removes from his position, apparently because of his pride. In his place, God calls Eliakim, whom he calls "my servant." The text does not detail everything Shebna did, so it is best not to assume more than it says.

For today: authority is an assignment from God, not a prize to show off. If you have responsibility over others, in your home, your work, or your church, exercise it with humility and care, like a father who protects and serves.
exp.41:10:
It says that even the driest and most remote places should raise their voices in praise. The "desert and its cities" are the villages that live in dry lands. "Kedar" was a nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert, a descendant of Ishmael. "The people of Sela" probably refers to Sela, a rocky city, though some believe it is a region or a high place.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. After announcing that he will bring new things, he invites everyone, even distant peoples, to sing a new song. God shows that his salvation is not only for Israel but for all nations. Then comes the image of God as a warrior who acts on behalf of his people.

For today: don't wait for your life to be perfect before praising God. Even in your "desert," in times of dryness or loneliness, you can choose to sing to him and thank him for his works.
exp.29:4:
The explanation says that the leaders of Judah will be put to shame for having trusted in a people who are useless to them. To be useless means to serve no purpose, and to bring shame means to bring disgrace or mockery. Egypt will bring them no help or benefit, but only the opposite: humiliation and disgrace.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God. Judah was under the threat of Assyria, and its leaders sent envoys with gifts to Egypt, seeking a military alliance, without consulting the Lord. Isaiah warns them that this alliance will be useless. Zoan and Hanes were Egyptian cities where the messengers arrived (the exact location of Hanes is debated).

For today: when you face a big problem, before rushing to your "resources from Egypt," whether money, connections, or plans, pray and seek God's direction. Human help can be useful, but it must not take the place of trust in Him.
exp.35:13:
Here Rabshakeh, a spokesman for the king of Assyria, speaks. He says the king orders them not to let Hezekiah deceive them, because Hezekiah cannot deliver the people. The word "deliver" means to rescue or save from danger. The phrase "do not let...deceive you" means not to let them be fooled by false hopes.

Jerusalem was surrounded by the Assyrian army, a few years before 700 B.C. Rabshakeh shouted in Hebrew, the language of Judah, so that the people on the wall would understand him and lose their confidence. His aim was to separate the people from their king and from their faith in God. He presents as deception the very thing Judah was meant to trust in.

When loud voices tell us there is no way out, it is worth remembering that they do not always speak the truth. Before surrendering to fear, we can pray and seek God's voice in his Word, trusting that he can act even when everything seems lost.
exp.29:19:
It says that God will allow hard times, described as "the bread of adversity" and "the water of affliction," that is, suffering and scarcity. But even so, your Teacher will no longer hide Himself. The people will see Him with their own eyes. Some understand this to refer to prophets who speak on God's behalf, and others to God Himself as the Teacher.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who trusted in alliances with Egypt instead of trusting in God. He warns them of the consequences, but he also promises that God will show mercy. Suffering is not the final word: after it comes God's guidance and the abandonment of idols.

For today: in your difficult moments, do not turn away from the Word of God. Seek out a church, a faithful teacher, or a daily time of Bible reading. God often uses difficulty so that you will listen to His voice with greater attention.
exp.2:6:
On that day he will cry out, "I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!" He says that, when the crisis comes, the person whom they want to make a leader will refuse. "He will cry aloud" means he will say it firmly and insistently. "I am not a healer" means: I will not take on that responsibility of setting things right. He says that in his house there is no food or clothing, and so he does not want to be made leader, that is, the one in charge of the people.

Isaiah speaks to Judah and Jerusalem, announcing God's judgment for their sin. Before this he says that God would take away their leaders and their provision. The land is left so weak and disordered that people look for a leader among anyone who has even a cloak. But even that man does not want to take on the ruin of others.

For today: leading is not only holding a position, but bearing responsibility. A people who turn away from God lose good guides. Pray for those who govern and, if God calls you to serve, do it with humility and honesty.
exp.32:0:
Here God announces a "woe", that is, a warning of judgment, against a destroyer. This man or nation destroyed others and betrayed them without ever having been destroyed or betrayed himself. A "traitor" is someone who breaks trust and deceives. The final message is clear: when his cycle of destruction and betrayal comes to an end, he will suffer the same fate he inflicted on others.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in God's name at a time of threat against Judah. The text does not name the destroyer, and many think it refers to Assyria, though others see it as a broader description of any oppressor. The following verse shows the people crying out to God and waiting on Him.

For today: do not envy those who prosper by doing harm, nor take revenge on your own. Trust that God sees injustice, and ask Him for mercy and strength, as the people do in the following verse.
exp.12:10:
God says he will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their wrongdoing. His judgment reaches those who do harm. He will put an end to the arrogance of the proud and bring down the pride of the ruthless. To "lay low" means to humble or bring down. "Arrogance" is the pride of someone who thinks they are better than others.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. This passage is part of a message against Babylon, which begins in chapter 13. The "day of the LORD" is described with images of darkness in the sky. Some see it fulfilled in the historical fall of Babylon, and others also see a look toward the final judgment. It can be understood in both ways.

For today: God opposes pride and the cruelty of the powerful. Today we can examine our hearts, set aside arrogance, and live with humility, trusting that God will do justice.
exp.8:19:
He says that the desperate people will grab violently whatever they find on the right and still be hungry; then they will eat whatever they find on the left and still not be satisfied. The word "carve out" here means to cut or tear away greedily. In the end, each one will devour the flesh of his own offspring, a very strong image: they end up harming their own children and families.

Some understand "offspring" as a relative or neighbor; others see it as a picture of self-destruction.

Speaking on behalf of God, Isaiah announces judgment on the northern kingdom, Israel, for its wickedness and injustice. The nation turns against itself: Manasseh against Ephraim, and both against Judah. It is the internal violence that follows when a people turns away from God.

Today it reminds us that selfishness and rivalry never satisfy and end up destroying families, churches, and communities. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that seeks peace and cares for a brother instead of competing with him.
exp.21:16:
The verse says that the LORD himself will take Shebna out of his land and carry him away into a harsh captivity. "Carry away" means to take far away, and the phrase about covering probably speaks of shame or a complete fall, though some understand it as an image of humiliation or death.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Shebna was a high official of the king, in charge of the treasury and the palace. He had made an elegant tomb, as if his place were permanent and his fame secure. God confronts him for his pride and for seeking his own glory. The Bible does not detail all of his sin, so it is best not to invent more.

For today: position, success, and prestige are not our security. We receive everything we have from God, so it is good to serve with humility and not to exalt ourselves.
exp.27:1:
God has someone strong and mighty ready to act. This one comes like a hailstorm, like a destructive tempest, like a driving rain or a flooding downpour. "Driving rain" and "flooding downpour" describe a sudden, heavy rain. The picture is of someone who smashes things and leaves everything in ruins. The idea of smashing a crown to the ground means striking something proud and bringing it down hard to the earth.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the eighth century B.C. against Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel. Its capital, Samaria, stood on a fertile hill, and its leaders lived proud and drunk. Isaiah announces judgment. Many understand that the "strong and mighty one" is the army of Assyria, used by God, although the text does not name it here.

Today it reminds us that pride and careless living do not hold up when God acts. Today we can ask ourselves in what things we trust more than in Him, and turn back to God with humility before the storm arrives.
exp.4:16:
After the judgment, the lambs will graze in peace, as if they were in their own pastures. And strangers, that is, outsiders, will feed in the ruins of the wealthy. The phrase "the ruins of the wealthy" here refers to fertile lands that have been abandoned. Some scholars understand the lambs to be the people who survive, and others take them to be simply flocks grazing among ruins. The text allows both readings.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah. He has just told the parable of the vineyard, which yielded sour grapes, and announced six woes against injustice, greed, and pride. This verse describes how the lands of the powerful would look after the judgment: empty and occupied by others.

Today it reminds us that accumulating wealth and power without justice does not last. What seems secure can be left abandoned. It is worth asking ourselves what we are building and whether it honors God and blesses others.
exp.55:8:
Here God calls out to the wild animals of the fields and forests to come and eat greedily. The verse uses the word "eat," and the picture is of a meal laid out for hungry predators. It is a strong image: those who should protect the people are leaving them defenseless, and the animals are invited to feed on them.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before, God promises to gather Israel and to welcome people from all nations into his house of prayer. Here the tone changes: the people are exposed to danger because the leaders who should guard them fail in their duty. The verses that follow describe these leaders as blind watchmen and silent dogs. Interpreters debate who the beasts are: they may be enemy nations, but this cannot be known with certainty.

For today: those who care for others, in the church or in the family, must be attentive, speak the truth, and not seek only their own advantage. Caring for others is a serious responsibility.
exp.44:1:
God tells Cyrus that he will go before him, preparing the way. "I will level the mountains" means that he will flatten whatever stands in the way, making the path clear. The gates of bronze and the bars of iron stand for obstacles that seemed impossible to pass, and God promises to break them down.

The LORD speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to Cyrus, king of Persia, whom he calls "his anointed," meaning someone chosen for a task. God would use him to defeat nations, among them Babylon, whose cities had great gates. The purpose is to help Israel, his people, and to make known that the LORD alone is God. Many see here a reference to the fall of Babylon, although the historical details are explained in several ways.

When you face closed doors or steep roads, remember that God governs history and can go before you. Trust, pray, and take the next step with humility, knowing that He fulfills His purposes.
exp.1:4:
The explanation says that the prophet invites the people of Israel, called "house of Jacob," to walk in the light of the Lord. "Come" is a call to action, and "let us walk" includes the prophet himself. The light represents guidance, truth, and God's presence. To walk is to live day by day according to his direction.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. Just before, he describes a future in which many nations will go up to Jerusalem to learn from God, and there will be peace. Then Isaiah shows that his own people were living far from God: they trusted in fortune-tellers, in riches, and in war horses. That is why the verse is an urgent call: do not wait for that future, but start living this way now.

For today: do not trust only in your own resources or plans. Before deciding something important, ask God for direction and search his Word for the step to take today.
exp.41:2:
It says that God's chosen servant will treat the weak with gentleness. A "bruised reed" is a reed already broken or split, and the "smoldering wick" is a lamp wick that barely gives off smoke, with almost no flame. He does not crush the fragile person or snuff out the one who is about to give up. The phrase about bringing forth justice means he will carry it out faithfully and surely.

God himself speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He presents his chosen servant, upon whom he places his Spirit. Christians see Jesus here, and Matthew 12:18-21 quotes this passage in that sense. God shows that his justice comes with patience and kindness, not with shouting or violence.

For today: if you feel tired, wounded, or low in faith, God does not discard you. And when dealing with weak people, imitate him: correct with firmness when needed, but care for them without crushing them.
exp.36:2:
Hezekiah sends word to Isaiah that this is a day of distress, of punishment, and of disgrace against God. He compares their situation to a woman at the point of giving birth: the children are ready to be born, but there is no strength to finish the delivery. The word "rebuke" here means humiliation or disgrace. "Blasphemy" means speaking with contempt about God.

The messengers of King Hezekiah speak, dressed in mourning clothes. Rabshakeh, spokesman for the king of Assyria, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. The king, with no human way out, seeks God in the temple and asks Isaiah to pray for the people who remained.

For today: when you feel weak and without a way out, do not hide it. Bring your distress before God honestly, and ask someone of faith to pray with you. He listens to those who trust in Him.
exp.50:22:
The promise here is that the cup of punishment will pass from God's people to those who humiliated them. Your tormentors are the ones who abused you. They told you, "Lie down, so we can walk over you." In that picture, you made your back like the ground, like a street for others to tread on. That describes extreme humiliation, like being trampled just as the surface of a road is walked over. "Your soul" here means the whole person.

The Lord speaks as the one who pleads, that is, who defends the cause of his people as in a court case. Jerusalem had suffered judgment for her sin and was left reeling in pain. Now God says that this time is ending and that he himself will deal with those who abused her. Most readers understand this to refer to the nations that oppressed Judah, such as Babylon.

For today: if you have been humbled or mistreated, God sees your pain and does not forget you. You can hand your wound over to him and leave justice in his hands, rather than carrying the burden of revenge.
exp.14:0:
This is a solemn message from God, called a "burden," against Moab, a people who lived next to Israel. In a single night its cities, Ar and Kir, were ruined and destroyed. The word "burden" refers to a heavy prophecy of judgment.

Isaiah, a prophet of Judah, delivers this message on God's behalf. Moab was a nearby people with a complicated history with Israel. Scholars do not agree on when or how exactly this destruction happened, and the text does not make it clear. What is clear is that God speaks as Lord over all nations, not only over Israel.

For today: let us not put our trust in what seems firm, such as money, power, or status. Everything can change in a night. Let us place our security in God, who endures and is just.
exp.54:1:
The explanation says that people spend their money and effort on things that do not nourish or satisfy. "Satisfy" means to fill someone completely so they are content. "Rich" refers to abundant, finest food, an image of joy and fullness. God invites us to listen carefully, to eat what is good, and to let our souls take real delight.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, probably to a people in exile or near it, tired and spiritually thirsty. He offers freely what money cannot buy: his grace and his covenant. The verses that follow speak of the promises made to David. Christian interpreters often see in this a sign that points to Christ, although the original text speaks first to Israel.

Today, ask yourself where you are investing your time and energy. Set aside a moment each day to listen to God in his Word and in prayer, and let him feed you.
exp.36:1:
Verse 2 tells that King Hezekiah sent three groups of men to the prophet Isaiah: Eliakim the palace administrator (the one in charge of the household and the affairs of the palace), Shebna the scribe (who wrote and kept the records), and the leading priests. All of them went wearing sackcloth, a rough clothing used as a sign of grief and humility.

King Hezekiah had just heard the threats and mockery of the Assyrian messenger against Jerusalem and against God. For that reason he tore his clothes, went to the temple, and sent his trusted men to ask Isaiah to pray for the people who were still left.

For today: when a crisis comes that overwhelms you, do not face it alone. Pray to God and seek the support of people of faith who can intercede with you.
exp.58:9:
This verse describes a people who have lost their way, like a blind person feeling along the wall to find the path. Feeling along the wall is the picture: moving forward without seeing, finding the way step by step. Even at midday they stumble as if it were twilight. And the verse says that among the strong and vigorous they are like the dead, a life without light or hope.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God's people and includes himself in the confession with "we." Earlier in the chapter he says that injustice and crooked paths have drawn them away from God. Then he acknowledges that their sins are the cause of this darkness. It is not that God is unable to help; the problem is the sin that separates them.

For today: when you feel confusion or stumbling, ask yourself humbly whether there is something you need to acknowledge before God. Confessing and returning to Him is the first step toward the light.
exp.26:1:
He says that, when that promised day comes, God's people will sing with joy about a fruitful vineyard. "Sing" is an invitation to celebrate. The vineyard represents Israel, and its fruitfulness points to a people who yield good fruit.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of the LORD. Earlier, God promises to judge Leviathan, a symbol of the powers of evil. Then He Himself says that He tends His vineyard, waters it, and does not leave it alone. This contrasts with Isaiah 5, where the vineyard produced bad grapes and was judged. Here there is restoration.

For today: if God cares for His own with such careful attention, you can rest in His protection. Before you worry, give thanks to Him and sing a song of praise for His daily care.
exp.36:36:
The explanation says that King Sennacherib of Assyria, after losing his army, left Judah, returned to his country, and stayed to live in Nineveh, his capital. "Broke camp and withdrew" means that he pulled his army out at once. "Returned to Nineveh and stayed there" means that he went back and settled in the city.

The one telling the story is the prophet Isaiah, who recounts what happened when Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem in the days of King Hezekiah. God had promised to defend the city, and that night his angel struck the Assyrian camp. This verse shows the result: the proud king who defied God went back humbled and without his army.

God keeps his promises, even when the danger seems greater than we are. When you face a problem that is bigger than you, pray as Hezekiah did and trust that God is faithful. He knows how and when to act.
exp.60:3:
This verse says that God's people will rebuild what lay in ruins. "Ancient ruins" and "places long devastated" refer to places destroyed and left abandoned for a long time. Cities ruined for generations will be renewed.

The context is a prophecy of comfort. The one speaking is a servant anointed by the Spirit of the Lord, and Christians see in him Jesus, who read part of this passage in Luke 4. It speaks to a battered and grieving people, most likely thinking of Israel after the exile. God promises to exchange their ashes for glory and their sorrow for joy, and that they themselves will take part in the restoration.

For today: God can restore what has seemed lost for a long time, such as families, relationships, or communities. We can trust that he invites us to work with him, step by step, in that rebuilding.
exp.56:15:
God says that he will not bring charges against his people forever, nor will he stay angry without end. If he did, the spirit of man would grow weak before him, worn down and unable to endure. The phrase "the breath of life I have made" in the verse above refers to the people God himself created.

God speaks, the High and Lofty One, who dwells with the humble and the broken. His people had fallen into greed and rebellion, and God corrected them. But here he explains that his discipline has a limit. His aim is not to destroy but to heal, guide, and comfort, as the following verses say.

For today: if you feel the weight of your mistakes or of a correction, remember that God corrects in order to restore, not to crush you. Draw near to him with humility and let him lift you up.
exp.8:4:
Every boot that tramples in battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. This verse says that the soldiers' gear from the fighting, the boots that trample in war and the clothing stained with blood, will not be kept. It will be burned, and the fire will consume it. "Trampling boot of battle" refers to the heavy footwear of soldiers marching through the fight, and "garment rolled in blood" means clothing dragged through and soaked in blood. "Fuel for the fire" means the material the fire feeds on.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who lived under threat and oppression. He announces that God will deliver them, as He did in the days of Midian. The verses that follow say that this deliverance comes with the promised child. Many Christians see in him Jesus. The burning of the gear of war shows that God will bring true peace.

For today: when you feel that your life is a battle, remember that God promises an ending of peace. Trust in Him and seek to be someone who brings peace, not more conflict.
exp.64:20:
It says that God's people will build houses and dwell in them, and will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. Here "dwell" means "live" in the house they have built. It is a simple picture of peace, stability, and rest from labor.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He promises a new heavens and a new earth, where Jerusalem will be a source of joy and there will be no more weeping. The verses that follow show the contrast: in the past others took what the people built, but now no one will take away the fruit of their labor. Some see here a future fulfillment; others see a promise that already began with the return from exile. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God cares about everyday life, such as home and work. You can trust that He watches over your effort, and in the meantime work with honesty and gratitude, waiting for His promise.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that the waters of Nimrim will dry up. So the grass will wither, the tender shoots will fade, and nothing green will be left. The vegetation is gone, and the greenery is no more, which is the picture of a fertile land left without life.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God about Moab, a neighboring people of Israel. He announces a destruction that leaves the people weeping and fleeing. Nimrim was in the region of Moab, although scholars are not sure of its exact location. It stands out that Isaiah says his heart cries out for Moab: the message of judgment is not delivered coldly, but with pain.

For today: what seems secure, like water, work, or riches, can disappear quickly. Place your trust in God and learn to feel compassion, even for those who suffer the consequences of their own ways.
exp.2:3:
He says that God will take away the capable leaders of the people and put in their place young people without experience. "Lads" are young men, and "children" can be understood as little ones or very immature people. "Leaders" and "rulers" are the people in charge. Some think it also speaks of rulers who act immaturely, even if they are not children.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The verses before it list the leaders God would remove: warriors, judges, counselors, and elders. When wise guidance is missing, disorder, violence, and despair would come, as what follows shows. It is the consequence of turning away from God.

For today: let us pray for our leaders and seek wisdom from God. Let us also patiently train the young, so that they grow with character and the fear of the Lord.
exp.32:10:
It says that God's enemies, and also those who trust in their own plans, conceive things of no value: chaff, which is dry straw, and stubble, which is the dry stalk left after the grain is cut. What they give birth to will be just as useless. Moreover, their own breath, that is, their fury and evil intentions, is a fire that will consume them. "Consume you" means that it will bring them to an end.

Here the LORD speaks, through Isaiah, to Judah and to the nations that threatened it, probably Assyria. The land is in mourning, and the fertile places, such as Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan and Carmel, are laid waste. Then God says that he will rise up. The plans of the proud fail when he acts.

For today: do not place your hope in plans made with pride, resentment or deceit, because they do not bear true fruit. Before you decide, ask God and seek what pleases him.
exp.45:10:
God calls a bird of prey from the east, a swift and determined figure, and brings him from a far-off land. He is described as "a man for My purpose," the one who will carry out God's plan. "I have planned it" means God has decided on it ahead of time. What God says, he does.

God himself speaks, at a time when Israel was in trouble. He asks them to remember that he alone is God, and that he announces the future before it happens, unlike the idols. Many understand this "bird" to be Cyrus, king of Persia, who would come from the east (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1), though some also see it as a broader picture of God's plans.

For today: when your situation seems out of control, remember that God has a plan and can use even unexpected people and places. Rest in his faithfulness and obey him with confidence.
exp.23:19:
The earth will stagger like a drunk man who cannot keep his feet, and it will sway like a flimsy shack that the wind batters. Earth's rebellion will weigh it down so heavily that it falls and never rises again.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing a judgment of God over the whole earth. These chapters (24 to 27) are often called the "apocalypse of Isaiah." Some see them as a final judgment, others as poetic language that also speaks of judgments within history. The text says that human rebellion is the cause, and that afterward God will act against the powerful.

For today: do not place your security in things that shake, such as money, power, or success. Trust in God, who does not move, and return to Him with humility every day.
exp.59:7:
Who are these who fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters? This question is full of wonder: the people come in such numbers and with such speed that they look like a cloud driven across the sky, and like doves rushing home to where they belong. The picture is of a great crowd arriving quickly, eager to be back.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, and God promises to restore her after the punishment. The verses that follow explain that these are her children returning from far away by ships, together with people from other nations who join to worship the LORD. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a broader fulfillment, with peoples from everywhere coming to God.

For today: God rejoices when someone returns to Him, and we too can rejoice and welcome with affection the one who comes back, without reproach.
exp.59:20:
It says that God's people will all be righteous, that is, they will be in a right relationship with Him and will live uprightly. They will possess the land forever. They are described as "the branch of My planting," shoots of a plant that God Himself has set in the ground. They are also "the work of My hands," and all of this is "so that I may be glorified," that is, to show who God is.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Jerusalem, a people who had suffered greatly. He promises them a future in which He Himself will be their light and their mourning will end. Interpreters differ on how this is fulfilled: some see restoration after the exile, others see something final and future, and others see both.

For today: if God is shaping you, you are not an abandoned project. Trust that He finishes what He begins, and let your life, with its processes, honor Him.
exp.21:19:
On that day, God says he will summon Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, whom he calls "my servant." In other words, he will choose him for an important task. Here, "summon" means to select someone and place him in an official position.

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just announced that he will remove Shebna, a high official of the king's palace, from his position because of his pride (Isaiah 22:15-19). Eliakim will take his place. God shows that he decides who serves and who falls. The verses that follow describe the authority he will be given as administrator of the kingdom of Judah.

For today: positions and influence are a responsibility to serve, not an occasion to boast. If God gives you a task, carry it out with humility and care for others, because he is the one who entrusted it to you.
exp.25:9:
Isaiah 26:10 says that a wicked person can be shown grace, yet still does not learn to live righteously. Even in a place where righteousness is the norm, he keeps acting wrongly. The word "grace" here means undeserved kindness; "wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God; and "acts unjustly" means doing evil. The phrase "fails to see the majesty of the LORD" means that he does not recognize the greatness of God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a song of trust by God's people. Earlier he said that when God judges, people learn righteousness. Here he contrasts this: there are those who do not change even when shown kindness. Interpreters understand this as a hardened heart, not merely a lack of information.

For today: do not assume that blessings will change the heart. Ask God for a humble heart, one that recognizes his goodness and responds with gratitude and obedience.
exp.12:11:
It says God will make people scarce, as rare and precious as the purest gold. Ophir was a region famous for its gold; no one knows for certain where it was. "Mankind" and "man" in the verse refer to human beings in general.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, in a message of judgment against Babylon. Before and after, the passage describes the day of the LORD: darkness in the sky, the end of pride, and the trembling of the earth. Many understand that very few people will be left because the judgment will be severe, and so each life that remains will be worth more than gold.
