For today: if God considers each person so precious, let us treat others with respect and care, and not with pride or contempt. Our worth comes from God, not from what we have.
exp.42:12:
It says that God existed before there was any time: "Even from eternity I am He." No one can snatch anything out of his hand or escape from it. And when God acts, no one can reverse it: "When I act, who can reverse it?" The question means who can stop or undo what he has done.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Israel, a people who would be carried off to Babylon. God reminds them that only he saves and that they are witnesses to what he has done for them. He gives them assurance before announcing that he will redeem them. Some understand "out of My hand" as God's power to deliver and also to judge.

For today: when you feel that your situation is out of control, remember that God is not caught off guard and is not weakened. You can rest in the knowledge that your life is in hands no one can overcome. Pray with confidence and obey, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.25:4:
He has humbled those who dwell on high, with their pride and their sense of security. The "lofty city" is a city that thought itself great and untouchable, but God lays it low until it is brought down to the ground and cast into the dust. The word "dwell" means to live, and "lofty" means high. "Humbled" and "lays low" describe the same action: God brings the city down.

Isaiah speaks within a song of trust that the people of Judah will sing in the future. He contrasts God, who gives peace to those who trust in Him, with the proud powerful ones who fall. Scholars do not agree on which city is meant: it may have been Moab, Babylon, or another, or it may be a symbol of all arrogant power.

Today: do not put your security in success, money, or reputation, since these can fall. Trust in God, and let Him teach you to live with humility and peace.
exp.22:17:
The verse says that the profits Tyre makes from its trade will be set apart for the Lord. They will not be stored away or saved up. Instead, the gain will go to those who live in the presence of the Lord, to provide plenty of food and fine clothing.

"Profits" and "wages" refer to what Tyre earns from its trade, and "set apart" means dedicated to the Lord. "Abundant" describes having more than enough.

Isaiah, as a prophet, announces judgment on Tyre, a city rich from its commerce. Earlier he says it will be forgotten for seventy years and then return to its trade, described with the image of a prostitute. This verse shows a final turn: its wealth will end up serving God and his people. Interpreters debate when and how this was fulfilled.

For today: money is not meant to be hoarded but to bless others. Today you can decide to set aside part of what you earn to help someone in need or to support the work of God.
exp.13:20:
The passage says that the sons of the wicked king will be handed over to death, as animals are led off to be slaughtered, because of the sins of their fathers. The verse begins with "Prepare a place to slaughter," which means that a place is being readied for this judgment. The result is that these sons will never rise up to take possession of a land or cover the earth with their cities.

Isaiah announces a mocking song against the king of Babylon, a cruel ruler who destroyed peoples. God speaks through the prophet, and the verses that follow confirm this. God promises to bring an end to that dynasty's name and descendants. Some believe the passage also reflects the wider danger of pride in power, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it unanswered. We can leave vengeance in his hands, trust his justice, and take care that our decisions bring blessing, not harm, to those who come after us.
exp.29:6:
Egypt's help will be of no use; it is futile and empty. For this reason God named her "Rahab Who Sits Still," pointing to the strength she claimed while doing nothing that would really protect anyone. God was saying that the true strength of His people lay in stillness before Him: not rushing after Egypt, but remaining calm and trusting in Him.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Judah faced a military threat, and its leaders were sending riches on donkeys and camels to Egypt to seek protection. God tells them that this alliance will bring them shame, because they did not trust in Him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, before rushing to find human solutions, stop for a moment to pray and ask God for direction. Being calm before Him is not passivity, but trust.
exp.4:18:
Here Isaiah quotes the mocking words of people who challenge God. They say: "Let him hurry and hasten his work so that we may see it!" They speak of God as "the Holy One of Israel" almost sarcastically, as if his warnings were nothing but a tale. The plan or purpose of God is what is meant here.

The prophet speaks to the people of Judah, who lived in sin and felt secure. In the "woe" just before this, Isaiah describes them dragging their wickedness along like animals tied to a heavy cart. They mocked the judgment announced against them because God had not yet acted. Another "woe" follows, directed against those who confuse good with evil.

For today: do not mistake God's patience for indifference. If He delays in acting, it is to give us time to return to Him. Use that time with humility, instead of mocking or hardening your heart.
exp.29:28:
It says that God's people will sing, as on the night of a holy festival, and that their hearts will rejoice like someone walking to the music of a flute as they go up to the mountain of the LORD. The phrase "the Rock of Israel" is a title for God, who is their firm foundation and refuge.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Judah, which was trusting in an alliance with Egypt against Assyria. Earlier, the prophet describes God's judgment against the nations. Here there is a contrast: while Assyria would be broken, those who are faithful to God would sing. Some think the night of the festival recalls the liberation from Egypt.

For today: when you face fear or pressure, remember that God has already rescued you before. Be encouraged to sing or to pray with gratitude, trusting that He is your strength.
exp.32:23:
It says that in the city of God no one will say they are sick, and that the people who live there will have their guilt for sin taken away. A "resident" is someone who lives in a place, and "forgiven of iniquity" means they will be pardoned, declared free of guilt. "There" refers to Zion, the city of God.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah in a time of threat and distress. The chapter shows God as judge, lawgiver, and King who saves. The verses before this compare the enemy to a poorly rigged ship that cannot hold together. This verse promises a future of restoration. Some see it fulfilled in part in the deliverance of Jerusalem, and others see it pointing to the fullness of God's kingdom. Both readings are possible.

For today: God's forgiveness is the greatest healing we need. Today you can bring him your guilt with confidence, knowing that he offers a future of fullness.
exp.13:5:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon struck the peoples in anger, and that the blows he dealt never stopped. "Subdued the nations" means he forced them under his control like a master over those he owned. "Rage" refers to violent anger. He also pressed the nations relentlessly and without mercy.

God commands Isaiah to raise up a taunting song, a mocking poem, against the king of Babylon. The prophet speaks on God's behalf to a people who were suffering oppression. Scholars debate whether it refers to one particular king or to all of Babylonian power. The text celebrates that God broke the scepter of the oppressors and that the earth rested.

No cruel power lasts forever, however invincible it may seem. If you suffer today from an injustice, trust that God sees and knows how to act in his time. And if you have authority over others, use it to care for them, not to wound them.
exp.21:21:
It says God will give Eliakim the key of David's house, as a sign of full authority. The key placed on his shoulder represents the right to govern the palace and decide who enters and who does not. What he opens, no one can shut; what he shuts, no one can open. The belt or strap of office is a sign of his role.

God speaks through Isaiah. Earlier he rebuked Shebna, the proud steward of the king, and announces that he will replace him with Eliakim, whom God calls "my servant." Eliakim would be like a father to Jerusalem and Judah. Later, the New Testament takes up this image in Revelation 3:7 to speak of Christ; Christians often see it that way, although Isaiah speaks first of Eliakim.

For today: true authority comes from God and is exercised through service. If you have any responsibility, use it with humility, caring for others, and trust that God opens and shuts the doors in your life.
exp.58:17:
This verse says that God will give each person what they deserve. The idea of repaying means responding with justice to what has been done. "Fury to His enemies" means God pays back His anger to those who oppose Him. "Recompense to the islands" probably refers to distant lands, and they too will receive God's judgment.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of a people full of injustice and wickedness. God sees that no one intercedes or sets things right, so He Himself acts, clothed in righteousness like a soldier in armor. His judgment is not caprice but a response to evil. And right after comes hope: the Redeemer will come to Zion, to those who turn away from their wickedness.

For today: do not take revenge with your own hands; trust that God sees all injustice and will judge it rightly. In the meantime, take up His invitation to turn back to Him, for His redemption is open to whoever repents.
exp.51:1:
God tells Jerusalem to rise up from the ground and shake off the dust, like someone coming out of humiliation. The command to "rise up and sit on your throne" points to taking back a place of honor and dignity. She is also told to remove the chains from her neck. "Captive Daughter of Zion" is a tender way of addressing the city and its people.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, announcing to a humbled and captive people that their situation is going to change. The verses that follow explain that they were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without payment. The text looks toward the release from exile, and Christians also read it in light of redemption in Christ.

Today, God invites us not to remain in shame or in old guilt. If He already offers freedom, we can respond with faith: praying, asking forgiveness, accepting His grace, and taking a concrete step to leave behind whatever still holds us bound.
exp.9:0:
It says God issues a strong warning, a "woe," against those who enact unjust statutes. It is not only personal wickedness: it is injustice turned into law.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's message to the people of Judah in the eighth century BC. The verses that follow explain the reason: justice was being denied to the poor, the widows, and the orphans. God asks them what they will do on the day He calls them to account, when destruction comes from afar.

For today: if you have any authority, whether at home, at work, in the church, or in the community, check whether your rules and decisions protect the most vulnerable. And if you do not have such authority, you can still stand up for those who have no voice.
exp.53:10:
God speaks to a city that is suffering and calls her "afflicted one": she is worn out, battered as if by storms, and without anyone to comfort her. But he promises to rebuild her with precious stones. The Berean Standard Bible says "antimony," a dark metallic substance used as a cosmetic, while the stones in the verse are not named clearly; scholars debate exactly which minerals are meant. The image speaks of a beauty and a firmness that she did not have.

The Lord is speaking to Jerusalem, the people of Israel, after the pain of exile. He has just promised that his anger has ended, just as he swore there would be no other flood, and that his mercy will not move even if the mountains tremble. The precious stones are poetic language for restoration, not necessarily a literal description.

For today: if you are exhausted from some storm, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Tell God how you feel and trust that he can lift up again what has fallen, on a firm foundation that is his faithfulness.
exp.7:11:
It says not to call "conspiracy" everything that people call by that name, nor to live in the same dread as they do. Explaining the wording: "conspiracy" is the verse's own word, and the phrase "do not fear what they fear" means "do not let yourselves be terrified by it."

God speaks through Isaiah, who tells that the Lord warned him not to follow the path of the people. Judah was threatened by neighboring kings, and the people saw danger and plots everywhere. God calls them to trust him, for "God is with us." Some scholars debate exactly what that "conspiracy" referred to.

Today, faced with alarming news and rumors, we can pause before repeating the fear of others. Before reacting, let us pray, ask for wisdom, and remember that God remains our refuge and the one who deserves our deepest respect.
exp.5:8:
God tells Isaiah to go and speak to the people. The words "Be ever hearing" and "be ever seeing" are commands to keep listening and looking, yet the result will be that they never understand or perceive. It is a harsh, almost ironic statement: they will hear and see, but without grasping its meaning.

The Lord speaks right after Isaiah was cleansed and said, "Here I am, send me." Isaiah is sent to a people who have hardened themselves against God. His message will be faithful, but many will not respond. Some understand this as God's judgment on a people who had already rejected his voice; the text does not explain every detail.

For today: obeying God does not depend on the results we see. We can speak faithfully, pray for those who do not listen, and ask God for a humble heart, one that hears and understands his Word.
exp.48:15:
God says he has inscribed his people on the palms of his hands, meaning they are marked there in a way that will not fade, like something carved in. The "walls" are the walls of Jerusalem (Zion), which lay in ruins. God keeps them always before him and does not lose sight of them.

The LORD speaks to Zion, the people of Israel in exile. They complained, "The LORD has forsaken me, and my Lord has forgotten me." God answers with the image of a mother who does not abandon her nursing child, and adds that even if she were to forget, he will not forget. Then he promises rebuilding and the return of their children.

For today: when you feel forgotten or overlooked, remember that God does not hold you in memory only, but has you inscribed on the palms of his hands. Speak to him openly about what hurts, and rest in the knowledge that he continues to think of you and of what you need to rebuild.
exp.51:13:
Many were appalled at him: his appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and his form was marred beyond human likeness. The explanation of the verse is as follows. "Appalled" here means they were horrified or shocked. "Appearance" refers to how he looked. The second half of the verse describes his form as marred beyond human likeness.

Here God speaks and presents his servant, who first suffers and afterward is exalted. Christians see Jesus in this passage, since the New Testament applies it to him. Some Jewish interpreters understand it as a reference to Israel. The text prepares the way for chapter 53.

For today: do not measure the worth of people, or the working of God, only by what is seen. God can bring salvation through pain and humility. Trust him when the path seems hard.
exp.53:16:
No weapon formed to harm God's people will succeed. You will prove wrong every tongue that accuses you. The inheritance the servants of the Lord receive is what God gives them as their share, and their vindication comes from God.

Speaking through Isaiah, the Lord comforts Jerusalem after promising restoration and peace. The people felt weak and threatened. God reminds them that he is the one who has authority over the blacksmith and over the destroyer, meaning that no enemy is outside his control. Some understand the promise in a general way, as applying to God's people as a whole; others see it fulfilled especially in Christ and his church.

For today: when you are attacked with criticism or lies, do not become bitter or seek revenge. Pray, keep doing good, and rest in the fact that God is your defender. The promise does not say there will be no attacks, but that they will not prevail.
exp.37:9:
He says that Hezekiah, facing his illness, thought he would die in the prime of his life. "The gates of Sheol" is a poetic way of speaking of the place of the dead. "Be deprived of the remainder of my years" means that he felt his remaining years were being taken from him.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks in a writing he composed after he was healed. He had been gravely ill and God had announced to him that he would die. This verse recalls what he felt in that moment of anguish, before the Lord heard his prayer and added years to his life.

For today: when you feel that your plans are being cut short by an illness or a crisis, do not hide your pain. Hezekiah expressed it honestly and put it in writing. Bringing our fear to God just as it is can open the way to receive his comfort.
exp.16:11:
Alas, the tumult of many peoples! It is a cry of grief over the roar of many nations, like the crashing of the sea or the thunder of mighty waters. It is an image of armies and nations stirred up with force and seeming impossible to stop.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in the name of God. The chapter concerns Damascus and Ephraim (the northern Israel), who joined forces against Judah and forgot God. Afterward the Assyrian invasion would follow. The verses that come next show that, although the noise is enormous, God rebukes it and everything vanishes like chaff before the wind. Many understand the warning to be both for the enemies of God and a comfort for His people. Scholars debate exactly which peoples are meant.

Today: when the noise of the world frightens you, remember that God remains above all things. Pray and trust in Him.
exp.19:5:
He says that when Egypt falls, the people of this coast will say, "See what has happened to our source of hope." They had fled to Egypt for help and deliverance from Assyria, and now they ask, "How then can we escape?" The word for "coastland" refers to the coast or region of the Mediterranean, and the idea of fleeing for help means that they had gone looking for refuge.

God speaks through Isaiah. Shortly before, Isaiah had walked naked and barefoot as a sign that Egypt and Ethiopia would be led away captive by Assyria. The peoples of the coast, perhaps including Judah, were trusting in that alliance. Scholars debate exactly who the dwellers of this coastland are, but the message is clear: that hope was false.

For today: check where and in whom you place your security. Money, connections, or plans can fail. Pray and trust God first, and use the rest wisely, without making it your refuge.
exp.36:21:
God answers Hezekiah's prayer with a message for the king of Assyria. He says that Jerusalem, described as the Virgin Daughter of Zion, despises Sennacherib and mocks him. The city's daughter, Jerusalem, shakes her head at him as he retreats. Shaking the head was a sign of scorn.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah had prayed in distress because Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was threatening Jerusalem and mocking God. God answers and declares that the city Sennacherib thought weak will not fall. The verses that follow show that his real sin was insulting the Holy One of Israel.

Today we can learn that when we feel small before a huge problem, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. God hears, and he does not ignore the pride of those who think themselves invincible.
exp.20:6:
He says the watchman sees chariots coming: one with teams of horsemen, another with riders on donkeys, and another with riders on camels. The verse describes horsemen as riders, so the word "horsemen" refers to men on horseback. On seeing this, he does not stay calm but becomes fully alert and begins to look much more closely, like someone who knows something important is approaching.

Isaiah recounts a vision about the fall of Babylon. God commands that a watchman be posted to report what he sees, while the leaders of Babylon eat and drink, confident. The riders on donkeys and camels probably point to an allied army arriving, although interpreters debate the detail. The message: "Babylon is fallen, is fallen."

Today we can learn to be alert and to pray with patience, without letting ourselves be lulled to sleep by comfort. God works even when we do not see it right away. Set aside a moment each day to listen to God attentively, trusting that He is greater than any power in the world.
exp.25:1:
The verse asks that the gates of the city be opened so that a righteous people may enter, a people who remains faithful. "Remains faithful" means a people who holds fast to and lives out what God has said. "Deliverance" in the verse before this one means being rescued.

Isaiah announces a song that Judah will sing "on that day," that is, at a future time of victory. The city is strong because God himself is its wall. Interpreters see it as Jerusalem or as an image of God's restored people. What matters is that the one who enters is the faithful person, not the one who merely boasts of belonging.

For today: it is not enough to say that we trust God; he invites us to live with integrity. Today, choose one truth from his Word and practice it in a concrete decision, even when it costs you. After that comes the peace that verse 3 promises.
exp.50:15:
God says that he has put his words in your mouth and covered you under the shadow of his hand. The phrases "to establish the heavens" and "to found the earth" mean "so that you might establish the heavens and found the earth." What God wants is to say to Zion, "You are My people."

The LORD speaks to Israel, who is distressed and in exile. He wants to comfort them and remind them that he is the Creator and has not forgotten them. Scholars do not agree on who the "you" is: it may be Israel as a nation, the prophet, or the Servant of God. What is clear is that God cares for the one who carries his message.

Today, if you share the Word of God, you do not depend only on your own strength. Speak with confidence and remember that his hand covers you and that you are part of his people.
exp.29:9:
This verse describes a people who did not want to hear the truth. They said to the seers (those who received visions from God), "Stop seeing visions!" and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us the truth!" They asked for pleasant words instead, and for prophecies that were illusions, that is, false and misleading.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to Judah, at a time when the people sought security in political alliances, especially with Egypt, instead of trusting the Lord. God calls them rebellious because they rejected his law. For this reason he commands that the message be recorded in writing, so that it may serve as a witness. The people preferred not to be confronted, and God warns that rejecting his word brings consequences.

For today: examine whether you seek out voices that only confirm what you want to hear. Ask God for humility to receive his Word, even when it corrects you, and surround yourself with people who tell you the truth with love.
exp.7:8:
The passage says that the enemy peoples may band together, arm themselves, and prepare for war, yet they will still be shattered. The word repeated three times stresses that the outcome is certain.

The prophet Isaiah speaks in a time of threat from Assyria against Judah. Shortly before, he had announced that Assyria would come like a flooding river, but now he turns his attention to the hostile nations. The name Immanuel means "God with us," and the following verse declares it: the plans against God's people will not succeed. Scholars debate exactly which peoples are meant, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel that troubles are gathering against you, remember that God is with you. Pray, trust, and take the next step without fear, knowing that his presence is greater than any threat.
exp.63:5:
Each of us has become like something unclean, and even our good deeds are like filthy rags, stained and impure. We also wither like a leaf, and our wrongdoing carries us away like the wind.

Here the prophet Isaiah speaks on behalf of God's people. It is a prayer of confession. The people admit their sin and their need for God. Afterward, the text asks that God, as Father and potter, not abandon them, because they are the work of his hands.

For today: do not rely on your own merits to be accepted by God. Humbly acknowledge your failings and come to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy and not in your own goodness.
exp.46:3:
This verse is a brief statement of who God is. The people of Israel call him "Redeemer," that is, the one who rescues and sets free his own. His name is "the LORD of Hosts," the Lord who holds all power, and he is "the Holy One of Israel," the one who is pure and wholly set apart from everything else.

Isaiah announces the fall of Babylon, called "the daughter of the Chaldeans." She had dominated Israel and was cruel to it. God himself allowed that punishment to fall on his people because of their disobedience, but now he judges Babylon for her lack of mercy. In the midst of that judgment, the prophet reminds us who defends his own.

For today: when you feel trapped by situations stronger than you, remember that God has not forgotten you. Pray to him as your Redeemer and trust in his care, even when deliverance is slow in coming.
exp.35:17:
Do not let yourselves be misled by Hezekiah when he assures you that the LORD will deliver you. "Do not let him mislead you" is a warning to be on guard. The speaker asks whether the god of any nation has ever rescued its land from the hand of the king of Assyria. The point is that, if none of them could, the LORD will not be able to either.

Rabshakeh, an officer of King Sennacherib of Assyria, speaks before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to stir up fear and distrust among the people so that they will surrender without a fight. He places the LORD on the same level as the gods of the conquered nations, so his argument is a mockery against God.

Today, many voices tell us that trusting God is naive when everything seems lost. We can remember that God is not like the idols people invent. When doubt comes, it is good to pray and rest in his faithfulness, as Hezekiah did.
exp.25:5:
It says that the proud city, already brought down to the dust, will be trampled underfoot. The verse says the feet of the oppressed and the steps of the poor will tread it down. In other words, those who were once oppressed now walk over what used to oppress them.

Isaiah 26 is a song of confidence that the people of Judah will sing in the future. Before that, the text invites trust in the LORD, the everlasting strength, because he has humbled the haughty city. Many think that city stands for the pride and violence of the nations; the text does not name it here. Afterward, the song speaks of the upright path of the righteous.

For today: if you feel small or mistreated, do not grow bitter or seek revenge. Trust in God and keep walking uprightly, because he cares for the humble and knows how to put everything in its place.
exp.36:25:
God asks the king of Assyria whether he has not heard that all of this was planned long ago. What is happening now, with fortified cities being crushed into piles of rubble, is something God himself ordained and now brings about. The phrase "long ago" simply means a long time back.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Sennacherib of Assyria, who had mocked God and boasted of his conquests. God makes clear that the king's victories were not his own achievement: God planned them and allowed them to happen. In this way the king is shown that he is not the master of history.

For today: when the powerful or circumstances seem to control everything, remember that God still governs history. You can rest in him and live with humility, without boasting of your achievements, because everything good comes from his hand.
exp.14:7:
Their cry of grief spread through the whole land of Moab, from one end to the other. "The border" is the edge or outer limit of the territory. Eglaim and Beer-elim were places near the edges of the land of Moab; their exact location is not certain. Their wailing is a loud cry of anguish.

The prophet Isaiah speaks for God in a message against Moab, a people who were neighbors of Israel. Before this, the destruction of its cities and fields is described, and afterward God announces further judgment on Dibon. Scholars do not agree on which exact historical event is meant. Even so, the text shows that the judgment reached everyone, and that the prophet also felt compassion for that people.

For today: God cares about the nations and sees the pain of people, even of those who are not his own people. We can learn to weep with those who suffer and to pray for them, instead of rejoicing in their fall. It also reminds us to live in humility before God.
exp.37:7:
God promises that he will make the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps, and it happens just as he says. The stairway seems to have been a structure that marked the time by the shadow of the sun, and the verse describes the sunlight returning the ten steps it had come down.

Isaiah speaks to King Hezekiah, who was seriously ill and had prayed with tears. God promises to heal him and to deliver Jerusalem from the king of Assyria. This sign confirms that God will keep his word. How the phenomenon happened exactly is not explained in the text, and it has been understood in several ways.

For today: when your situation seems to have no way out, remember that God is faithful to what he promises. Bring your fears to him in prayer and trust his word, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.57:11:
The verse promises that the people who live by justice and compassion will be used by God to rebuild what has lain in ruins for ages. The "ancient ruins" are the wrecked remains of long-abandoned places. The "breach" is a gap in a wall, and the "streets" are the roads where people live and travel. The people are promised that they will be called Repairer of the Breach and Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling, names that describe their work of mending broken places so that people can live in them again.

God speaks through Isaiah to a people who fasted and kept their religious rituals, yet who continued to treat others unjustly. He tells them that true fasting means sharing bread, freeing the oppressed, and caring for the afflicted. Many understand the restoration to refer to the rebuilding of the land after the exile, though the message reaches beyond that period.

Today, sincere faith shows itself in helping to repair what is damaged around us: a divided family, a neighbor in need, or a forgotten community. Today, choose one concrete act of service.
exp.56:20:
Those who live with their backs turned to God, the "wicked," do not know true peace. The word "wicked" refers to people who reject God and live without taking him into account. The peace mentioned here is more than calm: it means well-being, wholeness, and a good relationship with God.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Just before this, he offers peace and healing to both those who are far away and those who are near, that is, to those who are distant from him and to those who are close. Then he compares the wicked to a restless sea that cannot be calm and that throws up mire and dirt. The peace is offered, but whoever insists on evil does not receive it.

Today, if you feel restless, ask yourself honestly whether there is something you should let go of and give to God. Returning to him with humility opens the door to his peace and his healing.
exp.42:21:
God tells his people that they have not called on him in prayer. "Calling on" God means turning to him and asking him for help. Their having grown weary of him means that they had become bored with him and no longer cared.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier he had promised them water in the desert and his care. Here he rebukes them because, despite all his love, they offered sacrifices without a sincere heart. The verses that follow show that their religion had become empty ritual, while their sins weighed heavily on God. Even so, verse 25 announces forgiveness purely by grace.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly pray or only keep religious customs. God desires a close relationship. Take a few minutes today to speak to him honestly, without formulas, and to thank him that he always forgives.
exp.12:17:
The passage says that the soldiers who will attack Babylon will show no mercy. Their bows will strike down even the young men, and they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb, meaning the children, and they will not look on them with pity.

Isaiah gives a message from God against Babylon, the proud power of his day. God says he will stir up the Medes to bring judgment on her. These are harsh images of the violence of ancient war, and the text does not present them as something good, but as judgment on a proud and cruel nation. Some scholars see here a historical fulfillment, and others also see a foreshadowing of the final judgment.

Today it reminds us that God does not ignore the pride or the injustice of the powerful. We can trust that he judges with justice, and for that reason we should reject cruelty and treat the vulnerable with compassion.
exp.43:5:
God introduces himself with three titles: King and Redeemer of Israel, and the LORD of Hosts, that is, the LORD of all powers. To say "I am the first and I am the last" means that he was before everything and will continue after everything. "There is no God but Me" means that there is no other true God.

The same God speaks to Israel, his people, who lived surrounded by nations that worshiped idols. Just before this, he promises to pour out his Spirit and bless the children of the people. Here he reminds them who he is so that they will not be afraid. Later he calls them his witnesses.

For today: when you feel fear or uncertainty, remember that God was already there at the beginning and will be there at the end of your story. Bring to him in prayer today whatever worries you most, and trust that he remains the LORD.
exp.13:22:
It says God will turn Babylon into an abandoned place: a territory of owls and of swampy ground. It also says he will "sweep her away with the broom of destruction," meaning he will clear her out completely, like someone sweeping trash out of a house.

God himself speaks, "the LORD of Hosts," within a prophecy of Isaiah against Babylon, the great power that oppressed other peoples. That judgment answers its pride and violence. The nearby passages also speak of the fall of Assyria, which shows that God governs over all empires.

For today: no human power is eternal, and God has the last word over injustice. If you suffer from abuse or feel small before the powerful, you can trust that God is just and keeps what he says. It is also a call to personal humility.
exp.11:0:
It says that a day will come when God's people will sing to him with gratitude. It admits that God was angry with them, but that his anger has now turned away and he comforts them. The words "I will praise You" and "You have comforted me" are spoken directly to the LORD, the personal name of Israel's God.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah, who had been disciplined for their rebellion. This verse is a short song that closes the previous section, where a future king and a restoration are announced. "That day" refers to the time of salvation God promised. Some see it fulfilled in part in the return from exile, and others also in Christ or at the end of time.

For today: if you have felt God's discipline or have failed, do not stay in guilt. God forgives and comforts whoever returns to him. Answer him today with a sincere prayer of gratitude.
exp.37:10:
Hezekiah, believing himself close to death, thought he would never again see the LORD in the land of the living. He also thought he would no longer look on mankind, the people who dwell in this world.

King Hezekiah of Judah is the one speaking. He wrote this lament when he was seriously ill, before he was healed. He felt as if his life were being cut short in the middle. His grief was not only about losing his life, but about losing fellowship with God and with the people around him. Some think it reflects a limited view of the afterlife in his time; the text does not fully explain this.

When pain makes everything seem dark, we can be honest with God, as Hezekiah was. He did not hide his distress. Let us bring our fears to God and value each day of life so that we may stay close to Him and to others.
exp.23:11:
The explanation says the city was left empty and silent. "Ruins" here means the city has been wrecked and lies in pieces. Its gate, which used to be a place of trade and gathering, was reduced to rubble, that is, broken apart and scattered.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing God's judgment on the earth for its rebellion (Isaiah 24:5-6). The "city of emptiness" is a city that lives without God; interpreters debate whether it refers to a specific city or serves as a symbol of all human pride. After the judgment, the passage ends with hope: a group will sing about the greatness of the LORD.

For today: whatever we build without God, whether money, fame, or security, can crumble. Today you can ask yourself what you are trusting in and place your life in the hands of God, who endures.
exp.56:0:
The verse says that righteous people perish, and no one takes it to heart. The phrase "takes it to heart" means "stops to think about it." The devout are the godly, those who love God. "Taken away" means that they are removed from this world. No one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, announcing God's word to a people who had turned away from Him. The leaders and the people lived in idolatry and indifference, and did not value the faithful. The following verse explains that the righteous "enter into peace" and rest. Afterward God rebukes harshly those who practiced idolatry.

For today: when faithful people are taken away, or when life seems unjust, we can trust that God cares for His own and gives them rest. And let us value today the sincere believers around us, giving them thanks and support.
exp.18:2:
It says that Egypt will lose the courage and the wisdom that made it feel strong. God himself will bring its plans to nothing. Then, in their despair, the Egyptians will look for answers to idols, to spirits of the dead, to mediums and to spiritists. "Plans" means their strategies and their wisdom for governing.

It is a "burden," that is, a message of judgment that God gives to the prophet Isaiah. The LORD speaks, and announces that he will come against Egypt, a powerful nation full of idols. Before this verse it already speaks of divisions and internal fighting. Scholars debate exactly which historical moment it refers to, and there is no single certain answer.

When our plans fail, it is easy to run to anything that promises quick answers. Better that we bring our confusion to God in prayer and to his Word, where true wisdom is found.
exp.24:6:
It says that God will swallow up the shroud that wraps all peoples and the sheet that covers all nations. The "shroud" and the "sheet" are images of something that blocks sight, like a cloth that keeps one from seeing clearly. "This mountain" refers to Zion, the mountain of Jerusalem. Many understand this covering to be spiritual blindness and the shadow of death; the next verse speaks of God swallowing up death.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God and announces a promise for the future. Earlier he described a feast that the Lord will prepare for all peoples. Now he says that not only Israel, but all nations, will be invited to know him. Then comes the promise that God will wipe away every tear and save his people.

For today: if there are areas where you do not understand or where you feel pain, ask God to open your eyes. He promises light and hope, and you can trust that he will finish what he has begun.
exp.23:8:
It says that there will be no more feasts with songs and wine. "They no longer sing and drink wine" means that no one will raise a toast amid songs of joy. And the drink, which once gave pleasure, will taste bitter to those who consume it.

Isaiah is the prophet who speaks on behalf of God. In this chapter he describes a judgment upon the whole earth because of the wickedness and rebellion of the people. The harvests fail, and the music and celebration fall silent. Interpreters debate whether it refers to a near event, a final one, or both, and it is fair to say that not everything is entirely clear.

For today: do not place your joy only in passing things such as food, festivity, or money. Ask God to be the source of your gladness, because what he gives does not turn bitter.
exp.24:7:
He says that God will destroy death forever. The phrase "wipe away" means to dry, as the Lord himself will wipe the tears from every face. He will also remove the disgrace, that is, the shame and contempt his people have suffered across the whole earth. And all of this is certain, because the Lord has spoken it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to a people who live surrounded by threats and powerful nations. Earlier, God prepares a feast on this mountain, which many understand to be Zion or Jerusalem, for all peoples, and he removes the veil that covers the nations. Then the people respond with joy: "This is our God; we have waited for him." Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 15:54, and Revelation 21:4 recalls it.

When pain or loss weighs on you, do not keep it in silence. Bring it before God, who promises to comfort you and one day wipe away your tears.
exp.6:2:
God tells Isaiah to go out and meet King Ahaz. He is to take his son Shear-jashub with him, whose name means "a remnant will return." The meeting will take place at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field, the place where cloth was washed and worked.

God speaks to Isaiah, and the message is meant for Ahaz. Syria and Israel were threatening Jerusalem, and the hearts of the king and the people trembled like trees shaking in the wind. God sends His prophet with a message of calm. Perhaps Ahaz was checking the city's water supply, though the text does not say so for certain. The name of Isaiah's son was itself a message of hope.

When fear shakes us, God comes to meet us with words of calm. Before acting out of anxiety, stop and listen to what He says in His Word.
exp.44:20:
God invites everyone to speak up and present their strongest case, and to gather together and talk it through. Then he asks who foretold these things long ago, and who announced them from ancient times. His answer is himself, the LORD. He declares that there is no other God but him, that he is righteous, and that he is the Savior. There is none but him.

The LORD speaks through Isaiah, addressing the nations and those who trust in idols made of wood, which cannot save. God shows them that he has spoken openly, not in secret, and that what he says comes to pass. That is why he can call them to look to him and be saved.

For today: when you feel confused or tempted to trust in things that cannot rescue you, such as money, success, or the opinions of others, remember that God alone is faithful and saves. Pray sincerely today and entrust your need to him.
exp.48:14:
It is very rare for a mother to forget the baby she nursed and to stop feeling tenderness for the child she bore. "Compassion" means deep care and tenderness. The verse itself asks, "Can a woman forget her nursing child?" Even if a mother could forget, God declares that He will not forget you.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The people of Israel, discouraged in exile, had said that the LORD had forsaken them and forgotten them. God answers that complaint with a tender image. He also says that he has engraved Zion on the palms of his hands, and he promises restoration.

For today: when you feel alone, forgotten, or abandoned, do not trust only what you feel. Tell God honestly what hurts you, and remember this promise. His care for you is firmer than the strongest human love.
exp.13:30:
God tells Philistia to cry out in grief. "Wail" means to cry aloud in sorrow, and "gate" is the entrance of the city, where decisions were made. "Melt away" means to lose all courage and strength out of fear. "A cloud of smoke" comes from the north, probably an invading army. Scholars do not fully agree on this. No one will be left behind: none of them will straggle from the ranks, and all will be overtaken.

Isaiah delivers this message on behalf of God. The Philistines were celebrating the fall of a king who had struck them, but God warns them that something worse is coming. The following verse shows that, while they fall, God protects the afflicted of his people in Zion.

Today: do not place your security in a problem or an enemy disappearing, because another may come. Trust in God, who sustains the humble and offers firm refuge.
exp.21:18:
God tells Shebna that he will remove him from the position of power he holds. The phrase "I will remove you from office" makes the meaning plain: he will lose his position. The verse says he will be ousted from his post, so the sentence is clear.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. According to verse 15, the one accused is Shebna, the steward of the palace. The text shows him as someone proud, who cared about his own glory and not about serving the people. God removes him and puts Eliakim in his place, who would care for Jerusalem and for Judah like a father.

For today: any office or influence we have is entrusted to us, not owned by us. It is wise to use it with humility and to serve others, remembering that God is the one who raises up and the one who takes away.
exp.39:13:
No one advised God or taught him how to decide well. These are rhetorical questions, and the answer expected is "no one." To "enlighten" God means to instruct him or to make him wise, which is impossible for any creature. "Justice" is the right way of deciding, "knowledge" is understanding, and "understanding" is wisdom for acting well.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a discouraged people, who were living, or were about to live, in exile and felt that God did not see their situation. After announcing comfort, the prophet shows the greatness of God: he measured the waters and weighed the mountains. If God is so wise and powerful, his people can trust him, even when they do not understand everything.

Today, when something does not make sense, avoid judging God by your limited sight. Bring your anguish to him honestly and rest in the knowledge that his wisdom is perfect, even though you cannot yet see the way ahead.
exp.54:6:
This verse invites the person who lives in wrongdoing to change direction. The one who lives without regard for God is called "wicked," and the one who acts with evil is called "unrighteous." They are asked to leave behind both their actions and their thoughts, and to return to the LORD. The promise is that He will have compassion and will pardon freely, that is, without holding back.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah, addressing a weary people, probably during the time of exile in Babylon. Just before this, God invites people to seek Him while He can still be found. Afterward, He makes clear that His thoughts and ways are higher than ours, which helps explain why His forgiveness is so great.

For today: if something weighs on your conscience, do not wait until you have made yourself right first. Speak to God honestly today, leave that path, and trust that His forgiveness is free.
exp.11:1:
What it says: The verse affirms that God is the one who saves. "Salvation" here means being rescued and made whole, not just physical well-being. "I will trust and not be afraid" means "I will feel secure and rely on him." The verse uses the name LORD GOD, and the speaker says they will not be afraid, because the LORD is their strength and the reason for their song.

Context: Isaiah 12 is a short hymn of thanksgiving. The people of God, Israel, speak "in that day," that is, when they are restored after the judgment announced in the earlier chapters. They acknowledge that God was angry, but that his anger passed and he comforted them. Many Christians also see here a look toward the complete salvation in Christ, though the original text speaks first of Israel's deliverance.

For today: When fear overtakes you, do not just stare at the problem. Remember how God has sustained you before, and give thanks out loud, perhaps with a prayer or a simple song.
exp.33:3:
All the stars of heaven will be dissolved, and it means that everything in the heavens that seems firm and everlasting is going to come undone. "The stars of heaven" is the plain meaning here, and some think it may also point to spiritual powers. The idea of things being "dissolved" means they will be worn away or broken up. The skies being rolled up like a scroll means they will be folded up like an ancient parchment. The stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine and like foliage from the fig tree.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, announcing the judgment of the LORD on all the nations that oppose Him. Then the passage focuses on Edom, a people neighboring Israel. It is poetic and very intense language; not everyone agrees on whether it describes only a historical judgment, the end of the world, or both.

For today: do not place your security in anything passing, not even in what seems immense. Trust in God, who endures, and live today with humility and hope in Him.
exp.1:5:
It says that God has abandoned his people, Israel, because they are filled with influences from the East, practice divination like the Philistines, and make deals with foreigners. "Filled" means full. "Diviners" are those who try to foretell the future. "Foreigners" could refer to alliances with other nations or to adopting pagan practices; it is interpreted in several ways.

Isaiah speaks to the people of Judah. He has just invited them to walk in the light of the Lord, and now he explains why they are far from it. They were trusting in foreign influences, in riches, in horses and in idols, instead of trusting in God.

For today: check where you turn when you are afraid or need direction. Money, horoscopes, fashions or people can take the place of God. Seek Him first in prayer and in His Word.
exp.32:12:
God calls everyone to listen: those who are far away and those who are near. He wants them to know what he has done and to acknowledge his might.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Isaiah. Earlier, he has announced judgment on empty plans and the wickedness of the nations, compared to straw and burned thorns. Then the people of Zion become frightened and ask who will be able to stand before a God so holy. The answer describes the one who lives with righteousness and honesty. Some understand "those who are far off" as the nations, and "those who are near" as Israel.

For today: do not take lightly the might and holiness of God. Listen to him with humility, examine your heart, and ask him for help to live with honesty in everyday life.
exp.63:1:
The explanation says that God's presence would be like a very intense fire, like the fire that brushwood catches or the kind that makes water boil. "Brushwood" means dry twigs and small branches, which burn quickly. "Known" means made recognized by everyone. "Your enemies" and "the nations" are the peoples who do not acknowledge God. The speaker wishes that God would act with such power that the nations tremble before him.

It is part of a prayer by the prophet Isaiah on behalf of the people of Israel. The people feel far from God and in trouble, and they remember how God saved them before through astonishing deeds. For that reason they beg him to intervene again. Scholars debate at what historical moment this prayer is set, so it is wise not to state that with certainty.

Today we can pray sincerely and without fear, asking God to act in our lives and in our world. Remembering what he has already done gives us confidence to wait on him.
exp.40:28:
It says that the idols and those who make them are worth nothing. The word "delusion" describes something false and deceptive, and "images" refers to the idols shaped from cast metal in molds. Saying their images are "as empty as the wind" means they have no substance or power, like air that slips away.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. In this passage he presents a case against the nations and their false gods. He challenges them to announce what is to come or to give counsel, but they answer nothing. Only the Lord declares what will happen and brings good news to Zion and Jerusalem.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others, ends up being like air. Today you can identify where you are trusting too much and place your hope again in the God who really speaks and fulfills his word.
exp.21:3:
Here the prophet says he wants to be left alone to weep bitterly. He tells people not to try to console him, because his grief over the destruction of "the daughter of my people" (a poetic way of speaking of Jerusalem and its people) is too deep for comfort. The verse asks others to step back and let him mourn.

The speaker is Isaiah. The chapter is headed by a reference to Jerusalem, called "the valley of vision." It describes a city that thought itself safe and lived in festivity, but whose leaders fled and were captured. Isaiah does not rejoice in the judgment; he suffers for his people. Scholars debate which exact historical moment the passage refers to.

For today: sometimes pain needs time, not just quick words. We can accompany others with presence and silence, without rushing them. And when something hurts us, it is right to weep honestly before God.
exp.48:0:
The passage says that someone speaks to the islands and to distant peoples, that is, to nations all over the world, and asks them to listen. It affirms that the LORD called him before he was born and that, from his mother's body, the LORD had already given him a name. Saying that the LORD named him from the body of his mother means that God knew him and chose him for a purpose before his life had begun.

The one speaking is the Servant of the LORD, and his message reaches all the nations. In the verse that follows he is called "Israel," so many understand him to be the people of Israel. Others, based on what follows in the chapter, see in him the Messiah, and Christians apply it to Jesus. Some see both: a mission that Israel received and that Christ fulfills completely.

God knows and calls each person with purpose. Your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that God knows you and has had you in mind from the beginning. Today you can rest in that and serve with confidence.
exp.16:9:
It says the people forgot God, who is here called "the God of your salvation" (salvation here means safety and well-being) and "the Rock of your refuge," meaning the secure place where one runs for shelter. Therefore, although they cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines (shoots brought from other lands, perhaps tied to pagan worship), they will not see fruit.

Isaiah speaks on behalf of God to the northern kingdom, Israel (Ephraim), which was allied with Damascus. Many understand that they trusted in alliances and in idols rather than in God. The text does not make entirely clear what the plants were, and they are interpreted in several ways. The central point is that, without God, the effort comes to nothing.

For today: before you plan and work, pause to remember who sustains you. Set aside a moment each day to give thanks and to place your projects in his hands.
exp.6:11:
Here King Ahaz answers that he will not ask God for any sign. He says he will not test the LORD, that is, put him to the proof. It sounds very respectful, but God himself had offered him the sign.

Judah was threatened by two enemy kings, and Ahaz was already looking for help from Assyria instead of trusting God. So his answer seems like devotion, but it was really an excuse for not obeying. Isaiah rebukes him, and God gives the sign of Immanuel anyway, "God with us."

Today we too can pretend to be humble in order to avoid trusting God or doing what he asks. When God invites us to believe him, true faith responds with sincere obedience, not with excuses that merely sound religious.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that God's plan against Assyria is not something isolated. It is a plan devised for the whole earth, a firm decision of God that reaches every nation. The "hand stretched out" is an image of his power in action, reaching over all the nations.

Isaiah speaks in the name of the LORD, who swore that he would break the Assyrian, the empire that oppressed Judah. It was a message of comfort for a threatened people. It is then added that no one can overturn what God determines. Many understand that the judgment on Assyria is an example of how God governs all the nations.

For today: when the world seems dominated by unjust powers or by chaos, you can rest in the knowledge that God still governs. Bring your fears to him in prayer and trust that his purposes will be fulfilled, even though you cannot see how.
exp.9:2:
God asks three questions of those who oppressed the poor. The "day of reckoning" means the moment when God comes to hold people accountable. "Devastation" is total ruin, and it would come "from afar." "Flee for help" means running to seek refuge. They are asked: what will you do, where will you run for help, and where will you leave your wealth when that day arrives?

God speaks through Isaiah. He has just condemned the rulers who made unjust laws to strip the poor, the widows, and the orphans of their rights. What follows shows that the punishment would come through Assyria, a nation God would use as an instrument of judgment.

For today: God takes notice of how we treat the weak. Today you can ask yourself whether, at work, in your family, or in your community, you defend the vulnerable or take advantage of them, and correct whatever needs correcting before it is too late.
exp.50:19:
Your sons have fainted and lie at the head of every street, like an antelope caught in a net. They are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God. The prophet Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem, pictured as a grieving mother, after the destruction and famine that came as judgment. No one comforts or guides her. But the text that follows changes its tone: God, who defends his people, takes away the cup of his anger and promises that she will not drink it again.

For today: even when we live with the hard consequences of our mistakes, God does not abandon us. If you feel without strength today, come to him sincerely; he knows how to comfort and lift up.
exp.40:8:
God tells Israel that he brought them from the farthest parts of the earth and called them from its most distant corners. He reminds them: "You are my servant." He has chosen them and has not rejected them. The word "rejected" means throwing something away as though it no longer has any use. Some readers understand the "farthest corners" as the most remote places; others read the image in a different way.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. The neighboring nations make idols and encourage one another out of fear. In contrast, God comforts Israel, the people descended from Abraham, reminding them that they were chosen by grace, not because of their merits. The promise continues: "Fear not, for I am with you."

For today: when you feel small, rejected, or out of place, remember that God calls you and does not cast you aside. Tell him in prayer today: "Lord, I trust that you chose me and that you do not let go of me."
exp.13:16:
This verse continues the question asked by those who look at the fallen king: "Is this the man who..." It says that he turned the world into a desert, destroyed its cities, and refused to let the captives return to their homes. "Desert" describes a land left empty and barren. "Captives" are the people held against their will.

Isaiah presents a mocking song against the king of Babylon (v. 4). Those who see him dead are amazed that someone so feared now lies weak. Many believe he speaks of a historical king, and some also see a symbol of pride and evil in general. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: power used to oppress comes to an end, and God holds people accountable. We can use our influence, small or great, to help, to free, and to lift others up, not to dominate or harm them.
exp.46:9:
Babylon felt secure in her wickedness. She thought, "No one sees me," as if she could do whatever she wanted without consequences. Her wisdom and knowledge led her astray, and in the end she came to see herself as the center of everything: "I am, and there is none besides me."

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah against Babylon, a proud nation that had treated its people harshly. She trusted in her diviners and omens (signs they read to predict the future). God announces that her fall will come suddenly, and that these practices will not save her.

For today: let us be careful not to think that no one sees us. God sees the heart. It is wise to be humble, to recognize that our knowledge is limited, and to ask God to guide us, rather than trusting only in ourselves.
exp.41:23:
Isaiah 42:24 says that Jacob was given over to plunderers, and that Israel was handed to those who would rob them. The question is answered directly: it was the Lord, the one against whom they had sinned. To give someone up for plunder means to hand them over so that others can take everything they have. Plunderers are those who seize goods by force. The people admit their guilt, since they were unwilling to walk in God's ways and would not obey his law.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to a people who are suffering invasion and ruin, as described in the verses before. He asks a question and answers it: the punishment was not an accident, nor only the work of strong nations. Many understand that he is pointing toward the exile in Babylon, although the text does not give all the details. Then it says that, even in the fire of the trial, the people did not understand or take it to heart.

For today: when difficulties come, instead of blaming only others, let us ask God to show us whether there is something we need to correct. His discipline aims to bring us back to him, and he always welcomes the one who repents.
exp.48:10:
God says that he will turn his mountains into roads, meaning that the greatest obstacles will become open paths. "Turn" here means "I will change them into." The "roads" are routes prepared for travel, and "raised up" means they will be lifted high and made firm, ready for the passage of his people.

God speaks, addressing his Servant and, through him, Israel, who was held captive in Babylon. He promises to free the prisoners, care for them like a shepherd on the way, and bring them back from distant places. Interpreters see here the return from exile and, for many Christians, also a shadow of the work of Christ.

For today: when you face a problem that looks like a mountain, remember that God can open a way where you see only obstacles. Trust his guidance, take the next step in faith, and ask him to lead you with the tenderness of a shepherd.
exp.31:13:
It says that the palace will be abandoned and the busy city left empty. The hill and the watchtower will become caves, a place where wild donkeys delight to roam and flocks find pasture. And this will last "forever," meaning for a long time, until something changes.

The prophet Isaiah speaks to Judah. Just before this verse, he rebukes the women and the well-off people who lived calmly and confidently in their comfort. He warns that their prosperity will be lost through God's judgment. But the next verse brings hope: "until" God pours out his Spirit and everything is restored with justice.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, because all of that can disappear. Let us trust in God and ask him for his Spirit, who truly renews life.
exp.1:7:
The land is full of idols, Isaiah says, and the people bow down to what their own hands have made. The word "also" links this to the earlier list of troubles: their silver and gold, their horses, and their chariots. "Bow down" means they gave honor, trust, and their whole devotion to these things.

Isaiah speaks to Judah, the people of God, and brings his complaint before Him. God had allowed them to go their own way because they trusted foreign fortune-tellers, wealth, and military strength instead of Him. The verses that follow announce judgment, and when God rises to act, these idols will prove useless.

Today most of us do not carve statues, but we can still place our trust in money, success, or what we produce. Ask yourself honestly where your heart rests. Give that place to God, because only He can truly hold you up.
exp.0:8:
It says that, unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, the people would have become completely destroyed, like Sodom, and would have resembled Gomorrah. A "remnant" is a small number left behind, a few who remain. "LORD of Hosts" speaks of God's power over all things.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking to the people of Judah. Their land was devastated by invaders, and Jerusalem stood like a lonely hut. But the underlying problem was injustice and a religion that was only outward appearance. That is why, in the verse that follows, God calls their leaders "rulers of Sodom." Even so, the survivors show that God did not abandon them completely.

Today we can recognize that we stand firm by the mercy of God, not by our own merits. That gratitude invites us to return to Him with a sincere heart and to live with justice, not just with religious practices.
exp.28:8:
The passage says the people should stop and be amazed, because they are blind and confused. Their own words in the verse, "they are drunken, but not with wine," carry the picture: they stagger like drunkards, yet they have had nothing to drink.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to Jerusalem, which is called by a name that appears in the verses that follow. The verses after this one explain that God sent them a deep, sleep-like stupor because they did not want to listen. Many understand this as both a warning and a judgment: their spiritual blindness was real and had consequences.

For today: let us not assume we understand God simply because we know things about the faith. Let us ask him each day for humility to listen to his Word, before the heart hardens and no longer recognizes his voice.
exp.35:20:
The officials of Jerusalem stayed silent in the face of the mocking words of the Assyrian messenger. They did not answer him a single word, because King Hezekiah had commanded them: "Do not answer him."

Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, had just spoken with arrogance. He said that no god had delivered other cities, so the God of Israel would not deliver Jerusalem either. It was an attempt to frighten the people and make them doubt. Hezekiah, knowing that arguing would be useless, asked for silence. Afterward, his officials brought him the message with their clothes torn, a sign of grief.

There are moments when it is not necessary to answer every insult or provocation. Sometimes silence is wisdom, and it is better to bring one's worry to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did afterward.
exp.20:4:
This verse describes a scene of banquet preparations taking place while, at the same time, guards are set to keep watch and the leaders are called to get ready for battle. "Oil the shields" meant coating them with oil so that they were strong and blows would slide off.

The prophet Isaiah is speaking. In the passage before, he tells how a vision about the fall of Babylon filled him with anguish and dread. Many understand that the verse shows how the city was feasting with confidence, not noticing that the attack was already coming. Some scholars read it differently, and the text does not make this fully clear.

For today: do not live distracted by comfort. Stay alert and spiritually prepared, praying and trusting God, because troubles often arrive when we least expect them.
exp.33:14:
It says that in the ruined land there will be wild birds that make their home there. The phrase about gathering the brood under her shadow means that she will gather her young and care for them. The birds of prey are scavenging birds, and "each with its mate" shows that they gather in pairs.

Isaiah announces God's judgment against Edom and the nations that opposed his people. The city will be left desolate, and only wild life will inhabit it. This is presented as the fulfillment of the word of the LORD, written in his book.

For today: God is just and his word is fulfilled. When we see injustice, we can trust that he will not overlook it. That invites us not to take revenge, to live with humility, and to place our hope in his just judgment.
exp.43:26:
This verse says that God has power over the deep waters. He commands them, "Be dry," and they obey. The "currents" that dry up speak of great waters that seemed impossible to cross. "Depths" means the abyss or the deep waters of the sea.

The one speaking is the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, to a people who would be carried off captive to Babylon. God promises that Jerusalem will be inhabited again and that Cyrus, king of Persia, would help make that happen. Many believe the dried-up waters recall the Red Sea, and others think they allude to how Cyrus took Babylon, though this last point is debated.

For today: when you face an obstacle that seems too big, remember that God can open a way where you see no exit. Trust Him and take the next step in faith.
exp.43:24:
God says that he foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners. He also confounds the wise and turns their knowledge into nonsense. The word "foils" means that he brings their signs to nothing.

The LORD speaks, the Redeemer of Israel and the Creator of all things. The people are about to be rescued from exile, and God announces it as something certain. While the nations trusted in diviners and counselors, God shows that only he knows and directs the future. The verses that follow confirm this: he will fulfill his word and rebuild Jerusalem.

Today we can let go of the need to control the future through horoscopes, superstitions, or mere human calculation. We can plan wisely, but trusting in God, who keeps what he promises and sustains our lives.
exp.52:0:
The prophet asks two questions that express wonder and sorrow: who has believed the message we heard? And to whom has the power of God been shown? The "message" is what was heard or proclaimed, and the "arm of the LORD" is an image of his strength to save. The suggested answer is that very few have believed it.

This question opens the song of the suffering Servant, which begins in Isaiah 52:13. It seems to be spoken by a group ("our message"), which then confesses that it despised the Servant. Jews and Christians have interpreted it in different ways, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus (John 12:38).

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly believe what God says, even when his work does not seem great or impressive. Sometimes his power comes in a humble form, and we need faith to recognize it.
exp.12:5:
The explanation says that the people should cry out and wail, because the Day of the LORD is near. That day comes as destruction from the Almighty. "Wail" means a loud crying out, of pain and terror.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf. This chapter begins with a message against Babylon. The verses before describe a huge army gathered for battle, and God uses these nations as instruments of his judgment. The verses that follow show the fear of the people: weak hands and melted hearts. Some see here a historical judgment on Babylon, and others also see a picture of the final judgment.

Today we can take God seriously and not live distracted. Instead of fearing without hope, we can examine our hearts, ask for forgiveness, and live with humility, trusting in the mercy that God offers in Christ.
exp.46:10:
It says that disaster will come upon Babylon, and she will not know where it comes from. A calamity will fall on her that she cannot ward off. Devastation will strike suddenly and without warning. She will be unable to stop it or understand what is happening to her.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. He addresses Babylon, pictured here as a proud woman who trusted in her wisdom, her diviners, and her astrology, and who said, "I am, and there is none else beside me." God announces that these things will not save her. Scholars often see here a judgment on Babylon for her arrogance and cruelty.

For today: do not place your security in your own intelligence, your plans, or your superstitions. Live with humility, trusting in God, who sees everything and sustains what we cannot control.
exp.22:14:
In Isaiah 23:15, Tyre, the great trading city on the coast, would be forgotten for seventy years, "the span of a king's life." That may point to the length of one reign or of one lifetime. Afterward, the city would return to its old ways, going back to its trade and its fame the way a prostitute returns to her old life. Being forgotten means no one would remember the city or go looking for it.

Isaiah speaks on God's behalf within a message about Tyre (chapter 23). Tyre grew rich through sea trade. The Bible uses the image of a prostitute for its ambitious commerce, which was offered to every kingdom. Commentators do not agree on exactly how the seventy years were fulfilled.

For today: success and wealth do not give lasting security. Ask yourself whether your trust is in God or in your achievements, and use what you have with honesty and generosity.

sum.33: God calls all the nations to listen, because he is angry with them and will hand them over to judgment. Edom in particular will suffer its punishment, and its land will be left in ruins, burning and inhabited only by wild animals. The chapter teaches that God acts with justice and that his word is fulfilled.
sum.57: God tells his people that their fasting is fake, because they fast while they fight, exploit others, and look out only for themselves. The kind of fasting that pleases him is ending oppression, sharing bread with the hungry, and helping people in need. If they do this, God promises light, guidance, restoration, and joy, and he also invites them to honor the Sabbath.
sum.63: Isaiah 64 is a prayer from the people asking God to come down and act with power, as he did in the past. They acknowledge that their sins and their "righteousness" are worth nothing, but they rest on the fact that God is their Father and they are the clay in his hands. They ask for forgiveness and help in the face of the destroyed city and temple.
sum.17: Isaiah 18 speaks of a distant land, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, that sends messengers by sea. God says he will watch calmly and, when the time comes, will cut off what seemed ripe, as with pruning knives. In the end, a strong and mistreated people will bring an offering to God on Mount Zion.
sum.62: A glorious warrior comes from Edom with stained clothes, for he has punished the nations and saved his own people. Then the people remember the mercies of God toward Israel, even though they rebelled, and they pray that God would look upon them, because he is their Father and Redeemer.
sum.8: Isaiah announces that the people who walked in darkness will see a great light: a child will be born, called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace, who will reign with justice forever. But Israel, proud and not seeking God, suffers judgment, division, and violence.
sum.32: Isaiah announces that the plunderer will be plundered, and the people cry out to the LORD, asking for mercy. God rises up as judge and king, and he burns up the wicked like thorns. Only those who live with justice and righteousness will dwell securely, and they will see Zion in peace, with their sins forgiven.
sum.1: In the last days, Isaiah announces, all the nations will climb the mountain of the LORD to learn his ways, and there will be peace, with no more wars. But the people of Judah have filled themselves with wealth, fortune-tellers, and idols. Because of this, the day of the LORD is coming, a day that will humble all pride, and only God will be exalted.
sum.49: God says that his people were sold and abandoned because of their own wrongdoing, not because he lacked the power to save them. His servant speaks with the teaching God has given him, endures blows and mockery with firmness, and trusts that God is helping him. Whoever walks in darkness must trust in God, and whoever lights their own way with their own fire will suffer pain.
sum.47: God speaks to Israel, a stubborn people who claim to believe in him but do not live in truth. He reminds them that he announced everything beforehand so that they could not credit their idols. For the sake of his own name, he refines them and does not destroy them, and he calls them to leave Babylon. He laments that by disobeying, they lost their peace.
sum.52: Isaiah speaks of a servant of God who is despised and full of sorrow. He suffers in silence like a lamb, even though he never did any wrong. He carried the sins and rebellions of everyone, and through his wounds there is healing and forgiveness. God will lift him up and honor him. Christians see Jesus in this passage.
sum.55: God calls his people to practice justice and keep the Sabbath, and he promises that foreigners and eunuchs who join themselves to him will be accepted, with a place and an everlasting name in his house of prayer for all peoples. But he denounces the blind, self-serving leaders who neglect the people.
sum.54: God invites all who are thirsty to come and receive freely what truly nourishes the soul, and He promises an everlasting covenant. He calls people to seek Him and to turn away from wrongdoing, because He forgives generously. His ways are higher than ours, and His word accomplishes its purpose, bringing joy and renewal.
sum.53: God calls Jerusalem, pictured as a barren and abandoned woman, to rejoice and enlarge her tent, because she will have many children and will no longer live in shame. Although he left her for a brief moment, he promises everlasting compassion, a covenant of peace that will not be shaken, and protection against every attack.
